News.title: My abusive ex punched our puppy & forced me into sex after holding me hostage for 5hrs…before attack at our baby’s grave
News.content:
HAVING recently come out of a relationship, shy Charlotte Lewis was surprised when she got an unexpected message on Snapchat from a man named Josh who wanted to see her.

“It seemed a bit too much from someone I didn’t know but then I thought, ‘What’s the harm in meeting up with someone?’” she asks.



She was about to find out…

“My life changed, for sure, in 2021,” she says. “That was the year I realised, ‘I’m in something now that I don’t know how I’m going to get out of.’”



Ahead of a TV documentary called Paul C. Brunson: Red Flag in which relationship expert, Brunson, detects early warning signs in abusive partners, Charlotte tells us how she was mentally and physically abused which culminated in a devastating attack at the graveside of their baby.

Even though he is currently in prison she is dreading his early release next May after serving just half of his sentence.



“I don’t think his behaviour will be corrected by prison because he is completely different around men than he is with women and so he will have a different persona inside, because he’s scared,” she says.

“I have 100 per cent faith that he won’t change.”



When she first met Josh Kelly, she thought it was a case of opposites attract.

“He was wild, bouncing off the walls, and I was always very quiet, growing up. But I thought maybe I needed someone like him,” she says.

“He seemed to have his life sorted, which was a big part of the attraction. He was a plumber and training to be a gas engineer and he was on a decent amount of money. I thought he was doing really well for himself.

“He had a car and a flat, but I later found out that the flat and the furniture inside was all provided to him on discount by the foster care system.”

Things moved fast. Within two weeks she had met his mum, who had struggled to look after him when he was younger, and Charlotte was soon spending more time at his flat than she was at her parents’ home. But his love bombing quickly turned into escalating control, raging jealousy and violence.



“I wasn’t allowed to go on Facebook or to text my mum and dad because he would look at the messages at night. I couldn’t even brush my teeth without being accused of cheating on him.

“I was in this constant battle with myself over whether I was being reasonable or he was because, whenever I brought his behaviour up with him, he would say that I was the problem. But then I’d think ‘what would my mum say?’ And I’d know I was right.

“A lot of people think that abuse is about huge moments, but it’s not just about violence. A big factor of it is control. It’s often a series of little things that happen over time that gradually changes how you see yourself and who you are as a person.”

But things were about to turn very scary in a big way.

“Two months into the relationship, we were in the car, having just left the pub, and we were arguing. He was screaming at me and I knew it was serious. It wasn’t just messing around. I was petrified. I just thought, ‘What’s next?’



“He was shouting at me, calling me names. I felt I needed to get out of the car and when I managed to, I ran off and he got out and chased after me. I managed to hide and called my mum to get me.”

To her horror, he then drove to her parents’ house and screamed to her to get back in the car or he would kill himself.

“I was worried that he would do it and that it would be my fault. I called the police and they went to check on him and he was asleep.”

Over the next few days, he bombarded her with phone calls and messages.

“He was non-stop calling me, saying he loved me. I just wanted him to leave me alone because I didn’t want this anymore.”



One evening, Charlotte was out with her family, enjoying a meal, when he began texting her again, apologising for his behaviour and promising he would never do it again.

“He really got in my head,” says Charlotte. “There was a part of me that made me feel wanted and I just fell for that. And that was the time we got Reggie, our little puppy.

“He wanted the dog, because he saw it as our little family. Reggie was eight weeks old when we got him but a day or two later, Josh couldn’t deal with the fact that he was a puppy and not trained.

“He would bang on Reggie’s cage, clenching his teeth and frothing at the mouth because he was so angry. And then he just punched him in the face. Reggie didn’t really react and I thought, ‘What else has Josh done to him when I haven’t been around?’”

Yet, still Charlotte stayed with him.



“My self-esteem was so low. He just made me think that he was my only option. I felt trapped.”

A day or two later, Charlotte and her friend were getting ready at his flat, to go to a music festival, when he physically attacked her.

“I went into the bathroom to change into some cycling shorts, a vest top and a checked shirt and he came in after me and was up in my face. He put his hands round my neck and screamed at me about what I was wearing.

“It was the sort of thing I would wear on a normal day but now he was saying how much of a sl*g I was and why was I cheating on him with other men?”

The following day, Charlotte quietly arranged for her mum to pick her up, taking her belongings and Reggie back to her house. She had been seeing him, on and off, from April to September, but after so much manipulation and abuse, she wanted no more to do with him.



“It felt like such a relief when we drove away,” she says. “But it was far from over. He was constantly messaging me, begging me to return. I didn’t contact him for a whole month.

“He knew where my mum worked, where my dad worked and my brother, and he started listing them off, one by one, saying ‘I will turn up there and I will smash their head in.’”

In one angry voicemail to Charlotte, he shouted, “You’re dead! Watch yourself. You’re dead!”

In February the following year, Charlotte was alone at her parents’ home and was putting the dog out at night when she saw a shadowy figure at the bottom of the garden.



“I was terrified,” she says. “My dad works nights and my mum and my brother, James, also had night shifts on this occasion. I knew it was Josh in the garden and as he came nearer, he just pushed his way into the house, without saying anything to me.

“I asked him what he was doing there and he said, ‘I want to have sex with you.’ I said, ‘No. That is not happening.’

“It was 11pm and I fought tooth and nail against it for hours before I finally gave in around 5am, an hour before my dad came home, because I didn’t want him there when my dad came back. After having sex, he left.”

Ten days after her 21st birthday, Charlotte discovered she was pregnant.

“It was a really bitter-sweet moment because I loved the idea of having a baby but not with him.”



Her mum, Sharon warned her, “If you keep the baby, he will be in your life for ever.”

“It was a really difficult decision, whether or not I went through with it,” says Charlotte. “But I didn’t feel I could bear having an abortion.

“It was on a Facetime call that I told him I was pregnant and he just broke down, crying, saying he couldn’t believe it and that he was so happy.

“But I told him then and there, that I was never going to leave the baby in the room alone with him, purely because of how he was with Reggie. There’s no way he could deal with a crying baby on his own.

“We found out that we were having a girl and she had complications. She was diagnosed with Pallister-Killian syndrome which meant she would probably be blind, not be able to cry or move and I was told she had about five per cent chance of survival.



“After that, Josh’s behaviour went downhill. He went back to being abusive. He said to me, ‘If the baby doesn’t look like me, I’m going to stab you in the stomach.’”

Lottie Hope Lewis-Kelly was born on the morning of 24 November, 2022.

“It was amazing,” says Charlotte.

“I got told that she would probably pass away the moment she came out but she cried and she held my finger and I was so grateful. I was over the moon just to hold her. It’s the best feeling ever, being able to be a mum – even though it was only for less than two hours.”

But Charlotte realised that she would always be mum to Lottie and lovingly tended her daughter’s grave every day.



She had barely heard from Josh for six months when he messaged to say he wanted to put flowers on Lottie’s grave but that he wanted Charlotte there to do it with him.

“I didn’t want to be with him but I wanted him to be a dad towards Lottie. So he came and I was taking some pictures when I got a notification on my phone that he got really angry about.

For example, someone sentenced to three years’ imprisonment who would previously have been released after serving 18 months (50% of their sentence) will now be released after 12 months (one-third of their sentence). Likewise, someone who previously had to serve four years of a six-year sentence before release (two-thirds) will now be released after three years (50%).

“He probably thought it was a boy texting me. I told him to leave and he did go back to his car but then, as I sat by the graveside, he stormed over and started kicking me with his heavy work boots, over and over again, on my legs and thighs.

“I was in excruciating pain. I remember screaming but nothing coming out. I was in shock. I was next to my daughter’s grave and I was thinking he’s actually going to kill me but at least I’ll be with my daughter now.”

Lottie kept the attack secret from her family for two months before finally telling them. In the meantime. she had to deal with his sickening verbal attacks.



In one shocking voicemail message, he ranted, “F**k you! F**k your dead, retarded daughter. F**k your grief. F**k the lot of you. You’re all f*****g dead to me.”

After Charlotte reported the attack to the police, he was arrested and charged with coercive control. Six other women came forward to say they had also been assaulted by him.

It took four years to go to court but on 27 June, 2025, Josh Kelly, 23, admitted controlling and coercive behaviour towards seven former partners between 2020 and 2025 and was sentenced to four years and eight months, with a 10-year restraining order.

Today, Charlotte is working as a SEN (Special Education Needs) teaching assistant, helping children, and is in a new relationship with a supportive boyfriend who she has been with for a year.

“My mental health now is a lot better, but I still get triggered when I am in a car or see somebody who looks like him,” she says. “Even though he is in prison currently, I’m still scared.



“I got told earlier this year that he is only doing half of his sentence, so he will be getting out May next year, despite only being sentenced last June. I feel I have hardly had time to breathe.

“I’m still living in fear and dread every day, thinking I might see him in ASDA or walking down the street.

“The great thing that has come out of all of this was having my daughter. I wouldn’t change that for a minute. She is my inspiration. She was alive for an hour and 45 minutes.

“She defeated all the odds and I think that if she can fight for that long, I can do the same. I think to myself, ‘If she was here, I’d want to set a good example.’ I’m still being a mum to her now but just parenting in a very different way and I am so grateful that I can still do that.

“I have got to be strong for her and show her what’s wrong and what’s right.”

News.title: Four in 10 families cook at least three separate meals at dinnertime, new poll finds
News.content:
CHEF'S CHOICE Four in 10 families cook at least three separate meals at dinnertime, new poll finds

FOUR in 10 families cook at least three separate meals at dinnertime, as parents juggle different tastes, routines and dietary preferences under one roof.

The average family chef spends 30 extra minutes in the kitchen each week trying to meet everyone’s needs, leaving 60 per cent feeling pressured to make dinnertime work for the whole household.



But they do it to keep everyone happy (32 per cent), to accommodate flavour preferences (29 per cent) and because younger children want different foods (30 per cent).

Research of 2,000 parents with children aged 0 to 18 found that, overall, more than half (53 per cent) find mealtimes stressful.



However, 93 per cent think it’s important their family spends time together at dinnertime – even if everyone isn’t eating the same meal.

The research was commissioned by Dolmio, which has teamed up with podcaster and mum, Giovanna Fletcher, to celebrate its 40th anniversary and the return of Mama and Papa to our screens after more than a decade.

Giovanna said: “Mama and Papa Dolmio, and the whole Dolmio family, have been such iconic characters since I was a child, so I loved being part of their return.

“As a mum myself, I know how precious dinnertime can be – it’s often one of the few moments in the day when everyone can come together, catch up and connect.

“As Dolmio celebrates its 40th anniversary, it feels like the perfect opportunity to celebrate those simple family moments that make dinnertime so special.”

The research, from OnePoll.com, found perceptions of dinnertime have shifted across generations with 72 per cent agreeing dinnertime at home has become more flexible and less fixed than it was when they were growing up.



More than a third of Boomers (34 per cent) believe family mealtimes have changed significantly since they were parents of young children, with almost half (48 per cent) saying families eat together less often than before.

Meanwhile, Millennials pointed to families enjoying a wider variety of cuisines and dishes today compared with when they were growing up (39 per cent).

The study also found the average family eats the same meal together just four times a week with a quarter regularly having to cater to fussy or selective eaters.

Busier household routines (33 per cent), children having more say in what they eat (30 per cent) and parents having less time to cook from scratch (28 per cent) were among the biggest drivers behind the shift.

One quarter of families regularly rely on pre-made sauces (25 per cent), ready meals (19 per cent) and meal kits (16 per cent) to help get dinner on the table.



Overall, 51 per cent believe households are less likely to eat dinner at the same time now compared with 40 years ago.

While over one fifth (22 per cent) want mealtimes to become more about spending time together over the next 40 years, rather than what everyone is eating.

Hana Hutchinson, a spokesperson for Dolmio, said: “While modern mealtimes can sometimes be chaotic, they are still seen as integral – even when I look at my own family, the juggle of daily life and growing children means tastes and favourites change in an instant.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But what has remained is the dinner table, the place where, no matter the after-school sport club, friend visit or parent returning from work, it is the one moment to connect.

“That’s why, for 40 years, Dolmio has championed that there is no right way or rulebook to follow when it comes to preparing dinner – instead, it is about doing it your way, whatever is right for your family.”

News.title: Moment ‘violent’ sex attacker arrogantly moans ‘I can’t be arrested’ after he’s caught trying to rape woman in underpass
News.content:
THIS is the moment a sex attacker moans “I can’t be arrested” after he is caught trying to rape a woman in an underpass.

Syed Imam, 30, shouts “that’s a lie” when the police officers say he has been seen by a security guard.



The security staff had first noticed Iman while on patrol and bravely intervened when they saw him assaulting the woman.

The staff detained him and alerted the police.



Police arrive and arrest Imam for sexual assault, common assault and indecent exposure to which he objects: “Can’t be”.

In bodycam footage he is seen opening his mouth wide in disbelief as police say a security guard witnessed him.



Imam insists: “I have not been seen”.

He tells the cop “Good sir, I appreciate your right to a claim that you have.”



The officers arrived at the scene 30 minutes after the attack was reported on March 14 and Iman was taken into custody.

Before they arrived, the security staff at Canary Wharf detained Imam after witnessing him forcibly trying to rape vulnerable woman in the underpass of a train station.

The guards first saw Iman acting suspiciously while out on patrol.

The Metropolitan Police praised them for their quick thinking intervention which helped bring about a charge in 24 hours.

Iman, from Croydon Road, Beddington, was sentenced to six years at Snaresbrook Crown Court yesterday following a four-day trial.



Detective Constable Madeleine Powell, who worked on this case stated: “This case shows the important role everyone has to play in tackling violence against women and girls.

“If security staff at Canary Wharf had not bravely intervened, this violent offender could still be walking our streets, and the victim may have suffered even more harm than she already has.

“Everyone has a part to play in the joint action needed to protect women and girls and report concerning behaviour when they see it – you will be listened to and we will take action.

“I am proud of our officers who worked at an incredible pace to arrest Imam and present a compelling case, helping us to get justice for the victim and protect the public”

A spokesperson for the Met Police added: “Despite the victim having no recollection of what had occurred, the evidence secured through CCTV and fast-paced investigative work allowed the suspect to be interviewed, charged and remanded within 24 hours.



“The case was further strengthened through close collaboration between the officers, CPS and prosecution teams, ensuring the investigation progressed efficiently and without unnecessary delays.

“Throughout the process, dedicated support from specialist officers helped the victim understand the proceedings, remain engaged with the investigation, and navigate the significant trauma she had experienced.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The case demonstrates how effective partnership working, victim-focused policing and swift evidence-led investigations can combine to secure justice in the most challenging circumstances.”

News.title: Man, 25, who died after jumping in canal during police chase at Notting Hill Carnival is named – as new details revealed
News.content:
CANAL TRAGEDY Man, 25, who died after jumping in canal during police chase at Notting Hill Carnival is named – as new details revealed

A MAN who died after jumping in a canal during a police chase at Notting Hill Carnival has been named.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has revealed further details following the death of Karnell Kelly, 25, on Monday afternoon.



Officers briefly spoke with Karnell – who was wearing a face covering – at around 3.20pm as he approached the carnival area in West London.

He fled on foot and entered the canal near Meanwhile Gardens, according to the Metropolitan Police.



Officers and members of the public frantically sprung into action and managed to pull him from the water before CPR was carried out.

Karnell was urgently rushed to hospital but, despite the best efforts of medical crews, was sadly pronounced dead just before 4.45pm.

The IOPC are now probing his death – and will be reviewing body-worn footage from cops who chased him prior to the tragedy.

Investigators have so far spoken to ten officers who are being treated as witnesses in relation to Karnell’s death.

On Wednesday, divers from the Met’s Marine Policing Unit scoured the same area of the canal.

It has since been revealed that both Karnell and an officer were injured while in the water.



The cause of their injuries is still being investigated, the IOPC said.

Anyone with footage or who may have witnessed the events leading up to Karnell’s tragic death have been urged to come forward.

Investigators have spoken with Karnell’s family, who are currently being supported by specialist officers.

Amanda Rowe, IOPC director of engagement, said the watchdog needed to work out he “exact circumstances” of his death.

She added: “Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of Karnell Kelly and everyone affected by his death.



“We need to independently establish the exact circumstances of this incident given that he has died following an interaction with police officers.

“We are therefore appealing for anyone who may have witnessed and/or videoed any part of the incident to make contact with our investigators.”

The annual carnival is Europe’s biggest street party and billed as “the greatest community-led event on the planet” by organisers.

Scotland Yard responded to a number of incidents at Notting Hill Carnival, but said “the mood has been overwhelmingly positive and celebratory”.

The total number of arrests as part of the policing operation this year has been confirmed as 636, according to the Met Police.



Police arrested 394 people on Notting Hill Carnival’s final day as the party came to a close on Monday after millions flocked to the streets.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The arrests were related to several offences including possession of a handgun and sexual offender licence breaches.

Live facial recognition technology was expanded this year, leading to 214 alerts, 121 arrests and 86 registered sex offenders being stopped.

News.title: Autistic girl who was repeatedly raped by school taxi driver, 74, after ‘luring her with sweets’ demands life sentence
News.content:
'CRYING FOR HELP' Autistic girl who was repeatedly raped by school taxi driver, 74, after ‘luring her with sweets’ demands life sentence

AN AUTISTIC teen girl sobbed as she took the stand to testify at the appeal of a school taxi driver who repeatedly raped her and gave her sweets.

Lucie, whose name has been changed, was 11 when José B, now 74, repeatedly raped her while driving home from to school in Seine-et-Marne, east of Paris.



The taxi driver was convicted in July 2025, but claimed his sentence was “too harsh”.

He is appealing his 15-year sentence at the French court of appeal this week, and Lucie, now a teenager, has taken the stand to beg for a life sentence for her abuser.



She sobbed in her fathers arms, before reading a statement to the court.

The teen said: “I want him out of my life. I want him in prison for life.

“I’m angry. I’m furious.”

Prosecutor Rodolphe Juy-Birmann, said it was “very courageous of her to have come” to read her statement.

The child’s dad sobbed as her video testimony from four years ago was shown to the court.

A teaching assistant had asked Lucie where the sweets in her bag came from in April 2023.



She replied that they had come from José the taxi driver, who had driven her to and from school every day for five months.

Lucie mimicked what he was making her do in the back of the car, telling the school everything.

Police then found tissues with semen on and a packet of sweets in the taxi driver’s car and arrested José.

He would turn off the road and turn off the engine as he drove Lucie home, before forcing himself on the 11-year-old.

José vehicle’s tracking device showed he had taken 26 unusual detours and stops in the seven months between October and April 2023 when he drove the child to and from school.



He had retired as a bricklayer in 2015 and become a taxi driver, working for three separate providers of adapted taxis for disabled children.

Before Lucie, a 13-year-old had accused him of touching her thigh and moving up to her groin while he was teaching her to drive and shift gears.

He was suspended from his job, but wasn’t brought to trial until after Lucie’s case went to court in 2025, when he was given an 18 month prison sentence for the assault.

He continued to work with disabled children between between 2019 and 2023 for two different companies.

He was reportedly hired for his last job, where he raped and drove Lucie with just a phone call.



Lucie’s mum fought back tears as she recounted the amount of help and therapy her daughter had needed after her ordeal.

She said the trauma was “like a scar that will always be there but will heal”.

Lucie’s dad told the court: “Every night I hear my daughter crying for help.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A verdict in José’s appeal is expected on Friday.

News.title: Meet the Russians fleeing Ukraine war to work as strippers & £220 escorts in Thai sin city: ‘Why die when I can party?’
News.content:
SWEAT glistens on the muscled torso of a young Russian man as he finishes his workout to tell of his fears that the war with Ukraine will last another eight years.

But Sam, 23, from Moscow, is not honing his physique ready for a call up.





He is performing as a pole dancer in Thailand’s Sin City of Pattaya where Russian men are heading to work as male strippers and escorts to dodge a feared new round of conscription.

As he left the stage at the Big Tool strip club – where the men keep their trousers on despite its name – he was keen to talk about his new life in Pattaya.

With a huge grin he could hardly contain his enthusiasm for the coastal resort 90 minutes south of Bangkok where he moved just three weeks ago after first arriving in the capital.

But a dark cloud passed over his face when the discussion turned to the war and the devastating effect it has had on his family and friends.

He said: “Everything is so hard back home and every one of my age is terrified that they will be sent to fight.

“If that happens there is only one likely outcome.

“I have buried a lot of friends and relatives.

“I come from a big family – I have two brothers and two sisters and they miss me not being home but life is better here in Pattaya.





“I came here to have fun and to escape Russia and I am having a lot of fun while I am here. Everyone wants to escape Russia because this war is going to go on and on.

“I don’t think it will end until 2034.”

He doesn’t reveal how he comes to such a specific prediction but if he proves to be right it will have lasted 12 years, one of the longest conflicts between neighbouring states in modern history.

Sam appears happy to talk to men or women customers as long as they buy him a drink off the extortionate cocktail menu where prices reach 1,390 baht (£31).

His colleague Ilya, 25, was more interested in talking to just men – and much more up front to discuss what might follow an expensive cocktail.

He said: “It is 10,000 baht (£223) to go to a hotel. I work here six days a week and we stay open until 3.30am.

“It can be very busy and it is a lot of fun.”

Just like Sam, he is also happy to discuss the war and the crushing effect it has had on Russian society.



He said: “Five years ago Russia was a very rich country but now people have nothing.

“No money, no work and no hope.

“And it will not end soon

“If I was back home I would definitely have to join the army so you can see why I enjoy life in Pattaya.

“I love the freedom here. Someone like me can be myself here, I can’t be that at home.”

Despite all the problems back in Russia, Ilya, who comes from Putin’s home city of St Petersburg, revealed the tyrant does still retain some support.

He said: “Some people support him, some don’t, it’s probably 50-50.”

The Sun found the Russians working in Pattaya’s red light area after we travelled to Thailand to investigate the dark side of the Land of Smiles.



Russia is desperate to recruit young men like Sam and Ilya because it is losing 30,000 casualties a month.

But the growing fear among the population is that voluntary recruitment will be not be enough to replace this number and Putin may order another mobilisation

He last resorted to that tactic in September 2022, when a series of setbacks resulted in a call up of 300,000 reservists.

It was deeply unpopular and the Kremlin has avoided another one by targeting those from the poorest regions with the offer of lucrative salaries.

They also are lured by the promise of a huge payout to their families if they are killed.

Analysts reckon that approach is only just matching the number of casualties which Ukraine is claiming – around 1,000 a day on average.

But should Kyiv improve its “kill rate” it will pose serious problems for Putin.

Russia has dismissed rumours of a looming call-up but those young men who have fled to Pattaya are not taking any chances.

The Big Tool club on Walking Street, the popular tourist destination at the heart of the city’s sprawling red light district, is just one place where potential recruits would rather work than take their chances on the battlefield.

Both men and women work there – and both men and women are among the many customers the venue attracts each night.



After politely declining Ilya’s offer of a 10,000 baht hotel visit, I turned to talk one of the women dancers, Yana, 26, from Vladivostock.

She said: “Most of the guys in here are from Russia or Turkey.

“The Russian men would much rather be here than at home.

“If you are at home you could end up in the army. And if you end up in the army you could end up at the front and we all know what might happen then.”

Since the war began thousands of Russian have fled to Thailand.

In one four-month period shortly after the war began, 233,000 Russians arrived in Phuket, according to the local airport, making them the biggest group of visitors by far.

It helped drive property prices in the areas of the island popular with Russians to record prices as it dawned on them that Putin was in it for the long haul.

A Russian travel agent there said: “They just do not go home… they are here to get away from conscription.”



Back in the Big Tool, Sam, despite being a proud Russian, is in no doubt where his priorities lie.

He said: “Why would I want to join the army and fight and die when I can be in Pattaya having fun?”

News.title: Woman avoids jail after XL Bully named Prince mauled her cousin, 19, to death in horror attack inside flat
News.content:
DOG HORROR Woman avoids jail after XL Bully named Prince mauled her cousin, 19, to death in horror attack inside flat

A WOMAN has avoided jail after her XL Bully named Prince mauled her 19-year-old cousin to death.

Morgan Dorsett was attacked by the animal at a flat in Bristol on February 26 last year.



She suffered suffered catastrophic injuries to her neck – with the XL Bully later “humanely destroyed”.

Kelcie Reed, 24, wept as she was spared jail today and instead handed a suspended sentence.



She previously pleaded guilty to being in charge of a dog dangerously out of control, causing injury resulting in death.

Reed will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Judge Anna Richardson said: “Rather than putting everyone through the additional trauma of a trial, you accepted responsibility.

“You are someone who has over the last 18 months done what they needed to do to try and move forward. You need to continue to do that.”

Bristol Crown Court was told that just after 7pm on the day of the horror, a neighbour heard someone screaming: “Get down, get down”.

He went outside and then further heard a woman shout out: “She’s f***ing dead”.



After Reed called 999, emergency crews arrived to find Morgan lying on her back covered in blood.

She was declared dead shortly after, while Reed suffered cuts and bruises after attempting to stop the attack.

Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later “humanely destroyed”



The court was told Morgan had cocaine in her system which caused her to “act erratically”.

Judge Richardson said: “Morgan’s behaviour was unusual… she began to scream upon seeing Prince, that led to him barking and ultimately to attack her.”

In a victim impact statement, Morgan’s mum Marie Smith said: “She came to Bristol to experience something bigger than the small village she grew up in. Bristol with its vibrant lively culture would have suited her perfectly.

“Her death has cast a shadow over everything… A life that should have been so much bigger and brighter.”

News.title: Chris Mason: 'This is not what Farage wanted today to look like'
News.content:
Reform UK's annual conference is under way in Birmingham - a chance for the party to talk about its policies and what it hopes to do should it win a future general election.

Yet questions over money and donations are dominating the news after two of the party's senior figures stepped down on Friday morning following a Channel 4 News report.

Chris Mason reports from the conference.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.

However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

When asked about if the Prime Minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said the they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish".

"Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.

Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory.

"The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."

Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea â something that has never happened before."

He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".

It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

News.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister warns
News.content:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has warned.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El NiÃ±o that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Watch: Tensions flare as judge declines to remove juror in Lindsay Clancy trial
News.content:
The jury in the Lindsay Clancy case failed to reach a verdict on their sixth day of deliberations.

Clancy's lawyer asked the judge to remove a juror after the jury forewoman sent a court note saying one holdout would not follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.

The defence's request to remove the juror was denied by the judge.

The BBC's Ana Faguy breaks down how the dramatic day in court unfolded.

Read more

News.title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 BST on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are aware of some school closures in the area and have liaised with partners in the local authorities regarding the expected disruption today.

"Any decisions made by schools or other services to close has been a decision made by those organisations in isolation, and has not been a police recommendation.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authorities, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"There will be a proportionate visible police presence in the affected areas to ensure public safety, in line with our plans for any significant gathering."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil last week, for one of the young men who died, was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

Police said a total of 24 people had been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Russell Howard 'devastated' after his baby son died hours after birth
News.content:
This story contains content which some readers might find distressing

Comedian Russell Howard has revealed his baby son Felix died earlier this year, shortly after his wife Cerys had given birth.

In a statement, he said he and his wife had faced "unimaginable heartache" and described it as "the most devastating time of our lives".

Howard praised the "extraordinary compassion, kindness and humanity" of the hospital staff who cared for them over the period that followed Felix's death.

He also announced the launch of a new foundation in their late son's name to help families going through similar ordeals, with a comedy fundraiser set to take place next year.

In a statement posted on his social media accounts, external on Friday, Howard recalled: "During our time in hospital, Felix was placed in a cool cot, which meant that my wife and I were able to spend precious hours with our beautiful boy.

"We could hold him, talk to him and tell him how much we loved him. Those hours are among the most precious memories we have of Felix."

Howard and his wife had not publicly announced at the time that they were expecting their second child.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

He explained he and his wife had been assigned a bereavement midwife named Lauren, who had experienced a similar tragedy and retrained in order to help other families.

"Her care meant more to us than we could ever put into words," Howard said.

"We were overwhelmed by the care we received, and we made a promise to each other: that we would try to help other families who find themselves facing the same devastating circumstances."

As a result, Howard said he and Cerys were launching The Felix Foundation, which will aim to help families affected by miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, neonatal death or related bereavement.

A fundraising event, titled the Stand-Up Gala, will take place at London's O2 Arena in February to raise money for the charity,

Michael McIntyre, Jimmy Carr, Aisling Bea, John Bishop and Mo Gilligan are among the comics who will perform at the event.

Howard said he would "never forget the generosity" of his fellow comics, who were giving their time to the show "completely free of charge".

The 46-year-old is one of the best known stand-up comics in the UK, having appeared on shows such as Mock The Week and Russell Howard's Good News.

The comedian and his wife Cerys, an NHS doctor, have been together since 2004 and share another son, who was born in August 2024.

Howard recently played a string of shows at the Edinburgh Fringe festival, and is currently on a stand-up tour of the UK.

News.title: Warning after jobseekers targeted in interviews scam
News.content:
Jobseekers are being warned to be vigilant as scammers are targeting people on job listings websites to trick them into downloading bogus interview tools.

One victim was invited on LinkedIn by a fake recruiter to take part in a job interview process and downloaded a normal-looking document which turned out to be malicious software.

Within hours the hackers had drained his cryptocurrency accounts of Â£18,000 of savings and disappeared.

"It's a horrible feeling to be out a substantial amount - something I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy," the victim, who wanted to stay anonymous, said.

News.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing spotted back above Scottish coast
News.content:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".

News.title: Weekend heat for parts of UK before more rain next week
News.content:
Temperatures are on the rise again in time for the weekend with areas of the south experiencing 27C on Sunday.

However, before that, wet and windy conditions are in the Friday forecast for many across the northern half of the UK.

Low pressure systems continue to roll in from the Atlantic across the far north of the UK, affecting mostly northern and western Scotland.

Meanwhile, high pressure will block and weaken these fronts across the southern half of England and Wales, where drought conditions and hosepipe bans continue.

News.title: Anger as human poo and maggot-infested food left behind at beauty spot
News.content:
Lally said the weekend's fly-tipping was "one of the worst examples that we have come across", but it was not unusual to find discarded BBQs, beer cans and rotting food.

"Logic says it's lighter to carry back once you've eaten and drank it all than it is to carry it out there," said Lally.

"Come and have a nice time, but leave no trace."

She said the phrase "leave no trace", cited in the code, had been associated with beauty spots "for so long" but was "just as relevant today".

The Countryside Code also states that "dropping litter and dumping rubbish are criminal offences".

"Our wardens have gone from supporting firefighters with the wildfires and, the first rainy weekend, they're off finding abandoned wild camps. They have had quite the summer," said Lally.

"It has a knock-on effect on wildlife. There's still a fire risk. Pollution can contaminate water. It affects everything, not just it looking nice."

Steffan Edwards is a warden at Bannau Brycheiniog National Park and cleaned up the mess.

He told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast: "We've got plenty of things to get on with within the national park as warden's.

He said it was a "shame to see all that rubbish discarded on the hill" but added warden's like Edwards discover abandoned items "all the time", which they have to deal with.

"This isn't new to us and it's not new to other national parks and other beauty sites across Wales and the UK. But what we are finding is it's an increasing problem over the last couple of years.

"People are finding out about these nice places and taking literally everything up with them, which you would take to a campsite and just leaving it there."

Policy and Advocacy Manager at Wildlife Trust Wales, Joe Wilkins, said the discovery of the litter has come at a time where plants and animals "can't sustain another threat", following a summer of extreme heat.

Wilkins said it is "so important that people have access to these spaces" and the ability to enjoy them, adding it is "unfair" for people to "absolutely ruin that experience for others".

News.title: Is a whale fossil the leftovers of a Bronze Age Sunday roast?
News.content:
The head of a whale, believed to date back to the Bronze Age, has been discovered buried on a beach in Islandmagee.

A 10-year-old boy was out looking for fossils along the shore when he spotted the back of the skull protruding from a bank of earth - but could the fossil be the remnants of a prehistoric Sunday roast?

The find has been described as a totally unique, with geologists and marine specialists trying to establish the fossil's story and the Natural History Museum in London helping to identify it.

It was found on the same beach where Ireland's only dinosaur bones were discovered in the late 19th Century and the 1980s.

News.title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
News.content:
The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.

It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.

But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.

The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.

A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales.

It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apache helicopters.

This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year.

Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army â such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.

The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis.

Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.

Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.

An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness.

"We are also investing Â£2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."

On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030.

The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."

The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces.

Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.

The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

News.title: AI tools that take notes for GPs could miss vital information, study suggests
News.content:
The report concluded AI scribes can help with administrative work but more research needs to be done to understand how they work in specific healthcare settings and how their design supports both patients and clinicians.

It comes months after the BBC heard from doctors in the West Midlands, who said their workload had been significantly cut by using the transcription tool Heidi.

At one clinic in Dudley, the tool was credited with reducing a backlog of posting patient letters from six months to 14 days.

One of the key findings by the University of Edinburgh was that although AI tools can help capture what patients say, they can sometimes miss important aspects of consultations - such as facial expressions, gestures and emotional state.

The report said AI summaries tend to prioritise clinical information, which can come at the expense of the patients' stories and experiences of their illness.

It was also found that patients may be hesitant to reveal sensitive information - such as substance abuse, domestic abuse or mental health struggles - when they know the consultation is being recorded and processed by AI.

Researchers also highlighted that manual notetaking serves important functions for clinicians in their reasoning and reflection on what the patient has said.

Their report said using AI scribes could result in "cognitive offloading" for clinicians - which means the tools take on some of their mental effort.

This can have benefits, the report said, as clinicians can spent their efforts having more meaningful conversations with patients or concentrating on complex tasks.

However, it also said the tools can reduce memory recall and skill development and highlighted instances where clinicians do not recognise their own notes or remember the patient the next time they see them.

News.title: Golden retrievers to gather at the breed's ancestral Highland home
News.content:
A mass gathering of golden retrievers and their owners is to return to the ancestral home of the breed in July 2028.

The event will mark 160 years since the first golden retriever puppies were born at Guisachan House in Glen Affric, near Cannich, in the Highlands.

Meetings to celebrate the breed have been held in different formats by the Golden Retriever Club of Scotland since the late 1990s, with larger events taking place since 2006.

The last gathering held at Guisachan in 2023 involved almost 500 dogs from 12 countries.

The Golden Retriever Club of Scotland said a date for the 2028 gathering would be announced later.

After weeks of uncertainty over the publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, HarperCollins India has acquired the book and said it will be published in India on 10 November this year.

Ms Gandhi is one of the best-known figures in politics in India, as the widow of assassinated prime minister Rajiv Gandhi and then the longest-serving president of India’s grand old party, the Indian National Congress. She is also the mother of the current leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi and senior Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.

Her memoir is one of the country’s most hotly-anticipated political books in years, but became mired in controversy after a breakdown in the relationship between Ms Gandhi and its original publisher, Penguin Random House India.

It was reported by the Indian Express that Ms Gandhi’s representatives objected to “editorial changes and deletions” demanded by the publisher regarding sensitive political topics, including passages about current prime minister Narendra Modi. Penguin Random House India has denied facing any external pressure over the edits.

That put the book’s scheduled November release in India in doubt, until Friday’s announcement by HarperCollins. In a statement, the publisher said: “HarperCollins India will publish Belonging: A Journey of Love by Sonia Gandhi. The long-awaited memoir will be published in India on 10 November 2026.”

The statement said: “One of the most anticipated political memoirs of our time, Belonging is a dramatic and deeply personal story of love, identity, duty and belonging, and offers a rare insider’s view of India’s journey.”

The memoir covers Gandhi’s early life in northern Italy, her marriage to Rajiv Gandhi, and the assassinations of both her husband and his mother, his predecessor as prime minister Indira Gandhi. It also discusses her initially reluctant entry into politics, as well as interactions with other senior figures like Mr Modi going up to the present day.

HarperCollins India says about the memoir: “In this book, the once famously reticent Sonia Gandhi opens up with warmth and candour to tell the story of her remarkable life, from her childhood in post-war Veneto; to the romance that brings her to India; to the shattering losses that will reshape not only her own future but also that of her adopted home. We witness Sonia’s introduction to her formidable mother-in-law, Nehru’s daughter Indira Gandhi, India’s first female Prime Minister. We see Sonia gain confidence by Rajiv’s side, as she adjusts to the sounds and sights of her new home – learning to speak Hindi, to wear saris, to relish spicy cuisine.”

Earlier, in a statement, Penguin Random House India had indicated that it was still “willing and keen to publish” Belonging, while it disputed the characterisation in the Indian media of how the deal with Ms Gandhi broke down.

“Penguin Random House India is not the publisher of Belonging in India,” the statement read.

“As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in the best interests of their books. This is a normal part of the publishing process.”

The publisher told The Independent there had been “no external pressure whatsoever” regarding the edits under discussion.

A new 120-mile walking trail crossing the Pennines, Yorkshire Dales and Lake District is set to open in this month.

The Westmorland and Furness Way is a six-stage route from Alston in the North Pennines, England’s highest market town, to the ruins of the medieval Furness Abbey in Cumbria.

Cumbria Tourism will open the long-distance footpath at the Sedbergh Walking and Wellbeing Festival event on 15 September.

The walking route, developed by Westmorland and Furness Council, will take between eight and 17 days to complete and will utilise existing trails where possible.

All six stages have start and end points accessible by public transport; the longest stage is a 27-mile stretch from Sedbergh to Bowness-on-Windermere.

Trail highlights include the open moorland of the North Pennines, rounded fells of the Howgills and the Lake District National Park including the shores of Lake Windermere.

According to the Furness Way website, the route fits “three nationally protected areas, five distinct landscape types and a thousand years of history – all in 120 miles”.

It added: “The trail was conceived to celebrate the geography and identity of the Westmorland and Furness council area, formed in 2023.

“As well as being a walker's route, it is intended as an economic driver for the small towns and villages along its path – places like Kirkby Stephen, Sedbergh and Ulverston that richly reward an overnight stay.”

Councillor Adrian Waite, Westmorland and Furness Council’s cabinet member for Environmental Services and Transport, said: “We are incredibly proud to have developed the spectacular Westmorland and Furness Way, designed to connect both visitors and local communities with our rich heritage, nature and diverse landscapes.

“This new walking route will celebrate our stunning area and make it even more accessible, creating a connected path from Alston all the way to Furness Abbey.”

Katie Taylor is set to bid farewell to boxing this weekend, as she finally realises her Croke Park dream when she fights Flora Pili.

Taylor, a former Olympic gold medalist and two-weight undisputed champion, boxes on home soil in Ireland as she faces the unbeaten Pili, with all four major super-lightweight belts on the line.

Taylor, 40, brings the IBF, WBA and WBO titles into the iconic Dublin venue, while the vacant WBC strap is also up for grabs.

open image in gallery Katie Taylor (left) will fight Flora Pili at Croke Park ( PA Wire )

France’s Pili (12-0, 2 KOs) will aim to become just the second fighter to beat Taylor (25-1, 6 KOs), who is expecting 80,000 adoring fans at her final fight.

News.title: Could making fewer clothes create a fairer fashion industry?
News.content:

Fashion has become remarkably skilled at presenting small improvements as systemic change. A garment made with recycled fibres, a lower-impact collection or a resale scheme may suggest progress, yet the industry continues to manufacture clothes in quantities the planet cannot sustain.

For Safia Minney, the pioneering ethical fashion entrepreneur who founded People Tree and went on to establish Fashion Declares, and Indilisi incremental improvements are no longer enough. A genuine response to the climate crisis requires the industry to confront a far more difficult question: how can fashion produce dramatically fewer clothes without abandoning the millions of workers whose livelihoods depend upon making them?

open image in gallery Safia Minney, founder of People Tree, Fashion Declares and Indilisi, believes fashion must replace relentless volume with craft, regenerative agriculture and dignified livelihoods ( Copyright: Odi Caspi )

“Science tells us that we should be cutting back production and consumption of new clothing by between 75 and 95 per cent,” Minney says. “That is a reduction of 75 to 95 per cent, not 5 or 25 per cent.”

Such a contraction would represent far more than a change in seasonal trends or consumer habits. It would fundamentally reshape a global industry built on speed, volume and cheap labour. Factories would receive fewer orders and jobs would disappear, many of them in countries where garment work provides a vital, if often precarious, source of income.

“Obviously, what that means is that a lot of people will lose their jobs in fashion supply chains,” Minney says.

It is a reality that can be obscured by the seemingly simple instruction to “buy less”. Reducing consumption is essential, but without a plan for the people making our clothes, environmental progress risks coming at the expense of those who have benefited least from fashion’s profits and suffered most from its inequities.

For Minney, the answer lies in replacing volume with value. Rather than continuing to rely on vast quantities of industrially produced clothing, fashion could redirect investment towards handweaving, traditional textile skills and regenerative agriculture, creating work that supports communities rather than extracting from them.

“There is now a global trend for craft, but at the moment it is considered to be high-end luxury,” she says. “It’s incorporating craft, handweaving and traditional hand-skilled techniques into mid-market fashion and above.”

open image in gallery A weaver at Swallows in Bangladesh creates fabric for Indilisi, preserving traditional hand skills while supporting lower-impact production and dignified livelihoods ( Copyright: Safia Minney )

Craft is frequently celebrated on fashion’s most expensive runways, where evidence of the human hand helps justify the language and price of luxury. But Minney believes it should play a much broader role. If consumers bought fewer clothes, repaired what they owned and made greater use of resale and charity shops, they might also be able to spend more on an occasional handwoven garment.

“As consumers start to consume less and consume better and more consciously, there’s no reason at all why they wouldn’t be able to afford a handwoven shirt or dress or trousers,” she says. “We can buy second-hand very affordably through the various platforms or charity shops and, of course, we can repair clothes as well. We can keep things in circulation for longer.”

This is not simply about preserving beautiful techniques. Minney points to the millions of handweavers in India, Bangladesh and across Africa whose knowledge could form part of a lower-volume fashion economy. Investment in these skills could also create livelihoods outside the industrial centres to which many garment workers have migrated.

open image in gallery A craftswoman at Lesedi Cultural Village in South Africa uses traditional hand skills, an example of the knowledge and livelihoods Safia Minney believes fashion’s just transition must value and protect ( Copyright: Getty )

“Retraining people, providing livelihoods and opportunities in craft production in rural areas could actually make life much more comfortable for a lot of people who are living quite far away from their families, maybe only seeing their children a couple of times a year,” she says.

“There are some real advantages in creating craft livelihoods in rural areas, where people can live more affordably with their extended families and with their children.”

This is the social dimension of climate action that the language of lower-impact materials can miss. A just transition is not only concerned with how much carbon a garment produces, it asks who is being supported, who carries the risk and whether the new system gives people the means to build secure lives.

Minney describes conventional sustainability as an attempt to improve an existing model, protecting basic human rights, preventing excessive overtime and moving towards lower-impact materials or mono-fibre garments that are easier to recycle.

Important though those measures are, she argues that many should already constitute the basic conditions of doing business.

open image in gallery Safia Minney with a handweaver at Swallows in Bangladesh, where traditional skills are used to create fabric for Indilisi and support dignified, lower-impact livelihoods. ( Copyright: Safia Minney )

“Sustainability should be ticking all the boxes in terms of better practice, looking at what should be illegal, not covering people’s basic human rights in the supply chain, whether it’s paying workers badly or excessive overtime,” she says. “Sustainable fashion has been an embracing of human rights and nature, but I think we needed to go beyond that.”

Regenerative fashion demands a deeper relationship with the landscapes and communities which clothing depends. It means working directly with farmers through organic and Fairtrade agriculture, investing in soil health and GMO-free seeds, and paying producers fairly for fibres such as organic cotton.

Craft belongs within that model because its value can extend beyond lower-impact production. “Craft does use low-impact materials. It does use traditional hand skills. It can pay people a living wage,” Minney says. “If we were to use craft, that would be highly regenerative in its practices.”

For designers, buyers and merchandisers, this requires more than adding an artisanal piece to a collection. Brands need to change their production calendars and allow time for garments and textiles to be made by hand.

open image in gallery Indilisi brings traditional handwoven fabric into contemporary fashion, proving that heritage craft can feel every bit as modern as it is meaningful. ( Copyright: Steve Nyman )

“They can start to look at their critical path so that they can make allowances for hand production,” she says. “It’s not difficult. It’s perfectly doable. We did it at People Tree. We’re currently doing it at Indilisi.”

The guiding question, she suggests, should be: “How are you going to make products with as low an environmental impact as possible, but with as high a social impact as possible?”

Craft-based production cannot be expanded responsibly simply by placing larger orders. Brands must form close partnerships with craft organisations, learn what makers can produce and offer design input so that finished fabrics become high-quality garments people will want to keep.

Crucially, they must also reconsider when people are paid.

“Whilst working capital sounds really unsexy, it’s critical,” Minney says. A handwoven fabric can take three-and-a-half months to complete and sometimes as long as five. During that period, artisans still need to support themselves and their families.

“You need to be paying the handweaver, the hand-embroidery artisan or the hand-block printer as they’re finishing their work,” she says. “Every week or every month, not nine months, or three months after the product has arrived with you in the UK.”

Minney’s work in Bangladesh includes training in design, production and quality management, as well as the use of safe, GOTS-certified dyes and links to certified organic cotton. The aim is to make the journey of a garment traceable back to the people growing its fibres, while ensuring that respect for the farmer and the natural world is embedded in the product.

It is a slower system, but that is precisely the point. Craft cannot become another means of feeding fashion’s appetite for endless growth. The industry must reduce overall production while building strong networks that allow makers to work at a human pace.

After more than 30 years of campaigning, Minney’s vision extends beyond emissions reduction. Fashion companies must also prepare their supply chains for the climate disruption that is already unavoidable.

“We are not thinking about extreme heat and floods and how that’s going to impact the people within our supply chains,” she warns, “especially women who already carry the burden of making ends meet.”

Environmental, social and governance frameworks need to become more than corporate reporting exercises. They must help communities build resilience and adapt to increasingly dangerous conditions while recognising fashion’s dependence upon both people and nature.

The transition Minney describes is radical, but it is not a rejection of fashion. It is an argument for restoring value to it. Fewer garments, made with greater skill, from fibres grown in healthier soil, by people able to earn a dignified living close to their communities.

Buying less is only one part of that transformation. The greater challenge is ensuring that as fashion relinquishes its dependence on volume, it does not relinquish its responsibility to the people who have sustained it. A just transition cannot simply close the door on the old system. It must invest in what comes next.

open image in gallery Mountains of discarded clothing expose the scale of fashion’s waste crisis, a challenge explored through repair, reuse and circularity at Craft, Clothing & Circularity: Out of Fashion on 11 September ( Copyright: Tim Mitchell )

Minney will continue this conversation at Craft, Clothing & Circularity: Out of Fashion at Conway Hall in London on Friday 11 September. Created in collaboration with Selvedge magazine, the event brings together makers, menders and campaigners for hands-on workshops in rag-rug making, quilting, visible darning and clothing care, followed by discussions exploring repair as activism and how craft and circularity could underpin a genuinely regenerative fashion system.

“Fashion needs a wake-up call,” Minney says. “If you’re a fashion practitioner or fashion lover, join our interactive discussion and create powerful action with us.” Workshop tickets include access to the evening conversations and a curated pre-loved clothes swap, while evening-only tickets are also available.

Pierre Gasly has lost his podium finish at the Monaco Grand Prix in June after an appeal from McLaren and Red Bull was upheld by the FIA’s International Court of Appeal.

Gasly finished third at the chequered flag on track in the principality on 7 June, but was demoted ​to ⁠seventh when two ‌five-second penalties for pit-lane speeding were applied post-race, ‌with fellow Frenchman Isack Hadjar ‌(Red Bull) promoted to third.

However, that decision was overturned after a right ⁠to review on 12 June, with the stewards accepting Renault-owned Alpine's evidence that there had been a timekeeping error.

The FIA's International Court ‌of Appeal then met ​last month to ‌hear a ⁠McLaren and Red Bull ⁠challenge, with the verdict issued ‌on Friday during the start of the Italian Grand Prix – nearly three months later.

The verdict essentially reinstates Hadjar’s third-place finish and podium, with Gasly dropping back down to seventh, with his two five-second penalties reinstated.

In response, an Alpine statement read: "The team expresses its disappointment and frustration with the outcome reached by the FIA International Court of Appeal relating to the result of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

"While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that Car #10 did not exceed the Pit Lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

"While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive Championship fight.

"This outcome will not deter the team’s efforts and motivation in achieving its objectives by the end of the season."

Jai Arrow made an emotional 100th NRL appearance for the South Sydney Rabbitohs to mark his farewell from the sport at the Allianz Stadium.

After being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, Arrow had announced his retirement in May.

Special dispensation had been granted by the NRL and Rabbitohs to allow Arrow the opportunity to take to the field for the opening kick-off another two times – with the game against Sydney Roosters marking a century of appearances.

Arrow walked his team out onto the field, with ‘Stand By Me’ playing before ‘You’ll Never Walk Alone’ then rang around the stadium.

The 31-year-old forward had made 178 appearances overall in the NRL before his retirement announcement, playing at Brisbane Broncos and then Gold Coast Titans ahead of joining the Rabbitohs in 2021.

Arrow, also having featured 12 times for Queensland in State of Origin, fought back tears as he was presented to the crowd, who all stood in applause, many holding up banners of support in his name.

Ahead of kick-off, Arrow waved to the crowd before being embraced by his team-mates and then substituted off, with the Rabbitohs having been allowed an extra player in their squad list and an additional rotation.

Rabbitohs head coach Wayne Bennett offered out his arms to Arrow, who was overcome with emotion and could not hold back his tears before sharing an embrace with his wife Berina Colakovic.
