Sports.title: Liverpool seal new signing days after window shut ahead of January arrival
Sports.content:
Liverpool seal new signing days after window shut ahead of January arrival

The transfer window may have slammed shut on September 1, but Liverpool have managed to get a new signing over the line in the days after

View 3 Images Andoni Iraola's side have just announced a new signing (Image: Andrew Powell, Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Liverpool have announced the signing of Djylian N'Guessan from Saint-Etienne. The youngster's move was secured this morning, despite the transfer window slamming shut on September 1.

‌



At the age of 18 years old, he is considered to be a bright prospect in French football, having already racked up 13 senior appearances for the Ligue 1 side. He will officially move to the Reds in January.

‌



However, he will be spending his time on loan at Stade Brestois. It's understood Liverpool will pay a guaranteed fee of around £4.3m while also including a sell-on clause.

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd, Arsenal and Liverpool name Champions League squads as Reds snub two senior stars READ MORE :

8 players poised to miss Ipswich vs Liverpool as Reds see treble boost for Premier League clash READ MORE :

N'Guessan appeared at the 2025 Under-20 World Cup. He made seven appearances for France, who finished fourth after losing to Colombia in the third place play-off.

In the U17 European Championship last summer, he earned a place in the competition's Team of the Tournament, after scoring four goals for his country. In total, he boasts 11 goals in 11 games for France's U17s side.

‌



In January, Liverpool will decide to either allow him to stay at Brest or bring him to Anfield. He is not the only young talent to secure a late move to the Reds.

View 3 Images N'Guessan has 11 goals in 11 games for the French U17s (Image: AFP or licensors)

Andoni Iraola's side have also purchased young goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans from Genk. The 18-year-old is expected to cost a small fee at first, but once potential bonuses are added, it's understood the package as a whole could be worth as much as £30m.

‌



He signed a six-year contract at Anfield, suggesting he may be seen by the Merseysiders as the long-term replacement of veteran goalkeeping star Alisson Becker.

They are the final signings of a rollercoaster transfer window for the Reds. Including the late arrivals of N'Guessan and Brughmans, Liverpool spent just north of £200m on new transfers.

View 3 Images Brughmans was also signed by the Reds (Image: Liverpool FC)

‌



Victor Munoz arrived for £34.5m, and he is already making himself known by scoring a vital goal in the recent 2-2 home draw with Nottingham Forest.

Jeremy Jacquet finally arrived at the club, six months after the Reds agreed to pay Rennes £60m for the 20-year-old's services.

However, the major statement signing was undoubtedly the £123m purchase of Paris Saint-Germain superstar Bradley Barcola. The French international may even be handed his debut on the weekend when Iraola's side travel to Ipswich Town.

Sports.title: British Cycling star finally claims Tour of Britain road win to dispel nearly-man fears
Sports.content:
British Cycling star finally claims Tour of Britain road win to dispel nearly-man fears

The Cannock cyclist took victory in Lincoln with his grandparents watching on

View 2 Images Picture by Zac Williams/SWpix.com - 02/09/2026 - Cycling - UCI ProSeries - 2026 Lloyds Tour of Britain Men - Stage 1: Lincoln to Lincoln (182.5km) - Winner of Stage 1, Lewis Askey (NSN Cycling Team) celebrates with family

The career-high finishes and lauded strong performances had all come and gone for Lewis Askey this season, but at the top of Michaelgate he experienced the unbridled joy of victory he had been chasing.

‌



The 25-year-old from Cannock won stage one of the Lloyds Tour of Britain in the shadow of Lincoln Cathedral to dispel any fears of becoming the nearly-man.

‌



Askey had formed part of an 11-strong lead group through four laps of Michaelgate’s iconic climb before bursting away on the final lap to cross the line nine seconds ahead of the field.

‌



“It feels amazing, especially to have my grandparents there at the finish line. It was super special,” said the NSN Cycling Team rider. “I ride my bike to win races. It’s great when you come second, come third and do good performances, but nothing matches managing to put your hands up in the air.”

Askey rode to his best-ever Grand Tour stage finish on stage 17 of the Tour de France, having finished second at the National Championships a month before.

“I’ve been pretty close. I’ve had plenty of second places again. If I can do a year where I turn those seconds into firsts then it will change quite a lot for me,” he said prior to the race.

‌



View 2 Images Lewis Askey celebrates winning Stage 1 of the 2026 Lloyds Tour of Britain

And against some of Europe’s leading names, with Filippo Ganna and Matteo Trentin both part of the lead group, things did change for Askey who will wear the green leader’s jersey as the tour continues in Lincolnshire today.

Unlike Ganna and Trentin, Askey had no team support to help him up the cobbled climbs, instead relying on home crowds to will him up Lincoln’s notoriously steep ascent.

‌



“I didn’t really believe over the last two laps because I knew there were teams with multiple riders which is a really hard situation to manage,” he reflected.

“But I knew it was my chance to push for a chance at general classification and leadership. That performance grants me that opportunity.”

And British success continued as Walsall’s Adam Lewis won the combativity award, while Aberdeen’s Elliot Rowe collected the young rider jersey.

Sports.title: Defender Burghley Horse Trials kick off in style as crowds flock to Stamford
Sports.content:
Defender Burghley Horse Trials kick off in style as crowds flock to Stamford

Spectators thronged Burghley’s Main Arena as United States challenger Caroline Pamukcu set the ball rolling by presenting her two rides, HSH Tolan King and Defender Kentucky 2026 runner-up HSH Blake

View Image Clarke Johnstone and Domasco are one of the duos competing (Image: DBHT/Peter Nixon)

The Defender Burghley Horse Trials are officially underway after the Fairfax & Favor-sponsored first horse inspection saw 48 horses presented to the Ground Jury of Xavier Le Sauce (FRA), Joanne Jarden (IRE) and Sandy Phillips (GBR) on Wednesday afternoon.

‌



Spectators thronged Burghley’s Main Arena as United States challenger Caroline Pamukcu set the ball rolling by presenting her two rides, HSH Tolan King and Defender Kentucky 2026 runner-up HSH Blake.

‌



Caroline’s horses were accepted, along with both rides of New Zealand’s former Burghley winner Tim Price, the current world number one, plus the British trio Holly Richardson, Tom Jackson and Harry Meade, whose hopes again include Cavalier Crystal following three successive third-place finishes at Burghley, and Ireland’s Susie Berry on Clever Trick and John The Bull.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

A number of Burghley first-timers included Suffolk-based Mary Edmundson, making her debut at an event that her mother Debbie competed at 40 years ago, the 2022 world champion Yasmin Ingham aboard Goliath Du Loir, Jack Pinkney on Claragh Olala and Switzerland’s Robin Godel with Dealer De La Bride. All 48 horses presented passed the first horse inspection and will start the dressage phase on Thursday and Friday.

‌



Winner of the Fairfax & Favor best dressed lady award was Jonelle Price (NZL), who wore a striking cream coat by ME+EM, while Clarke Johnstone (NZL) was best dressed man, clad in a Dior cashmere jacket and navy trousers.

Judge Andrew Ransford, of Hiho Silver, said: “It is about attention to detail. The way the riders present themselves for the first horse inspection these days is very professional. Clarke looked incredibly trendy, and he stood out. The ladies’ prize this time was a lot more difficult, but Jonelle looked unbelievable.”

Competition begins at 10am on Thursday with Caroline Pamukcu and HSH Tolan King taking centre-stage after Olympic gold medallist and two-times Burghley winner Ros Canter has completed the traditional “guinea pig” test aboard MHS Seventeen.

Article continues below

As one of only six CCI5* competitions around the globe, Defender Burghley always attracts the very top athletes, and ranks alongside Wimbledon and The Masters as a sporting “major”. The event offers superb shopping opportunities, delicious food and drink, elegant hospitality options and lots to entertain children and less-horsey members of the family. HRH The Princess Royal is visiting Burghley – where she won the European Eventing Championships in 1971 – on Sunday, 6 September to present the prizes after the final showjumping, and in her role as President of Burghley’s supported charity for 2026, World Horse Welfare, and as President of the British Eventing Support Trust.

Every minute of the action from Defender Burghley, from the first horse inspection to the final trophy lift, as well as the Dubarry Burghley Young Event Horse Finals and the Main Arena Masterclasses, is broadcast on Burghley TV.

To purchase a Burghley TV subscription, and for a full timetable and to buy tickets, visit www.burghley-horse.co.uk.

Sports.title: Scottish windsurfing star Andy Brown sets out 2028 Olympic ambitions
Sports.content:
Scottish windsurfing star Andy Brown sets out 2028 Olympic ambitions

Andy Brown learned his trade in the Scottish Highlands and heads to Weymouth looking to retain the world title he won in 2025

View 2 Images Andy Brown celebrates becoming iQFOiL world champion in Aarhus in 2025 (Image: © Sailing Energy / iQfoil Class)

Andy Brown is taking an attacking approach to home waters in Weymouth as he bids to retain his title as world champion.

‌



The Scottish windsurfer enters the Musto iQFOiL World Championships 2026 as the man to beat and both reigning champions belong to the host nation, with Emma Wilson defending her women’s crown. Brown is hoping to make the most of his local knowledge as he bids for a repeat in an event he sees as a key marker two years out from the LA Olympics.

‌



He said: “There’s lots of sailing and water sport that happens in Portland, it’s the biggest spot in the UK. I’ve been sailing here for 10 years. I know the place and I know the waters.

‌



“The Worlds show where you are at, it’s the most accurate test. You need those tests on the way to the Olympics and the plan is gold at LA 2028. Winning the Worlds did bring a new pressure but that’s dissipated over the last year and I’m in the process now.

“I’m confident that it’s going to come together but there’s all sorts of conditions that we could face. I’m attacking to win my next world title, not defending last year’s crown.”

View 2 Images Windsurfer Andy Brown is targeting gold at the LA 2028 Olympics (Image: © Sailing Energy / iQfoil Class)

‌



Success in iQFOiL, a fast-paced and exciting version of windsurfing, reflects the British Sailing Team (BST)’s position as the most successful Olympic sailing nation in history, with 64 medals, 31 of them gold.

Brown missed out on selection for Paris 2024 but has been in fine form in this cycle so far and is looking to continue that at the first World Championship in UK waters in an Olympic windsurfing discipline since 2009. The investment in upgrading facilities and hosting of world-class events reaffirms the BST commitment to Weymouth and Portland as the long-term home of British Sailing.

Brown’s own journey began at the other end of the UK, in the Scottish highlands, roots he holds to his core as he reflects on his achievements since.

‌



“I have pictures somewhere of me rigging up during the snow,” Brown said. “It shows my passion for windsurfing even then. I’m definitely losing the accent. I didn’t have a strong accent to begin with since Mum is from Yorkshire, but it’s hanging on for dear life these days.

“I got into the sport in the Scottish Highlands, sailing every Sunday and travelling around Scotland. Islay Watson (fellow windsurfer) is a couple of years younger than me, but her Mum and Grandma used to drive me down south quite often.

“Her family have been supporting me for a long time, and I’ve been racing with her for many years. Every summer was spent in Nethy Bridge for a busy summer holiday."

Sports.title: 'I can even be with my dog!' - Windsurfing star hopes home comforts help world title defence
Sports.content:
'I can even be with my dog!' - Windsurfing star hopes home comforts help world title defence

The Nottingham-born windsurfer grew up on the Dorset coast in Christchurch and is based near the Weymouth & Portland National Sailing Academy, which is hosting next week’s Musto iQFOiL World Championships

View 2 Images iQfoil Worlds Aarhus, Denmark 11 July, 2025 © Sailing Energy / iQfoil Class (Image: © Sailing Energy / iQfoil Class)

Emma Wilson hopes home comforts can propel her to a successful defence of her world title.

‌



The Nottingham-born windsurfer grew up on the Dorset coast in Christchurch and is based near the Weymouth & Portland National Sailing Academy, which is hosting next week’s Musto iQFOiL World Championships.

‌



Wilson completed her set at the event with gold in Aarhus last year, having won bronze and silver in 2023 and 2024 respectively, and the two-time Olympic bronze medallist is eager to show what she can do on home waters.

‌



“It’s definitely a bit different,” she said. “I haven’t had to travel around the world to compete, I can just get out of bed each morning and cycle down to the club, do my thing and go home. I can even be with my dog!

“I always feel the pressure, probably mainly on myself, but I’ve never had a big competition here at home. I’ve been competing in Weymouth since I was 12, it’s where you come to enter the British team, so I have experience racing here. It’s cool that we can show how good windsurfing is as a sport.

“The British squad is pushing hard, and all the British sailors are excited to show how cool Weymouth-Portland is. Hopefully, we can get more events in the UK off the back of the World Championships. In Weymouth-Portland, we get every condition possible. We have flat water in the harbour then waves into the bay – you don’t know what you’re going to get. People have been training here all summer and the level is super high, so I think it will be a big old battle.”

‌



Both the men’s and women’s reigning champions are British, with Andy Brown joining Wilson in entering the week with a title to defend.

Success in iQFOiL reflects the British Sailing Team’s position as the most successful Olympic sailing nation in history, with 64 medals, and the fast-paced, exhilarating discipline is set to thrill fans on the south coast ahead of its return to the Olympic programme in LA. Wilson, the daughter of two-time Olympian Penny Wilson, is relaxed ahead of her title defence and the pressure, as she sees it, is on the challengers looking to steal her crown.

View 2 Images Emma Wilson is a two-time Olympic medallist in windsurfing (Image: World Sailing)

‌



She said: “It’s super nice and pretty chill. Obviously, there’s maybe a bit more pressure on me, but I think I will enjoy it and make the most of the situation.

“What I achieved last year was amazing and no one can take that away from me. I’m really happy to have won at the World Championships but I also know that at this Championships, everyone will be gunning for the title. I don’t see the pressure being on me, I see everyone going for the title and giving me a good challenge, which is why we do sport.

“I’ll sail with a smile on my face. If someone told me when I was 12 that I would be in this position, I would say, ‘dude, that’s so cool! There’s quite a few people planning to watch. Normally I’m competing all over the world but my family and friends can watch this year, which is great.”

Sports.title: 8 players poised to miss Ipswich vs Liverpool as Reds see treble boost for Premier League clash
Sports.content:
8 players poised to miss Ipswich vs Liverpool as Reds see treble boost for Premier League clash

Liverpool travel to Ipswich Town on Friday evening in the Premier League, but both sides will be without a number of key players for the encounter at Portman Road

View Image Andoni Iraola will be without a number of first-team players against Ipswich (Image: Liverpool FC, Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Up to eight players combined could miss Ipswich Town's Premier League clash with Liverpool on Friday evening. The Reds will look to secure their first win of the season when they travel to Portman Road at 8pm.

‌



Liverpool were held to a 2-2 draw by Newcastle United at St James' Park in their opener last month, before running out against Nottingham Forest at Anfield to the same scoreline. As a result, Andoni Iraola's men sit 13th in the Premier League table, yet to really get going in the English top flight.

‌



Ipswich, meanwhile, sit a place higher following a 2-1 win over Sunderland AFC in their own opening match of 2026/27. They will look to quickly forget last weekend's 5-2 rout from Manchester United, however, and build momentum as they look to survive their first season back among the elite.

‌



That's no straightforward task, however, given the considerable gulf in quality between the Tractor Boys and the Reds, not to mention the injury concerns heading into the match. Ipswich will be without at least three first-team regulars for the game, with Gary O'Neill confirming that Jaden Philogene , Jack Taylor and Azor Matusiwa will all miss out.

Philogene is recovering from an ankle problem, and is anticipated to be sidelined for at least another week. The timescale for Taylor and Matusiwa is identical, as they continue their comebacks from respective knee and thigh injuries.

While Florentino Luis and Emersonn were both originally doubts for the fixture, O'Neill has since confirmed that both are in contention for selection. Ipswich aren't the only team carrying injuries heading into this weekend's clash, however.

‌



Iraola appears to be without at least five players when the 8pm kick-off arrives, with several long-term absences to contend with. Hugo Ekitike remains in rehabilitation for an Achilles tendon rupture suffered in the Champions League earlier this year, and isn't anticipated to be back until the end of the year.

Joe Gomez also remains sidelined from first-team action due to a muscular injury, leaving Liverpool looking somewhat thin on the ground when it comes to centre-back cover. Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
