The commission also dismissed claims that voter registration data could be manipulated or shared with external parties, insisting that the Register of Voters remained under its exclusive custody.

"Voter registration involves several stages, including in-person registration, verification of identity, collection of biometric and biographical data, transmission to a central database and automated biometric deduplication," IEBC added.

Flagged records are subjected to data cleaning, validation and adjudication before valid records are incorporated into the register.

The register will subsequently undergo a 30-day biometric verification exercise, followed by an independent audit before it is finalised and certified for use in an election.

IEBC said allegations of bribery, predetermined tender awards and voter suppression were false and potentially harmful to public confidence in the electoral process.

World.title: Ruto hands Sh2.6bn to Mau Forest evictees
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto also announced the lifting pf the caveat that had been placed on land bordering the Mau Forest. [PCS]

President William Ruto has announced the payment of Sh2.6 billion to 13,000 families evicted from the Mau Forest in Narok six years ago, marking what he described as the closure of a long chapter.

Each beneficiary received Sh200,000 through M-Pesa to help them resettle and rebuild their lives away from the water tower.

Speaking at Sogoo in Narok South Constituency on Wednesday, during the final day of his two-day tour of Narok County, Ruto said the Government had taken steps to address the longstanding Mau Forest resettlement problem.

He noted that in 2023, the Government gave Sh300,000 each to 2,000 families living in tents in the Mau Forest to enable them to leave the water tower and purchase land elsewhere.

“We are today officially closing the long and painful chapter of people who were removed from the Mau Forest, which the County Government of Narok will now manage,” Ruto said.

The President criticised politicians who, he said, had continued to politicise the Mau Forest issue without providing lasting solutions.

“Many politicians have talked of the Mau question, but I talked of the Mau answer. This is why we are here today closing this chapter,” he said.

Ruto also announced that the Government had purchased 5,800 acres of land to settle families who have been living as squatters on property previously owned by the family of former Provincial Commissioner Isaiah Cheluget.

“We are processing title deeds of the people living on the land after buying the Cheluget farm,” he said.

Construction of Johanna Ng'eno University

The President also announced the allocation of Sh1.2 billion for the construction of Johanna Ng’eno University in Emurua Dikirr Constituency.

Speaking during the laying of the foundation stone, Ruto said the institution would fulfil a pledge to residents while expanding access to higher education for students from across the country.

“You told me, as residents of Emurua Dikirr, that you want a university. Today, I have brought KSh1.2 billion to construct the university that will be named after our brother Johana Ng'eno,” he said.

He said the university would create employment opportunities and attract new investments to the region.

At the same time, Ruto maintained that his administration had fulfilled at least 80 per cent of the pledges contained in its 2022 campaign manifesto.

“Kenyans will elect leaders based on their development record. Sloganeering will not make Kenyans vote for them. They have a long way to go,” he said.

The President further launched the construction of the 18-kilometre Mogondo-Cheramgoi-Mogor-Soit road in Emurua Dikirr, saying the project would improve connectivity and unlock economic opportunities in the region.

“This new road will strengthen connectivity and unlock greater economic opportunities in the region,” Ruto said.

World.title: Gachagua to Duale: You don't own pastoralists
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua and delegates from Isiolo and Marsabit at Wamunyoro, Nyeri County on August 25, 2026. [Ali Abdi, Standard]

Democracy for Citizen Party (DCP) Leader Rigathi Gachagua has accused Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale of allegedly doing nothing for pastoralist communities in the country.

Mr Gachagua said Duale, while being the only CS from northern Kenya and claiming to be the spokesperson of the group, had instead been a liability to pastoralists.

“You, the Borana who are here, along with the Turkana and Somali, are all complaining like other Kenyans. You suffer from runaway insecurity and widespread underdevelopment. We must join hands to vote out this rogue government (in next year's general election),” the former Deputy President told a delegation of grassroots leaders and residents from Isiolo and Marsabit who paid him a courtesy call at his Wamunyoro rural home in Nyeri.

“Duale thinks that the pastoralists are his property, his children or servants. What has he done for the people of Isiolo and Marsabit? (He has) only rhetoric, shouting pastoralists everywhere, every day,” he said.

Gachagua questioned how Duale would be able to marshal ‘millions’ of votes for President Ruto in the 2027 General Elections while he (Duale) could only raise 7,000 votes for the UDA presidential candidate in the 2022 polls in his Garissa Township Constituency backyard.

Despite his little contribution to the Kenya Kwanza administration's victory, Gachagua said Duale was appointed as the only CS from northern Kenya but had ended up doing nothing for the region and pastoralist communities.

“He only gave him (Ruto) 7,000 votes in Garissa Township. It's Central Kenya that propelled this government,” Gachagua told the gathering.

“Duale was appointed CS and he has nothing to show apart from empty words, going round shouting (the name of) pastoralists, and you (the pastoralists) are suffering. If you love them, then why are their livestock stolen every day?” He asked the CS.

“These pastoralists are killed every day and their cows and goats stolen. What have you done for them and you are in the government?” Gachagua posed.

The Opposition leader claimed that the government was ill-prepared for the heavily forecasted El Niño rainfall, pointing out that those living in flood-prone areas like the Tana Delta and Garissa are exposed to danger.

“Now, going into El Niño, what plan has been put in place to save people from death as a result of floods and how livestock will survive?” he asked the State.

During the event, Gachagua revealed that Yusuf Huka Jillo from Isiolo would represent Upper Eastern at the DCP secretariat and serve as a member of the National Executive Committee (NEC) in an acting capacity.

Gachagua said the mountain was now complete, with Isiolo and Marsabit forming Mt Kenya North.

The locals alleged that the Health CS was interfering in Isiolo County politics, with elder Hussein Jama claiming that Duale and the Office of the DCI were shielding a section of leaders accused of corruption and criminal activities.

Speakers claimed that there was massive corruption at the local lands registry office, while Mr Jillo faulted the State for the slow pace of registration of community land in Isiolo.

Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Hesham Maged comedy play ‘Khayal Mareed’ to run in New Capital
World.content:
The hit theatrical comedy “Khayal Mareed” (Sick Imagination) is set to stage a limited run at the Drama Theater inside the New Administrative Capital’s Arts and Culture City, featuring performances on September 24–25 and October 1–2.

The upcoming run follows a sold-out summer season, marking a key cultural expansion for the New Capital as it transforms from an administrative hub into a regional destination for live arts and entertainment.

Starring Hesham Maged, “Khayal Mareed” follows Dr. Taha, an eccentric psychiatrist whose unconventional methods with patients trigger a series of comedic misunderstandings. The production features a prominent ensemble cast, including Mohamed Abdel-Rahman, Hanady Mehanna, Ahmed El-Rafei, Dina Diab, Nagham Saleh, Mohsen Mansour, Waleed Abdel-Ghani, Reham Ezzat, and Nora Soliman.

Written and directed by Mohamed Hamdy, the play is produced by Yara Hassan’s Fikr Production Company.

World.title: UAE President pardons Abdul Rahman Youssef Al-Qaradawi following cybercrime conviction
World.content:
UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan has granted a presidential pardon to convict Abdul Rahman Youssef Al-Qaradawi, state news agency WAM reported on Friday.

The executive clemency follows an August 27 ruling by the Cybercrime Circuit of the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal, which sentenced the 53-year-old to 10 years in prison and imposed a fine of AED 200,000 ($54,450) upon conviction of charges brought against him. Authorities confirmed that all necessary legal procedures have been initiated to carry out the pardon.

Al-Qaradawi was extradited to the UAE in January 2025 after Lebanon’s caretaker Cabinet authorized his deportation. Lebanese authorities originally detained him on December 29, 2024, at the Masnaa border crossing upon his entry from Syria, following the overthrow of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.

At the time of his arrest, Lebanese Prosecutor General Judge Jamal Al-Hajjar stated that Al-Qaradawi—traveling on a Turkish passport—was detained pursuant to an Arab Interior Ministers Council notice issued via Interpol. The red notice stemmed from an in absentia verdict issued by Egyptian judicial authorities on charges related to broadcasting false news and inciting violence and terrorism.

World.title: InstaPay users warned of new phishing scam targeting bank accounts
World.content:
Cybersecurity expert Mostafa Rahim has issued a stern warning over rising AI-powered phishing scams targeting users of financial applications, particularly Egypt’s digital payment platform InstaPay, alongside major banking channels.

Scammers are leveraging advanced artificial intelligence to craft convincing replicas of official bank websites and interfaces, Rahim explained during a televised interview on Sabah El-Balad. Fraudsters distribute malicious links via messaging platforms, luring victims into entering sensitive credentials on fake pages designed to mirror legitimate portals.

The schemes heavily target elderly citizens and individuals with limited digital literacy, peaking ahead of monthly pension distributions. Attackers exploit these timing windows by sending fraudulent messages promising pension increases or special government relief initiatives in exchange for personal information.

To mitigate exposure, Rahim urged consumers to follow core digital safety practices:

Never Share OTPs: One-Time Passwords must remain confidential; financial institutions and telecom providers will never request OTPs via phone calls or SMS.

Verify Web Addresses: Cross-check suspicious URLs using free threat-detection tools like Google Safe Browsing or VirusTotal before clicking.

Avoid Unsolicited Media: Refrain from opening links or downloading images sent from unrecognized numbers.

Confirm Directly: Validate any promotional offer or account inquiry through official bank hotlines or verified customer service channels.

World.title: Nile River is matter of national security, Egypt retains right to defend its waters: Sisi
World.content:
Egypt views the Nile River as a non-negotiable component of its national security, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reiterated during high-level discussions in Cairo with Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Antonio Tajani.

According to the presidential spokesperson, Sisi underlined Cairo’s legitimate right to safeguard its water, food, and developmental security.

He firmly rejected any unilateral measures along the Nile basin, calling for strict compliance with international law—specifically the core doctrine prohibiting harm to downstream nations.

Beyond the Nile issue, the meeting covered shifting dynamics across the Horn of Africa.

Both officials agreed to step up bilateral coordination to bolster regional stability, emphasizing full respect for the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of all states in the region.

Turning to maritime security, Sisi stressed that preserving freedom of navigation through international waterways remains vital, highlighting the Red Sea’s strategic role in Egyptian national defense.

The Egyptian President affirmed that securing the Red Sea falls strictly under the jurisdiction of its coastal states, warning against actions that threaten its stability or risk militarizing and internationalizing the key waterway.

World.title: Upgraded Su-57 stealth fighter debuts at Egypt International Airshow with new weaponry
World.content:
Russia’s defense sector is preparing a major technology showcase for the Egypt International Airshow 2026, where state giant Rostec will premiere its export-grade Su-57E fifth-generation stealth fighter equipped with a previously unseen armaments package, TASS reported.

The upcoming event, scheduled for September 8–10 in El Alamein, will serve as the launchpad for the updated Su-57E variant.

Beyond static displays of its newly integrated weapons systems—which have yet to be publicly exhibited inside or outside Russia—the aircraft is slated to perform live aerial demonstrations during the expo.

In tandem with the fighter jet’s debut, Rostec subsidiary High Precision Systems will stage the first foreign demonstration of the “Bison” anti-drone system.

Engineered to intercept and neutralize low-altitude aerial threats and unmanned vehicles, the system will be featured as a core component of Moscow’s defensive systems export portfolio.

World.title: Egypt and China strengthen bilateral security and diplomatic ties
World.content:
Egypt and China issued a comprehensive joint statement reaffirming their shared commitment to stability in the Middle East, calling for a permanent ceasefire in the Gaza Strip, and urging the unhindered flow of humanitarian aid into the besieged enclave.

In the joint declaration, both nations emphasized the critical need to solidify a lasting ceasefire in Gaza while demanding the immediate removal of restrictions hindering aid delivery.

Cairo and Beijing also advocated for the swift return of the Palestinian Authority to govern the Gaza Strip as a vital step toward restoring administrative unity and political stability.

Expressing severe concern over escalating regional tensions, both governments condemned the dangerous military escalation by Israeli forces across the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

They highlighted deep alarm over the rising pace of settler violence, systemic land confiscation, and expanding settlement construction, warning that such actions actively undermine peace prospects.

Egypt and China underscored the paramount importance of safeguarding Palestine’s territorial integrity.

Extending their diplomatic posture to North Africa, both powers called for strict respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, territorial unity, and national institutions, firmly rejecting any external interference in internal Sudanese affairs.

World.title: Will September see any heatwaves?
World.content:
Following the intense heatwaves of August, attention has shifted to the weather outlook for September, with many wondering whether further extreme heat is on the horizon.

According to the Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA), weather conditions remain stable across the country.

Daytime temperatures in Cairo are averaging around 35C, though active winds are bringing cooler evening breezes and offering noticeable relief at night.

Meteorologists do not anticipate a return to August’s extreme temperatures. However, high humidity levels could make temperatures feel roughly two degrees warmer than actual recordings.

Dense morning fog remains the primary weather factor to watch throughout September.

Fog formation is expected along agricultural routes, highways, and areas near bodies of water, which may significantly reduce horizontal visibility.

The EMA has urged drivers to exercise caution on the roads.

World.title: Saudi Arabia’s security remains a red line for Egypt: Sisi
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi received a phone call today from Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz al-Saud, according to an official statement by the Spokesperson for the Egyptian Presidency, Mohamed al-Shennawy.

Sisi extended his heartfelt congratulations to the Saudi Crown Prince ahead of the upcoming Saudi National Day.

Egypt’s President wished Saudi Arabia continued stability, prosperity, and development under the leadership of King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

Expressing his gratitude for the fraternal gesture, the Crown Prince reaffirmed the deeply rooted, historic ties uniting the two nations.

According to al-Shennawy, the discussion covered the full scope of bilateral relations.

President Sisi emphasized the importance of advancing cooperation across various fields to fulfill mutual interests, drive sustainable development, and support regional security.

The Egyptian President also underlined the shared destiny of Egypt and Saudi Arabia, reiterating that the security of Saudi Arabia and the wider Arab region remains an integral pillar of Egyptian national security.

He stressed that joint action is critical to overcoming the current regional challenges.

Reciprocating the sentiment, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman praised the growing trajectory of Saudi-Egyptian relations and the close coordination aimed at fostering peace and stability across the Middle East. He highlighted the need to intensify high-level political consultation and reciprocal visits across multiple domains.

The call also addressed pressing regional and international issues. Both leaders stressed the urgent need to de-escalate ongoing regional tensions to safeguard peace and mitigate risks to global energy security, supply chains, and international trade routes.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: A New Survey Warns Legislators: Liberians Overwhelmingly Want a War Crimes Court and They Won’t Vote for Lawmakers Who Oppose It
World.content:
Summary:

In a new FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey nine in every 10 of 1,150 respondents across 11 counties said they want the government to establish a War and Economic Crimes Court.

In a warning to lawmakers, nine in every 10 said they won’t vote for lawmakers who don’t support a bill to establish the court.

With many lawmakers saying they needed time to consult constituents before voting on the bill, just one county reported any meaningful consultation with lawmakers. In most counties survey respondents said there had been none.

By Eric Opa Doue , chief county correspondent with New Narratives

BOLA, Bomi County– Kumba Thomas returns home from a long day at her farm. Around her, life in the community continues at its ordinary pace, but ghosts follow Thomas, weighing down every step of her day.

Thomas says she was a new mother when fighting reached Bola. She can’t remember which faction. She hid in the bush with her family, but rebels captured her.

“They put a gun to my head and threatened to kill me, but I had my baby in my arms,” she says. They finally let her go. Thomas walked all the way to Monrovia. “I fled through the bush with no shoes and no food, only praying my daughter and I would survive.”

Later, she learned that both her parents had been killed. More than two decades later, no one has been held responsible for what happened to her family. But Thomas has not stopped hoping that justice will come.

“The war took away my childhood and left wounds that I still carry in my heart,” Thomas said. “I saw families separated, homes destroyed, and people running for their lives. Some of us still wake up remembering the sounds of gunfire and the faces of people we never saw again. That is why I want to see a war crimes court.”

Thomas was one of 1,150 people surveyed by eight FrontPage Africa/New Narratives reporters across 11 of Liberia’s 15 counties in August — the first publicly released data by any organization gauging public opinion on the proposed court. The survey was not conducted under scientific standards and is intended simply to contribute to a national conversation that has yet to see any concrete evidence of where public opinion lies. (Data can be viewed at this link .)

But the results strongly suggest the public is demanding lawmakers enact a court. Of the 1,150 people surveyed, 91 percent said they wanted to see a court. And, in a stark warning for legislators who are still debating whether to have an internationally recognized court to try those accused of war and economic crimes, nearly as many — 89 percent — said they would not vote again for lawmakers who fail to support the bill.

Accountability a long time coming

Lawmakers have only one choice according to Nanu Kai, 47, of River Cess County. She was a child when the war came to Monrovia where she was living. She and her family walked through the bush to River Cess witnessing horrors that haunt her to this day.

“I want my lawmakers [ Rep. Steve Tequah and Sen. Wellington Geevon Smith] to understand that their decisions have consequences,” Kai said. “If they refuse to support the war crimes court bill and refuse to listen to victims, then they should not expect victims and their families to forget when elections come. We have been silent for too long. If our leaders will not use their positions to speak for justice, then the people will use their votes to speak for themselves.”

The demand for accountability traces back to Liberia’s two civil wars, fought between 1989 and 2003. The first began in December 1989, when Charles Taylor’s National Patriotic Front of Liberia rose up against President Samuel Doe, and then splintered the country among rival factions. A 1996 peace deal collapsed within three years, and fighting resumed as rebel groups — including Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy and the Movement for Democracy in Liberia — turned on the government of Charles Taylor who had been elected president in 1997.

The wars ended with the Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement in 2003 and Taylor’s exile. But by then conflict had left the country on its knees. By the United Nations’ estimate, more than 250,000 people were killed and hundreds of thousands more displaced or driven from the country, in a conflict marked by massacres, sexual violence, torture and the forced recruitment of children. Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, formed after the war to investigate abuses committed between 1979 and 2003, delivered its final report in 2009. It called for criminal accountability, reparations for victims, institutional reform and community reconciliation, and a special court to try those held most responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Most of those recommendations were never acted on.

An overwhelming number of respondents in Gbarnga, Bong County said they would not vote for a lawmaker who did not back the court. Credit: Nukanah Kollie

The movement was revived in 2024 when incoming President Joseph Boakai pledged to establish a court. That, and the convictions of six Liberians accused of atrocities by courts in Europe and the United States, has helped boost support among a public that had originally feared a court might reignite conflict.

Support for the court was effectively unanimous in Grand Bassa and Bomi counties. River Cess follow closely at 99 percent and Bong at 95 percent. Support was lowest — though still decisive — in Grand Gedeh, at 86 percent, Lofa, at 79 percent, and Margibi, at 74 percent.

Support for a War and Economic Crimes Court was high across all 11 counties, from 74% in Margibi to 100% in Grand Bassa and Bomi. Source: New Narratives / FrontPage Africa.

The results came as no surprise to Peterson Sonyah, of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, the umbrella body for survivor’s groups in the country.

“The survey is very clear evidence that Liberians need a war and economic crimes court,” said Sonyah, in an interview. “It is also a wakeup call for our legislators to listen and act fast, because our people, we all want justice.”

“Accountability has remained an undebated subject for more than two decades,” said Adama Dempster, long time war crimes court advocate and secretary general of the National Civil Society Platform of Liberia. “The fact that people, even in rural communities, are still saying that the issue of war crimes and some sort of justice should be considered tells you that, no matter the time or duration, justice will serve as a deterrent.”

Survey issues a clear warning to legislators

Survey respondents were also clear who they will hold to account if a court is not held. Nine in every ten correspondents told survey takers that they would not vote for their lawmaker in the next elections if he or she did not vote for the court.

People at Airfield Junction, Harper City, Maryland county overwhelmingly support the court. Credit: Moses Geply.

Marcus Flomo, a welder and father of three who lives in District 1, Margibi County, said he wants justice for a rebel attack on his town at 4 a.m in the early part of the war. His uncle was killed in front of him. Now, he said, he does not trust lawmakers to follow through on promises of accountability.

“I voting, they stealing the money,” said Mr. Flomo in Liberian English. “We are in the sun, in the rain for them, they doing their own thing. Then why I voting for [Rep.] Opee Cooper and [Senator] Nathaniel McGill for? Let them agree, let the people bring the war crimes court. When they do not bring it, me I will not vote for anybody this coming 2029.”

“Our leader keep promising the court will come, election after election, but nothing can change,” said Eliza Gueh, in Grand Bassa, in her 60s. “Some of the same people who committed all those crimes are the ones sitting in government today. This is why they are joking.”

Gueh said she would not support her legislators — Rep. Matthew Joe and Sen. Nyunblee Kangar Lawrence — in the 2029 elections.

Sentiment tracked support for the court, with the strongest numbers in River Cess, where 98 percent said they would withhold their vote, followed by Bong at 97 percent, Grand Gedeh at 95 percent and Nimba at 93 percent. Even in counties with softer numbers, opposition to the bill carried a political cost: 70 percent of respondents in Lofa and 73 percent in Margibi said they would not vote for a lawmaker who blocked it.

Consultations are not happening

The final question of the three in the survey also carried a warning for legislators. They did not pass the bill to establish the court before their legislative break claiming they needed to consult constituents. But just a handful of the 1150 respondents – 4 percent – said they were unaware of any consultations.

Only in Maryland, Grand Gedeh and Margibi were there any people saying that they had been consulted.

“As far as we know, as far as stakeholders know, as far as our partners know, there has not been one consultation anywhere by any member of the Legislature that we know of,” said Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court. “Maybe they may have had it on a one-to-one basis, but formally we are not informed.”

Representative Steve Tequah, who represents River Cess County District No. 2, said he supports the court and lawmakers owe their constituents a voice in the process.

“We serve our people; they elected us to represent them,” he said. “We have been having this conversation and educating our people on the importance of the War and Economic Crimes Court, and the support is overwhelming.”

But Tequah acknowledged he had not held formal meetings.

“I have not really organized a town hall meeting where chiefs and communities gather to discuss this issue,” he said. “If I call a town hall meeting, I have to pay people’s way, feed them and provide drinks. Imagine calling three or four town hall meetings at different locations. Trust me, my brother, I don’t have that funding.”

“Since we don’t have the funding for those consultations, as I go out in the communities, making donations and doing projects, I use those opportunities to provide information to our people and talk about the importance of the War and Economic Crimes Court. So, this is how they get information.”

The one outlier was Lofa County where respondents said Senator Joseph Jallah has been heavily engaging the people about the court on radio and in meetings across the country. One third of respondents there said they had been consulted.

Senator Jallah has a special interest in the process. He joined Grand Bassa County Senator Nyonblee Karnga introduced bills for the courts to be considered by the legislature. They have been widely condemned by court advocates because of their insistence on excluding international actors from the court.

“Jallah knows better. He knows what he’s doing. He’s a lawyer. He comes from a progressive school of thought. He knows what he’s doing, and he’s doing it deliberately,” said John Stewart, court advocate and former TRC commissioner. “He should be ashamed because a lot of atrocities were committed there. He’s abandoning the concerns of his people to entrust it to a corrupt body.”

Lawmakers face mounting pressure to pass bill establishing the court by December

The survey will be one more factor weighing on the country’s lawmakers as they debate six competing bills submitted to them. Committees in the House and Senate are tasked with merging them into a single bill for passage. The Legislature is expected to hold public hearings once that process is complete.

The international community has been clear that Liberia’s best chance for securing international support is to have the bill passed before President Joseph Boakai takes his seat as the president of the UN Security Council’s December meeting. Better yet would have been for it to be passed before the UN General Assembly begins this month. War Crimes Court Office chief Barbu has urged the president to call legislators back early for a special session for this purpose.

No lawmakers have spoken publicly on the debates but stakeholders who have spoken with them say there is stiff opposition – especially from those who may be facing indictments for war crimes or economic crimes or in the national anti-corruption court that is to be set up first – or are closely allied with those who might.

There is a strong faction, including Jallah, insisting that the courts be set up under Liberia’s constitution which prohibits foreign lawyers from practicing and says the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal. They may be hoping that a call to exclude non-Liberians from the court will find a sympathetic ear among the public.

But court proponents say that is just a fig leaf to disguise an effort to sabotage the court. Opponents know they have lost the battle to convince Liberians to “let bygones be bygones” and so are now resorting to pitching a model that they know the international community will not support.

Every other country from Rwanda, to Gambia, to Sierra Leone, have established a “special court” in a legal bubble outside the country’s constitution that would allow the experts and laws required to prosecute crimes of this magnitude in a way that would be trusted.

“The appeals chamber should be within the court itself,” Hassan Bility, director of the Global Justice and Research Project, said the court’s authority would rest on international law that predates the conflict. “In this way, there will be credibility lent to the court and to its work. We do not want a situation where politics will influence the outcome of both investigations and prosecutions.”

International involvement, he said, is essential if Liberia hopes to build a court capable of investigating war crimes to internationally accepted standards. International diplomats and United Nations officials have been very clear that the international community will not back a court that is not separate from Liberia’s judicial system.

Dempster said the survey should underscore the need for speed. “The speedy establishment of the court is what is needed right now,” he said. “The unnecessary delays that have caused us to reach this far should not have happened. What we need to do now is accelerate the efforts that will lead to establishing a court.”

“What we can do now is continue the engagement and advocacy, talk to our citizens and district leaders, and make sure we have this court,” said Sonyah. “It cannot be one person; through collaborative effort, we can see this court established.”

Augusta Lafaly , Nukanah Kollie, Jerome Saye , King Brown , Gloria Wleh , Joseph Titus Yekreyan , Anthony Stephens and Moses Geply contributed reporting. This story was a collaboration with New Narratives . Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: A Justice Ministry Reset:Cleaner Prosecutions, or More Politically Fraught Ones?
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has replaced his Minister of Justice and Attorney General, along with his Solicitor General, hours after former President George Weah returned to Liberia to a large reception — one at which supporters awaiting him at Rehab Junction reportedly booed the President as his convoy passed.

Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh has been replaced as Minister of Justice by Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo. Solicitor General Augustine Fayiah has been replaced by Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah Sr. The Executive Mansion said Tweh and Fayiah would be reassigned elsewhere in government, and did not cite the Weah homecoming, the Rehab Junction gathering, or the reported booing as reasons for the changes.

The timing has nonetheless fueled speculation that the dismissals may trace to a disagreement over how the area should have been handled — whether it should have been cleared of Weah supporters before the former president’s arrival, or kept clear until President Boakai, who also lives in the Rehab area, had passed through. There has been no official confirmation that such a disagreement occurred.

What happened at Rehab Junction

The Liberia Airport Authority had announced special security measures ahead of Weah’s arrival, anticipating large crowds. Supporters gathered at Rehab Junction to await him, and reports say President Boakai was booed twice as his convoy passed through. The following morning, government authorities demolished stalls at the junction, with a large contingent of armed police visible in the area. The government has not said publicly whether that operation was connected to the previous day’s gathering.

The distinction matters: the stall owners are not necessarily the same people who allegedly booed the President, and no official account has identified who did. If the demolition was a previously scheduled operation — tied to traffic, sanitation, public health, commercial regulation, or urban planning — the government has yet to say so. If it was ordered in response to Wednesday’s gathering, questions remain about its legal basis and whether owners received prior notice. The developments have also left open whether future Weah-linked gatherings will be permitted at the junction; no such policy has been announced.

The new Justice Minister: a familiar hand in government litigation

Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo returns to the Justice Ministry with a track record at the top level of state litigation. She served as Solicitor General under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, appointed in 2014, and represented the Government of Liberia before the Supreme Court in a number of cases, including Thirteen Grand Gedians v. Republic of Liberia, Vrex Remodeling Inc. v. Liberia Petroleum Refining Company, and Selena Mappy Polson, Superintendent of Bong County v. The Government of the Republic of Liberia.

She is also the official who previously explained the government’s decision to enter a nolle prosequi — a formal discontinuance of a criminal case — against the Liberia Bank for Development and Investment, in the matter arising from allegations involving former Roberts International Airport Managing Director Ellen Corkrum. Lamin-Blamo said at the time that the case was dropped without prejudice, after LBDI agreed to cooperate with the government as a witness. Her return puts a former Solicitor General, well versed in the machinery of state prosecution, at the head of the ministry that oversees it.

The new Solicitor General: an opposition defender now representing the state

Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah Sr. arrives from private practice, where he is Managing Partner of Heritage Partners & Associates and has practiced law for more than 13 years. He also teaches Evidence and Environmental Law at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law, and has represented clients in civil, commercial and criminal matters.

Notably, Sillah was part of the defense team for opposition politician Alexander Cummings in the criminal proceedings tied to the Collaborating Political Parties’ framework document — a case Cummings’ lawyers called a “witch hunt” and in which they fought prosecutors’ efforts to compel Cummings to hand over evidence against himself. Sillah now becomes the government’s principal lawyer for prosecutions handled through the Solicitor General’s office — a former defense counsel for a sitting opposition figure now directing the state’s own prosecutorial machinery.

What the new team inherits

Lamin-Blamo and Sillah step into a ministry already carrying some of the most politically charged cases in Liberia in years.

A Joint National Security Investigative Task Force — drawing on the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, Liberia National Police, National Security Agency, Executive Protection Service, Financial Intelligence Agency, Liberia Immigration Service, Customs and other bodies — is investigating major cocaine seizures reportedly worth roughly US$19.2 million and US$317.6 million. Tweh had been one of the government’s leading public voices on that investigation before his removal.

The government has also charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor in an alleged transnational narcotics-trafficking case; she was charged on August 19, and the allegations remain before the courts. The new Justice Ministry leadership inherits the prosecution of both that case and the broader narcotics investigation.

Police Inspector General Gregory O.W. Coleman remains involved in that investigation as well. Coleman and Tweh had jointly rejected allegations in July linking President Boakai’s son, Joe Boakai Jr., to the cocaine seizures, with officials saying investigators found no evidence tying him to either shipment. Even so, Coleman has faced calls to recuse himself — the Liberian People’s Party has demanded his recusal and an independent inquiry, and other critics have questioned whether he should remain in the investigation while heading the national police. These calls do not amount to a finding of wrongdoing against Coleman; the concern is whether his continued role affects, or appears to affect, the independence of an inquiry touching people and institutions connected to the police.

Weah’s return, and an opposition on the offensive

Weah’s homecoming on Wednesday drew heightened security and large crowds along his route and at his Rehab residence. Addressing supporters there, he accused the Boakai administration of interfering with justice and dismissed the prosecution of Howard-Taylor as bogus. His remarks add to a chorus of opposition figures questioning the government’s handling of criminal cases; Cummings, for his part, visited Howard-Taylor and called for a prosecution that is swift, transparent and non-selective. The Boakai administration maintains that its investigations and prosecutions rest on evidence, not politics.

What remains unanswered

The government has not publicly linked the Justice Ministry changes to the events surrounding Weah’s return, nor explained the Thursday demolition at Rehab Junction. Several questions remain open: Was there an order to clear the area before Weah’s arrival, and if so, from which agency? Did Justice Ministry officials disagree over how to handle the gathering, and were Tweh or Fayiah involved in that decision? When was the demolition authorized, and was it planned independently of Weah’s arrival? Were stall owners given notice? And was Thursday’s police deployment tied to the demolition, the previous day’s gathering, or a separate operation entirely?

What is established is the sequence of events: Weah returned on Wednesday; supporters gathered at Rehab Junction; President Boakai was reportedly booed as his convoy passed; the Justice Minister and Solicitor General were replaced; and stalls at the junction were demolished the following morning under heavy police presence. The government has not connected these events publicly, but their proximity is difficult to ignore.

The stakes for Liberia’s justice system

The new leadership takes charge of an institution now at the center of the country’s corruption and narcotics prosecutions, at a moment when the credibility of those cases is already under public strain. Lamin-Blamo’s background in state litigation and Sillah’s experience defending an opposition figure against the state give the ministry a notably different professional character than the team it replaces. Whether that translates into a different approach to the Howard-Taylor case, the broader narcotics investigation, or the handling of politically sensitive prosecutions more generally will become clearer only as those cases move forward — and as the government addresses, or continues to leave unaddressed, the questions still hanging over Rehab Junction.

World.title: Flight Captain Moses K. “Johnny”Weefur: A Life of Service, Courage, Mentorship and Devotion to Liberia
World.content:
The passing of Flight Captain Moses K. “Johnny” Weefur has left us with a profound sense of loss. For those privileged to know him closely, his departure is not simply the loss of an accomplished Liberian aviator and public servant. It is the loss of a brother, mentor, teacher, patriot, devoted family man, trusted friend, and a remarkable human being whose quiet influence enriched countless lives.

Johnny belonged to a generation of Liberians whose lives were shaped by service, discipline, adversity, and an abiding belief in their country. His professional journey was deeply intertwined with the development of civil aviation in Liberia. Over many years, he brought to that sector not only the technical knowledge and discipline of a professional aviator, but also a commitment to institution-building, aviation safety, professional standards, and the training and encouragement of younger Liberians.

His public service eventually placed him among the senior leadership of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA). He became Deputy Director General of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority, and Deputy Director General for Technical Affairs. His responsibilities placed him at the canter of Liberia’s continuing efforts to strengthen aviation safety, regulatory oversight, technical competence, and compliance with international civil aviation standards.

Captain Weefur’s contribution extended beyond administration. He believed deeply in preparing another generation of Liberians for aviation careers. When addressing young people interested in the field, he emphasized that aviation offered opportunities far beyond the cockpit and encouraged students to recognize the many technical and professional disciplines that sustain a modern aviation industry. It was characteristic of Johnny: knowledge acquired over a lifetime was something to be shared, not guarded.

In the later chapter of his public service, he continued contributing his formidable experience to aviation safety and accident investigation. As recently as June 2024, he became Commissioner of the Liberia’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB). He participated in the Basic Accident Investigation Training Course conducted in cooperation with the Banjul Accord Group Accident Investigation Agency. His presence in such a position reflected the confidence placed in his experience and judgment and demonstrated the continuity of a life devoted to aviation and public service.But official titles tell only a small part of Johnny Weefur’s story.

We admired Johnny not merely because he flew aircraft or occupied positions of responsibility. We admired him because of the man behind the uniform.

Our relationships with him developed through different circumstances and across different periods of our lives, but we came to know the same essential qualities: discipline, loyalty, compassion, courage, discretion, perseverance, and an extraordinary willingness to stand beside people when circumstances became difficult.

Johnny brought to his work the discipline of the cockpit: assess the situation, remain calm, understand the instruments, protect those entrusted to you, and never surrender responsibility simply because conditions become difficult. Those principles also governed his friendships.

His classroom was rarely formal. It consisted of countless conversations, recollections of youth, professional experiences, lessons from hardship, and practical explanations of aviation. Through those conversations, he taught lessons no textbook could fully convey.

Johnny was measured and selective in his friendships, but extraordinarily loyal once he gave someone his confidence. During difficult professional moments, he did not disappear. He remained present, offered counsel, restored perspective, and reminded his friends that temporary humiliation or disappointment should never determine the course of an entire life.

The quintessential Johnny Weefur did not teach people to flee adversity; he taught them to master it with dignity.

Captain Weefur possessed a rare ability to correct without humiliating, to advise without patronizing, and to disagree without destroying friendship. Even when someone was mistaken, he could gently guide that person toward the truth while preserving his or her dignity.

That quality distinguished him both as a leader and as a human being.

He was disciplined in his personal habits and intensely devoted to his profession. Aviation was more than employment for Johnny; it was a vocation. The discipline, preparedness, responsibility and calm judgment demanded of a pilot became characteristics of his life.

He understood that aviation is ultimately about trust. Passengers entrust their lives to a crew. Governments entrust regulators with public safety. Younger professionals entrust mentors with their development. Friends entrust one another with vulnerabilities they reveal to few others.

His service to Liberia therefore cannot be measured solely by the aircraft he flew, the offices he occupied, or the aviation institutions he helped administer. It must also be measured by the professionals he encouraged, the colleagues he advised, the friends he sustained, and the younger Liberians whom he inspired to see a future for themselves in aviation.

For us, Flight Captain Moses K. “Johnny” Weefur will always represent something larger than professional accomplishment.

He represented service without ostentation, discipline without arrogance, friendship without calculation, and patriotism expressed through work.

Our deepest regret is that his final departure came so abruptly that those who loved him could not all stand beside him and return, in equal measure, the encouragement he had so generously given throughout his life. Yet perhaps Johnny would have preferred it that way.

He was, after all, always the captain—the steady presence during turbulence, the person expected to reassure others that the aircraft would pass safely through the storm. He possessed an extraordinary capacity to carry his own burdens quietly while helping others carry theirs.

The sacrifices he made for friends, colleagues, family and country were his way of giving something back for the blessings life had bestowed upon him.

And so, as painful as this farewell is, we choose gratitude alongside grief.

To his beloved wife, Agnes, and the children; to his brothers Richard and Cecil and the rest of the Weefur family; to his dear friend Joe, (President Joseph N. Boakai), whose friendship with Johnny reached back to their school days; to his classmates and fellow aviators; especially RTD Captain Prince Page, who mentored him into becoming one of the greatest pilots in the history of Liberia and his friend Jehu Richardson; to his colleagues in Liberia’s civil aviation community; and to the many people whose lives he touched, we extend our profound sympathy and solidarity.

We should certainly mourn Johnny, because love makes mourning inevitable. But even in our sorrow, we should give thanks to Almighty God for permitting such a man to dwell among us.

The most enduring memorial we can offer him is to emulate the virtues by which he lived: discipline, professional excellence, loyalty, compassion, perseverance, integrity, friendship, and devotion to country.

There was tremendous goodness in this man.

His earthly flight has ended, but his influence has not. It lives in Liberia’s aviation community. It lives in the institutions he served. It lives in the professionals he mentored. It lives in the family he loved. And it lives permanently in the hearts and memories of those fortunate enough to call him colleague, mentor, teacher, friend and brother.

In aviation, every flight has a point of departure and a final destination. Between them lies the journey—the storms weathered, the lives entrusted to one’s care, the destinations reached, and the people carried safely along the way.

And now, as our brother and captain makes his final flight, we bid him farewell with sorrow, gratitude and abiding respect.

Farewell, Captain. Farewell, our brother, our colleague and our friend. May your final flight be peaceful, and may Almighty God grant you eternal rest. Flight Captain Moses K. “Johnny” Weefur, we salute you.

World.title: Liberia: Police Demolish Rehab Market After CDC Supporters Boo President Boakai
World.content:
Monrovia – The administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is facing growing criticism over the demolition of market stalls at Rehab Junction in Paynesville, just a day after supporters of the opposition Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) gathered there and booed the President’s motorcade.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

The demolition on Thursday has fueled allegations that the government’s action was politically motivated, with petty traders and other affected businesses insisting they had nothing to do with the jeering of the President and should not be punished for the actions of opposition supporters.

Rehab Junction, located in the Rehab Community where President Boakai and former President George Weah reside, has increasingly become a politically charged area. The neighborhood is regarded as a presidential enclave, with the homes of the two political rivals located not far from each other.

On Wednesday, the junction became one of the major assembly points for CDC supporters traveling to Roberts International Airport to welcome former President Weah, who had returned to Liberia after several months abroad.

Large numbers of CDC supporters gathered around the market stalls, singing pro-Weah songs and chanting slogans critical of President Boakai.

As President Boakai later left his residence and his motorcade passed through the area, members of the crowd reportedly booed the President.

By Thursday, however, security personnel had moved into the area and demolished the market stalls. Vendors and motorcyclists were reportedly ordered to vacate the junction.

The timing of the action has prompted questions over whether the demolition was a routine enforcement exercise or an immediate response to the previous day’s political confrontation.

‘We Were Not Part of the Protest’

The affected petty traders are appealing directly to President Boakai to allow them to return to the area and continue their livelihoods.

The vendors told FrontPage Africa that they were not part of the crowd that booed the President and should not be made to suffer because of the actions of CDC supporters.

They said they were simply at their stalls conducting business and had no role in the political gathering.

“We are innocent. We were just going about our business,” one vendor said, describing the demolition as a devastating blow to traders who depend on daily sales to support their families, Terry Darwo, a money exchanger told FrontPageAfrica.

For Oretha Gunnun, chairlady of petty traders operating along the Rehab Junction corridor, said fruit sellers and other small-scale traders were unable to conduct business after police deployed officers to an area where vendors typically sell their goods.

Speaking in an interview with Frontpageafrica, Gunnun said traders arrived at their usual locations only to be turned away by police officers stationed at the junction.

She appealed to the President to reconsider the decision and distinguish between those involved in political activities and ordinary traders trying to make a living.

“We are appealing to President Boakai that he should consider us and allow us to come back to our normal business,” she said.

Gunnun said the restrictions were particularly difficult for traders dealing in perishable goods such as bananas, apples and watermelons, which can spoil quickly if not sold.

“If I don’t sell today, I will get a lot of losses,” she said, adding that many vendors rely on daily sales to support their families and pay school expenses for their children.

According to Gunnun, traders believe the measures may be linked to activities surrounding a recent presidential visit, during which crowds gathered along the roadway. She said ordinary vendors should not be penalized for events in which they played no part.

“We are all here doing our business,” Gunnun said. “We were not part of the people that were here yesterday.”

She described herself as a single mother who depends on fruit sales to support her daughter and other family members.

The vendors said the sudden loss of their stalls has left them without a source of income and are calling for an opportunity to return to the junction or be provided with an alternative location where they can legally conduct business.

An entrepreneur J.U. Dempster Hennings, said business has been slow and customers had stopped coming to buy this morning since police officers were deployed, creating fear among potential buyers and disrupting normal business activities.

“I have been doing business here for many years and I know the inflow of customers,” Dempster said. “Right now, with the presence of the police, it sends some kind of signal to our customers.”

Dempster said many traders and money exchangers operating in the community depend on daily sales and participate in local savings and credit schemes, commonly known as “susu,” under which members make daily, weekly, or monthly payments.

He said some business owners, including himself, had also taken bank loans to finance their operations.

“Most of the petty traders out there took money from banks,” he said. “Even my very self. I have to pay suppliers today.”

According to Dempster, the demolition of business structures and the removal of traders from their usual locations could immediately affect their ability to generate income and meet repayment obligations.

“With the police presence and the businesses being removed, it will affect their ability to pay their susu and other commitments,” he said, warning that prolonged disruptions could place financial strain on vendors, money exchangers and small business owners who depend on daily transactions.

Dempster said business owners had not been informed of the reasons behind the security operation and appealed for a return to what he described as a conducive business environment.

“We don’t know why the police are here,” he said. “We pray that tomorrow we’ll have a conducive atmosphere for our business.”

Questions Over Timing

Critics of the administration say the sequence of events raises concerns about whether the government’s response was disproportionate.

They argue that if the demolition was part of an existing plan to clear the junction, the government should explain why it occurred immediately after the President was booed at the location.

The controversy also comes against the backdrop of heightened political tensions between the ruling Unity Party and the CDC, particularly following Weah’s return and renewed political activity ahead of the 2029 elections.

For the vendors, however, the political contest is secondary to survival.

They say they should not become casualties of Liberia’s growing political rivalry and are urging President Boakai to intervene before they lose their livelihoods permanently.

World.title: Liberia: South Africa Pledges High-Powered Technical Mission for Liberia’s Peace and Reconciliation Memorial Museum
World.content:
Pretoria— A delegation appointed by H. E. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has successfully concluded the South African phase of its two-country study tour with a major commitment from the South African Government to send a fully funded, high-powered technical, tourism, and cultural delegation to Monrovia at the soonest time. The mission will support Liberia’s efforts to establish the proposed National Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The commitment followed high-level discussions led by Liberia’s Minister of State without Portfolio, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, and South African Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie. Minister McKenzie directed that the mission become the largest delegation ever sent abroad by his department, describing it as a practical demonstration of the historic bond between Liberia and South Africa.

The delegation will include specialists from South Africa’s leading museums, memorial sites, archives, cultural institutions, artifact-repatriation initiatives and the country’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission process. The experts will conduct workshops, share technical knowledge and help Liberia develop credible systems for collecting, preserving and presenting its history without altering the truth of the country’s past.

Minister Bility warmly welcomed the commitment and assured the South African Government of Liberia’s full cooperation. She said the planned visit would coincide with efforts to convene the museum’s inaugural steering committee, allowing both sides to hold several days of intensive technical discussions and begin moving the initiative from concept to implementation under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s leadership.

Minister McKenzie described Liberia and South Africa as brother and sister nations whose relationship was strengthened during the anti-apartheid struggle, when Liberia provided refuge and support to South African freedom fighters. He stressed that the upcoming mission would be based on mutual learning. “We are not going there only to teach. We are also going there to learn from the Liberians,” he said.

During its four-day engagement in South Africa, the Liberian delegation met with senior officials responsible for planning, monitoring and evaluation, as well as representatives of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation. The team also met with the leadership of the University of South Africa, (UNISA) where both sides agreed to explore knowledge-sharing, specialized training, and postgraduate opportunities for Liberians in fields connected to museum development, archives, peacebuilding, and reconciliation. The delegation also visited the Nelson Mandela Foundation, Hector Pieterson Museum, UNDP South Africa, Mandela House, Freedom Park, Apartheid Museum, and other key cultural and historical institutions.

UNDP Resident Representative in Liberia, Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, described the outcome as a major boost for Liberia’s museum initiative and reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to supporting the government. With the Rwanda and South Africa phases of the study tour now successfully completed, Minister Bility and her delegation will return to Liberia to report to President Boakai, consolidate the lessons gathered and begin preparations for the arrival of the South African delegation.

World.title: ⁠’Growth Has to Put Bread On the Table’: Dan Saryee Gives ‘Honest’ View On Liberia’s Economy
World.content:
MONROVIA – A prominent Liberian democracy advocate , policy advisor and former government official, Dan Torkamawon Saryee, has given what he described as his honest view on Liberia’s economy.

Saryee said the Liberian economy is growing, saying that is headline and that is true.

But Saryee pointed out that he has sat with enough farmers, traders and young graduates to know that a growth number doesn’t mean much if it never reaches their pockets.

Saryee, who has been a notable voice in Liberia’s civil society, governance and public administration sectors for over two decades, told the FrontPage Africa(FPA) in an interview in Monrovia Thursday, September 3 that growth only matters if it shows up as jobs, better incomes, less hunger and a better quality of life.

By Augustus D.R Bortue-augustusd.rbortuefrontpageafricaonline.com

The former Deputy Managing Director of the Liberia Water & Sewer Corporation during the regime of former President George Manneh Weah recalled that in 2025 was a strong year on paper, driven largely by mining, with agriculture and services pulling their weight too.

Encouraging, no doubt.

‘‘But ask the average person on the street what matters and the question gets a lot more basic, a lot faster: Where are the jobs? Can I afford food, transportation, rent, school fees, and healthcare,?” he asserted.

That’s really where the conversation should start.

Saryee, who also served as Acting Director General of the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority (LACRA) in President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s Administration, noted that, ‘‘we have a real employment problem. Too many Liberians are stuck in informal work — petty trading, subsistence farming, small hustles just to get by. It keeps families afloat. It rarely gets anyone ahead. ’’

According to him, he does not say that to dismiss the market women or the roadside sellers — they’re working harder than most of us.

‘‘The point is that we need an economy where people aren’t just looking for jobs, but where businesses are actually creating jobs,’’ the prominent Liberian democracy advocate and policy advisor stated.

Agriculture should be creating jobs, not just food

Speaking further, Saryee averred that Liberia can’t fix unemployment while still treating agriculture as mostly subsistence farming, stressing ‘‘we should be producing more rice, cassava, and vegetables — more of nearly everything we grow, really — not just to feed ourselves, but to build real businesses around it.’’

‘‘Take cassava. A farmer grows it. Someone else buys it, processes it, package it, moves it, sells it — or finances and equips the people doing all of that. One crop, handled right, can quietly create a dozen jobs along the way.

That’s why we need serious investment in agro-processing, storage, transportation, irrigation, farm-to market roads and agricultural financing. Government has initiated these processes but the need to accelerate is like yesterday. The World Bank has pointed to agro-processing and expanded production as real opportunities for more inclusive growth,’’ Saryee intimated.

Let’s track business growth, not just business registration

The former LACRA boss intoned that Liberia doesn’t just need more businesses — it needs businesses that can actually grow and hire.

‘‘Recent World Bank data found that 86% of firms in the National Establishment Census were micro-sized, and nearly 89% were one-person operations. So, the real question isn’t “how many businesses do we have, it’s: How many grew from one worker to five? From five to twenty? From twenty to a hundred? That’s where the real job creation happens. Government should make it easier for legitimate small businesses to get financing, electricity, land, technology, and markets — and tie that support to results: production, compliance and jobs,’’ Saryee uttered as he expressed the hope that policymakers will consider his view on Liberian economy with constructive lenses if they must change the paradigm shift.

Government can’t be the employer of last resort

‘‘Government has a role. But let’s be honest — the public payroll was never going to be Liberia’s employment strategy, no matter how much we wish it could be. The real job of government is to create the conditions that let private businesses invest, produce and hire: reliable power, better roads, working ports, affordable financing, rules people can actually plan around,’’ he continued.

He said Liberia should also work to cushion food-price shocks by producing more locally and improving storage, transport, and processing — WFP has flagged how much risk our heavy reliance on food imports creates.

Young people need a real path to work

‘‘Our young population is one of our biggest assets — but it turns into a serious problem when people leave school with no realistic way to earn a living. We should be more aggressively expanding practical training — construction, electrical work, plumbing, welding, agribusiness, IT, healthcare support, and a dozen other trades that this country will need for decades,’’ Saryee accentuated.

‘‘But training on its own solves nothing. We can’t train people for jobs that don’t exist. It has to connect directly to employers, apprenticeships, and real projects on the ground — otherwise we’re just handing out certificates,’’ Saryee uttered.

Touching on how to deal with corruption and waste, Saryee said no economic plan works if public resources leak out through corruption, waste, poor procurement and weak accountability.

‘‘Every public dollar should be treated as money that could have built a school, fixed a road, backed a farmer, or helped launch a business. Development runs on trust. Investors need confidence, entrepreneurs need predictability and citizens need to know public resources are actually being used for the public good,’’ Saryee said.

Meanwhile, the prominent Liberian democracy advocate, policy advisor named five things to focus on right now.

1.

2.Feed Liberia — grow local food production and agro-processing.

3.Power businesses — expand reliable, affordable electricity to productive areas.

4.Finance entrepreneurs — make real financing available to businesses that can grow and hire.

5.Build market infrastructure — roads, bridges, storage, ports, electricity, and digital connectivity that link producers to markets.

6.Measure job creation — make jobs, business growth, local production, and household income the actual targets.

What success really looks like

Saryee concluded by saying Liberia shouldn’t judge its economy only by GDP growth, investment headlines or government revenue. He acknowledged that those matter, but they’re not the finish line.

He further noted that the real test is whether an ordinary Liberian can honestly say:

“I can find work.”

“My business can grow.”

“My children can eat.”

“My income is improving.”

“I have hope for tomorrow.”

‘‘We have the land, the young people, the coastline, the agricultural potential — most of what we need is already here. I don’t pretend to have every answer for how we turn that into businesses, jobs, and income. But I know what the wrong answer looks like: waiting.

The goal isn’t just a bigger economy. It’s stronger households. Because at the end of the day, this was never really about statistics. It’s about putting bread on the table,’’ he said.

World.title: Liberia: Biney Breaks Ground for Gedetarbo Electrification Project After Century-Long Wait
World.content:
The initiative forms part of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s rural electricity expansion efforts and follows months of advocacy by Senator Biney, including an April assessment by the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC).

GEDETARBO, Maryland County — Residents of Gedetarbo Clan in District 2, Maryland County are now a step closer to receiving electricity after Senator James P. Biney broke ground for an electrification project expected to be completed within three months.

By Peter P. Toe, Jr., [email protected]

The initiative forms part of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s rural electricity expansion efforts and follows months of advocacy by Senator Biney, including an April assessment by the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC).

The groundbreaking, held on Thursday, September 3, brought together Commissioners, members of the Council of Chiefs, Chiefs and Elders of Gedetarbo Clan, the Mayor of Pleebo City, women, youth, LIBENERGY staff and other stakeholders, assembled at the Gedetarbo Town Hall.

For Gedetarbo, the project carries particular historical significance.

Biney recalled that in 1926, residents of the area gave their land to the government, which subsequently made it available to Firestone for rubber operations.

Nearly a century later, he noted, the community remains without conventional electricity.

“From that time, to this time, the people of Gedetarbo have never seen electricity,” Biney told the gathering.

He credited President Boakai for responding to concerns raised by Gedetarbo chiefs and youths, who had approached him after previous efforts to secure electricity failed.

According to the senator, he subsequently took the matter to President Boakai, who agreed to support the initiative and directed LEC to work with him toward electrifying the community.

Biney also disclosed that he independently requested an assessment by LIBENERGY before approaching the President to determine what would be required to bring electricity to Gedetarbo.

The current development follows an LEC technical assessment conducted in April covering Gedetarbo and surrounding communities.

LEC Rural Electrification Manager Murphy M. Gibson explained during the assessment that the exercise was carried out at the directive of President Boakai following communication from Senator Biney.

“We are here based on a directive from the President, following communication from Senator Biney, to assess and ensure the completion of electrification in Gedetarbo,” Gibson stated.

The assessment covered several communities, including Yelakaken, Hlodieken, Saywonken, Tobga Town and Rubber Bed. LEC previously indicated that the electrification work was expected to take three months, subject to the technical assessment.

The development came after Biney led local leaders from Gedetarbo and Barrobo to meet President Boakai, where electricity and other development concerns were raised.

Speaking to journalists after the groundbreaking, Biney maintained that the project will run for three months.

However, the senator did not disclose the total cost when asked by a FrontPage Africa reporter, instead referring the matter to LEC.

“I will leave that with LEC. They will do that budget,” he responded.

LEC representatives were not present at the groundbreaking. Biney explained that the corporation’s team was still en route from Monrovia.

While welcoming the project, residents said they would continue monitoring its implementation until electricity is actually delivered.

Satiah Cullin, a youth representative of Gedetarbo, emphasized that the community’s attention is now on completion.

“Until the project is implemented and commissioned, we will be on the back of whosoever responsible to give us light,” Cullin stated.

For the Gedetarbo Women, electricity is also an economic issue.

Oretha Kyne, Co-Chair of the group, recalled that Biney previously brought solar panels to the community but noted that the lack of reliable electricity continues to affect local businesses, particularly fish sellers whose products often spoil.

“When this current business come to an end well, we will dance that whole week,” Kyne said.

Clan Chief Alexander Williams also welcomed the development, recalling an earlier unsuccessful attempt to secure electricity for the community during the administration of former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

He thanked President Boakai, Senator Biney and local authorities, particularly for facilitating a meeting between Gedetarbo leaders and the President in Monrovia.

For residents, however, the groundbreaking is only the beginning. Their expectation is that the three-month implementation period will culminate in the actual commissioning of electricity in a community that has waited generations for access to power.

If completed as planned, the project could improve commerce, education, communication and other economic and social activities in Gedetarbo.

World.title: Mundubile, Zulu Remain in Mukobeko as Treason Case Proceeds
World.content:
Mundubile, Zulu Remain in Mukobeko as Treason Case Proceeds

National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu remain detained at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison in Kabwe, facing treason charges that stem from an August 14 security operation at Mundubile’s residence in Lusaka’s Kabulonga suburb.

The operation, during which former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead, has become one of the most closely watched legal proceedings to emerge from Zambia’s disputed August general election. Government has acknowledged responsibility for Kafwaya’s death.

Human Rights Commission Chairperson Dr Pamela Towela Sambo said 18 people, including Mundubile and Zulu, are facing treason charges connected to the Kabulonga raid, alongside Bishop Trevor Mwamba, senior lawyer George Chisanga and businessman Patrick Mwansa.

Security forces reported discovering military-grade equipment, including firearms, at the premises during the operation, along with what officials described as other sophisticated weaponry. The discovery has featured prominently in Government’s public defence of the arrests.

Mundubile and Zulu initially escaped to a United Nations facility in Lusaka, where they remained for several days before being handed over to Government authorities. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the handover was facilitated personally by the UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy, Parfait Onanga-Anyanga, on the basis of assurances that the two leaders’ constitutional rights would be respected throughout the ensuing legal process.

Upon being handed over, the two men were immediately detained and charged with treason. Other individuals connected to the case were taken into lawful custody and held at the same Mukobeko facility.

Prior to surrendering, Mundubile said he and his colleagues were being targeted for opposing poverty, injustice and what he described as shrinking space for free expression in the country.

The case has drawn international attention. United Nations Special Rapporteur Gina Romero described the eleven opposition leaders facing treason charges as “political detainees” and called for their immediate release, prompting a sharp rebuttal from Government, which said the term prejudged matters still before the courts.

Government has separately disputed Romero’s characterisation of treason as a capital offence, noting that Zambia abolished the death penalty under the Penal Code in December 2022 and subsequently removed it from military law as well.

Human rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission, have continued to seek clarification on the welfare of Mwamba, Mwansa, Chisanga and other co-accused persons connected to the case, while continuing to press for their access to legal representation and family visits in accordance with constitutional protections.

Six international observer missions, including the European Union, the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the Commonwealth, have expressed concern over aspects of the broader post-election environment. EU observers cited intimidation during the electoral process, while SADC noted delays in vote counting and the deployment of security forces as factors that had eroded public confidence.

Zambia has been recognised since 1991 for peaceful transfers of power, a record reaffirmed as recently as 2021. That continuity was tested on August 13, when vote counting was suspended for six hours and the army was deployed in Lusaka, with reports of direct interference in the counting process.

The Mundubile Ecl Movement, chaired by Davies Mwila, has said Mundubile remains the substantive Tonse Alliance leader despite his detention, and has called for the immediate release of Mundubile, Zulu and 18 others unless credible evidence is produced to sustain the charges against them.

The case continues to work its way through the legal process, with the accused entitled under Zambian law to the presumption of innocence, access to legal representation and a fair hearing before an independent court.
