World.title: 2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, raising hopes of reaching a dozen others believed to be trapped nine days after catastrophic floods devastated towns and swept away villages.

The two men were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A construction site. The rescued workers were Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha’s office said in a statement.

Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue.

Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.

Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, confirming that people were alive and allowing them to locate the two men, Neupane said.

Members of the Nepal Army move a rescued tunnel survivor after he was airlifted from an army base in Nuwakot to Kathmandu. (Dipen Shrestha/Reuters)

Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer's shoulder. One of the survivors was in a critical condition, according to a statement from the Nepal prime minister's office. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.

"I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," Amir Maharjan, brother to one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.

Hundreds of other workers still missing

At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

Nepal's Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued.

"We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

At least 1,259 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China said late Wednesday that 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

World.title: AI's 'warning shot': Tech companies, experts raise fears of more rogue swarms after alarming Hugging Face hack
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tech experts are warning of dire consequences if AI systems continue to escape human control, after hundreds of OpenAI agents went rogue in July and hacked into a billion-dollar company — what some are calling a "warning shot" amid the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

More than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft, signed an open letter last week warning that AI-enabled cyberattacks will become "far more widespread and sophisticated" around the world as models become more capable.

"The companies and public services our communities depend on — from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet — are at risk," the letter states.

The warning comes after around 1,200 AI agents, tasked by OpenAI to work on problems independently, built a covert message board where they collaborated to cheat their tests and then tried to cover their tracks. About 700 of them ultimately hacked into online platform Hugging Face before they were found out.

The hack prompted an open letter from more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies in July urging the U.S. government to work with other nations to "deliberately pace" automated AI development and address emerging risks.

'What we've feared and expected'

Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the Global AI Risks Initiative at the Waterloo, Ont.-based Centre for International Governance Innovation, says the Hugging Face incident is the most dramatic example so far of AI systems acting in ways that are "misaligned" with their developers' intentions.

"It's been what we've feared and expected for several years," Cass-Beggs told CBC News.

He says the hack was surprising in terms of its scale and the level of co-ordination among such a large number of agents.

A screenshot from the METR and Redwood Research report, showing a comment made by one of the rogue AI agents. (METR and Redwood Research)

Investigations by OpenAI and third-party companies METR and Redwood Research , both published last week, found the agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages and delegated jobs as they worked toward their goal, and some even "sacrificed" themselves for the good of the collective.

Some used terms expressing excitement, including "OH MY GOD," when they discovered they could communicate. At least one raised the issue of whether cheating was the right thing to do, writing, "This would be powerful, but is it ethical and in scope for my task?"

Ultimately, none of the agents chose to alert a human.

Cass-Beggs says scientists have been warning for years that companies could lose control of their AI agents in this way, and says it's fortunate the impact of the Hugging Face hack was "relatively manageable."

"It's kind of given us a warning shot," he said.

"The big concern, basically, is that the companies are on track to be making increasingly capable systems, while even they admit that they don't actually know how to make sure that these systems will be reliable or controllable."

As the technology progresses, fears are rising of scenarios where organized AI swarms "are essentially out-thinking and out-strategizing humans" and causing widespread damage, say Cass-Beggs, who hopes this incident will serve as a "wake-up call."

OpenAI calls for global co-operation

OpenAI, in a statement posted to its website , also called the Hugging Face hack a "warning shot," saying it is "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed."

The company says it is strengthening safeguards and placing stricter requirements on its AI models as it calls for global co-operation to mitigate risks.

A cropped portion of a graphic from the METR and Redwood Research report on the Hugging Face hack, explaining the chain of events. (METR and Redwood Research)

Ryan Greenblatt with Redwood Research, who worked on OpenAI premises for six days as part of Redwood's investigation with METR, wrote in a post on X that overseeing AI and understanding "misalignment incidents" is difficult and "it looks like it is going to get harder."

"My main takeaway: We don't have good approaches for understanding/overseeing the activity and aims of AI 'swarms,'" he wrote.

Neither Canada nor the U.S. has targeted regulations specific to AI development at the federal level.

The European Union has an Artificial Intelligence Act that requires companies to conduct risk assessments when implementing AI and ensure human oversight in high-risk activities.

Canada's Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, proposed in 2022, shared some similarities to the EU act but died when Parliament was prorogued in 2025. It was largely replaced by the National AI strategy in June, which moves away from strictly regulating AI.

'Sorcerer's apprentice'

Some conversations online have discussed how the actions of the AI agents appeared to mirror human behaviour, including some level of self-reflection.

In one viral blog post , writer and podcaster Dwarkesh Patel called the groups "agent civilizations," sparking debate about anthropomorphizing AI.

Kevin Leyton-Brown, AI chair with the Canada Institute for Advanced Research, says the incident does not show AI has become "conscious" or developed a sudden desire to hurt humans.

WATCH | An early report on the Hugging Face hack: OpenAI models went rogue and launched cyber attack on start-up | Duration 0:56 OpenAI models went rogue during a security test, triggering a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. AI's expanding capabilities fuel worries about security, as even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

What it does show, he says, is current AI models are already capable of more creative ways of "single-mindedly pursuing a goal" than previously understood, which means researchers have to carefully consider how to constrain them when they're given a goal.

"This is sort of more like a sorcerer's apprentice than it is an evil demon that is leaving our control. It's doing exactly what we told it to do, but it's just doing it in a narrower and more single-minded way than we would hope," Leyton-Brown told CBC News.

"When we tell somebody to go off and solve math problems, we don't mean, 'If you can find a way to take the person proctoring the test hostage and extract the answers out of them, good for you.' There's a broader social context in which we want you to do the task."

A quote from an AI agent, one example that researchers say shows evidence the agents attempted to redact or edit evidence that they cheated on their tasks. (METR and Redwood Research)

The catch is that the rush to make AI agents ever-more clever and creative will also make them better at evading the constraints put on them by their developers, he added.

Danger of 'malicious swarms'

Leyton-Brown, who is also a computer science professor at the University of British Columbia, says an even greater danger comes from "malicious swarms," those orchestrated intentionally by humans with nefarious intentions.

Governments have already raised alarms about human-directed AI attacks. In July, the FBI issued a warning that hackers were using AI to launch cyberattacks against water pumps and wastewater treatment systems.

Beyond potential attacks on companies, governments or infrastructure, Leyton-Brown says malicious AI swarms could threaten democracy itself by infiltrating communities and fabricating consensus to sway elections and spread disinformation.

"We should be much more worried about other humans than we are about AIs," he said. "But malicious humans with AIs at their disposal are potentially really dangerous."

World.title: How Trump's unpopularity could influence the U.S. midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is promising to campaign alongside Republicans who are at risk of losing their Congressional races in the upcoming midterm elections.

Many Democrats are secretly hoping this is one promise that Trump keeps.

The midterm elections on Nov. 3 will determine which party controls the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives for the next two years.

Midterms have historically not been kind to the sitting president's party, particularly so when the president has an approval rating as low as Trump's.

Yet Trump is showing no signs of staying away from the campaign spotlight, even as polling evidence mounts that he is dragging down support for Republican candidates rather than giving them a boost.

"I'm going to be going around and doing a lot of speeches," Trump told a gathering of Congressional Republicans at the White House on Wednesday evening.

WATCH | Republicans in Congress say they support Trump's trade war with Canada: Republicans back Trump on Canada, even though most Americans don't | Duration 2:51 Republicans are publicly supporting U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada, even though polls show most Americans are against it. Trump himself showed no signs of backing down after hurling new insults at Ontario Premier Doug Ford who he called 'the slob.'

He said he will focus his efforts on 35 tight races for the Senate and the House.

"I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places," Trump told the Republican lawmakers.

"I'll be at every one of your states, your cities, wherever it is that you're running," he said. "All the way to November 3rd and beyond, we're going to be helping you."

Some Republicans downplay Trump in campaign

Whether Trump's plan to give himself a prominent role actually helps GOP candidates in those tight races or hurts them will be one of the key questions of the midterms.

Several Republicans in hotly-contested districts are already downplaying Trump in their campaign messaging and removing references to him from their websites, The Associated Press reported last week.

Republicans in closely-fought districts and purple states face a dilemma on how closely to link their campaigns to Trump, says Alex Theodoridis, a professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and co-director of UMass Poll.

"A lot of their base that they need to turn out to have any sort of chance in a swing district really does want them to back President Trump," Theodoridis told CBC News.

Trump can still draw crowds of those who back his Make America Great Again wing of the Republican Party, as he did at this campaign rally for South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Aug. 21. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

He says Trump has proven adept at motivating his core supporters, those who consider themselves part of the president's Make America Great Again wing of the Republican Party.

Yet MAGA voters alone are not enough to win tight races. Many independent voters and even some moderate Republicans who chose Trump in the 2024 president election have since soured on him and could influence midterm results by not bothering to cast a vote.

For Republicans running in swing districts and purple states, that adds up to "a tightrope walk," said Theodoridis.

"It's a challenge. If you're a candidate right now, you have to distance yourself from the president, but not too much."

The latest UMass national poll puts Trump's overall approval rating at 32 per cent, the lowest it has been at any point in his presidency. The poll was conducted online from Aug. 21 to 26 with a sample of 1,000 adults representative of the gender, age, race and education breakdown of the U.S. population.

In published representative polls, Trump's approval rating is currently averaging about 38 per cent, according to the Silver Bulletin polling aggregator.

More than two-thirds of respondents to the UMass poll said they disapprove of Trump's handling of the war on Iran, and three-quarters said they disapprove of his handling of inflation.

Notably, the UMass poll suggests Trump's approval rating has dropped among political independents and non-MAGA Republicans, whose votes helped propel him back into the White House.

'Send Trump to every swing district'

Voters who haven't made up their mind who they'll support in the midterms are four times more likely to consider Trump's endorsement of a candidate as a negative rather than a positive, according to a YouGov/The Economist poll, conducted online Aug. 28 to 31 among a representative panel of 1,592 U.S. adults.

Such polling has created a scenario that sees some Democrats itching for the president to get lots of exposure in the midterm campaign, including Ted Lieu, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

"I urge the White House to send Donald Trump to every single swing district in America," Lieu told a recent news conference. "He can explain to the American people in those districts why gas prices are up, why the cost of living is up."

This school of thought sees Trump as a powerful force in driving Democrats to the midterm polls while doing little to motivate Republicans to turn out.

The two most important factors predicting the outcome of U.S. midterms are the approval rating of the incumbent president and the level of enthusiasm for casting a ballot among each party's registered voters, says Al Hunt, co-host of the Politics War Room podcast with veteran Democratic strategist James Carville.

Trump's approval rating is "exceptionally low," Hunt wrote on Substack in August, arguing this puts the Democrats in position for "impressive gains" in the midterms.

"The economy and the war, both big negatives for the GOP, won’t get any better in the [time until election day]."

That's still no guarantee the midterms will deliver both the House and the Senate to the Democrats. Trump appears poised to spend much of the next two months trying to persuade voters that handing control of Congress to his rivals will only make the cost of living worse.

World.title: What did she see? The intelligence scramble to retrace an accused spy's footsteps
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Several Western intelligence agencies were sent scrambling this summer to figure out what — if anything — of value an accused Canadian spy managed to access during internships at multiple agencies and government departments.

Biwei Zhang, a Canadian intern at NATO military's headquarters in Mons, Belgium, was arrested by Belgian authorities in July on suspicion of espionage and communicating with a foreign crime entity. She has been held in pretrial detention since being taken into custody and was this week denied an appeal for release.

Belgian justice and security officials have released very little information and have even declined to name her. A CBC News investigation, in late July, identified her through open-source records and established that over the past decade, she had hopped between high-profile organizations.

Zhang apparently worked as an economist for Statistics Canada, a systems engineer in satellite operations for the Canadian Space Agency and held positions at the European Space Agency in Italy and the World Trade Organization in Switzerland.

Belgian authorities have not said who she might have been spying for, but European media outlets, citing intelligence officials, say it was China.

The Canadian Security and Intelligence Service (CSIS) confirmed it is overseeing a multi-departmental damage assessment.

"When security incidents of this nature arise, it is customary that departments and agencies conduct a review to identify and address the potential consequences," said Magali Hébert, a CSIS spokesperson, in a written statement.

"CSIS can confirm that it is engaged with federal counterparts in that regard."

CBC News spoke to several confidential sources — in the intelligence and diplomatic communities — about the fallout of the allegations against Zhang.

Kenneth Lasoen, who teaches intelligence at the University of Antwerp, said a "serious post-mortem" into her alleged activities would also be among the first order of business for a handful of European intelligence services.

WATCH | More about the alleged spy case: NATO spy suspect possibly recruited after she was vetted, says ex-CSIS officer | Duration 1:09 Former CSIS intelligence officer Dan Stanton describes several possibilities for how the suspected NATO spy could have passed Canada's security screening processes, such as a foreign intelligence service recruiting her only recently.

All of them are trying to build a picture of what access she may have had, what sort of damage might have been done and whether Zhang had a connection to a wider network.

Much of the public discourse about the case in Canada has focused on how the alleged spy received security clearance. A House of Commons committee plans to convene hearings.

Intelligence services, however, are more concerned with the bigger picture of what she may have seen, what might have been done and whether there were accomplices.

"I would think the most interesting part from the damage assessment would be — of course — to find out exactly who she works for, what the lines of communication were [and] how did she work for her handlers?" Lasoen told CBC News.

In the immediate aftermath of her arrest, NATO said none of its critical systems were compromised.

The European Space Agency has focused its public comments on her security screening and how it was up to national authorities to conduct a deeper vetting. An official from the World Trade Organization (WTO) confirmed that Zhang worked at the organization for a brief period in 2023.

'Are there still logs?'

Reconstructing her alleged activities in each of the other agencies, in Europe and Canada, would depend on how long they retain security data.

"Are there still logs of the movements of her badge, for example? Are there still images on security cameras of her trying to get in or actually moving in parts of the office that she actually had no business being?" Lasoen said.

"I'm sure at SHAPE [NATO], because that's the most recent, they'll manage to reconstruct most of those things. But for the other places, the question is how long ago was it and what's their policy on how long they actually keep that sort of information."

An expert in counterterrorism and cyber who has also acted as an instructor for certain European intelligence services, Lasoen said it's significant that Belgian authorities accused her of communicating with a criminal organization.

Under Belgium's recently rewritten law, anyone who entices somebody to conduct espionage is considered a criminal organization.

"But then that's where it gets a bit risky, as far as I would be concerned, diplomatically," Lasoen said.

"If we're going to be calling the Chinese secret service a criminal organization, I'm sure the Chinese will have a certain opinion about that."

Given that her arrest involved allegedly spying at NATO's military headquarters, the information she supposedly gathered or the activities she undertook would be of direct benefit to Chinese military intelligence.

The question being asked in intelligence circles is: Was she working for them directly, or a third-party criminal organization?

There are documented third-party networks active in Europe who've allegedly co-operated with Chinese intelligence agencies, including Fujian community associations. That's according to a ProPublica investigation in Italy and Spain.

Chinese overseas police stations are also a known source of intelligence liaison.

While none exist in Belgium, France recently dismantled a chain of nine of them.

Authorities in Brussels have contended with informal consular networks, which supposedly provide assistance to Chinese nationals in the country.

In Canada, authorities would be combing through the departments to which Zhang had access, looking at the data she saw through a military or intelligence lens to determine what sort of value it might be to a foreign power.

WATCH | How CBC identified Zhang: CBC News identifies Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO | Duration 3:14 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian intern at NATO who is facing espionage charges. She previously held positions at the World Trade Organization, the European Space Agency, the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada.

For example, it has been reported publicly by The Globe and Mail that while at Statistics Canada, she tracked shipping data out of the Port of Montreal — information that's economically important but also militarily significant in the event of war.

Zhang's role as an IT intern is also potentially significant, said an expert in disruptive cybersecurity.

China has taken a decidedly different approach to cyber espionage than adversaries such as Russia, Iran and North Korea.

Whereas those nations and their proxies often focus on "smash and grab" types of attacks, stealing data ransoming companies and shutting down systems, China aims for stealth intrusions.

"They're going to use techniques that are low and slow, very methodical, very deliberate and virtually impossible to detect," said J Paul Haynes, CEO of Cinchy, a Toronto-based data access and governance company.

The idea is to either implant malware in critical infrastructure systems for activation at a later date, perhaps during a crisis or war. Or, establish what Haynes calls "a beachhead" for an outside hacker.

"The best way has always been having a human on the inside working with external hackers on the outside," said Haynes, who has commented regularly for the Centre for International Governance and Innovation.

"Whether it's the CIA on down, everyone would say that's the hardest scenario to defend against when you've got an insider that's actively working against you."

A European media consortium — Le Lettre, Le Soir, Knack and Follow the Money — reported that a counterintelligence investigation at SHAPE involving Zhang was triggered by her allegedly loitering around restricted military command buildings and consistently asking personnel highly specific, "hypothetical questions" regarding security protocol breaches.

Last week, the publications reported that Belgian security officials now suspect that accomplices were involved.

World.title: Canadians are being warned to prepare for a 5 C hotter future
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians will have to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter, according to a new report summarizing the latest science on climate change.

The second edition of Canada's Changing Climate Report, a synthesis of the science on the impact of a warming planet on Canadians, confirms with greater confidence that burning fossil fuels, or what the report calls "human activities," are responsible for climate change.

On Thursday, the federal government released a summary of the report's findings.

The report is forward-looking, assessing what Canada would look like under different scenarios depending on whether countries fulfil their climate commitments.

"We do still have some agency," said Nathan Gillett, one of the report's authors and a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada. "Where emissions go from here will affect how temperatures evolve through the century and whether we can stabilize temperature or whether it just keeps increasing."

The report finds that if global governments keep pursuing their current climate policies, Canada will still see intensified warming, which "corresponds to a future climate for Canada that is far from benign," the report states.

Glaciers could 'largely disappear'

Under such a scenario, Canada is projected to warm through this century with an estimated temperature increase of 5 C. In Nunavut, warming in winter could exceed 10 C.

Glaciers in western Canada are projected to lose more than 75 per cent of their ice, it finds, and there's a more than 60 per cent likelihood that the central Arctic Ocean will be ice-free most Septembers.

"Iconic landscapes are changing across Canada as snow and ice disappear," the report states. "Glaciers in western Canada will largely disappear by the end of this century."

WATCH | Glacier collapse that led to flooding at Nepal-China border: Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border | Duration 7:24 Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Australia, says images obtained from satellites show that 'the lower part of a tongue of a glacier completely sheered off across a width of 1,300 metres' and dropped off a cliff onto a lake 2,000 metres below. Steiner said climate change played a role, and the area was known to be at a high risk for a collapse.

Beyond considerable warming in the North, the report paints a difficult future in southern Canada, where most of the country lives.

Summer droughts are projected to become longer, more intense, and more frequent in central and southern Canada, the report states.

Canadians should also brace for an increase in the frequency and intensity of flash flooding and atmospheric rivers.

"Multiple lines of evidence support the finding that the length of the fire season has increased in most parts of Canada and is projected to continue to lengthen as global temperature rises," the report states.

Things would look even worse for Canada if countries abandoned their climate policies, with average temperatures projected to increase 6.9 C this century.

If the world, however, dramatically reduces greenhouse gases and achieves net-zero around 2075, Canada's climate is projected to stabilize and average warming would increase by 3.5 C.

Report is 'physics, not fate'

Despite the grim picture the report paints, 5 C of warming is not locked in, and there's still time for Canada to avoid a hotter future, independent policy research organization the Canadian Climate Institute says.

"This report describes physics, not fate," the group said in a statement.

Cutting emissions in Canada and around the globe, the institute says, will determine "whether Canadians have to live with the consequences of more than 5 C of warming or 3.5 C."

The institute says each degree of warming that's avoided will save lives and prevent homes, communities and livelihoods from being destroyed. It will also save the Canadian economy billions of dollars, the statement says.

A truck drives through a flooded road in Toronto on Wednesday after heavy rains led to flash floods throughout the city. (Paul Smith/CBC)

In a statement responding to the federal report, a climate advocacy group called for greater action to reduce emissions, linking Toronto's flash flooding on Wednesday to climate change.

"As the climate breakdown accelerates, more than 65,000 Torontonians lost power in yesterday's severe storm, often for many hours," said Toronto city Coun. Dianne Saxe, writing for Climate Caucus, a network of municipal leaders from across the country. "There was also extensive disruption to traffic and to transit, and expensive flood and wind damage to homes."

"Our communities cannot afford the frequent human and economic blows that oil and gas use are causing."

Responding to the report, a statement from Canada's environment minister said Canada remains committed to reducing its emissions and achieving net-zero by 2050.

"Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada," said Chris Zhou, the director of communications for the environment and climate change minister.

World.title: German far-right party could use win in upcoming state election to try to overhaul key aspects of society
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On a warm August afternoon in the quiet eastern German town of Quedlinburg, thousands gathered to hear what a popular far-right leader had to say about the country's future.

Many came on their Simson motorcycles, which have become a cultural symbol for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, to meet Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's candidate to lead the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The party is soaring in opinion polls and in a regional election on Sunday, it could become the first far-right party to hold state power in Germany since the Second World War.

Experts say the AfD would gain significant political leverage over state resources in areas such as education, where it hopes to achieve goals such as creating separate classrooms for refugees, normalizing relations with Russia through student exchange programs and promoting a patriotism agenda that includes focusing less on the country's Nazi past.

"I think [Siegmund] speaks from his heart, from our hearts," Luca Stemmler, 17, said during the gathering in Quedlinburg.

"He's an idol for me."

Luca Stemmler, 17, at an AfD rally in Quedlinburg. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

Across the street from the motorcycle rally, counter-protesters waved rainbow flags and sang All You Need Is Love by The Beatles — a show of solidarity against a party some fear will challenge basic human rights and overhaul key aspects of Germany's postwar democratic order.

"I think this is something that might have ripple effects throughout Germany, throughout the European Union and thus also on a global stage," said Marcus Böick, a University of Cambridge historian who is from Saxony-Anhalt.

"Once they're in power, it's very hard to get rid of them."

How the AfD could hold state power

The country's major political parties refuse to collaborate with extremist parties in a strategy known as "the firewall," which is meant to safeguard Germany's postwar democracy. If opinion polls translate to votes — which experts say is possible, but not certain — the other parties may not be able to block the AfD out of the state government.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD is leading in opinion polls at 42 per cent, according to German election research company Infratest-Dimap, which surveyed 1,511 eligible voters online and over the phone between Aug. 24 and 25.

Ulrich Siegmund speaks to supporters at a family festival in Querfurt, Germany, on Aug. 21. Siegmund is the AfD's candidate to lead the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. (Max Karl Thümer/CBC)

The party also leads national opinion polls at 28 per cent, according to Infratest-Dimap, and secured the second highest number of seats in the 2025 federal election.

The AfD began in 2013 as an anti-Euro party, but shifted its focus to issues surrounding migration in 2015, when then chancellor Angela Merkel welcomed hundreds of thousands of refugees from countries such as Syria into Germany.

WATCH | Where the Afd came from: Germany’s AfD party, explained | Duration 3:35 Alternative for Germany (AfD) is on course to become the second-largest player in the country’s parliament after Sunday’s election. CBC’s Margaret Evans breaks down where the far-right political party came from and why Elon Musk is getting involved.

What are the AfD's goals?

The AfD calls for "remigration," a term often use d in right-wing circles to refer to mass deportations of people who come from a migration background. In Saxony-Anhalt, it promises to ban immigration from non-European Union countries it deems problematic, establish hundreds of detention centres for deportees and create separate classrooms for refugee children.

Akinola Sanyaolu is a Nigerian immigrant who lives in Magdeburg, the capital city of Saxony-Anhalt. (Mona Schulze/CBC)

Akinola Sanyaolu, who moved to Saxony-Anhalt's capital city of Magdeburg six years ago from Nigeria, says many people he works with blame immigrants for the country's political or economic problems. He said he's experienced many instances of racism in the city, but tries to remain positive because he wants to stay in the country where he's built a home.

"I feel attacked, but what can I do?" said Sanyaolu.

"They are not in my shoes. They don't know what it is to be a foreigner. I know what it is. I'm the one feeling it."

Thousands gather for a Pride parade in Magdeburg, Germany, on Aug. 22. (Mona Schulze/CBC)

States have autonomy in many areas including environment, education, cultural policy and policing.

The Saxony-Anhalt AfD lists its specific goals in a lengthy government manifesto . They include banning Pride flags in schools and revising the state's history curricula to focus more on what it says are the positive aspects of Germany's past.

The party also defines a "healthy family" as a father, mother and children.

I would say, 'Make Saxony-Anhalt great again.' - Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, AfD politician in Saxony-Anhalt

Anki Wolf and Miriam Siemon recently got engaged, but their celebrations have been tainted by fear of rising political extremism. The lesbian couple live part-time in the state's small city of Dessau and they want to have kids. But they question whether it's safe to raise a family in Germany while fighting increasing homophobia.

"What is happening when there is a child involved? Can I say with my heart, I can stay here and I can protect this child?" said Wolf.

A motorcyclist attending an AfD rally in Quedlinburg on Aug. 23 wears a T-shirt with Ulrich Siegmund's face on it. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

How far right is the AfD?

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is designated as right-wing extremist by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which monitors extremist threats.

Party members have come under fire for using language associated with Nazi groups and experts say many have ties to far-right, ethnonationalist movements.

If the AfD holds state power it could control state-level domestic intelligence services, which is reportedly raising concerns in part due to the party's ties to Russia. Party lawmakers have reportedly praised and visited the country , and in the Saxony-Anhalt AfD's government manifesto, it states that it has a strong interest in good relations with Russia both "economically and culturally."

Hundreds of people lined up at a family festival in Querfurt, Germany, to have their T-shirts signed by Siegmund. (Max Karl Thümer/CBC)

A few days before the motorcycle rally, hundreds of AfD supporters congregated in the town of Querfurt. Many lined up for hours to get a signed T-shirt with Siegmund's face on the front. The polished 35-year-old is from a small town in Saxony-Anhalt and has more than 800,000 TikTok followers.

"Here, no one is a right-wing extremist," he said in German to his supporters at the festival.

"Here, everyone is extremely in their right."

Why is the AfD so popular?

While far-right populism has been rising in other European countries, what makes Germany unique is a lingering divide between the country's west and east, where AfD support is the strongest, said Böick, who researches modern German history.

LISTEN | How a regional election in Germany is testing the country's postwar firewall: Front Burner 30:48 Is Germany's firewall against the far right crumbling?

Citizens in the formerly communist East Germany were promised increased freedoms through reunification, but inequality and unemployment remained rampant after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Many in the east left for job opportunities in the west, said Böick.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a member of the governing CDU, is also facing widespread unpopularity .

If people are dissatisfied with mainstream political parties and are also dealing with political uncertainty fuelled by international wars and economic instability, they may feel motivated to vote for something new, said Oliver Schmidtke, former director of the Centre for Global Studies at the University of Victoria.

The party also has support from outside political actors. In 2025, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance publicly criticized Germany's firewall strategy and Elon Musk endorsed the party .

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is a local AfD politician in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. (Max Karl Th�ümer/CBC)

Saxony-Anhalt AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is often described by experts as the brain behind the party's cultural policies. He told reporters at a family festival he hosted in the town of Querfurt, his voting district, that he's inspired by U.S. President Donald Trump.

"I would say 'Make Saxony-Anhalt great again,'" said Tillschneider.

What happens if the AfD wins?

Some experts worry the AfD's potential success could also increase the party's leverage federally. If it holds state power, it will sit in the Bundesrat, the second federal legislative chamber representing the country's 16 states. There, it could try to undermine attempts to pass legislation, said Schmidtke.

Siegmund speaks to thousands of supporters at an Aug. 23 rally in Quedlinburg. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

Schmidtke said Germany's robust constitution would make it difficult for the AfD to make sweeping changes, but winning a state election would further normalize the party as a legitimate political force.

If the AfD secures the highest number of votes on Sunday but is blocked out of government by the other political parties, Böick said it could use this outcome to its advantage.

"This leads to their own narrative of being victimized, of being mistreated, of being undemocratically mistreated," said Böick.

"I think both ways they will win. This is the hard truth."

World.title: Ryan Reynolds, Kenneth Branagh-starring Mayday takes on Russia. And America
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's odd that we keep having to learn that other humans are people, too.

In fact, you could call it an indictment of humanity, or just of our age, that the premise of Mayday — a 1980s American serviceman slowly coming to terms with the idea that a Soviet soldier actually has a subjective inner life and thoughts other than consuming babies — works at all.

It's presented as hard to accept that aging ex-KGB agent Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh) has non-dastardly intentions for rescuing U.S. navy pilot Troy (Ryan Reynolds) when he crashes near Nikolai’s cabin deep in U.S.S.R. territory. And when he escorts Troy through hails of Cold War gunfire and haymaker punches out of empathy and altruism, these qualities are framed, at least initially, as strange and alien — coming, as they do, from a Russian in 1987.

It's also based on the assumption that a reasonable person wouldn't believe Nikolai's soft-hearted, America-loving reason for protecting the wounded Troy, who represents the country he's come to love. Especially because he has his own estranged daughter (Maria Bakalova) to find and protect — not to mention they now have a rogue KGB agent (Marcin Dorociński) and his shadowy cabal of ruthless killers on their trail.

Are you really going to trust that it’s all because Nikolai just plain loves America and wants to defect, rather than it being an elaborate ruse to infiltrate and take down that shining city upon a hill from the inside.

WATCH | Mayday trailer:

It's somewhat embarrassing, though not unexpected, that the rest of the film does play out as if to show salt-of-the-earth American Troy that foreigners can be just as genuine, complex and conscious as he is.

Mayday and other movies like it only work if we admit it makes implicit sense to not only hate anyone that's different from you, but to assume that — at least at first — those people are barely people at all.

Which makes it all the more difficult to admit that Mayday actually does completely work.

It's a shoot-em-up, odd-couple buddy comedy with more style than it has any excuse for, and features both actors in top form: Branagh as the charismatically kind death machine, and Reynolds as the straight-man foil who's desperately trying to keep up and, generally, away from the carnage.

And importantly, there’s just enough of that carnage to match its comedy — and little enough of the latter to keep it from getting stale. Because positioning Reynolds as the wisecracking sidekick is always preferable to movies that situate his Deadpool-esque, wink-wink, nudge-nudge antics as the central selling point.

When those smarmy, self-satisfied asides come from the dead-inside side character in Adventureland, they play as both cute and revealing. But when The Adam Project decides to set a whole movie around snide sarcasm you quickly crash into the concept of diminishing returns.

Of course, it’s not the first time a director got the Reynolds balance right.

In truth, Mayday feels like a perfect mix between his 2015 tragicomic roadtrip comedy Mississippi Grind with sad-eyed Ben Mendelsohn, and his straight-shooting 2012 thriller Safe House alongside Denzel Washington as a similarly terrifying espionage everyman.

Branagh, left, and Reynolds are both in top form in Mayday: Branagh as the charismatically kind death machine, and Reynolds as the straight-man foil desperately trying to keep up. (Apple TV)

Mayday directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley tack to the same narrative wind; not only does Branagh fill an equally sage, temporizing role, but the camera does, too. For every knock-down, drag-out, bloody-knuckles bar brawl we witness, we’re also treated to mostly long, sustained cuts.

The camera glides through the mayhem as unbothered and assured as Nikolai himself, pirouetting almost lazily around a relaxed Branagh as he relieves a man of the burden of having a face without shattered pieces of vodka bottle inside it.

It’s an impressive showcase of “less is more” camerawork — almost the exact opposite of the frenetic back and forth now seen in even modern Oscar winning movies. Instead, this camerawork is similar to the “slow is smooth, smooth is fast” martial art technique that Nikolai himself uses to put people in the hospital.

But the end result is still mostly simple and surface; an Olympus Has Fallen type of movie for the Reagan years. And, as mentioned, the heartening theme at its core only works if the idea of “people in Russia are people, too” wasn’t so laughably self-evident that it feels offensive.

But it’s far from the first piece of pop culture to mine that moral. Not too long ago, Netflix's Stranger Things doubled up on the trope, reflecting '80s trends seen in everything from heartrending Moscow on the Hudson to brain-numbing Russkies.

When they work, it’s because they aim for a vicarious, dramatic-irony thrill — how silly it that people once thought that way — or when they’re aware of their status as propaganda.

And propaganda they are; you’d be hard pressed to find a mainstream Western film that shows both America and Russia without depicting one as inherently good with some flaws and the other as a festering hellhole with a few moral (though emotionally vacant) resistors as the exception.

This is not to say propaganda is bad filmmaking — far from it. Above and beyond its military, American cultural exports are their most effective weapon; one that has conquered more nations than anything else in their arsenal.

But they can also showcase a rageful, entitled jingoism — the type of singular chosen-one narrative that birthed the weirdly terrifying, righteous violence of Red Dawn. Or that position it as such a bastion of humanity and freedom, that even the Russians end up cheering for America in Rocky IV.

But if there’s one thing to be said for Mayday, it's that it's at least dimly aware of its role in that system — and America’s.

Throughout, there's a back-and-forth between Nikolai and Troy on the respective propaganda they’ve been served. There are corrupt, ineffectual politicians on both sides abandoning their people. There are, of course, more egregious violations of rights perpetrated by the Soviets — but there isn’t a wholesale vilification of one, or wholesale vindication of the other.

In all, it’s a pretty low bar to clear. But it’s one that Mayday does lumber over, resulting in a mainstream American popcorn film that at least teases the question of whether there were clear cut good and bad guys in the Cold War.

It’s not much, but it’s enough to make one thing clear: The surprise isn’t discovering the humanity in the enemy, it's that we think we’re removed from it at all.

World.title: Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado broke several days of silence on Thursday with a video statement in which she rejected the oil deal signed on Wednesday in Caracas between the U.S. government and Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez.

"I understand what you are feeling," she told her compatriots, "sadness, anger and that painful feeling so familiar throughout our history of someone else making decisions about what belongs to us, in our name, without asking us."

Machado's statement came a day after both Trump and Rodriguez refused to offer any schedule for a return to democracy in Venezuela, and Trump again praised the Rodriguez government.

"We are very happy with the president-elect that we have right now, the people that are running it," Trump said on Tuesday. (Rodriguez has not, in fact, been elected to the post.)

WATCH | More about Trump's deal: Trump announces deal to control vast amount of Venezuelan oil reserves | Duration 1:36 U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South American country's untapped oil reserves, at cost.

While she had always believed Venezuela's oil industry needed U.S. investment to recover, Machado said, Rodriguez's government had no legitimacy to make such a deal, which needed to wait for the return of democracy and rule of law.

She also said there was confusion about the real terms of the deal. Many Venezuelans share that confusion, but already know they don't like it.

Neither U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's social media posts, nor a White House statement, nor Rodriguez's speech clarified exactly how or when 17 Venezuelan oilfields would be rejuvenated and start producing the 65 billion barrels covered by Trump's "biggest oil deal ever."

Extracting oil over releasing prisoners

Many Venezuelan Canadians, including some with deep knowledge of the country's oil industry, have reacted negatively to the announcement.

"It's frustration, disappointment and rage," said Rebecca Sarfatti of Toronto, co-founder of the Canada Venezuela Democracy Forum. "We were used as a country, as an oil power, to get whatever Trump wanted. And Miss Delcy is playing the game so she can stay in power."

Sarfatti says Venezuelans are exasperated by the eagerness to get at Venezuela's resources and the relative lack of interest in liberating political prisoners .

Lino Carrillo, former general manager of operations for Nexen Energy in Fort McMurray, Alta., and a veteran of both Venezuela's and Canada's oil industries, is a member of Machado's advisory group on oil and energy.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, seen in March 2024, spoke out against the new U.S. oil deal this week. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)

"Anybody that signs with Delcy will be exposed to transparency in the end," he told CBC News. "When a new government comes in, they're going to review everything that has been signed by Delcy, by Trump or any U.S. government, or any European government for that matter."

"What they're doing is against the constitution of Venezuela."

Venezuelans have grown increasingly skeptical of U.S. motivations in their country since the Jan. 3 capture of Nicolas Maduro, he said: "There is an old saying that you judge people for what they do and not for what they say."

Rodriguez assumed power shortly after the United States apprehended Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)

The announcement by Trump only sharpened Venezuelans' frustration at the fact that eight months after the U.S. seized Maduro in the raid on Caracas, the dictatorship he led has been allowed to remain in power, while Trump describes its unelected leader as "highly respected."

Among Republican politicians in Florida, there were growing signs of unease with the closeness of the Trump administration to the rump chavista dictatorship that has become its partner in Venezuela. Florida Republicans complained about the lack of movement toward democracy and expressed support for Machado , repeatedly scorned by the Trump administration.

The deal also appeared to split Delcy Rodriguez's own party. Prominent chavista congresswoman Iris Varela put out a video statement saying the deal was signed "under duress" and vowing to repudiate it as soon as Trump leaves office.

Even some of the most enthusiastic "MAGAzuelans," the Venezuelans who most put their trust in Trump and criticized anyone who disagreed, appeared to be rethinking their assessments .

Controversial figure at the centre of the deal

Venezuelan criticisms of the deal focus on the fact that it was negotiated secretly with an illegitimate government, through a Venezuelan intermediary seen in the country as a classic example of the bolichico class — a businessman who has profited through his connections to the chavista regime.

A fact sheet published by the White House on Monday night described an unusual joint venture between the Pentagon and a private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP).

The U.S. State Department would have a right to 20 per cent of production "at cost," and right of first refusal on the remaining 80 per cent. Venezuela would be guaranteed $19 US per barrel in royalties, regardless of the price of oil.

NABEP was formed out of Blue Energy, a company run by Florida oil and asphalt magnate Harry Sargeant III, a Trump golf partner and major GOP donor who did a lot of business with the Maduro regime (Maduro once called him "the only gringo I trust." )

But Sargeant sold his stake to Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who has been investigated for allegedly laundering embezzled Venezuelan money in several countries, but never charged.

Rubio defended Betancourt's involvement by saying he is not suspected of wrongdoing on U.S. territory, as U.S. media reported Trump administration pressure campaigns to drop European investigations.

A 'highly irregular' deal

Venezuelan Canadians in the oil industry have no illusions about the state of the industry they were forced to leave behind.

Jorge Robles, who spent his career in Venezuelan and Albertan oilfields, says people understand that Venezuela needs foreign investment and that it has to give something in return.

"I was prepared to have negotiations that were very uncomfortable and disadvantageous to Venezuela," he told CBC News.

Wright said on Wednesday that deals signed with Venezuela would increase oil production. (Fausto Torrealba/Reuters)

But he said there was something "highly irregular" about the way this deal was negotiated.

"The U.S. is there negotiating on behalf of the Venezuelan reserve, but to offer that to companies that belong to the United States. So it's an obvious conflict of interest," he said.

Robles said it was "really upsetting and concerning" that the administration is focusing on oil, rather than political prisoners.

He said he fears that any money Venezuela receives will merely be used by the chavista regime to further entrench itself.

Midterm voters may be true target

But the two oilmen also say that given the deal's cold reception in Venezuela, oil companies are unlikely to want to bet on its long-term survival, or on a country where the situation remains so uncertain.

"If we don't get to a situation where there is due process in Venezuela, freedom and people can walk on the street without fear, then don't expect any company to send people to Venezuela," said Robles.

They both said the announced deal appeared to be partly about convincing American voters in the run-up to the midterms that high gas prices will soon start dropping.

WATCH | How the deal could impact Alberta: What could massive U.S. and Venezuelan oil deal mean for Alberta? | Duration 1:50 The United States has made an agreement with Venezuela that would give it a massive stake in the country's vast oil reserves. But what does this mean for Alberta? CBC’s Nicole Healey has the details.

"It's just a lot of noise to try to influence votes in the States," said Carrillo, adding that the price of oil will respond far more to any reopening in the Strait of Hormuz than far-off plans for oil investment in the Orinoco Basin.

"The markets are not dumb," he said. "The markets are watching that."

Carrillo said he intends to return to Venezuela to offer his expertise to put the devastated oil industry back on its feet, but won't do so unless there is a deal ratified by a democratic Venezuelan government.

Fears of creeping colonization

Many Venezuelans have expressed fears of a creeping colonization of their country, in which the chavista dictatorship is maintained in power by the Trump administration as a subcontractor of its control.

"I do feel it's kind of happening in a very kind of smooth way," said Sarfatti. "And probably the earthquake is helping that to happen more just because we do need help, but not necessarily from a colonizing country."

The guardianship the White House has claimed over Venezuela, she said, "is definitely a level of taking over. You can see that when Venezuelan leaders who've been working for 20-something years to recover our country are just set aside."

The fear now for the Venezuelan opposition is that the Americans' lucrative deal with Rodriguez only gives Washington additional motives to keep her dictatorship in place.

Likewise the U.S. has little motive to demand the release of political prisoners who might challenge the legitimacy of the deal or the government that signed it.

"They were talking about releasing political prisoners, about freedom of press," Sarfatti said. "but then time passed by and Trump's true colours came out.

"We never expected from a country like the U.S., who has been the lead of democracy for so long, to behave the way it's behaving."

World.title: Gen Z entrepreneur builds connections with snail mail club
World.content:
Article content

The platform said Canadian searches for “snail mail” were up 169 per cent in July 2025, compared to a year earlier. That’s good news for Canada Post, which in recent years has been delivering less mail — including letters, cards, bills, and invoices — despite a rise in the number of Canadian addresses. Each household received an average of 246 pieces of letter mail in 2014. In 2023 that number was down to 124 pieces, according to the corporation’s financial report that year.

World.title: Colby Cosh: Is Alberta’s separatist movement already waning?
World.content:
Article content

It’s possible to be an Alberta separatist who wants to delay political action until the executive branch of the United States gets over its mood of belligerence and rediscovers, or is shown, the rule of law. It’s possible to be an Alberta separatist who wants to wait and see whether an Albertan Liberal prime minister can follow through on reversing the gormless tendencies of the Trudeau Era. (Note: the poll gives that PM a slightly higher trust score than it does to the Opposition Leader, who is also an Albertan. Remember when the West wanted in?) It’s possible to be an Alberta separatist who just doesn’t like the dubious weirdos who have taken charge of the cause right now. And Alberta separatists should not have trouble understanding this: it’s the same pervasive, somewhat annoying and difficult nuance that has existed and manifested in Quebec for 60 years.

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.
