The route will strengthen Los Cabos’ air connectivity with the U.S. East Coast market — a key source of international tourists for the Baja California Sur destination.

These new routes will join planned winter seasonal services, including Vancouver-Mazatlán with Air Canada and Puebla-Chicago O’Hare with Volaris.

With reports from Northern Virginia Magazine and Grupo Aeroportuario de Chiapas

World.title: Sheinbaum touts Mexico’s trade position amid US tariff talks: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕯️ Sheinbaum addresses Atizapán family murders: The president called the killing of musician Jonathan Meléndez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker a “very sad, terrible situation.” She noted that two alleged perpetrators had been arrested and said the motive for the crime was a dispute between two families.

🏭 Mexico seeks lower US tariffs: Sheinbaum said her government is working hard to secure a better agreement with the Trump administration on tariffs affecting Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. Her remarks came after Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday.

💬 Sheinbaum discusses politics and AI with Petro in CDMX: Sheinbaum said former Colombian president Gustavo Petro spoke to her about a book he is writing on attempted influence over elections by “the international right.” She said they also spoke about artificial intelligence and its potential impacts. During the meeting, Sheinbaum said she outlined Mexico’s political context and invited the leftist politician to return for a talk at a federal historical institute.

Why today’s mañanera matters

A multiple homicide case and the United States’ trade barriers were among the significant issues President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke about at her Thursday morning press conference.

Official statistics — disputed by some — show that homicides have declined significantly during the term of the current government, but, violence remains a major problem in Mexico, where, on average, more than 48 people were murdered on a daily basis in the first seven months of 2026.

The killing of four people in a México state apartment this week has attracted more attention than many other homicides as one of the victims was a well-known musician.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments about her meeting on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, who served as the first leftist president of Colombia until his four-year term ended last month. As president, Petro held face-to-face talks with Sheinbaum on several occasions, including at Mexico’s National Palace in December 2024.

Sheinbaum comments on multiple homicide in México state

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about the murder of a family in Atizapán de Zaragoza, a municipality in México state that is part of greater Mexico City.

Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker were found dead on Tuesday in an apartment in an affluent area of Atizapán. A golden retriever was also found dead in the apartment.

Sheinbaum said she was briefed on the case on Wednesday.

“It’s a very sad, terrible situation,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that arrests have been made in connection with the crime. Authorities on Wednesday reported the arrest of two men who are alleged to have committed the murders.

Sheinbaum said that the murders were related to a dispute between two families. She also said that the México state government is supporting relatives of the victims and that the federal Interior Ministry is also ready to provide assistance.

Mexico seeks reduction of US tariffs on steel, aluminum and vehicles

Asked about the meeting on Wednesday between Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Sheinbaum said her government is working very hard to reach an agreement with the Trump administration that results in a reduction of the U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

“There is ongoing dialogue,” she said, noting that Ebrard is a frequent visitor to Washington, D.C.

“… We’re seeking the best possible agreement for Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. “… We’re doing well and we hope to be able to reach a beneficial agreement.”

Sheinbaum reiterated that Mexico is among the “best-positioned countries” in terms of trade with the United States, as its exports — most of which enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA free trade pact — are subject to lower tariffs than those from other nations.

“The majority of [Mexican] goods that are exported to the United States don’t have tariffs, but we want an even better agreement on steel, aluminum and automobiles,” she said.

Sheinbaum summarizes her meeting with Gustavo Petro, former president of Colombia

Asked about her meeting in Mexico City on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, Sheinbaum told reporters that the ex-president of Colombia spoke to her about a book he is writing.

She said that Petro, in the book, “touches on some issues that we’ve spoken about here.”

“But obviously it’s from his perspective,” Sheinbaum said. “… It has to do with the use of digital platforms [e.g. social media] to externally influence election results.”

She said Petro is writing about how the “international right” has organized itself to exert influence in different parts of the world.

Acabo de salir de hablar con la presidenta de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, @Claudiashein pic.twitter.com/e9msOf0CZd — Gustavo Petro (@petrogustavo) September 2, 2026

Earlier this year, Sheinbaum agreed with a reporter who suggested that an “international media” campaign designed to “impose narratives in Mexico” was taking place.

“There are a lot of people who have come to an agreement. This international right-wing movement we talk about moves in many places in the world and there are a lot of people who are betting on the defeat and failure of the Mexican government for ideological reasons and for political reasons,” she said on May 13.

On Thursday morning, Sheinbaum said that Petro is also writing about artificial intelligence and “the impact it could have at a national and international level.”

“We spoke about that, about the reflection he’s making in his book [and] I spoke to him about Mexico,” she said.

“[I told him that] our perspective is very different because here there is a large majority of Mexican people who support the transformation and the results we’ve achieved, and the people are happy with the work the government is doing,” Sheinbaum said.

“… They were some of the issues we spoke about,” she said, adding that she had invited Petro to return to Mexico to speak at the National Institute of Historic Studies of the Revolutions in Mexico.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: How to move money into Mexico from abroad without losing a bundle
World.content:
Most foreigners who relocate to Mexico arrive with most of their liquid assets sitting in a bank outside of Mexico’s borders. Before long, they are wondering about the best ways to move money from there to here to fund everyday expenses.

Whether it is money for rent and groceries, or a big-ticket item like a car or real estate, finding the most economical way or ways to move money across borders is not necessarily intuitive.

Below are the best — and worst — ways to accomplish this boring but necessary task.

Factors to consider before choosing a money transfer method

If you’re new to living abroad and have never done a cross-border money transfer, it is natural to feel fear and uncertainty about the safety and reliability of the transaction. And that is before you even consider cost.

The truth is, there is no “one size fits all” best method for moving money across borders. The best option depends on three things. How much you need to transfer? How soon you need the money? In what form do you want the funds?

The best ways to move small amounts across borders

When you have no bank account in Mexico and only need to access small sums from a foreign bank account, a Mexican bank ATM is your best option.

At a Mexican ATM, two different fees are applied to cash withdrawals. The first is a “convenience” fee, which ranges from 30 to 200 pesos per transaction. The second is the exchange rate commission applied when converting money from your home country’s currency to Mexican pesos.

As a non-bank customer, it is wise to test out different brands and locations. BBVA and HSBC tend to charge larger transaction fees to out-of-network users, while fees from Banorte and Santander are typically lower. Even within the same bank, ATMs in touristy areas often have higher fees than those in non-touristy neighborhoods.

While the ATM’s convenience fee cannot be avoided (though some U.S. banks will refund them), foreigners can avoid exchange rate markups at Mexican ATMs that can reach 6%. To protect yourself, always decline the Mexican bank’s conversion rate when withdrawing funds. The transaction will still process, but at your foreign bank’s exchange rate, which is almost certainly better.

In addition, take care to avoid standalone ATMs that are not tied to major banks, such as those in convenience stores, gas stations and other public venues. These are easy for criminals to tamper with and can also apply exorbitant fees.

How to move large sums across borders

Because the daily limit on ATM withdrawals in Mexico is about 11,000 pesos (US $645), there are times when this method will not meet your needs. For transfers exceeding ATM limits — such as US $1,000 to US $50,000 — electronic transfers (also called EFTs or ACH transfers) are the most cost-effective option.

Money transfer specialists like Wise, Remitly, Revolut and others handle a large volume of these transactions. But they are not all the same.

Transaction fees and wait times from one provider to the next vary widely, so it pays to shop around. While Wise can move US $1,000 to Mexico in seconds, with Remitly it could take three to four days. Exchange rate markups with these services can range from 0.8% to as much as 3% over the mid-market rate.

In addition, while most who use these services have a Mexican bank account to receive the funds, some providers like Western Union or Remitly allow senders to pick up cash at Mexican retail chains like Oxxo or Walmart. Others give customers the option to send money to a mobile wallet.

Besides helping foreigners living in Mexico access their funds in overseas banks, these service providers also handle a large share of the nearly US $62 billion in annual remittances sent home by Mexicans working abroad.

In rare cases when a foreigner might need to move an even larger sum of money to Mexico — such as US $500,000 for a home purchase — a standard money transfer service may not suffice.

Among top specialists, platforms like OFX and Wise can accommodate high-value transactions of this size. Even when they do, it is common to experience longer wait times.

International wire transfers

In these cases, the most reliable option is an international bank-to-bank wire.

International wires use the SWIFT payment system and a unique code for each banking institution, ensuring funds reach the correct destination. They may also require a phone call to verify the sender’s identity.

This method is considered the safest of all, though keep in mind that international wires may take several days to reach the destination bank. Additionally, traditional banks add big exchange rate markups (2% or more) and fees (up to US $50) on international wires.

Due to these shortcomings, international wires only make sense when an ACH transfer does not satisfy your needs, or when you insist on having a person assist you for peace of mind.

How to lose a lot of money while moving it into Mexico

Convert physical cash you carried to Mexico

This old-school method of moving cash across borders carries some of the highest commissions. At money changers in Guadalajara, exchange rate markups can reach 5%. At a kiosk inside the arrivals hall of an international airport, it is even worse, with markups reaching 10% to 20% over the spot exchange rate. These places tend to target desperate travelers and should be used only in an emergency.

Choose a money transfer service without comparing fees first

Because quality and reliability are a moving target with money transfer specialists, it pays to collect multiple quotes and periodically check customer reviews. That said, some providers routinely fall short, hitting customers with 3% or higher fees, such as PayPal and its subsidiary, Xoom.

Fail to manage exchange rate risk

For anyone who needs to send large sums of money to Mexico with an uncertain time horizon, managing exchange rate risk is critical. In the case of a foreigner buying Mexican property with funds sourced from abroad, if the peso strengthens against your home currency while you wait months for paperwork to finish, you could end up paying tens of thousands more than intended.

Fortunately, there are now services for this, too.

With MexEdge, it is possible to purchase a forward contract for a fee of about 1% that locks in the current exchange rate for up to two years. While forward contracts do not make sense for small transactions, the savings can add up on larger ones.

Conclusion

No matter which service you use, U.S. citizens should know that banks and money transfer services are legally obligated to report cross-border transfers exceeding US $10,000 under the Bank Secrecy Act. The law applies to U.S. financial firms as well as foreign banks with branches in the U.S. to combat money laundering.

For foreigners living in Mexico without a local bank account, many of the best money transfer options will not be available. It is a key reason to consider opening a local account, which will be the topic of the next article in the “Mexico and My Money” series.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Ariane 6’s First Geostationary Mission Lifts Off From French Guiana
World.content:
FRENCH GUIANA · SPACE INDUSTRY

Key Facts — What happened Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket flew its first geostationary orbit mission from French Guiana on August 27, 2026.

— How big The rocket carried MTG-I2, a European weather satellite, into an elliptical orbit reaching 36,000 km above Earth at its highest point.

— What it means The success proves Ariane 6 can handle high-value weather and telecom satellite missions.

— The catch No local employment or revenue figures for French Guiana were disclosed with this mission.

— Who it affects The launch base near Kourou, French Guiana, serves as Europe’s main spaceport on South America’s coast.

— What comes next The satellite now moves under its own power to its final operational position.

Ariane 6’s first geostationary mission from French Guiana proves the rocket can handle Europe’s most valuable satellites. That keeps Kourou at the center of a busy 2026 launch year.

Ariane 6 lifts off from French Guiana’s spaceport, the Centre Spatial Guyanais, near Kourou. (Photo: Ariane 6 with P160C Boosters.jpg — ESA – S. Corvaja (CC BY-SA 3.0 igo), via Wikimedia Commons)

Ariane 6 flew its first mission to geostationary transfer orbit from French Guiana on Thursday, August 27, 2026. The launch happened at 5:11 p.m. local time, from the Centre Spatial Guyanais, or CSG, Europe’s spaceport near Kourou.

The mission, designated VA270, carried MTG-I2, the second Meteosat Third Generation Imager weather satellite. Both CNES, France’s national space agency, and Arianespace, the launch operator, declared the flight fully successful.

A Milestone for the Rocket

This was Ariane 6’s first flight to geostationary transfer orbit, or GTO. GTO is an elliptical orbit that leads toward a satellite’s final position.

Thirty-six minutes after liftoff, MTG-I2 separated from the rocket. It then used its own power to reach a final spot 36,000 km above Earth.

CNES called the mission a milestone that “confirms Ariane 6’s capacity to serve geostationary orbit.” That capacity matters because weather and telecom satellites, among the most valuable payloads in the industry, all need this orbit.

A Busy Year at Kourou

The flight was Ariane 6’s ninth overall and its eighth commercial mission. It was also the fourth Ariane 6 launch from French Guiana in 2026.

The mission was also the sixth flight in the two-booster Ariane 62 configuration. That configuration uses solid-fuel boosters known as the P120C.

That cadence marks a sharp turnaround for the CSG. This outlet has covered the trend closely through 2026.

A June piece asked who profits from Europe’s busiest new rocket. Another reported on Spain’s PLD Space investing $41 million in a private launch pad there.

What the Satellite Will Do

MTG-I2 was developed by the European Space Agency (ESA) for EUMETSAT, Europe’s meteorological satellite agency, and built by Thales Alenia Space. Officials say it will strengthen Europe’s next-generation weather satellite system, improving early detection of severe storms, weather forecasting, and climate monitoring.

The satellite is the second of its kind in a planned series. Its predecessor, MTG-I1, launched in 2022 and became operational in 2024.

Local Impact Remains Unclear

No specific employment, revenue, or GDP figures for French Guiana’s local economy were disclosed in connection with this mission. Those numbers were not made public, so this launch’s local economic effect remains unknown.

What is clear is the CSG’s standing as the launch base France and ESA use for their rockets. Officials describe it as “Europe’s spaceport,” and the rising launch rate in 2026 keeps that role central to the region’s identity.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Centre Spatial Guyanais?

The Centre Spatial Guyanais, or CSG, is Europe’s spaceport, located near Kourou in French Guiana. France and the European Space Agency use it as the launch base for their rockets.

What is geostationary transfer orbit?

Geostationary transfer orbit, or GTO, is an elliptical orbit used as a stepping stone toward a satellite’s final position. It is the orbit needed for high-value weather and telecom satellites.

What satellite did Ariane 6 carry on this mission?

Ariane 6 carried MTG-I2, the second Meteosat Third Generation Imager weather satellite. It was developed by the European Space Agency for EUMETSAT and built by Thales Alenia Space.

Why was this launch a milestone?

This was Ariane 6’s first mission to geostationary transfer orbit, proving it can serve high-value satellites. CNES said it confirms Ariane 6’s capacity to serve geostationary orbit.

How many times has Ariane 6 launched from French Guiana?

This was Ariane 6’s ninth flight overall and its fourth launch from French Guiana in 2026 alone. It was also the rocket’s eighth commercial mission.

Sources: Arianespace newsroom and launch kit, CNES (Centre National d’Études Spatiales), Centre Spatial Guyanais (CSG) official site, European Space Agency (ESA) media materials.

World.title: Suriname Gas Prices Rise as EBS Director Rebukes Parliament
World.content:
SURINAME · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Suriname’s state utility, EBS, raised cooking-gas cylinder prices on September 1, 2026.

— How big A 28-lb cylinder now costs SRD 535 (about US$14.12), up from SRD 508 (about US$13.40).

— What it means Households face higher costs from a scheduled quarterly price increase.

— The clash EBS’s own director publicly told parliament to pay its unpaid electricity bill.

— The family tie That director, Leo Brunswijk, is the younger brother of Ronnie Brunswijk, parliament’s vice chairman.

— Who it affects Households buying cooking gas, and taxpayers who cover parliament’s power bills.

— What comes next The 14-kg cylinder faces one more scheduled increase, on December 1, 2026.

Suriname’s state utility, EBS, raised cooking-gas prices this week in a scheduled quarterly increase. Days later, the utility’s own director publicly clashed with parliament over its unpaid electricity bills.

Suriname’s state energy company, N.V. Energiebedrijven Suriname, known as EBS, raised cooking-gas cylinder prices on September 1. The increase follows a scheduled quarterly adjustment set under a 2023 ministerial decree.

The same week, EBS’s own director publicly clashed with parliament over its unpaid electricity bills. The director is Leo Brunswijk, the younger brother of a senior parliamentary leader.

Cooking-Gas Prices Rise Again

The 28-lb propane cylinder now costs SRD 535 (about US$14.12), up from SRD 508 (about US$13.40). The 14-kg composite cylinder now costs SRD 556.50 (about US$14.68), up from SRD 530 (about US$13.98).

EBS says the increase is part of a subsidy phase-out that began in 2023. The 28-lb cylinder has now reached its final price under the current decree.

The 14-kg cylinder will rise once more, on December 1, 2026. Households that buy the smaller cylinder face one final increase before the year ends.

Prices have climbed in steps since the subsidy phase-out began. The 28-lb cylinder cost just SRD 441 (about US$11.64) as recently as March 2026, according to Suriname Herald.

EBS Director Rebukes Parliament

EBS General Director Leo Brunswijk hit back at parliament in comments published Thursday. Lawmakers had criticized the utility’s performance, including recent outages.

Brunswijk told the broadcaster Sun Web TV that lawmakers should look at their own conduct first. His message was blunt: “DNA, pay your electricity bill.”

Brunswijk said parliament runs several buildings with heavy air-conditioning use. He said parliament still owes EBS money despite that spending, according to Suriname Herald.

He challenged lawmakers to reveal when they last paid and how much they owe. Suriname’s parliament has not made that figure public.

A Family Tie Inside Parliament

Leo Brunswijk is the younger brother of Ronnie Brunswijk, a well-known Surinamese politician. Ronnie Brunswijk served as the country’s vice president from 2020 to 2025.

He now serves as vice chairman of Suriname’s parliament, De Nationale Assemblee, known as the DNA. That makes him a leader of the very body his brother just criticized.

This family connection has drawn conflict-of-interest concerns in Suriname before. There is no evidence Ronnie Brunswijk was involved in this week’s dispute over parliament’s bill.

Cost of Living Pressures

The gas price increase adds to household costs across Suriname. Many families rely on propane cylinders for daily cooking.

For a typical household, the 28-lb cylinder now costs SRD 27 more than before, about US$0.71. That adds up over a full year of quarterly increases.

The dispute over parliament’s unpaid bill raises separate questions about accountability. It remains unclear whether lawmakers will respond to Brunswijk’s challenge.

More: Suriname news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is EBS in Suriname?

EBS is the abbreviation for N.V. Energiebedrijven Suriname, the state-owned energy company that supplies electricity and cooking gas across Suriname. It sets regulated prices for propane cylinders under a ministerial decree.

How much does cooking gas cost in Suriname now?

As of September 1, 2026, a 28-lb cylinder costs SRD 535 (about US$14.12), up from SRD 508 (about US$13.40). A 14-kg cylinder costs SRD 556.50 (about US$14.68), up from SRD 530 (about US$13.98).

Why did EBS’s director criticize parliament?

EBS General Director Leo Brunswijk publicly told Suriname’s parliament, De Nationale Assemblee (DNA), to pay its unpaid electricity bill. The exact amount parliament owes has not been disclosed.

Are the Brunswijks related?

Yes, EBS General Director Leo Brunswijk is the younger brother of Ronnie Brunswijk. Ronnie Brunswijk is a former vice president who now leads parliament as vice chairman.

Will cooking gas prices rise again in Suriname?

The September 1 increase was the last scheduled increase for the 28-lb cylinder under the current decree. The 14-kg cylinder faces one more scheduled increase, on December 1, 2026.

Sources: Starnieuws (Sept 1, 2026), Suriname Herald (Sept 2-3, 2026; June 1, 2026; March 4, 2026), De West (Sept 3, 2026), Government of Suriname (gov.sr), Central Bank of Suriname.

World.title: Guyana Barima Ferry Inquiry Makes First Site Visit, Critics Seek Answers
World.content:
GUYANA · INVESTIGATION

Key Facts — What happened Guyana’s Commission of Inquiry made its first site visit to the MV Barima accident area on September 2.

— The scale The July 18 ferry sinking killed at least 72 people, with about 31 still unaccounted for.

— What it means The inquiry is gathering documents and witnesses, but no public hearing date has been set.

— The catch Opposition leader Amanza Walton-Desir says key questions remain about the site survey and vessel recovery.

— Who it affects Families of the dead and missing, plus all Guyanese who depend on coastal ferry travel.

— What comes next Hearings will be held at the Arthur Chung Conference Centre once the schedule is announced.

Six and a half weeks after Guyana’s deadliest maritime disaster, investigators made their first site visit — but questions remain.

A river ferry approaches Bartica, Guyana. The MV Barima capsized on a similar coastal route on July 18, 2026. (Photo: Turani approaching Bartica – panoramio.jpg — Marco Farouk Basir (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons)

Guyana’s Commission of Inquiry (CoI) made its first preliminary visit to the MV Barima accident site on Wednesday, September 2. The visit came about six and a half weeks after the ferry capsized, killing at least 72 people.

The five-member panel is chaired by Belizean Justice Godfrey Philip Smith. It surveyed the wreck site off the Essequibo Coast, where the 87-year-old ferry sank on the night of July 18.

The Commission is gathering documents on the ferry’s seaworthiness and how the crew operated it, according to a report from Demerara Waves.

It is also collecting records from Guyana’s Maritime Administration Department, known as MARAD. Other sources include the Transport and Harbours Department and the Guyana Defence Force’s Coast Guard and Air Corps.

A Slow-Moving Investigation

The Commission is compiling a list of potential witnesses and preparing a hearing schedule. No public start date has been announced yet.

Hearings will eventually be held at the Arthur Chung Conference Centre in Greater Georgetown.

The disaster remains Guyana’s worst maritime tragedy. The official manifest listed 133 people, but authorities believe roughly 179 were actually aboard.

That gap points to possible overloading of the vessel. Seventy-six people were rescued, and 72 bodies have been recovered so far.

That leaves about 31 people still unaccounted for.

Opposition Demands Answers

On Thursday, September 3, Amanza Walton-Desir, leader of the Forward Guyana Movement, issued a public statement. She was responding to the Commission’s first substantial public update.

Walton-Desir welcomed the update, which included a notice inviting public submissions. But she said it left major questions unanswered.

She asked who conducted the preliminary site survey and which commissioners took part. She also asked what technical experts and methods were used.

Walton-Desir questioned whether investigators actually examined the sunken ferry, or only visited the general area where it went down.

She pressed for details on any written records or photographs from the visit. She also asked how any evidence was secured.

Walton-Desir asked what role MARAD played in the investigation. She also asked what has been done to recover the vessel or find remaining victims.

Concerns Over Accountability

Walton-Desir’s most pointed remark targeted the government’s handling of the process. “The President cannot use that process as a constitutional waiting room in which ministerial responsibility is suspended until the Commission reports,” she said, according to the Guyana Standard.

President Irfaan Ali announced the independent Commission of Inquiry in late July. It will examine pre-departure procedures, cargo handling, emergency response, and possible regulatory violations.

The panel was sworn in on July 30. Justice Smith chairs it, and Javed Shadick serves as Secretary.

The inquiry must also recommend maritime safety reforms for Guyana. Coastal communities across the country depend heavily on ferry connections.

The ferry’s captain and first engineer tested positive for marijuana after the accident. Three men, including the captain, have already been charged with murder in the case.

What Happens Next

The Commission has not yet announced when public hearings will begin. Its witness list also remains under preparation.

The panel is expected to release more details on its schedule soon. It will also explain how the public can make submissions to the inquiry.

For the families of the dead and missing, the wait continues. The gap between the manifest and the estimated number aboard has fueled public anger.

Many suspect the ferry was overloaded on its regular Georgetown-to-Port Kaituma route.

More: Guyana news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the MV Barima ferry to sink?

The exact cause is still under investigation, but authorities believe the ferry may have been overloaded. The official manifest listed 133 people, while authorities now estimate about 179 were actually aboard.

How many people died in the MV Barima disaster?

At least 72 bodies have been recovered, with about 31 people still unaccounted for. Seventy-six people were rescued from the water.

Who is leading the Commission of Inquiry?

The five-member Commission is chaired by Justice Godfrey Philip Smith of Belize, with Javed Shadick serving as Secretary. The panel was sworn in on July 30, 2026.

When will public hearings begin?

No public hearing start date has been announced yet. Hearings will be held at the Arthur Chung Conference Centre in Greater Georgetown once the schedule is set.

What concerns has the opposition raised about the inquiry?

Amanza Walton-Desir of the Forward Guyana Movement has asked who conducted the site survey and whether the sunken vessel was actually examined. She also questioned how evidence was secured and what role MARAD played in the investigation.

Sources: Demerara Waves, Guyana Standard, UPI, Jamaica Observer, The St Kitts Nevis Observer.

World.title: Argentina Airport Strike May Resume September 7-8
World.content:
Argentina · LABOUR

Key Facts — What happened Airport workers postponed a strike that was set to begin on September 3.

— New dates ATE has floated September 7-8 for a new stoppage but has not formally confirmed it.

— Who is striking ATE members at ANAC, including ground staff and firefighters; air traffic controllers are not involved.

— Why Workers say the government has not paid wage increases it previously agreed to.

— The catch No verified figure exists for flights or passengers affected.

— What comes next ATE awaits a Labour Ministry hearing on essential-service rules before deciding whether to strike.

Argentina’s airport strike was postponed just before it began on September 3. The union ATE has warned it could resume on September 7 and 8 if wage talks fail.

Aerolíneas Argentinas and JetSMART aircraft at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery in Buenos Aires. The airport strike may resume on September 7 and 8. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Argentina’s airport strike could resume on September 7 and 8, after being postponed just before it began. The union ATE says it will wait for a Labour Ministry hearing before deciding whether to proceed.

Strike Postponed After Government Warning

Argentina’s airport workers called off a planned 48-hour strike just before it was due to start on September 3. The government had ordered the union to guarantee at least 75% of services during the stoppage.

The State Workers Association (ATE), which represents state employees, suspended the action on September 3. It requested a hearing with the Labour Ministry to discuss wages and the strike’s legality.

New Dates: Still Not Confirmed

The Buenos Aires Herald reported on September 2 that a new stoppage was expected for September 7-8. The stoppage would use the same two daily windows as the original plan, 09:00-12:00 and 18:00-21:00.

As of September 4, the union had not formally confirmed the new dates. No outlet has reported that ATE has dropped the plan either.

The strike could still be called off if the Labour Ministry hearing produces an agreement. It could also go ahead exactly as first floated.

Who Is ATE

ATE stands for Asociación de Trabajadores del Estado, the State Workers Association, one of Argentina’s largest public-sector unions. Its general secretary is Rodolfo Aguiar.

The union is organizing this strike through its section at the National Civil Aviation Administration, known as ANAC. ANAC is the government body that oversees airports and air navigation in Argentina.

ATE members work at more than 27 airports nationwide, including Ezeiza and Aeroparque Jorge Newbery in Buenos Aires. The union has raised similar strike threats at ANAC earlier in 2026.

Which Airport Workers Are, and Are Not, Striking

ATE members covered by this action include ground traffic controllers, firefighters, healthcare staff, inspectors and administrative personnel. These are ANAC employees, not airline staff.

Air traffic controllers, pilots and cabin crew belong to separate unions and are not part of this strike, the Buenos Aires Herald reported. Ground-handling and airline staff outside ANAC are also not involved.

The Wage Dispute

ATE says the government has not paid wage increases, including extra-paritario items, that a previous Transport Secretary agreed to. The union also wants sector-wide pay talks for ANAC staff reopened.

ATE says wages have lost more than 40% of their purchasing power since President Javier Milei took office. The union also wants more funding for operational tasks and airport oversight.

No specific peso figure or percentage increase has been confirmed as of September 4. ATE says the conflict will deepen if no negotiation table is opened.

The Legal Basis for the 75% Rule

Argentine law requires unions to guarantee minimum service levels during strikes affecting essential activities. That framework comes from Law 25,877, as amended by Law 27,802.

The reform set the minimum at no less than 75% for services declared essential. National air navigation falls into that category.

ANAC applied the rule to aviation strikes through Resolución 173/2026, issued in March 2026. That resolution sets out how the 75% minimum must be calculated and enforced.

How the 75% Rule Works in Practice

The resolution measures the 75% minimum against scheduled flights during the affected time window. It does not simply guarantee three of every four individual flights.

Some flights are always exempt from a stoppage: official, medical and humanitarian flights, plus organ-transport flights. Aircraft already in the air cannot be grounded.

Routes with only one daily frequency must still be served. These carve-outs aim to limit the strike’s impact on essential travel.

Why the September Plan Was Ruled Non-Compliant

The government said ATE’s original plan for September 3-4 did not meet this threshold, according to EFE. Mercedes Cabezas, ATE’s assistant general secretary, said the Labour Ministry called the measure illegal.

The ministry argued the plan did not guarantee the required “essentiality” of the service. That finding is what pushed ATE to postpone the strike.

Passengers boarding at Aeroparque. A minimum-service rule limits any stoppage. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

No Verified Impact Numbers

No verified figure exists for the number of flights or passengers affected. Reports mention possible delays and cancellations, but no exact counts.

The original strike was suspended, so operations on September 3-4 were normal. If the new strike goes ahead, its impact will depend on how many workers take part.

What Aeroparque and Ezeiza Passengers Should Expect

Aeroparque Jorge Newbery and Ezeiza are Argentina’s two main Buenos Aires hubs and would likely feel the heaviest impact. Aeroparque handles most domestic routes, while Ezeiza handles most international flights.

Under the 75% rule, most scheduled flights should still operate even if the strike goes ahead. Delays are more likely to cluster around the start and end of each stoppage window.

Travelers flying on September 7 or 8 should check with their airline for updates. Arriving early is advisable during the 09:00-12:00 and 18:00-21:00 windows.

How the Strike Was Postponed at the Last Minute

On the morning of September 3, the strike was set to start at 09:00. ATE postponed it minutes before that time, according to La Nación.

Mercedes Cabezas said the Labour Ministry had notified the union that the plan did not guarantee the required essential-service level. An ATE source said the measures “quedaron postergadas hasta el lunes” — postponed until Monday.

ATE called the postponement a gesture of goodwill toward the government. The union said it would hold assemblies at airport facilities on September 4 to decide its next steps.

The Role of the Ministry of Labour

ATE requested a hearing with the Ministry of Labour before postponing the strike, according to Infobae. The union wants that hearing to define the scope of aviation’s “essentiality” before any new stoppage.

The ministry can also issue a “conciliación obligatoria,” a mandatory conciliation order that forces both sides to negotiate. Such orders typically suspend strike action for a fixed period, often 15 days.

As of September 4, no such order had been reported for this dispute. Both sides remain under pressure to reach a deal before September 7.

A Precedent: The March 2026 Dispute

This is not the first time in 2026 that ATE has threatened a strike at ANAC over the same wage claim. In March, the government issued a formal conciliación obligatoria that halted a similar 27-airport strike planned for March 18-24.

Some headlines that month described the dispute as involving air traffic controllers. The union involved was again ATE, representing ground and support staff, not the controllers who manage aircraft in flight.

Aguiar said at the time that the underlying wage claim remained unresolved. That same claim is now driving the September dispute.

What Happens Next

As of September 4, talks between ATE and the government continue. The Labour Ministry has not announced a formal conciliation order for this dispute.

ATE has warned the conflict will deepen if no negotiation table is opened, a warning reported by La Gaceta on September 1. The strike could still be called off, or could go ahead as planned.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the airport strike postponed?

The government said ATE’s strike plan did not meet the legally required 75% minimum service level. The union postponed the action and requested a hearing with the Labour Ministry.

When is the new airport strike scheduled?

ATE has floated September 7 and 8, in the same 09:00-12:00 and 18:00-21:00 windows. As of September 4 the union had not formally confirmed the dates.

Which airports are affected?

The strike covers more than 27 airports, including Ezeiza and Aeroparque. These are the main airports serving Buenos Aires.

Will my flight be canceled?

It depends on the timing. The government requires at least 75% of services to keep running, so most flights should proceed even if the strike goes ahead.

Sources: Buenos Aires Herald; Infobae; La Nación; EFE; 0223; La Gaceta.

World.title: El Salvador Wins IMF Staff-Level Agreement Worth US$140 Million
World.content:
El Salvador · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened IMF staff and El Salvador reached a staff-level agreement on 3 September 2026.

— How big The deal could unlock about US$140 million, pending board approval.

— The catch The money is not paid yet; board sign-off and prior actions are needed.

— Who it hits El Salvador’s government and its Bitcoin policy are directly affected.

— What comes next The IMF board must approve the agreement before any funds are released.

The International Monetary Fund and El Salvador have agreed on a staff-level deal. It could release about US$140 million once the board approves.

The IMF headquarters in Washington. El Salvador has reached a staff-level agreement worth about US$140 million. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

El Salvador has reached an IMF deal that could bring about US$140 million in new funding. The staff-level agreement, announced on 3 September 2026, still needs approval from the IMF’s executive board.

What the IMF Deal Means

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and El Salvador have reached a staff-level agreement. This is a technical step, not a final payment.

A staff-level agreement means IMF experts and the country’s officials have agreed on a plan. The IMF’s executive board must still approve it.

IMF missions negotiate this kind of agreement after reviewing a country’s economic data on site. Staff then write a report for the Executive Board to consider.

Details of the Agreement

The agreement covers the combined second and third reviews of El Salvador’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF). This is a 40-month loan programme.

If approved, El Salvador could access about US$140 million. That is equal to SDR 101.96 million, the IMF’s unit of account.

The full EFF programme is worth about US$1.4 billion, equal to SDR 1,033.92 million. That is roughly 360 percent of El Salvador’s IMF quota.

Board Approval Still Pending

The IMF says the deal is ‘subject to approval by the IMF Executive Board.’ Disbursement also depends on completing agreed prior actions.

Prior actions are specific steps the country must take before the money is released. They are part of the conditions of the loan.

Bitcoin Commitments

The IMF said El Salvador’s Bitcoin accumulation since 27 June 2025 came from private donations. No public funds were used for that accumulation.

IMF staff said no further Bitcoin accumulation beyond documented donations is expected. The Fund did not describe this as a formal pledge by El Salvador.

El Salvador held about 7,762 Bitcoin in its reserves as of early September 2026. Acceptance of Bitcoin by businesses became voluntary under a 2025 legal change.

Chivo Wallet Changes

Public participation in the Chivo Bitcoin wallet has been reduced. Most ownership and control have moved to a private operator.

This change is part of the understandings with the IMF. It aims to reduce the public sector’s role in crypto activities.

The December 2024 agreement had called for El Salvador to sell or wind down Chivo. The government instead transferred majority control to a private firm, keeping a minority stake.

Regulatory Reforms

El Salvador and the IMF agreed to modernize the legal and regulatory framework for digital assets. They also plan to strengthen governance for public crypto holdings.

These reforms are meant to manage risks. They are part of the conditions tied to the IMF deal.

IMF staff also list the reforms under the programme’s wider financial-sector stability goals. They sit alongside the separate fiscal and governance conditions.

What Is the Extended Fund Facility?

The Extended Fund Facility (EFF) is an IMF loan programme for countries with balance-of-payments problems. It typically runs three to four years, with repayment stretched over four-and-a-half to ten years.

El Salvador’s EFF is a 40-month programme. The staff-level agreement of 3 September 2026 covers its second and third reviews.

Those reviews check whether the country has met the conditions set in the programme.

What Are Special Drawing Rights?

Special Drawing Rights, or SDRs, are an international reserve asset created by the IMF. They are not a currency but can be exchanged for usable currencies like US dollars or euros.

The potential disbursement is about US$140 million, which equals SDR 101.96 million. That is about 0.4 percent of El Salvador’s 2025 GDP.

An SDR’s value is set daily from a basket of five major currencies. That basket includes the US dollar, euro, yuan, yen and British pound.

The port of Acajutla in El Salvador. The programme sets fiscal targets the country must keep meeting. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

How Does the IMF Board Approval Work?

The IMF Executive Board has 25 directors representing member countries. They meet to approve loan reviews and disbursements.

After a staff-level agreement, IMF staff prepare a Board report. The Board must approve it, and the country must complete prior actions before funds are released.

Board approval of a review also rests on measurable performance criteria, not only prior actions. Missing either can delay a disbursement.

What Are Prior Actions?

Prior actions are conditions El Salvador must meet before the IMF board approves the loan. For this agreement, the specific actions have not been published.

They differ from the numeric targets checked at each review. Prior actions must be finished before the Board vote, not after it.

What Did the IMF Mission Chief Say?

Reports reviewed for this article do not quote the IMF mission chief for El Salvador directly on this deal. The IMF’s mission chief for the country, Mr Torres, was not quoted by name in the 3 September 2026 statement.

IMF staff said ‘no further accumulation beyond documented donations is expected.’ That line appeared in the update issued on 3 September 2026.

What Happened Before This Agreement?

El Salvador adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021. The IMF was cautious about this policy.

In December 2024, IMF staff and El Salvador reached a staff-level agreement on the new EFF programme. The IMF Executive Board approved it on 26 February 2025.

The first review was completed in June 2025, releasing further funds. This staff-level agreement now covers the combined second and third reviews.

What Earlier Reviews Found

IMF staff reached agreement on the first review on 27 May 2025. The Executive Board completed it on 27 June 2025, releasing about US$118 million.

The IMF said most targets set for that first review were comfortably met. It also said the agreed structural benchmarks were progressing well.

The Fund reported El Salvador’s economy grew by about 3.9 percent in 2025. That growth outpaced earlier forecasts for the year.

Fiscal Targets and Governance Reforms

The programme targets a 3.5 percentage-point improvement in El Salvador’s primary fiscal balance over three years. It also calls for the country to rebuild its foreign currency reserves.

Governance conditions include stronger transparency and anti-corruption safeguards across public institutions. Pension reform and anti-money-laundering rules are also among the structural benchmarks.

El Salvador secured a separate US$500 million loan from the Inter-American Development Bank in March 2025, to support its budget. The IMF says its own programme should help catalyze over US$3.5 billion more from other lenders.

What Are the Next Steps?

The next step is for the IMF Executive Board to review the staff-level agreement. The Board will decide whether to approve the reviews and the disbursement.

The Board meeting’s exact timing is not yet announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a staff-level agreement with the IMF?

A staff-level agreement is a technical deal between IMF staff and a country’s authorities. It is not final until the IMF’s executive board approves it.

How much money could El Salvador receive?

El Salvador could receive about US$140 million. This amount is subject to board approval and prior actions.

What are the conditions of the IMF deal?

Conditions include fiscal targets and Bitcoin-related measures. The IMF expects no further Bitcoin accumulation beyond the private donations already recorded.

When will the money be paid?

The money will be paid only after the IMF board approves the agreement. The board meeting date has not been announced.

Sources: International Monetary Fund; CryptoBriefing; Crypto.news; Coinfomania.

World.title: US Sanctions Hit Cuba as Havana Widens Private Business
World.content:
Cuba · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened US Treasury sanctioned Raúl Castro’s grandson and five Cuban state firms on September 3, 2026.

— How big The action targets one individual and five entities, including a bank and an oil trader.

— The catch Cuba had just widened rules for private chains, but US sanctions still block most American business.

— Who it hits Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis, grandson of Raúl Castro, and state-linked firms in banking and energy.

— What comes next Designated persons and firms face asset freezes and US travel bans.

Washington hits Cuba’s state elite and key firms. Havana, days earlier, opened retail and restaurant chains to private owners.

The Capitolio in Havana. New US sanctions landed in the same week Cuba widened the space for private business. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

New US sanctions hit Cuba on September 3, 2026, naming a grandson of Raúl Castro and five state firms. They landed days after Havana widened the space for private business.

US Sanctions Target Castro Family and State Firms

On September 3, 2026, OFAC added Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis to its Specially Designated Nationals list. He is Raúl Castro’s grandson and the son of Alejandro Castro Espín, who Treasury sanctioned in June 2026.

The action also designated five Cuban state-linked entities: Banco Exterior de Cuba, Comercial Cupet S.A., Nicarotec, Cexni and Abapet. They operate in banking, oil trade, mining and nickel trade, according to OFAC’s published list.

The OFAC entry reads: “CASTRO CALIS, Fidel Ernesto, Cuba; DOB 16 May 1995; nationality Cuba; Gender Male.” It links him to his father, Alejandro Castro Espín.

Who Is Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis

Castro Calis was born on May 16, 1995, making him 31 years old. He is one of two known sons of Alejandro Castro Espín, a former Cuban intelligence and security adviser.

His father is a son of Raúl Castro, Cuba’s former president and Communist Party leader. That makes Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis a grandson of Raúl Castro, per the State Department fact sheet.

His brother, Raúl Alejandro Castro Calis, was designated alongside their father in June 2026. OFAC designated Castro Calis as an adult family member of a previously sanctioned official.

The Legal Authority Behind the Sanctions

The designation relies on Executive Order 14404, signed by President Trump in May 2026. It targets people responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security.

OFAC cited Section 2(a)(i)(I) of that order for Castro Calis. That clause covers adult family members of people already designated under the same order.

The same day, OFAC issued Cuba General License 4A. It authorizes certain transactions for third-country diplomatic and consular missions operating in Cuba.

What the Sanctions Mean

Being on the SDN list freezes U.S.-based assets and bars American citizens and companies from business with the designee. It also generally prohibits U.S. travel for the individual.

The U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place since 1962, restricts most trade and financial transactions between the two countries. These new designations extend that policy to specific people and companies linked to the Cuban government.

Foreign banks and firms that keep dealing with a designee can also face U.S. penalties. That secondary exposure often discourages business with sanctioned entities beyond U.S. borders.

The Five Sanctioned Entities Explained

Banco Exterior de Cuba, founded in 2000, handles foreign trade and international transactions for the Cuban state. Comercial Cupet S.A., founded in 1991, runs wholesale commerce for Cuba’s fuel sector.

Abapet imports machinery and equipment for the petroleum industry. Cexni handles wholesale trade linked to Cuba’s nickel industry, while Nicarotec provides support services for mining.

All five entities have operated for decades under different Cuban ministries. Each now appears on OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals list for the first time.

US Officials’ Statements

U.S. officials described the action as targeting Cuba’s elites, financial channels and resource-exploitation networks. The designations cover banking, energy and mining-linked entities, officials said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the designations reflect “President Trump’s unwavering vision for a free Cuba.” A State Department fact sheet named Castro Calis as a grandson of Raúl Modesto Castro Ruz.

Cuba’s Response to the Sanctions

Cuba’s government rejected the sanctions and called them illegitimate, CiberCuba reported. Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez defended the designated officials and companies in public remarks.

Cuban authorities had already framed their private-sector opening as a response to U.S. pressure. In July 2026, officials said the reforms aimed to help the economy withstand American sanctions, according to Arab News.

Cuba’s Private Business Opening

On August 28, 2026, Cuba published rules authorizing private retail and restaurant chains nationwide. The rules let micro, small and medium firms, cooperatives and foreign investors run one brand across multiple provinces.

The measures appeared in Decree 167 ‘On Domestic Trade’ and Resolution 15/2026, both in Official Gazette No. 69. Resolution 15/2026 also relaxed wholesale trade rules for private MIPYMES and non-agricultural cooperatives.

The new chains may sell goods in both Cuban pesos and foreign currency. Regulators require registered businesses to display permits and identify their operator type.

A vintage taxi on Havana’s Malecón. Cuba’s private sector has grown since 2021. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

When the New Trade Rules Take Effect

Decree 167 takes effect on September 4, 2026, seven days after publication. A companion measure, Decree 168, updates Cuba’s Central Commercial Registry for the new chains.

Resolution 23 sorts the new chains into three categories: high-end, mid-level and neighborhood stores. It also defines four activity types, including retail, dining, lodging and services.

Registered businesses must use electronic payment systems accessible to customers. The rules apply equally to state and private operators of retail and restaurant networks.

Broader Reforms in Cuba

The same Gazette issue carried Decree-Law 129/2026, which repealed a 1994 rule on seizing goods for trade-registry violations.

A separate Council of State decree-law, issued August 19 and published September 2, removed the 100-worker cap on private firms. It updated Decree-Laws 88, 89 and 90 of 2024.

Cuba’s Economic Reforms Package

The private-business rules form part of a wider package of 176 economic measures. Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel’s government approved the package in June 2026 to address the economic crisis.

Officials have floated further steps, including new forms of financial services, though details remain undefined. The package also revisits limits on how large private firms can grow.

MIPYMES Growth Since 2021

Cuba first allowed private micro, small and medium enterprises in August 2021, capped at 100 employees. By 2023, roughly 8,000 such firms had registered, according to published economic data.

That reform built on an earlier opening of self-employment in 2011. More than 400,000 Cubans had registered as entrepreneurs under that earlier system.

Private-sector employment has grown alongside those changes. It rose from about 23 percent of jobs in 2000 to 35 percent by 2023.

Cuba’s Economic Crisis

Cuba’s national power grid collapsed in March 2026, leaving millions without electricity for days. Blackouts, fuel shortages and medicine shortages have continued through the year, as reported by UPI.

Fuel shortages have disrupted transport and farming across the island for months. Cuba’s school year still began in late August despite the ongoing energy crisis, UPI reported.

The government has cited the crisis as a reason for its economic reforms. Officials say a wider private sector could ease shortages and create jobs.

Contrast Between US and Cuban Actions

The two announcements came within days of each other. Washington tightened pressure on Havana’s state sector while Havana moved to widen its private one.

Analysts say the timing appears coincidental, since Washington and Havana work on separate calendars.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the new US sanctions on Cuba?

On September 3, 2026, the US Treasury sanctioned Raúl Castro’s grandson and five state firms. They are added to the SDN list, freezing US assets and banning US business.

Who is Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis?

He is a grandson of Raúl Castro and son of Alejandro Castro Espín. He was born on May 16, 1995, and is now sanctioned as an adult family member.

What did Cuba announce on August 28, 2026?

Cuba published rules authorizing private businesses to operate retail and restaurant chains nationwide. This lets MIPYMES and cooperatives run multiple locations.

How do the sanctions affect ordinary Cubans?

The sanctions target specific individuals and firms, not the general population. However, they may worsen economic conditions by restricting trade and financial flows.

Sources: Arab News; CiberCuba; Deutsche Welle; Infobae; MENAFN; Reuters/Internazionale; RIA Novosti; UPI; U.S. Department of State; OFAC.

World.title: US Deportation Flight Lands 101 People in Haiti
World.content:
Haiti · MIGRATION

Key Facts — What happened US deported 101 people to Haiti on a charter flight on September 3, 2026.

— Where it landed The plane landed in Cap-Haïtien, not Port-au-Prince, due to security concerns.

— The pattern This was the third consecutive Thursday deportation flight, marking a shift to weekly flights.

— The catch The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Haiti at all.

— Who it hits Deportees include men and women, but whether children were aboard is not known.

— What comes next Nearly 200,000 people have been forcibly returned to Haiti in 2026 so far.

The United States flew more than 100 deportees to Haiti on Thursday, even as its own advisory tells Americans not to travel there. The flight landed in Cap-Haïtien, not the capital, because of gang violence.

Cap-Haïtien on Haiti’s northern coast, where the deportation flight landed. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The United States deported 101 people to Haiti on a charter flight on Thursday, September 3, 2026. This deportation flight to Haiti landed in Cap-Haïtien, not the capital, because of gang violence.

Flight Details and Weekly Pattern

The U.S. government deported 101 people to Haiti on a charter flight from Louisiana that landed in Cap-Haïtien, in northern Haiti. The flight was reported by The Associated Press (AP) on September 3, 2026.

Nicolas Mardochée, a Haiti foreign affairs coordinator, told AP that exactly 101 deportees were aboard.

Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor said this was the third straight Thursday flight to Haiti. It marked a shift from monthly to weekly deportation flights to Haiti.

Why Cap-Haïtien Instead of Port-au-Prince

Deportation flights were redirected from the capital due to security concerns. Port-au-Prince’s main airport has long been considered too dangerous for regular commercial service.

The U.S. State Department separately keeps a do-not-travel advisory covering the whole of Haiti, not just the capital.

As a result, the deportation flight to Haiti landed at Cap-Haïtien International Airport instead of Port-au-Prince.

Previous Deportation Flights

On Thursday, August 27, 2026, the U.S. deported 57 people to Haiti on a charter flight to Cap-Haïtien. Le Nouvelliste, cited by UPI, reported 51 men and 6 women, including children born in the U.S. and Brazil.

It was the second U.S. deportation flight to Haiti within eight days. The U.S. had already deported more than 160 people to Cap-Haïtien on August 20, 2026.

The exact composition of the September 3 flight, including whether children were aboard, is not known.

Temporary Protected Status and Its End

TPS is a U.S. program letting people from certain countries stay temporarily because of dangerous conditions at home. Around 350,000 Haitians held TPS before its termination.

A federal judge blocked the termination with a stay in February 2026, days before it was due to take effect. The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Mullin v. Doe on June 25, 2026, that courts cannot review such terminations.

A district court lifted its stay in August 2026, and TPS protections for Haitians then formally ended. Related litigation over the termination continues in the lower courts.

The Kenscoff Attack

On August 23-24, 2026, an overnight gang attack in Kenscoff killed at least 47 people, including three boys and two girls.

The same attack displaced about 2,647 people, according to the International Organization for Migration’s Displacement Tracking Matrix.

Security forces had cut violence in Kenscoff by 66% earlier in 2026, per UN figures. The August attack reversed much of that earlier progress.

Gang Violence in the Capital’s Plain

Gang clashes in La Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, including Cité Soleil, killed at least 613 people between March 6 and July 31, 2026.

BINUH, the UN mission in Haiti, said 375 more people were injured in the same five-month period. It reported the toll to the UN Security Council in an August briefing.

The same clashes displaced about 18,000 people around Cité Soleil, according to BINUH figures reported by Le Nouvelliste.

Displacement Crisis

As of May 2026, 1.47 million people were internally displaced in Haiti, per the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, citing BINUH data.

That is about 12% of Haiti’s population. Women and children make up more than half of everyone displaced.

The UN Security Council later cited about 1.5 million people displaced by June 30, 2026, including 751,000 children.

Forced Returns in 2026

In 2026’s first eight months, nearly 200,000 people were forcibly returned to Haiti, up about 10% from the same period in 2025.

Indrika Ratwatte, the UN’s acting humanitarian chief, told the Security Council of the total at an emergency briefing on August 28, 2026.

He said the figure was at least 20,000 more people than in the same period of 2025.

Cité Soleil in Port-au-Prince. Gang violence has displaced more than a million people. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

IACHR Concerns Over TPS

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights expressed concern about ending Temporary Protected Status for Haitians. It cited BINUH’s casualty and displacement figures directly.

The commission stressed the principle of non-refoulement, which bars returning people to places where their safety is threatened.

It said any such determination must be assessed considering the prevailing conditions on the ground in Haiti.

US Advisory Contradiction

The U.S. State Department advises Americans not to travel to Haiti at all, citing kidnapping, crime and civil unrest. Yet the U.S. continues to send deportees there on a weekly basis.

The deportation flight to Haiti landed in Cap-Haïtien, but the advisory itself covers the entire country, not just the capital.

The advisory sits at Level 4, the State Department’s highest warning category. It also lists terrorism among the risks Americans face there.

Reception at Cap-Haïtien

Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, director general of Haiti’s National Office of Migration, oversees deportee reception at the airport. He has said the office’s mission is to welcome migrants of forced return.

Officials give returnees up to $65 in cash along with food and water on arrival. Those unable to reach home the same day are given shelter overnight in secure spaces.

Gangs control routes to Haiti’s south, complicating onward travel for some deportees. The government has said it will help with family reunification where needed.

What Happens to Deportees

Local authorities and aid groups try to assist arriving deportees, but resources across Haiti remain badly stretched.

Many deportees have spent years in the U.S. and have no family or home left in Haiti. The Haitian government has repeatedly expressed concern about the growing influx.

Groups like the International Organization for Migration try to connect deportees with longer-term support and services.

Bahamas and Regional Returns

Other regional countries also return migrants to Haiti. On August 27, 2026, Bahamian authorities returned 104 Haitians to Cap-Haïtien.

That was the same day as a separate U.S. flight of 57 deportees, taking that single day’s combined arrivals above 160 people.

Rights groups have criticized this regional pattern of returns, arguing that conditions in Haiti remain unsafe for anyone.

US Policy and Legal Context

The U.S. government says it has the right to deport non-citizens who are in the country illegally. The end of TPS made many more Haitians newly eligible for deportation.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is responsible for carrying out deportation flights. DHS has not commented publicly on the specific flight of September 3.

Haiti is struggling with political instability, gang violence and a deepening humanitarian crisis. The arrival of deportees adds further pressure to an already strained system.

How Deportation Flights Are Tracked

Human Rights First, a group that monitors immigration enforcement, runs a tool called the ICE Flight Monitor. It tracks flights operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

This information helps the public see how often deportation flights happen and where they go.

The dashboard has tracked ICE flight routes and deportation patterns since 2020.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the US deport people to Haiti despite the do-not-travel advisory?

The US government has a legal obligation to deport non-citizens who are in the country illegally. The advisory is for American citizens, not for deportation policy.

Where did the deportation flight land?

The flight landed in Cap-Haïtien, in northern Haiti. It did not land in Port-au-Prince because the capital’s airport is considered too dangerous due to gang violence.

Were children on the deportation flight?

It is not known if children were aboard the September 3 flight. A previous flight on August 27 carried 57 people, including children born in the U.S. and Brazil.

What is Temporary Protected Status (TPS)?

TPS is a U.S. program that lets people from certain countries stay temporarily due to dangerous conditions. It ended for Haitians in August 2026 after a Supreme Court ruling, though litigation continues.

Sources: Associated Press; Yahoo News; Chicago Tribune; UPI; Le Nouvelliste; AOL; DW; Security Council Report; HaitiLibre; The Rio Times; Africanews; UN; IOM; BINUH; Human Rights First; Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

World.title: Mexico Faces Fresh Warning on Investment Grade as Pemex Debt Looms
World.content:
Mexico · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch warn Mexico’s investment grade faces risks from Pemex and fiscal deficits.

— How big Mexico’s public deficit hit MXN 559 billion (US$32.98 billion) in the first half of 2026.

— The catch Mexico is one notch above junk at Moody’s and Fitch, with S&P on negative outlook.

— Who it hits The warning affects investors in Mexican bonds and the government’s borrowing costs.

— What comes next The 2027 budget must show credible fiscal consolidation to protect the rating.

Mexico’s credit rating is under renewed scrutiny. The warning centers on Pemex debt and the 2027 budget.

A Pemex filling station at night. Mexico’s investment grade is under fresh scrutiny, with Pemex debt at the centre. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)
