We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices. However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. ❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego. Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW — Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026 Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures. They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.” The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations. Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year). There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year. Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules. If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector. EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals https://t.co/0Y5nzfZZYF — Financial Times (@FT) August 30, 2026 The measures have been subject to intense debate within the ruling coalition. When the legislation was first submitted to parliament in July, some parts that had previously been included, such as provisions allowing municipalities to ban short-term rentals in certain areas, were removed. That prompted a backlash from two junior coalition partners in particular, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), prompting further discussions over the summer, resulting in the bill now being toughened again. The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”. The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. Previously, her party had accused the government of watering down the original bill due to industry lobbying. Znowu wbiliśmy lobbystom gola. Właśnie spłynęła nowa wersja rządowej ustawy o Airbnb. Jest decyzyjność wspólnot, spółdzielni i samorządów. Patohotele strzeżcie się – idziemy po was. Czasem warto być „kłótnicą” rządu 😉@PL_2050 — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) August 31, 2026 It also appears that the bill could obtain support from the opposition. In July, after the government initially removed parts of the legislation, the largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for them to be restored, saying that power should be put in the hands of local communities. If the bill is approved by parliament, it also requires the signature of Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, before becoming law. He has vetoed a record number of government bills, but has signed an even larger number. It remains unclear what his position on short-term rentals is. ‼️ To mieszkańcy najlepiej wiedzą, co służy ich wspólnocie. Dlatego wspólnota powinna mieć prawo powiedzieć NIE, jeśli chodzi o najem krótkoterminowy. 👉 Udostępnij! pic.twitter.com/dWURZ9awAY — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 27, 2026 Poland has seen a boom in tourism in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). However, the growth in tourism has also prompted tensions. In 2024, Kraków, which is Poland’s second-largest city and its main tourist destination, appointed a new “night mayor”, who is responsible for reconciling the needs of the city’s residents, business owners and tourists. Previously, in 2020, the city formed a partnership with Airbnb to promote responsible and sustainable tourism. The following year, it launched a “tourist patrol scheme” to inform visitors of the “rules and norms they should follow”. In 2024, Kraków also appealed to the government to allow it to introduce a new tax on tourists. It warned that “overtourism has led to tensions and social discontent in many places in Europe…because residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. World.title: NfP podcast: How small towns became a testing ground for Poland’s far right
World.content: In our new podcast, Notes from Poland’s editor-in-chief Daniel Tilles speaks with deputy editor-in-chief Alicja Ptak about her research into how four contentious issues – migration, women’s rights, Jewish heritage and LGBT+ rights – have played out in 19 smaller towns and cities in Poland. They discuss how national far-right talking points are being imported into smaller towns, how these issues are covered and contested at the local level, and what this all means ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. This conversation was based on a report produced as part of Notes from Poland’s new bespoke service offering our expertise to clients. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Tusk noted that there had been “some very disturbing incidents and events in Poland and Germany over the past few [days]”. “This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” he continued. “Unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Najbliższe tygodnie i miesiące będą krytyczne nie tylko jeśli chodzi o zdarzenia na froncie i w ogóle całą wojnę rosyjsko-ukraińską, ale te tygodnie i miesiące będą także bardzo dużym wyzwaniem dla wszystkich państw w tej części Europy, ze względu na… pic.twitter.com/ZcjVMjhWc0 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 2, 2026 On Sunday, a fire broke out at a production facility in the Polish city of Lublin belonging to JFG Composites, a company that produces components for the aerospace industry, including for military helicopters. Then, in the early hours of Monday morning, another fire occurred at a plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna, south-central Poland, belonging to WB Electronics, a Polish firm that is the largest producer of drones in the European Union. It supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. By Monday afternoon, Polish prosecutors and the security services had confirmed that they were investigating the Skarżysko-Kamienna fire as a potential “crime of a terrorist nature” carried out with the involvement of “foreign intelligence”. On Tuesday, improvised explosive devices were found at one electricity substation in Germany near the border with Poland while another substation in the west of the country was attacked. That came on the same day that Germany announced it held Russia responsible for a drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into whether a fire last night at a facility belonging to WB Electronics, the EU's largest drone maker, was a “crime of a terrorist nature” committed with the “participation of foreign intelligence” https://t.co/rBKmy2A13V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 In his remarks on Wednesday, Tusk said that “there is no doubt” that the incident in Skarżysko-Kamienna “was deliberate arson, meaning an act of sabotage”. “In the case of Lublin, we do not have such evidence but, considering the nature of the production, it cannot be ruled out that deliberate arson occurred there as well,” he added. “I am in constant contact with the leaders of the countries in our region, and everyone realises that the coming weeks and months will be critical, not only in terms of events on the front and the entire Russian-Ukrainian war,” continued the prime minister. “These weeks and months will also pose a very, very significant challenge for all countries in this part of Europe, precisely because of Russia’s plans to escalate tensions and destabilise.” On Tuesday, a deputy interior minister, Czesław Mroczek, told broadcaster RMF that surveillance cameras had recorded a masked person entering the WB Electronics plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna. He said it was “obvious” that Russian involvement was suspected, pointing to previous similar cases in which agents working on behalf of Russia have carried out acts of sabotage in Poland. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe. Last year, Poland confirmed that Russia was behind the fire that in 2024 destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre. The Polish authorities are also seeking to detain two men believed to have sabotaged a rail line last year on Russian orders. However, in contrast to Tusk’s remarks on Wednesday, Kierwiński said that the fires in Lublin and Skarżysko-Kamienna are “two separate incidents and likely unrelated” to one another. “Regarding the Lublin incident, with the information currently available, I’m not so convinced that we were dealing with sabotage,” he explained. “In the case of Skarżysko[-Kamienna], all signs point to an act of terror and sabotage.” Minister @MSWiA_GOV_PL @MKierwinski: Jeżeli chodzi o kwestię pożaru hali w Lublinie, z dostępnymi obecnie informacjami nie mam takiego twardego przekonania, że mieliśmy do czynienia z sabotażem.https://t.co/cspYL5Bn0w — Radio Lublin (@RadioLublin) September 1, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish court orders Catholic diocese to compensate child sex abuse victim and priest to apologise
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A court has ordered a Catholic diocese in Poland to pay 550,000 zloty (€128,250) in compensation to a woman who suffered sexual abuse as a child at the hands of a priest over four decades ago. It has also ruled that the priest himself must publish an apology to his victim and admit his guilt. The ruling, which can still be appealed, represents one of the largest compensation orders ever issued against Poland’s Catholic church, which has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations of clerical child sex abuse, as well as of negligence by bishops in dealing with such cases. Iwona Dudzik-Osińska, who has allowed her name to be published, was first raped in 1981 at the age of 12 by a priest, who has only been named so far as Father Jan and is now 76 years old, in the city of Kielce. The abuse continued for a period of three years, she revealed to the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. In 2007, Dudzik-Osińska decided to report the crimes to prosecutors, but was told that the statute of limitations had expired. In 2019, after the release of a major documentary on sex abuse in Poland’s Catholic church, she also informed Jan Piotrowski, the bishop of Kielce, of what she had suffered. Dudzik-Osińska said that the bishop was sympathetic but told her he could not meet her request to provide church funds to pay for therapy. However, she later received a bank transfer (for an amount that has not been revealed) from Piotrowski’s personal account. Meanwhile, Father Jan was suspended by the diocese of Sosnowiec, where he had been working since the 1990s, banned from contact with children, and brought before an internal church court. A spokeswoman for the Sosnowiec diocese confirmed to Gazeta Wyborcza that, in 2023, the church court removed Father Jan from public exercise of priestly ministry (though he remains in the priesthood) and ordered that he must reside at a location designated by the bishop (which has not been publicly revealed). In the meantime, Dudzik-Osińska launched a civil case against the church, demanding 900,000 zloty in compensation and an annual lifetime payment. The case lasted over four years, but in July the district court in Kielce issued a ruling, which is only now being reported. It ordered the Kielce diocese to pay the victim 550,000 zloty. Moreover, Father Jan must send a personal apology to Dudzik-Osińska in which he admits to sexually abusing her, and also publish such an apology and admission of guilt, under his real name, in a local newspaper, reports Catholic magazine Więź. The ruling can still be appealed by any of the parties involved. A spokesman for the diocese, Paweł Ścisłowicz, told Gazeta Wyborcza that they would only decide on further steps once the court had sent the justification for its decision. Dudzik-Osińska’s attorney, Michał Sochański, celebrated the ruling as “one of the first of its kind in Poland” and said that it “reflects an extremely important trend in case law that can offer hope to those sexually abused by clergy many years ago”. “Institutional mechanisms for resolving cases of sexual abuse in the church have proven insufficient for victims, but fortunately the court system remains an option,” he added. “Justice may come very late, but this verdict demonstrates that it is not unattainable.” A Catholic diocese has been ordered to pay compensation to a man sexually abused as a child by a priest. The victim was treated as an “accomplice in the sin of adultery” at a church trial that acquitted the priest, who was later convicted by a state court https://t.co/IHay5h56SG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2022 Poland’s Catholic church has in recent years faced a growing number of claims of sexual abuse by clergy and of negligence in dealing with the issue by bishops. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Holy See announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. Meanwhile, the Polish church has introduced new rules intended to protect children and other vulnerable people from abuse,held meetings with victims, and apologised for its neglect in dealing with such cases in the past. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 In 2018, a court in the city of Poznań ordered the Society of Christ, a Polish Catholic congregation, to pay 1 million zloty in compensation as well as lifelong monthly payments of 800 zloty to a woman who had been abused by one of its priests as a child. In 2022, the Catholic diocese of Toruń was ordered by a court to pay 600,000 zloty in compensation to a man who was sexually abused for almost a decade while serving as an altar boy. Last year, Bielsko-Żywiec diocese was ordered to pay 400,000 zloty to another victim, who is also seeking a further 20 million zloty in compensation from the archdiocese of Kraków A court has begun hearing the largest-ever compensation claim against Poland’s Catholic church by a victim of clerical sexual abuse. Janusz Szymik, who says he was raped hundreds of times by a priest as a child in the 1980s, is seeking 20m zloty (€4.7m) https://t.co/8ENcjyKsi1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland grants Ukraine permission to search for remains of Ukrainians massacred by Polish partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. The decision marks the latest step towards reconciliation between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Following a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv has also granted Poland permission to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists. On Tuesday, Ukrainian deputy culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi announced that the Polish authorities had granted a permit for a Ukrainian group to conduct exploratory work in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. The search aims to uncover the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), a major underground resistance movement that emerged in Poland during the German occupation of World War Two. Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population, was attacked by a Peasant Battalion unit on 10 March 1944, with some estimates suggesting around 300 civilians were killed. Among those who died was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), Poland’s largest armed resistance movement, also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń. According to estimates, they killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Dariusz Kopciowski, the conservator of monuments in the Lublin province where Łasków is located, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that a permit for exploration work in Łasków had been granted. The issue had recently begun to cause tension, with Ukrainian media reporting last week that Ukraine has been waiting over a year for permission to carry out searches in Łasków. By contrast, Kyiv has granted permission for Poland to conduct such searches on its territory. Those Polish efforts are focused in particular on finding and exhuming the remains of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards those massacres as a genocide. However, Ukraine strongly rejects that label and also points to the fact that Polish partisan units killed Ukrainian civilians during the war. Poland, in turn, argues that many such incidents were acts of reprisal for the massacres carried out by Ukrainians. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine introduced a moratorium on search and exhumation work on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA led the Volhynia massacres but is still celebrated by many in Ukraine for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Last year, following negotiations with Poland, Ukraine lifted that moratorium and again began issuing permits for searches and exhumations of Polish victims on its territory, a number of which have already taken place. Last Sunday, Verbytskyi attended a funeral ceremony for 55 Polish massacre victims, around half of them children, whose remains were recently found and exhumed in a former Polish village located in what is now Ukraine. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, as well as those moves towards reconciliation, there have also been regular clashes between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, in particular following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision in May this year to name a military unit after the UPA. That triggered strong protests from Poland, whose president, Karol Nawrocki, stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Poland has also expressed concern over a new national pantheon being established by Ukraine. It has warned that, if figures associated with the massacre of Poles are included, that could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
