World.title: Robot penguins make a splash at Wakayama theme park
World.content:
Two robot penguins that move realistically are gaining popularity at the Adventure World theme park in the town of Shirahama, Wakayama Prefecture.

The robots — one modeled after a rockhopper penguin and the other after a gentoo penguin — are exhibited among real penguins at the theme park, the world’s only facility to house 10 species of penguins.

Visitors looked amazed to see one of the robots deftly move its flippers to change direction and dive deeper into the water as it swam next to real Humboldt penguins. “I thought it was real,” one visitor said.

The robots were created by Ikuma Okada, the 34-year-old leader of a group within the Adventure World operator.

The robot penguins were created by Ikuma Okada, the 34-year-old leader of a group within the Adventure World operator. | JIJI

Established in 2019, the group began developing robotic animals to let people who cannot visit the park feel closer to animals. It has made robots of many types of animals, including dolphins and tuna.

“We take meticulous care to make (robots) as realistic as possible,” Okada said. “If you look closely and notice that what you’re looking at are robots, it can provide an opportunity to take a fresh look at real animals.”

The robot penguins are covered in a material used in wetsuits. Toothpicks were used to form feather-like patterns on the material. The robots are remotely controlled by staff members.

Okada said he plans to improve the robots, including by making them more waterproof and using highly wear-resistant parts, so that they can move automatically for longer periods.

World.title: Nidec says investigation found 844 quality-control irregularities
World.content:
A third-party investigative panel set up by Nidec said Friday that it has identified 844 cases of misconduct involving some of the company’s products, such as changes to materials, manufacturing processes and designs without customer approval.

The panel was set up in May after the major Japanese motor maker disclosed more than 1,000 suspected cases of quality irregularities committed between 2020 and 2025 in its home appliance, automotive, information technology and other businesses.

The third-party body comprising outside experts said in a report that inappropriate decisions had accumulated “under pressure from various business processes, including performance targets, cost reduction and delivery deadlines,” which led to the formation and entrenchment of an “unsound state.”

Toshihiko Itami, chairman of the investigative committee and a lawyer, told a news conference that “misconduct on this scale in an area that lies at the core of manufacturing is extremely serious.” He stressed that the company “must take the matter seriously and implement corrective measures.”

The report called on Nidec’s current management to centralize the management of quality-related information and establish investigation frameworks involving an independent in-house team and outside experts.

Nidec said in a statement that the company sincerely acknowledges the reported issues, adding that it will return to the basics of monozukuri (manufacturing) and shift toward quality-centered management.

World.title: Almost anyone can make money selling electricity with AI, batteries and solar panels
World.content:
For many Europeans, this summer’s heat was a powerful reminder of the damage climate change has wrought — from illness and devastated crops to high energy bills. For Andrew Austin, a 34-year-old homeowner in Shropshire, England, the stubbornly high temperatures were a chance to make some money.

Power demand was rising as London crossed 34 degrees Celsius on June 24. Energy prices spiked as the sun set and solar panels across the U.K. stopped generating electricity. That’s when Austin knew he could take advantage of his 200 kilowatt-hour home battery, which he had charged up using cheap power from the grid during the daytime. He sold the power back to the grid for £60 ($82) from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. In just a few hours, Austin had earned about as much as an apartment dweller would typically pay for electricity every month.

All this happened without Austin having to press a single button. He has set up a computer to conduct this energy trading while he goes about his life as normal. The computer downloads electricity prices for every 30-minute period from his utility Octopus Energy, which publishes them at 4 p.m. each day. That allows him to know when electricity will be cheap to charge his batteries, and when power prices on the grid are high, the computer sells it back to the grid.

World.title: Nepal floods ruin merchants, traders ahead of crucial festival season
World.content:
The clothes Ashok Kumar Chaurasiya wore as he fled his textile shop in Nepal’s Trishuli Bazaar last week were almost all he has left after the floods.

The 62-year-old trader, who moved from India to Nepal about four decades ago, had built six shops and stocked up ahead of the festival season.

Last Wednesday, with only minutes between the warning and the water reaching the settlement, Chaurasiya, his son and mother raced to higher ground on a motorcycle. “If we had been 20 seconds late, three of us in the family would have gone,” he said.

World.title: Panel may consider restricting evidence use in civil trials in Japan
World.content:
Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi said Friday he will ask an advisory panel to consider a law revision barring the use of evidence submitted in civil trials for purposes not directly related to court proceedings.

Hiraguchi told a news conference that he will ask the Legislative Council, which advises the justice minister, at its meeting on Sept. 14 to consider the change to the Code of Civil Procedure.

The request will come after video evidence submitted by the government in damages lawsuits against the state involving improper interrogations by prosecutors was played in court and broadcast by television and other media outlets. The proposed law revision may restrict the public release of such videos.

World.title: Corporate venture capital develops in Japan
World.content:
Fast-evolving technologies, such as robotics and artificial intelligence, are making the business climate more unpredictable, and leveraging corporate venture capital (CVC) is seen as a critical strategic option.

“As we are in this era of uncertainties, we think companies with the capability to scout what’s next will continue to win,” said Shiro Matsuzaki, managing partner at Japan Airlines Ventures, Japan Airlines’ venture capital arm.

“I believe the primary role of CVCs is to use investment as a means to uncover and make sense of what we don’t know yet.”

World.title: Late Japanese researcher wins Ig Nobel Prize for study on blowing one’s nose
World.content:
The late Professor Emeritus Tokuji Unno was awarded the Ig Nobel Medicine Prize — a satirical prize awarded to promote public engagement with scientific research — on Thursday for his research on how best to blow one’s nose.

Unno, who passed away in 2022 at 89, was the inaugural professor of otolaryngology — or the study of the ear, nose and throat — at Asahikawa Medical University in Hokkaido.

A specialist in respiratory physiology, he won the award for work detailed in his 1977 paper, “How to Blow the Nose — An Aerodynamic Study of the Nose Blowing.”

World.title: Influencers and content creators test boundaries of tennis etiquette at U.S. Open
World.content:
Influencers and content creators armed with smartphones and ring lights have featured prominently in the stands at this year’s U.S. Open, as they try to grab the spotlight away from the on-court action at one of tennis’ marquee events.

Around 100 content creators were given credentials for the tournament, organizers said, with 20 of those dedicated to providing coverage of the food and beverage scene alone, where caviar-topped chicken nuggets and the famed “Honey Deuce” cocktail promise viral attention.

Thousands more amateur social media hounds can be found throughout the plaza and in the stands — after shelling out for their own tickets.

World.title: Dairy Queen to make Hong Kong comeback with 4 stores. Is it scooping up cheap rents?
World.content:
American ice cream chain Dairy Queen will open four Hong Kong outlets in the fourth quarter of this year, as part of an ambitious expansion plan amid the widespread closure of food and retail shops.

Dairy Queen, an 85-year-old brand, said on Friday that it would launch its flagship store at the One Causeway Bay shopping centre on Hong Kong Island in November, followed by three other outlets in Kowloon, the New Territories and the outlying islands before the end of the year.

“Following Causeway Bay, the Kwun Tong store in Kowloon is already under hoarding,” the company said. “A total of four stores are set to open this quarter, strategically covering Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, the New Territories and the outlying islands.”

The Kwun Tong store is located in The Angle shopping centre. The coming stores mark the brand’s return to Hong Kong after a short-lived opening in Causeway Bay in 1979.

The company said it had a fresh store concept tailored for Hong Kong, featuring five product lines, including milkshakes, parfaits and uniquely designed ice cream cakes.

It said the city’s products would include its signature soft-serve dessert, which it described as “thick enough to hold when the cup is turned upside down” and made with an exclusive full-fat dairy mix and an air overrun of about 40 per cent to maintain texture.

Edwin Lee Kan-hing, founder and chief executive of Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management, said Dairy Queen’s entry into the market comes after a sharp fall in retail rents and shop values, creating lower entry costs for foreign brands even as legacy merchants using older business models continue to shut down.

World.title: Hong Kong Disneyland Hotel to close from October 12 for major renovation
World.content:
Hong Kong Disneyland Hotel will temporarily close from October 12 for a comprehensive renovation and upgrade, with no completion date announced, as the resort shifts focus to seasonal culinary offerings and immersive storytelling.

Hong Kong Disneyland announced on Friday that the Victorian-style property, open since 2005, will be revamped with Disney movie-themed rooms, while retaining the hotel’s classic charm.

“As the world’s only Disney resort backed by mountains and facing the sea, this place perfectly blends Disney magic with natural scenery, bringing guests a unique holiday experience,” said Anita Lai Pui-shan, vice-president of communications and public affairs.

“The renovated hotel will retain its classic charm while integrating immersive story experiences, innovative design and better service, further consolidating Hong Kong Disneyland’s leading position in regional tourism.”

The closure leaves the resort’s two other properties to absorb demand. Disney Explorers Lodge offers 750 rooms while Disney’s Hollywood Hotel has 600 rooms.

Lai noted that average occupancy across all three hotels exceeded 80 per cent during the recent summer holiday, in line with the broader Hong Kong market.

World.title: 5 ParknShop and contractor staff who forged pay claims plead guilty to fraud
World.content:
Five former employees of Hong Kong supermarket chain ParknShop and its contractors have pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud by falsifying workers’ attendance records to cheat the retail giant of HK$3.2 million (US$408,000).

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Friday that an investigation revealed that the former supermarket employees colluded with contractor staff over two years to deceive ParknShop by falsifying attendance records for 13 warehouse workers who were not on shift at the chain’s distribution centre.

The defendants – Lau Kin-pong, 44, then a senior supervisor at ParknShop’s eCommercial Distribution Centre, Tai Kin-man, 43, then assistant manager of Earnward Warehouse, and three former warehouse workers employed by Logistics Network Management, Wong Wai-fung, 27, Wong Pak-kan, 28, and Lau Tsz-pan, 28 – all pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud at the District Court on Friday.

The corruption watchdog said the scheme was carried out at ParknShop’s eCommercial Distribution Centre, where logistics personnel sorted online orders and packed goods for delivery to customers.

The workers were supplied by a contractor, Logistics Network Management, but supervised by another company, Earnward Warehouse.

According to the watchdog, Logistics Network Management facilitated wage payments and billed ParknShop based on workers’ shift hours, while daily attendance sheets were verified by Earnward Warehouse’s assistant manager.

Between June 2019 and April 2021, the five defendants used an identical clocking machine to fabricate the attendance records for the 13 logistics warehouse workers.

World.title: Louis Koo’s production firm disputes HK$149m lawsuit, says claim ‘incomplete’
World.content:
Hong Kong film actor and director Louis Koo Tin-lok’s production company has rejected allegations that it owes HK$149 million (US$19 million) in outstanding debts to an offshore firm, saying the claim is incomplete and violates confidentiality principles.

In a statement published on social media on Friday, One Cool Film Production said the civil lawsuit lodged by Sino Hero Ventures on Wednesday had concealed crucial details about a HK$70 million loan extended to Koo’s film production business in September 2019.

“The case presented by the plaintiff is incomplete. In particular, the plaintiff did not reveal the fact that [it] had been removed from the company registry and dissolved for nearly three years, during which we could not contact its authorised personnel,” the statement said.

The defendant in the High Court case also alleged that the plaintiff, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, had unlawfully disclosed details of their agreement that were protected by legal privilege.

“The company reserves all rights to pursue the matter. We will handle this matter with lawyers in a solemn manner,” the statement added.

Actor Louis Koo has appeared in more than 110 local productions since rising to fame in the late 1990s. Photo: K.Y. Cheng

Koo, one of Hong Kong’s most recognisable home-grown film stars, has appeared in more than 110 local productions after rising to fame as a television actor in the late 1990s.

World.title: Fake customer service drives 56% jump in phone scam losses to HK$900 million
World.content:
Impersonating customer service staff is the “most rampant tactic” used by phone scammers, Hong Kong police have said, revealing the number of such fraud cases rose by 45 per cent to 4,830 in the first half of 2026 compared with a year ago.

Despite the increase, deception cases overall fell slightly between January and June, dropping by 0.7 per cent compared with the same period last year, Superintendent Kwok Ching-yee of the commercial crime bureau said on Friday.

Losses also fell by 0.8 per cent to HK$3.51 billion (US$447.6 million), she noted.

“Among phone scams, impersonating customer service was the most rampant tactic, accounting for nearly half of the cases. In other words, in the first half of this year, one resident fell victim to a phishing scam every four hours,” Kwok said.

“Every one hour, a resident falls for a scam after answering a fraudulent call. On average, victims of each phone scam lost at least around HK$270,000.”

Although the numbers of most online scam cases registered a year-on-year decline, phishing scams rose by 61 per cent to 1,113 cases, and phone scams rose by 45 per cent to 4,830.

World.title: Suspect deemed unfit to stand trial for alleged role in deadly hold-up 35 years ago
World.content:
A mainland Chinese man has been deemed unfit to stand trial for his alleged involvement in a deadly shooting during a botched robbery in Hong Kong 35 years ago, after he was diagnosed with a cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer.

A High Court jury of four men and three women ruled on Friday that Shenzhen resident Wen Wenye, 61, could not be held criminally liable for murder and attempted robbery because he was unable to understand the legal proceedings and give instructions to his lawyers.

A “special hearing” will still be held before the jury to decide whether Wen indeed took part in the crimes at Shun Fat Company, a second-hand goods shop on Pei Ho Street in Sham Shui Po, on June 9, 1991.

The defendant will not be convicted in any event, but the court can impose appropriate measures if the jury decides that he committed all the acts alleged in the original indictment.

Wen has been remanded in custody since his arrest at the Shenzhen Bay control point on November 11, 2023.

During his incarceration, he was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer, with mutated cells spreading to his brain.

He underwent surgery to remove damaged brain tissue on July 24, 2024, but has used a wheelchair since.

World.title: Hong Kong’s City University disciplines students over orientation camp misconduct
World.content:
Hong Kong’s City University has disciplined students over an orientation event with a disco theme in which a half-naked man was seen carrying a woman wearing only a bra and shorts, two days after the institution said it had “zero tolerance” for improper conduct.

The institution said on Friday that all students involved in the orientation camp incident on August 27 had admitted their mistakes, formally apologised to the university and accepted disciplinary action.

“The university’s student discipline panel has completed its investigation into the incident and imposed disciplinary penalties on the organisers and the students involved,” it said.

“In accordance with established procedures, further details will not be disclosed to protect student privacy.”

It added that the event organiser, the Management Sciences Society under the CityU student union, had acknowledged serious mismanagement, immediately dissolved its executive committee and apologised to the community.

The university took disciplinary action two days after expressing “grave concern” over the “serious mismanagement and inappropriate behaviour by certain individuals” at the event.

The orientation camp sparked public discussion after a video showing the conduct at a disco-themed party went viral online.

World.title: John Lee urges banks to finance city’s tech growth, expand offshore yuan business
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has urged the banking sector to support financing the city’s creation of a new economic engine in innovation and technology (I&T) while expanding offshore yuan business, a key area for aligning with national strategies.

Speaking at a Hong Kong Association of Banks’ event on Friday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu called for closer partnership between the government and banking sector in four areas.

They comprise expanding offshore renminbi business, encouraging I&T through finance, developing commodity trading, and strengthening financial security and market integrity.

“Strategic growth hinges on technological self-reliance and high-quality development. That very much includes the Northern Metropolis,” Lee told the Distinguished Speaker Luncheon.

The Northern Metropolis would integrate university town areas with I&T and industry, providing an environment for living, working and travelling, he noted.

“It will become a breakthrough point for our city’s rapid development,” he said.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.title: Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.content:
Under the blazing July sun, Zhang, a high school teacher from northern China, stood outside the Digital Exhibition Center of the Mogao Grottoes, a modern building designed to resemble the surrounding dunes. A shuttle bus would soon take him and other tourists to the foot of Mingsha Mountain, where they would see the original Mogao Grottoes: 492 caves containing Buddhist murals and painted sculptures spanning more than a thousand years, now strictly protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Zhang had just watched two introductory films at the center, “A Thousand Years of Mogao Caves” and “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace,” the latter screened in its dome theater. His eyes sparkled with excitement. “It is so spectacular that I am speechless! I hope other heritage sites in China can be presented like this.”

The Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang, northwestern China’s Gansu province, are the product of more than a millennium of cultural exchange between East and West along the historic Silk Road. Renowned for the extraordinary aesthetic and cultural value of their cave art, they attract large numbers of tourists. Yet the grottoes are intrinsically fragile, threatened by both the surrounding desert and the carbon dioxide and humidity generated by visitors.

To reduce pressure on the caves and ensure their long-term preservation, the Dunhuang Academy, which manages and researches the site, has been developing the Digital Dunhuang project since the late 1980s. More than 200 caves have been documented through photography, image stitching, and laser scanning, with the material transformed into online and on-site experiences spanning films, virtual and augmented reality, and museum exhibitions. These digital experiences have become an increasingly prominent part of visiting Mogao.

Putting “cultural heritage” and “digital technology” together creates an immediate tension. Heritage looks backward, toward the past and the old; technology looks forward, toward the future and the new. When the two are brought together, digital representations exist alongside the physical heritage itself, raising questions such as: what qualities of the original are irreplaceable, and to what extent can they be reproduced or conveyed digitally?

I conducted a year of fieldwork at the Mogao Grottoes between 2024 and 2025, spending long periods in both the physical caves and digital exhibitions and talking with visitors. While physical and digital exhibitions at heritage sites can tell separate stories, at Mogao they are closely intertwined. The tension between heritage and technology highlights both their differences and how they complement each other, as visitors often observed.

Among the visitors I spoke with was a middle-aged British artist traveling with her partner. The two had sharply contrasting reactions. She was fascinated by the distinctive smell inside the caves, a mixture of dust, moisture, and history that would be difficult to reproduce digitally. Her partner, by contrast, was perfectly content with the digital exhibitions. “I really got my fix! I could just go with the digital,” he said. He drew parallels with Lascaux Cave in France, where replicas receive visitors while the original, closed to the public since 1963, is preserved.

For some caves, digital representations are the only way visitors can experience their fragile artworks. Cave 285, built during the Western Wei period and containing inscriptions dated to 538 and 539, is one of Mogao’s most important early caves, renowned for its rich murals and diverse artistic styles. It is currently closed to the public for conservation, but a virtual reality exhibition immerses visitors in the stories depicted on the murals and even lets them use handheld controllers as drumsticks to play music alongside mythological beings.

Wang, visiting from the southern city of Shenzhen with her young child, told me: “I like it very much, and it is also child-friendly. The VR shows real scenes from the cave while telling the stories in detail. It even surpasses the real cave!”

For visitors like Wang, VR not only reproduces the physical cave but creates a space of its own, allowing them to experience it in a playful, multisensory way impossible inside the original. “I am so touched that I almost cried,” another visitor told me. “I know Cave 285 is not open to the public, so I am very grateful for the opportunity to see it up close.”

For caves that remain open, experiencing both their physical and digital versions can offer a more nuanced perspective on the art. Cave 61 contains the largest surviving Buddhist historical landscape painting at Mogao. Based on the geography of the Tang dynasty (618–907), the mural depicts pilgrimage routes leading to the sacred Mount Wutai, over 2,000 kilometers east of the caves. It is also featured in “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace” in the center’s 360-degree dome theater.

Later, on a poplar-shaded path, a college student, Xiaoyang, reflected on the contrast. “When I saw the mural from Cave 61 on the big screen, it was so bright. It really looked real, but I knew it wasn’t. I couldn’t feel the traces of time. But when I actually stood inside the cave and faced the mural, I began wondering how ancient cartographers had trudged through Mount Wutai and how painters had depicted the scene on the wall.”

Her response points to what digital reproductions can lose even as they make the art more visible. On-screen, details are easier to see, but this digital representation weakens the power of age and decay that connect viewers to the mural and the people who created it centuries ago. The digital image shows what can be difficult to see inside the cave, while the physical mural confronts visitors with the passage of time. Together, they encourage visitors to consider both the image and the history behind it.

Another crucial component of Digital Dunhuang is the digital repatriation of manuscripts and artifacts now held overseas. In the early 20th century, the discovery of more than 70,000 manuscripts, paintings, and other objects in the Library Cave, or Cave 17, opened a new chapter in Mogao’s history. Most were removed amid the era’s turmoil. Now dispersed around the world, they are being brought together digitally through collaborations between the Dunhuang Academy and international institutions.

Adjacent to Caves 16 and 17 is a museum housing the exhibition “Treasure in Caves,” which recounts the artifacts’ dispersal and virtual reunification. Replicas of objects now scattered among collections worldwide stand side by side in rows of glass cases.

Visiting the caves and exhibition offers complementary experiences, making this place marked by loss feel slightly more complete. A woman in her 50s discussing Cave 17, a memorial cave containing a statue of the Tang-dynasty monk Hong Bian, said: “Cave 17 is a physical place that has endured these historical events. The exhibition tells their story and shows the artifacts, so I can hear the echoes of history and finally breathe a sigh of relief.”

Like these visitors, I have found my own answers to questions about the authenticity. Now writing about Dunhuang from afar, I often revisit photographs from my fieldwork. Yet when I close my eyes, I can still recall the original caves: their warmth, their solemnity, and their sense of history.

The tension between the digital and physical does not necessarily have to be resolved in favor of one or the other. Digital representations can make inaccessible caves available, reveal otherwise difficult-to-see details, and reunite objects that have been physically dispersed. But they can also erase the traces of time and distance that give the originals much of their power. At Mogao, the two forms are most effective not when one substitutes for the other but when they work in tandem to deepen the experience.

By presenting the grottoes from multiple perspectives while carefully controlling access to the physical caves, the Dunhuang Academy shows how digitization can expand our understanding of authenticity rather than simply imitate the original. Perhaps another thousand years from now, the Mogao Grottoes will still move us, both through their carefully preserved physical form and through the digital versions that capture, interpret, and transmit them.

According to research guidelines, all names in this article are pseudonyms.



Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.title: China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.content:
Amid falling primary school enrollment, multiple regions in China are combining primary and secondary school levels, encouraging primary school teachers to transfer to higher grades, and creating schools with flexible enrollment.

Starting this September, several newly built schools designed to allow more flexible enrollment in Yiwu, in the eastern Zhejiang province, as well as the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, have opened and welcomed their first classes of students.

The change comes amid decreasing numbers of new students enrolling in primary school. In 2025, 14.6 million students were reported to have enrolled in primary schools nationwide, down nearly 10% from the year before and 22% from the enrollment peak in 2023. The number of junior high school students is also expected to peak this year, according to the Ministry of Education.

Previously, primary schools have generally acted as independent institutions with relatively fixed sizes and facilities. But as student numbers decline, some regions are launching schools that adjust capacity according to fluctuating enrollment, known as “tidal,” or chaoxi, schools.

Two of the first such schools opened this fall in Yiwu. Of them, the New Silk Road School’s Choucheng campus accepts students from primary school through junior high school, and features facilities that can be “dynamically allocated to different grades,” according to the local government. The other, Suxi Middle School — which hosts both junior and senior high school students — has implemented a flexible enrollment policy that accommodates classes of different sizes depending on the year.

Huli Innovation Experimental School in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen also expanded from a nine-year to a 12-year school this year, cutting its primary and junior high classes to make room for 30 senior high school classes.

Another school in Xiamen, Lianhua Middle School’s Longshan campus, originally intended to be a primary school, was converted into a 36-class junior high school this fall.

In March, authorities in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, announced plans to build the city’s first tidal school, with construction set to be completed in 2028. Over the next three years, four more such schools are planned for the city’s Xiaoshan District, with a total investment of over 1.5 billion yuan ($223 million). In addition to space for 8,100 junior and senior high school students, local education authorities estimate that the model could save 18.7 hectares of land and nearly 900 million yuan in public funds.

Since June, several regions, including the eastern Fujian, Anhui, and Jiangxi provinces, have also released announcements recruiting junior high school teachers from primary and senior high schools. A teacher transfer training program was also recently launched in Shanghai, helping teachers make the move from kindergartens to primary schools and from primary schools to junior high schools.

On social media, users claiming to be primary school teachers said they had been asked to transfer to other grades. Data shows that the number of full-time primary school teachers in China fell by 131,900 in 2025.

The topic has received more than 14 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many users expressing concerns about the quality of teaching, arguing that teachers accustomed to teaching primary school may struggle to adapt to the curriculum and student needs at the junior or senior high school level.

Some teachers who have transferred to other educational levels face issues such as lower pay and inadequate training, Chen Chunyong, a researcher at the National Academy of Educational Sciences, wrote in an online commentary.

Chen called for national and provincial authorities to establish certification standards for teachers transferring between educational levels, including clear requirements for academic qualifications, assessments, and training.

Xiong Bingqi, deputy director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Beijing, also said the new reforms may undermine the country’s recent promotion of small-class teaching.

“Many regions still use traditional class size to calculate teacher staffing allocations, leading to the conclusion that there is a ‘surplus of primary school teachers and they need to be transferred to other levels to reduce excess,’’ he said. “This kind of traditional logic hampers the implementation of small-class reforms and affects the long-term distribution of teaching resources.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Students on their first day of school in Kunshan, Jiangsu province, Aug. 30, 2022. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.title: Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.content:
SHAANXI, Northwest China — “You have gone off route. Recalculating.” For the fourth time that day, Zhao Yushun and his wife, Yuan Zhenzhen, ignored the GPS. By then, jujube trees, signs advertising local specialties, and a view of distant mountains had already pulled them off course.

Now it was a farmer sorting pears beneath a black sunshade by the roadside in Dali County, northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.

“What kind of pear is this? I’ve never seen it before,” Zhao asks after they pull over. “How’s the harvest this year? Have people here been growing pears longer, or jujubes?”

“Jujubes,” the farmer says with a wry smile. His family has grown them since he was a child, but over the past decade more and more people have started planting them, and the returns are no longer what they once were. “Things are worth more when they’re scarce.”

As he speaks, Yuan raises her camera and starts recording, keeping it around waist height to make it less conspicuous.

The farmer soon moves beyond pears, telling Zhao about his years as a migrant worker in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen and his eventual return home to care for his children and aging parents. With jujube profits falling, he has also begun growing pears, hoping for a better return.

Thirty minutes later, Zhao and Yuan are back on the road. The encounter becomes the closing scene of the fifth episode of their “Yellow River” series.

Since 2021, Zhao and Yuan have traveled through more than 1,100 villages and towns, turning roadside conversations and unplanned stops into short documentaries about rural China. Their account, Yuzhenjishi, or “Encountering Reality,” has more than 530,000 followers on Bilibili, one of China’s largest video platforms.

Many of the people Zhao and Yuan film are farmers in their 60s or older who grew up working the land, spent years as migrant workers in cities, then returned home after being aged out of many urban jobs. They now farm through falling crop prices, increasing mechanization, extreme weather, and the departure of younger generations.

Since July, Zhao and Yuan have been traveling along the Yellow River, one of China’s longest and most historically important waterways, filming a six-episode series on the farms and pastures along its banks. Sixth Tone joined them for three days as they traveled through Henan, Shanxi, and Shaanxi provinces.

Down to earth

For Zhao and Yuan, leaving rural China had once seemed the obvious measure of success. Both grew up largely in the care of older relatives while their parents worked in cities, part of a rural generation known in China as “left-behind children.”

When Zhao did well in school growing up in a village in central China’s Hunan province, villagers would tell him: “Your hands aren’t meant to hold a hoe. They’re meant to hold a pen. You have to get out and go to the big city.”

He studied journalism; Yuan, who grew up in a small town in the southern Guangdong province, studied Chinese literature. Both made it to university, but neither found the stable urban life that education had seemed to promise.

As graduates of second-tier universities, they moved between media jobs in Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and other cities, rarely earning enough to feel settled.

“We moved so many times,” Zhao said. “Every time we moved, we wondered whether we should hire a medium-sized truck, only to find that our stuff filled barely half of a small one. After we left, there wouldn’t be any trace of us in the city.”

By 2021, Zhao and Yuan were both 27 and living in a rented apartment in Beijing. Zhao spent about three hours a day commuting by bus and subway. He came to recognize the passengers who got on and off at particular stops without ever knowing who they were.

The routine made him feel like “a cog in the machine.” Yuan described herself as “someone stuck in a corner.”

One night in 2021, they decided to start their own video account. They named it Yuzhenjishi, combining one character from each of their names with the slogan: “Let the overlooked be seen.”

Their first post was an edit of news footage about a herd of elephants that had wandered north from their habitat in the southwestern Yunnan province. At the end, they added a caption: “A herd of elephants drifting north, just like us leaving home to make a living.”

The couple soon moved to Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, where they continued working in media while filming in their spare time. At first, they focused largely on small cities around the province. But after making a video about left-behind children in a mountainous area, they found themselves increasingly drawn to villages and towns.

Within a year, Yuan proposed a more drastic move: quitting their jobs and making videos full time. After spending much of their childhoods trying to study their way out of rural China, Zhao and Yuan began returning to it with cameras.

For Zhao, the change brought a sense of connection he had rarely felt while covering new skyscrapers and suburban redevelopment in cities. The rural stories were “things I genuinely care about,” he said. “I finally felt grounded.”

As they began filming rural communities, viewers increasingly responded with stories of their own. Some left comments 400 or 500 words long.

One viewer from Hunan described growing up in a mountainous area where families had little land to farm and few ways to save money. “We all ended up taking the same path: leaving home to find work,” the viewer wrote. “It was all just to make a living.”

An agricultural university student wrote that after drought destroyed an experimental crop, they began searching for coverage of similar losses and were struck by how little they found. “Farmers and real rural communities barely have a voice of their own,” the student wrote.

The responses became important enough that Zhao and Yuan later printed a selection in a leaflet accompanying their first book, an anthology adapted from the written narratives of their videos. They came to see their videos as only half the story; viewers supplied the other half.

“We’re like a little public square,” Zhao said. “I pick up a loudspeaker and shout, ‘If anyone has something they want to say, come over.’ And then people really do come and tell their stories.”

On record

In practice, Zhao’s “loudspeaker” is usually just a question.

In a cornfield, he picked up an ear the harvester had missed and called to a farmer gleaning nearby: “Do you still want this?” Soon, the man was telling him about a nearby reservoir he had helped repair years earlier.

On the banks of the Yellow River, Zhao approached two men overseeing repairs to an embankment. “We’re from the south and have never seen this kind of embankment,” he said. “Could you explain it to us?”

Few turn him away. And once they begin talking, Yuan watches for the moment to start filming.

After filming a group of peach farmers packing nectarines for delivery to a foreign trade company, Zhao and Yuan were offered some fruit. When they asked how much they owed, one farmer waved them off.

“No need to pay,” he said. “Just put this in your video.”

Zhao remembered another farmer telling him much the same thing: “Little brother, there’s no money in farming these days. Look how hard life is for us farmers. Film this and put it on people’s phones. I’ll give you a like.”

“Farmers actually really want to talk,” Zhao said after returning to the car. “They just don’t have a channel to do so. So we bring the microphone to their doorstep.”

Zhao and Yuan describe these farmers as “standing at the crossroads of an era,” perhaps the last generation shaped primarily by traditional small-scale farming.

Their conversations often return to money and work, from falling crop prices and thin margins to years of physical labor and pensions that leave many older rural residents with little to live on.

Zhao argues that rural life is often viewed from outside in one of two ways. “People tend to imagine the countryside either as an idyllic retreat or as a place of poverty and hardship,” he said. “But both are ways of looking in from the outside.”

“We’re part of this world ourselves,” Zhao said. “What we do is document it from within and then communicate it outward.”

One of their most watched videos underscored the point more directly. Released in 2022 under the title “China’s 760 Million Farmers Don’t Need Praise,” it has nearly 5 million views.

“Since primary school, textbooks have taught us to praise farmers and applaud their hard work, but they never taught us to truly understand them,” the video said. “For farmers, mountains and rivers are not poetic, and rural life is no pastoral idyll. Farming is about survival.”

They have also tried posting on YouTube, with limited success. Zhao believes many of their stories require too much background knowledge for overseas audiences.

“After all, we are not Li Ziqi,” he said, referring to the hugely popular Chinese creator known internationally for idealized videos of rural life. “We are not making a pastoral fantasy.”

Still rolling

This spring, Zhao and Yuan hoped to film elderly porters who haul oranges out of the mountainous Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River.

But by the time they went looking for them, drones had taken over most of the work. Only a handful of porters still do it today, mainly on plots with too few orange trees to meet the minimum charge for drone transport.

“And of course, that’s a good thing. It’s a sign of progress that people no longer have to do such grueling work,” Zhao said. “But what that generation of porters went through, the lives they lived, and the labor they endured, was never recorded.”

They have encountered the same problem while trying to document people who built reservoirs, canals, and other water projects more than half a century ago.

Yuan’s grandmother had helped build an irrigation canal when she was young. Before she died, Zhao and Yuan took her back to see it. “Canal, reservoir — I’ve come to see you with my walking stick,” she said.

Children were playing nearby. Yuan’s grandmother tried to strike up a conversation with a gray-haired man in his 60s. “Did you help build the canal?” she asked. “It was such hard work back then.”

“How could I have?” he replied. “Anyone who worked on it would be at least 80 or 90 by now.”

Yuan’s grandmother smiled and said nothing more.

Many of the projects were built more than 60 years ago, and Zhao said it is increasingly hard to find surviving workers who can still tell their stories.

During the Yellow River trip, they met a man who had worked on one such project. Later, Zhao repeated a line the man had uttered in his local accent: “Once it was finished, it had nothing more to do with us.”

“If we don’t film these stories now, in another 10 years, there’ll be no one left who remembers them,” Yuan said.

The couple says they plan to spend 10 years documenting rural China. They are not worried about running out of stories, because many of the questions they pursue — about farming, migration, aging, and the changes reshaping villages — have no simple answer.

For Zhao, putting those questions on camera is a necessary first step. “First it has to be seen,” he said. “Once it is seen, people can start paying attention.”

Keeping that space open also costs money. After quitting their jobs in 2022, Zhao and Yuan burned through their savings and accumulated more than 250,000 yuan ($37,000) in debt.

They bought their camera, drone, and car on installments and took on outside commercial projects to support their documentary work. Even now, they sometimes sleep in the car while filming and get a hotel only when they need to do laundry.

It was not until 2025, the year they married, that they felt for the first time that they had actually made some money. After paying down debts and heading out to film again, much of it was soon gone.

“We were constantly moving money around just to keep things afloat,” Yuan said. “At the beginning of the year, we landed some other commercial deals, and it barely made us feel alive again. It’s like dying and coming back to life, then dying and coming back again.”

The two have nevertheless settled into a division of labor that requires little discussion. Zhao does most of the interviewing, appears on camera and narrates; Yuan films and edits. On the road, they often know without speaking when Zhao should deliver a piece to camera, when Yuan needs another shot, or when they should stop and try again.

But they differ over what they expect the work to achieve.

For years, Yuan wrote the same sentence on every résumé she sent to prospective employers: “Images have the power to change the world.” Zhao often repeated it too.

She is less certain now.

“I’m just going through a bit of a period of uncertainty,” Yuan said. “Change is difficult. Video may not necessarily change the world, but it can record the world.”

“I want to change things; he wants to record them,” she added. “I’m the more radical one.”

For Zhao, the record itself is reason enough to continue. “These are precious historical records,” he said. “A hundred years from now, someone may look through our videos to understand what this generation of farmers was thinking.”

Along the Yellow River, Zhao and Yuan collected water in plastic bottles at different points on their journey. At the river’s estuary in the eastern Shandong province, they opened the bottles one by one and poured the water back in.

Editor: Apurva.
