World.title: Kazakhstan Completes Track Connection on Moiynty-Kyzylzhar Railway Line
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has completed the track connection on the 323.3-kilometer Moiynty-Kyzylzhar railway line, marking a key milestone in one of the country’s major transport infrastructure projects.

The new line, being built across the Ulytau and Karagandy Regions, is designed to strengthen Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics potential, expand international routes and increase export and transit capacity.

Once commissioned, the line will become an important link of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, improving regional connectivity and freight transportation efficiency.

The project will shorten freight routes by 149 kilometers, ease pressure on the Moiynty-Zharyk railway section, increase container train speeds and expand capacity for freight and transit traffic.

The project comes amid growing international attention to the need for expanded rail infrastructure along the Middle Corridor. According to experts, the pace of rail infrastructure development could have a “huge impact” on demand for freight rail services, while infrastructure development, coordination and supply-chain resilience remain key to the corridor’s long-term viability.

Construction is progressing according to schedule, with around 2,000 specialists and more than 700 units of equipment deployed at the site. The railway line is scheduled for commissioning this year.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Laos Seek to Expand Trade Through Agriculture and Transport Links
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Laos are seeking to expand bilateral trade by using Kazakhstan’s position as a trade and logistics bridge to connect Lao products with Central Asian and wider Eurasian markets, while opening greater access for Kazakh goods to Southeast Asia.

Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith, who arrived in Kazakhstan for his first official visit on Sept. 3, discussed implementing agreements reached between the two countries’ Presidents and identified agriculture, transport, logistics and digitalization as key areas for closer economic ties.

Agriculture offers immediate trade potential

Agriculture emerged as one of the main areas with potential for expanding trade. Kazakhstan, a major exporter of wheat and flour with extensive arable land and pasture resources, is ready to increase supplies of grain, oilseeds, feed and meat products to Laos, reported the Prime Minister’s press service.

The Lao side expressed interest in Kazakh agricultural products, while Kazakhstan is looking to increase imports from Laos, including coffee, rubber and other goods.

The officials also discussed joint processing and storage of agricultural products and the introduction of modern irrigation technologies, which could broaden cooperation beyond the exchange of finished goods.

Transport links could connect two regions

Transport and logistics offer a longer-term opportunity to link Central Asia with Southeast Asia.

Kazakhstan is developing major transcontinental corridors connecting China and Europe and has extensive logistics infrastructure that could facilitate Lao exports to Central Asian and European markets. At the same time, Laos could provide Kazakhstan with an additional gateway to Southeast Asian markets.

Both countries see scope for using existing transport infrastructure to strengthen these links. Kazakhstan’s logistics network includes facilities connected to major international routes, while Laos’ position and transport links with China offer access to Southeast Asian markets.

This could give both landlocked countries an opportunity to turn geography into a practical economic advantage.

Digitalization adds a new dimension

Digital development was another area highlighted during the visit. Kazakhstan and Laos exchanged a Memorandum of Cooperation on information and communication technologies and e-government services.

The document is intended to support cooperation in digital development and create opportunities for exchanges of experience and joint initiatives.

President Sisoulith emphasized the importance of strengthening friendly relations with Kazakhstan and implementing joint projects.

Cooperation extends beyond trade

The two countries also signed intergovernmental documents covering political consultations, law enforcement, digital development and cooperation between their capitals.

As part of the visit, Kazakhstan’s Prosecutor General Berik Assylov and Prosecutor General of the Supreme People’s Prosecutor’s Office of Laos Livong Laoly signed a memorandum on cooperation in asset recovery. The document provides a framework for exchanging information and experience and for mutual assistance in identifying, tracing and returning illegally transferred assets.

From diplomatic ties to economic links

The talks also underscored the broader regional dimension of the relationship. Kazakhstan views Laos as an important partner in Southeast Asia, while Laos can benefit from stronger connections with Central Asian and Eurasian markets.

The countries established diplomatic relations in 1997, with 2027 marking their 30th anniversary. Sisoulith’s visit is the first official visit by a Lao President to Kazakhstan.

The two officials also exchanged intergovernmental documents covering political consultations, law enforcement, digital development and cooperation between their capitals.

For Kazakhstan, closer ties with Laos could open another channel toward Southeast Asian markets. For Laos, stronger links with Kazakhstan offer access to a broader Eurasian economic space, making trade and transport the most immediate areas to watch as the agreements reached during the visit move toward implementation.

World.title: Top Experts Argue Central Asia Needs Stronger Agency in Emerging Global Order
World.content:
ASTANA – Central Asia’s best defense against challenging and fragmenting global order lies not in choosing a geopolitical camp but in deeper regional coordination, diversified partnerships and stronger international rules, top experts said during an Aug. 31 discussion in Astana.

The five Central Asian states are unlikely to become a separate pole in the emerging global order. However, their geography, resources and growing cooperation give them an opportunity to shape how that order operates provided they can turn regional coordination into lasting institutions and economic resilience.

The expert discussion brought together Nargiza Murataliyeva, an associate professor at the American University of Central Asia in Bishkek, Dauren Aben, deputy director of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies and Akram Umarov, first vice rector of the University of World Economy and Diplomacy in Uzbekistan. The panel followed the launch of German political analyst Marc Saxer’s book, “Geopolitical Conflict in the Wolf World: Great Power Competition and the Illiberal Revolt against the Liberal Order.” Saxer uses the term “wolf world” to describe a fragmented international system in which institutions are weakening, geopolitical competition is intensifying and power increasingly determines outcomes.

For Central Asia, that challenge is particularly notable. The region sits between Russia and China, borders Afghanistan and is surrounded by ongoing conflicts. It also depends heavily on external markets, infrastructure and technology. At the same time, demand for its critical minerals, uranium, energy resources and transit routes has increased its strategic value.

Stronger regional agency

The experts emphasized that Central Asia should no longer be viewed merely as an arena in which outside powers compete or an object of the so-called great game that many Western experts use extensively.

“For a long time, we have been considered through the prism of great-power rivalry: who has the greatest influence, whether China is replacing Russia and so on,” Aben said. “All of these are legitimate questions, but they are increasingly insufficient.”

Murataliyeva stressed that discussions about Central Asia did not put the region at the forefront. Some experts referred to it as a “buffer,” a “transit zone,” or a “place things pass through on the way somewhere more important.” Murataliyeva said that vocabulary has become obsolete as the five countries develop greater regional agency.

Since 2018, the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state, with the latest held in Cholpon-Ata in July, have created a form of cooperation distinct from conventional regional organizations. It can further serve as a model for other regions throughout the world.

“The five states have built something that doesn’t look like any existing regional organization. There is no supranational authority, no binding laws, no court, no commission, no pooled sovereignty. Decisions are made by consensus among presidents, and implementation is voluntary,” she said.

The results are tangible. Murataliyeva pointed to the reopening of borders, settlement of long-standing border disputes and the growing intraregional trade. This format has also made the region’s voice stronger and made it more recognizable to outside partners as a single negotiating counterpart.

“This is a part that other regions might learn from,” she added.

Umarov said the enhanced regional coordination is a natural response to the changing world order.

“And our task is to make sure this regional coordination will bring necessary strategic resilience to the region, because I believe our development is inevitably linked to each other,” he said.

Strategic philosophy

Aben sees regionalism as an instrument of strategic autonomy. Rather than seeking isolation or alignment with one power, Central Asian states are trying to preserve the widest possible range of choices. He stressed the region’s vast experience in “strategic balancing.”

“We want good relations with Russia, but we do not want to be absorbed into the Russian sphere of influence. We want to deepen strategic partnerships, especially with China, but we do not want to become an exclusive zone of influence of China,” Aben said.

The region also wants strong ties with the United States and Europe without becoming another front in geopolitical confrontation, he added. Central Asian states are simultaneously expanding connections with South Asia, the Middle East and the broader Islamic world.

“Our determination is not to choose a camp, but to enlarge the space in which choices remain possible,” Aben said. “It is not just tactical hedging. It is our strategic philosophy.”

Regionalism faces limits

According to Murataliyeva, the region’s flexible model also has clear vulnerabilities.

“First of all, this model runs on personal trust between a specific group of leaders. It has no mechanism for resolving a dispute if the trust fails, and no institutional memory to survive a difficult succession,” she said.

The five states also remain competitors in several areas. Each seeks to become a regional transport hub, manufacturing center or gateway between Europe and Asia. “Soft regionalism is excellent at removing friction. It hasn’t yet been tested on a genuine conflict of interest, in fact,” said the expert.

Security cooperation is similarly fragmented. Central Asian countries participate in overlapping and sometimes competing arrangements, including the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, C5+1 platforms and bilateral or trilateral mechanisms covering Afghanistan, water and energy.

“As a result, Central Asian security can be understood as networked and institutionally fragmented, rather than organized around a single regional security provider or institutional framework,” she explained.

However, Murataliyeva suggested this fragmented structure can be both a weakness and a potential form of adaptation. Rather than relying on a single security provider, states can work through different networks depending on the issue. The question, she said, is whether Central Asia can develop a meaningful regional security agency without creating a unified security architecture.

Multivectorism under pressure

The experts warned that the space for Central Asia’s traditional multivector diplomacy is narrowing.

“What is also becoming challenging for the region, we talk a lot about this multilateral policies, non-alignment, but the space for this multilateralism is shrinking, and we are coming to the politics where there are no ideal choices, so you have to balance, but still this balancing is very steep and very fragile in some aspects,” said Umarov.

In the past, the region could balance relations among external partners that were not in direct confrontation with one another. That is no longer the case. Russia’s confrontation with the West and the deepening strategic rivalry between the United States and China make that balancing act more costly.

“Multivector foreign policy has changed character, in fact, because classical multivectorism was balanced among partners who were not fighting each other. The vectors are in open conflict now,” said Murataliyeva.

The region has an interest not simply in the emergence of multiple centers of power but in preserving rules that protect sovereignty and territorial integrity. According to her, the Central Asian agency depends on major powers continuing to compete without allowing that competition to escalate into direct conflict.

According to Aben, Central Asia needs an order that offers “sovereignty without being isolated, connectivity without being overly dependent and cooperation without the need to choose alliances.” The region already practices a version of this model through overlapping partnerships.

“We cooperate with China on infrastructure. We want to cooperate with Europe on connectivity, critical raw materials. We cooperated extensively with the United States on nuclear security and non-proliferation, and we want to continue this cooperation with Russia on trade and transport,” he said.

“We cannot prevent the wolves from competing,” he said, referring to the central premise of Marc Saxer’s book. “Our task as middle and small powers is to ensure that this competition is not organized according to the logic of the wolves.”

Weakening institutions raise the stakes

Umarov said the erosion of universal international institutions poses a particular threat to small and middle powers, which have traditionally relied on international law and multilateral organizations to protect their interests.

“It is quite obvious that usually small and medium powers rely on international norms, rely on international institutions to secure their interests and to promote their interests and to make sure that these interests are taken into account. But in a world where no one is quite serious about norms and taking them very simply, this is a big challenge for us,” he explained.

A world in which several powerful leaders can make agreements behind closed doors and impose them on others would leave smaller states with little influence over decisions affecting their security and development, he said.

The rise of selective coalitions and the weakening of universal multilateralism are therefore deeply concerning for Central Asia, Umarov said. Since independence, the region’s states have joined numerous international organizations partly to reinforce their sovereignty and secure platforms from which to advance their interests.

According to Aben, the objective is not to preserve the old order unchanged. Central Asian states have also experienced its double standards and unequal distribution of influence. Instead, the region needs rules that constrain power rather than serve as instruments of power politics.

Umarov called on Central Asian countries to become more active defenders of international law while also proposing reforms to existing institutions and developing regional norms of their own.

“We need to be proactive, not reactive to the changes in the world,” he said.

Connectivity

Geography is becoming an asset as well. “The world looks at us as a landlocked space between Russia and China, close to Afghanistan, rich in energy, critical minerals, located along the Silk Way,” said Aben.

“All of this, of course, is true, and all of this can produce vulnerability, but it also makes us strategically relevant,” he added.

Disruption of traditional routes and supply chains has also drawn increased interest to Central Asia as a continental bridge between China, Europe, Russia, South Asia and the Middle East.

Umarov rejected the idea that Uzbekistan’s double landlocked status should define it primarily as isolated. He believes that assumption overlooks the region’s historic position along the Silk Road and its growing relevance as maritime trade routes become more vulnerable. “This continental connectivity is very important,” he said.

Murataliyeva also noted that making the region a strong connectivity hub will remain largely rhetorical if governments do not address physical and economic constraints.

“For instance, mismatched rail gauges, customs delays, thin processing capacity. The corridor agenda only pays off if it is paired with an industrial agenda,” she said.

The experts agreed that Central Asia cannot eliminate the pressures created by its location or prevent larger powers from competing. However, it can reduce the risks by strengthening regional trust, building economic and technological capacity and acting collectively where interests converge.

World.title: Alatau City: Can Kazakhstan Build Regional Economic Hub from Scratch
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is betting that Alatau City can evolve from a planned development outside Almaty into a regional economic hub. Backed by a special legal regime and billions of dollars in proposed investment, the project seeks to combine manufacturing, logistics, technology and finance with new transport and digital infrastructure, but its success will depend on whether ambition can be translated into sustained investment and effective governance.

The latest government review on Aug. 28 shows that the project is moving from planning toward implementation. Alatau City’s investment pipeline has expanded to 67 projects worth nearly $6.9 billion, with the potential to create around 55,000 jobs. Projects involving PepsiCo, Sunny Paper, Mars Petcare KZ, Griffin Logopark, DanaFlex and G-Trans Service are at different stages of implementation, while additional projects are being developed with Korean and Chinese partners.

The scale of the investment pipeline is only one measure of the project’s potential. The larger question is whether Alatau City can generate a new concentration of economic activity rather than simply shift some activity from neighbouring Almaty.

From a new city to a new economic center

The government has given Alatau City an unusually broad mandate. PepsiCo and Sunny Paper are in the active implementation phase, while work has begun on production and logistics projects involving Mars Petcare KZ, Griffin Logopark, DanaFlex and G-Trans Service. Other proposed projects include sustainable aviation fuel and green energy initiatives by Full Vision Capital, a branch of South Korea’s KAIST research institute, logistics and data-center projects involving CIMC and a high-tech agricultural complex by Sinomach.

Several Korean companies are also being considered for projects in investment, food production, hospitality, energy, urban air mobility, smart mobility and hydrogen technologies.

Yernar Serik, a trading and investment analyst, founder of the Tradereport Telegram channel, said Alatau City has the potential to become a new center of economic activity, particularly in sectors where Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify its economy.

“For Kazakhstan’s economy, where a significant portion of business, capital, and human resources is concentrated in Almaty and Astana, the emergence of another major center would be an important structural change,” Serik told the Astana Times.

“At the same time, I wouldn’t contrast Alatau City with Almaty. A more realistic model is a polycentric agglomeration, where Almaty remains the financial, educational, and cultural center, while Alatau gains its own specialization,” he added.

According to Serik, Alatau’s proximity to Almaty could itself become one of its advantages, providing access to the country’s largest consumer market, human capital, airport, universities and established business environment.

Geography is part of the proposition

Alatau City’s location is central to the government’s economic rationale. The city sits between Almaty and Konayev and close to the Almaty International Airport. The broader region is connected to major transport routes linking China with Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe and the Middle East, including the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route.

That gives the project an opportunity to combine two roles that are often developed separately: a production center and a logistics hub. The proximity to Almaty also provides access to a large consumer market, financial services and an established labour pool, while the city’s location within the broader Eurasian transport network could help manufacturers connect more efficiently with export markets.

A legal experiment as much as an urban one

Perhaps the most distinctive feature of Alatau City is not its construction program but its legal framework. A constitutional law adopted on May 8 established a special legal regime under which Alatau City operates as a “city of accelerated development.” The legislation creates specific rules for public administration and allows a separate regulatory framework for areas including entrepreneurship, digital assets, finance, urban development and other aspects of the city’s development.

This makes Alatau City an institutional experiment as much as a construction project. The government is creating a separate administrative architecture through Alatau City Authority, alongside an Operational Committee and Regulatory Commission.

The long-term plans are equally ambitious. A development master plan to 2040 and a long-term development plan to 2055 are being prepared with international firms ARUP and BCG.

The limits behind the ambition

The scale of the project also raises a more fundamental question: can preferential regulation and large-scale infrastructure create a genuinely new economic center, or could some of the apparent growth simply reflect the relocation of existing economic activity.

Economist Anuar Nurtazin notes that the answer will ultimately depend on factors beyond the special status granted to the city. In a comment published on his Telegram channel, he questioned whether Alatau City’s location and institutional model are sufficient to overcome the structural advantages enjoyed by established global economic hubs.

He noted that major technological and financial centers have typically emerged around major ports, logistics hubs or established financial agglomerations, where capital, talent and trade already generate a natural flow of economic activity.

Nurtazin also cautioned against measuring the success of a special economic regime through the number of registered companies or investment announcements alone. Companies can relocate their activities within a country without necessarily creating significant additional economic value.

“If the key argument is a special regime, there is a risk of statistical growth without a genuine economic breakthrough,” he said, highlighting that the key indicators should instead include exports, technological supply chains, localization of production and productivity growth.

According to Nurtazin, such incentives are justified only when they generate measurable economic returns. Without transparent indicators for evaluating those returns, he said, a fundamental question remains: where is the line between a strategic investment and an expensive experiment?

“The sustainable development of cities depends on three factors coming together: the market, capital and institutional stability,” Nurtazin wrote.

Shenzhen, Dubai, Songdo: three models, three lessons for Alatau

While no model can be replicated directly, the experiences of Shenzhen in China, Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and Songdo in South Korea offer three different lessons about what can make or limit the development of a new economic center.

Shenzhen provides perhaps the most relevant comparison. Kazakhstan has explicitly said it is studying the Chinese city’s experience. During a June 9 meeting with Shenzhen Mayor Qin Weizhong, Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev said the country was taking into account international practices, including Shenzhen, when developing Alatau City’s special legal regime and development model.

Shenzhen’s development was supported by proximity to Hong Kong, access to international capital and markets, large-scale infrastructure investment, manufacturing supply chains and the rapid concentration of companies and talent. Its experience suggests that a special regulatory regime can be an important catalyst, but it works most effectively when it is combined with strong market access and an expanding business ecosystem.

Dubai offers a different lesson, centered on international connectivity. The emirate built its economic position by combining infrastructure, global aviation and logistics links, investment-friendly business environments and specialized economic zones. Its experience is particularly relevant to Alatau’s ambition to use its location between major Eurasian markets.

Songdo in South Korea provides a more cautionary comparison. The planned smart city near Seoul was conceived as an international business and technology hub, built around advanced infrastructure, digital services and sustainability. For Alatau, this distinction could prove important. The city is pursuing similarly ambitious projects in smart mobility, artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, data centers and tokenized assets.

Infrastructure before the city

The government is also trying to avoid one of the most common problems associated with large new-city projects: building housing and industrial facilities before the infrastructure required to support them is ready. Energy efficiency is also being incorporated at the planning stage.

Timur Tashmukhambetov, director of the Department of Design and Construction Standards at Alatau City Authority, said the city should integrate energy efficiency into its development from the beginning.

“For Alatau City, it is important to lay the foundations of energy efficiency already at the city design stage,” he said, pointing to technologies that can reduce energy losses, peak-load management and distributed renewable generation.

The approach is significant because a new industrial and digital center could create substantial additional demand for electricity. The ability to meet that demand efficiently could become an economic advantage.

What would success look like?

The $6.9 billion investment pipeline and projected 55,000 jobs provide an initial measure of ambition. But they will not, by themselves, determine whether Alatau City has succeeded. The city will also have to demonstrate that its special legal regime creates tangible advantages for businesses rather than simply another layer of administration.

That question is particularly relevant because the project’s stated horizon extends well beyond the current investment cycle. The master plan runs to 2040, while the long-term development plan is being prepared through 2055.

“Moreover, Alatau City should not be viewed as a project starting from scratch, but as a new attempt to implement a concept that has existed for almost two decades. Previously, it was called G4 City and involved four separate satellite cities. Today, these four specializations are combined within a single city, Alatau,” Serik said.

The challenge will be turning that institutional advantage into an economic one. If infrastructure arrives ahead of demand, the regulatory system remains predictable, investment projects move from announcements to operating businesses and the city develops a skilled workforce and international connections, Alatau could become an important new node in Kazakhstan’s economy.

“For me, the main criterion for a city’s independence will be a fairly simple indicator: who goes to work and where. If residents of Alatau travel to Almaty every day, we will primarily get a large suburb of the southern capital. But if people from Almaty and other regions start coming to Alatau for work, business, education, and technology, then we can talk about an independent economic center,” Serik said.

World.title: Kazakh Elections: Another Stage in Long-Term Political Modernization
World.content:
It would be a mistake to assess the significance of Kazakhstan’s parliamentary elections, held on Aug. 23, solely through the distribution of mandates or the results achieved by individual parties. What is far more important is the broader political and institutional process of which these elections are both a consequence and another stage. In recent years, Kazakhstan has embarked on a distinctive path of evolutionary political modernization, the central element of which is not the sudden dismantling of the existing system, but its gradual transformation.

The elections were held within the framework of the new constitutional system. Following the March referendum, the former bicameral Parliament ceased to exist, and a unicameral Kurultai consisting of 145 deputies was established. Therefore, these elections were not merely about electing a new parliament; they represented the first real test of the functioning of Kazakhstan’s renewed political institutional system.

From this perspective, voter turnout deserves particular attention. According to official results, around 9.35 million citizens took part in the vote, representing a turnout of 74.08%. This is significantly higher than the 54.19% turnout recorded in the 2023 parliamentary elections. Of course, high voter turnout alone does not prove the democratic nature of a political system, but it does indicate that a significant part of society regarded the elections as a relevant political act.

The clear winner of the elections was Adilet, which received 71.17% of the vote and secured 110 seats. At the same time, four other political forces also entered the Kurultai: Auyl, Respublica, Aq Zhol and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party. This, of course, does not yet amount to a competitive multiparty democracy in the Western sense. Kazakhstan’s political system remains strongly presidential, and the dominance of Adilet is unlikely to change this fact in the near future.

Nevertheless, it is important to distinguish between the current democratic condition of a political system and the direction of its democratic development.

I believe it is primarily the latter that should be examined. The reform process launched after 2022 — the concept of a Just Kazakhstan announced by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev — has gradually been changing the relationship between the state and society. This process has included constitutional reform, the transformation of political institutions, changes to the party system, amendments to the electoral system, and efforts to expand institutional channels for political participation. For this reason, the current elections should not be interpreted in isolation, but rather as part of this multi-year reform cycle.

At the same time, criticism should not be ignored. According to the preliminary assessment of the OSCE/ODIHR, the elections were technically well prepared; however, political pluralism remains limited, and concerns were raised regarding media freedom, the legal framework and certain aspects of the vote-counting process. These are precisely the issues that Astana will need to address substantively during the next phase of reforms.

On the other hand, the complexity of Kazakhstan’s development model is reflected in the fact that the European Union itself acknowledged the significant reform of the political system carried out in recent months, as well as the fact that, despite the short preparation period, the elections were organized and conducted in an orderly manner. The EU also encouraged Kazakhstan to continue further democratic reforms. This latter formulation is particularly important: democratization should be understood as a process, not as a one-time event.

One of the fundamental dilemmas of political development in Central Asia is how to preserve state stability while gradually expanding political participation, institutional accountability and social pluralism. Given the historical, social and geopolitical realities of the region, it is hardly realistic to expect these countries to transform into Western European-style political systems within just a few years. The real question is rather whether the direction of change points toward greater or lesser political participation.

Perhaps the most important feature of President Tokayev’s reform policy is its attempt to reconcile political modernization with state stability. The events of January 2022 clearly demonstrated the serious consequences that may arise when social and economic tensions accumulate without proper political channels for expression. One of the deeper objectives of the current reform process may therefore be to create more institutional opportunities for the articulation of social interests, while preserving the functionality of the state and the country’s geopolitical stability.

This is particularly important for a country located between Russia and China, while at the same time building increasingly intensive relations with the European Union, the United States, Türkiye and the broader Turkic world. Kazakhstan’s domestic political stability is one of the foundations of its foreign policy room for manoeuvre. A destabilized Kazakhstan would have serious consequences not only for Central Asia, but also for the wider Eurasian transport, energy and trade systems.

Therefore, the success of Kazakhstan’s political modernization should not be measured by whether the country meets all Western democratic standards overnight. A much more relevant question is whether political institutions have become stronger, whether citizens now have greater opportunities for participation, whether the political space has become more pluralistic, and whether the feedback mechanisms between the state and society function better than they did five or ten years ago.

From this perspective, Kazakhstan’s progress is difficult to deny.

The current elections, therefore, do not mark the end of the reform process, but rather the beginning of a new stage. The real question for the coming years will be whether the new Kurultai will be able to become an independent political institution; whether the parliament’s oversight function will be strengthened; whether genuine political competition will emerge both within and beyond the currently dominant party system; and whether the institutional strengthening of the rule of law and media freedom will continue.

The key message of the 2026 elections is that Kazakhstan continues to choose the path of controlled, evolutionary political modernization. From the outside, the pace of this process may appear slow, its results imperfect, and the need for further reforms obvious. Yet, based on Central Asia’s historical experience, a gradual transformation that preserves stability and is based on institution-building may prove to be a more sustainable model in the long term than a rapid political transformation imported from outside.

The story of Kazakhstan’s democratic development, therefore, is by no means over. In fact, it has just entered a new and perhaps even more interesting phase.

The author is Professor László Vasa, the Chief Advisor, Senior Research Fellow of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, research professor of the Széchenyi István University.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Abkhazia to review how effectively agricultural grants are being spent
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to review how agricultural grants have been spent. President Badra Gunba has ordered the government to return to the budget any money spent on ineffective projects.

The grants come from the Agriculture Ministry’s “Agricultural Development for 2025” programme and the Economy Ministry’s programme supporting small and medium-sized businesses.

The president’s decision to review how the grants are used was most likely prompted by numerous complaints from farmers on social media, who say the government is providing little or no support to actual producers.

Badra Gunba does not rule out some violations given the large amount of funding involved.

“If violations are found — and with such a huge amount of funding, they are bound to occur — we must respond to them. But most importantly, we should not simply punish those responsible. We must make sure they compensate the state for all the costs it has incurred and return the money to the budget,” the president said.

The opposition media outlet Respublika believes that the president’s decision to order law enforcement agencies to set up an interagency group to oversee state support programmes for small and medium-sized businesses can only mean one thing: something is clearly wrong with these programmes.

“It looks like someone has already decided to make a tidy profit from state support for entrepreneurs. Now law enforcement agencies have several options:

simply scare them so they stop stealing;

investigate what they have already managed to steal;

or get in on the deal themselves.

Which option do you think they will choose?” Respublika asks, making it clear that it believes the answer is obvious.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Georgian businessman Elizbarashvili charged over alleged threats
World.content:
Elizbarashvili charged with making threats

Prosecutors have charged businessman and animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who is known for his outspoken criticism of the government, with making threats. He is accused of an offence under Article 151, Part 1 of the Criminal Code, which carries a maximum prison sentence of one year.

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Lekso Svimonishvili, seven alleged victims are involved in the case. Prosecutors say Elizbarashvili threatened them and that they regarded the threats as genuine.

Svimonishvili said his client categorically rejected the charges and maintained that he was completely innocent.

What do investigators accuse Elizbarashvili of?

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, an investigation by the Interior Ministry established that at around 2340 on 30 August, Tamaz Elizbarashvili and one of the alleged victims encountered each other by chance at a restaurant in Tbilisi. A verbal altercation broke out over a comment Elizbarashvili had previously posted on social media about the individual and his family.

According to investigators, during the altercation Elizbarashvili threatened the alleged victim and the people accompanying him. In particular, he allegedly said he would not let the matter rest and would return in about 30 minutes, while demanding that they remain at the restaurant.

“Since the alleged victims knew that Tamaz Elizbarashvili possessed a weapon that could be used against them, they had reasonable grounds to fear for their lives and safety and therefore decided to leave the restaurant.

At around 0020, Tamaz Elizbarashvili returned to the scene intending to carry out his threat. He was armed and attempted to enter the restaurant, conspicuously keeping his hand on a weapon tucked into his waistband. He also continued to threaten and insult the alleged victims. Those who had not managed to leave and remained near the restaurant had reasonable grounds to fear that the threat would be carried out.

Despite being barred by security staff, Tamaz Elizbarashvili nevertheless entered the restaurant premises. After establishing that the alleged victims were no longer there, he left,” the Prosecutor’s Office said.

What does the lawyer say?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, prosecutors cite comments previously made by the businessman on social media as the reason for the confrontation. However, the defence says the indictment makes no mention of any personal conflict between Elizbarashvili and the alleged victims.

“Mr Tamaz does not admit guilt, and his account of what happened is radically different [from the one presented]. During the incident, he left his wife and children at home to shield them from any potential confrontation and returned alone, believing that if anyone had questions, they could put them to him in person. However, no-one was there when he arrived,” Svimonishvili said.

The case materials also refer to a firearm, although Elizbarashvili denies possessing one illegally. According to his lawyer, he has not at this stage been charged with the illegal acquisition, possession or carrying of a firearm.

Svimonishvili said the only firearm seized during a search of Elizbarashvili’s apartment was officially registered in his name and had been sent for forensic examination.

The defence will ask the court not to impose any pre-trial restrictions on Elizbarashvili. Alternatively, the lawyer will request that he be released on bail.

Prosecutors have not yet specified what pre-trial measure they will ask the court to impose.

Background

On 1 September 2026, Elizbarashvili was placed under administrative arrest for allegedly failing to comply with a lawful police order. His arrest followed searches of his car and home conducted as part of an investigation launched under Articles 151 (threats) and 236 (illegal acquisition, possession and carrying of firearms) of the Criminal Code.

Elizbarashvili said the complaint against him had been filed by employees of the Imedi TV channel, with whom he had a verbal altercation at a restaurant on 30 August. He alleged that the Imedi employees had initiated the confrontation and threatened him over his political views.

World.title: Ex-Georgian PM questioned in prison over his statements on a human rights defender who died by suicide
World.content:
Georgia: Gharibashvili questioned in Jorbenadze case

As part of the ongoing investigation into the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, law enforcement officers questioned former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili at Prison No. 12 in Rustavi on September 3.

Jorbenadze had publicly criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili recently published a letter expressing doubts about the officially stated cause of the human rights defender’s death — suicide.

Following several hours of questioning, prosecutor Medea Tsiramua and Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, spoke to journalists.

Former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in January 2026 for legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. He pleaded guilty and reached a plea deal with the prosecution. On August 24, he was charged with a second offence — accepting a particularly large bribe. Gharibashvili denies the new charge.

What the lawyer and prosecutor said

How it started. On September 1, 2026, Irakli Gharibashvili published another letter from prison on social media, calling on government officials to answer questions about the true circumstances of Lazare Jorbenadze’s death. Gharibashvili pointed out that Jorbenadze, a former human rights defender, had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze in an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze and died by suicide shortly after its publication. Gharibashvili also noted that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, where the article was published, had publicly questioned the suicide theory.

According to the prosecution, Gharibashvili’s public suspicions about the circumstances of Jorbenadze’s death have no direct factual basis. The prosecutor said the former prime minister provided investigators with no new or significant information.

She said the questioning showed that Gharibashvili was neither a direct witness to Jorbenadze’s death nor someone with specific information about it.

“Gharibashvili’s public letters were based solely on information from various publications, rather than any specific facts. He categorically stated that he has no specific information about Lazare Jorbenadze’s suicide,” prosecutor Medea Tsiramua said.

Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, who is his wife’s sister, said the former prime minister’s questions arose after he read specific publications while in prison and later learned of Jorbenadze’s death.

“His questions arose after he was sent a letter containing an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze in Asaval-Dasavali. The article was critical of Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili later learned about Jorbenadze’s death, put the facts together and raised questions publicly. During the questioning, he repeated the same questions he had raised in his public letter,” the lawyer said.

According to the defence, Gharibashvili was not trying to provide investigators with previously unknown sources or information. His questions were based on suspicions about a possible connection between the articles published in the media and Jorbenadze’s sudden death.

Series of interrogations in the Lazare Jorbenadze case

Before Gharibashvili was questioned, politicians and public figures were questioned at the Digomi police headquarters in Tbilisi. They were asked about the former prime minister’s letter published on social media.

Investigators questioned Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the opposition coalition For Change, analyst Gia Khukhashvili and several activists.

Gvaramia said he had no information about the details of the case and knew only what had been published on social media.

Opposition politicians Khatia Dekanoidze and Tazo Datunashvili, as well as journalist Nanuka Zhorzholiani, refused to appear for questioning at the police station. They told investigators they would give evidence only in court, in the presence of a magistrate judge.

World.title: ‘If Russia decides to withdraw its military base, we will not object’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia.

“If Russia decides to withdraw its military base from Armenia, we will not object. But if they want to stay, we are ready to discuss that too,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during his regular weekly briefing.

He also said Yerevan does not consider the presence of Russia’s 102nd military base in Armenia vital.

Putin raised the issue after his meeting with Pashinyan in Bishkek, although the Armenian prime minister says they did not discuss the issue either during those talks or before them. Putin said:

“If Armenia believes that Russia’s military base is not needed in Armenia, we will leave tomorrow if necessary. Is Armenia ready for that? Fine, we will not impose anything on anyone. But if the Armenian people want some kind of Russian military ‘wing’ there, we will stay. We will work and cooperate.”

Pashinyan also commented at the briefing on the issues he discussed with Putin in Bishkek. In particular, he once again explained Armenia’s position on its membership in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, Russia’s concession to operate Armenia’s railways and the construction of a new nuclear power plant.

Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum

“And who said that all EAEU member states swore allegiance and would remain members of the EAEU for their entire existence?”

That was Pashinyan’s answer to a question about Armenia’s membership in the Russian-led EAEU. He gave it among the first answers at the briefing. The issue also dominated the open part of the Pashinyan-Putin talks.

For several months, Russia has been calling at various levels for Armenia to hold a referendum on membership of the EAEU or the European Union. The Russian president also insisted on this at the meeting in Bishkek.

“The adoption of the law to begin Armenia’s accession to another organisation amounts to a declaration that it is leaving ours,”* Putin said.

Pashinyan explained to the Russian president, and repeated at the briefing, that under the union’s charter, a country must give six months’ notice before ending its membership. However, Armenia has no such intention for now.

He said he continues to explain this to his Russian partners, trying to make Armenia’s position “clearer and more acceptable”.

One journalist who raised the issue described Putin’s tone towards Pashinyan as “harsh”. He said Moscow was taking a tough line and forcing Yerevan to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenia’s prime minister replied:

“I am also giving the Russian president a tough choice. I say: this cannot continue, the issue of the railway concession must be resolved. Why is there no headline saying ‘Pashinyan gives Russian president a tough choice’?”

Pashinyan himself believes Armenian media do not use such headlines because the country still follows the “logic of subordination to the Central Committee of the USSR”. In his view, that logic produces the following reaction: “They called from Moscow, we urgently need to bring out the cognac.”

At the same time, the prime minister stressed his position: Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum.

He said the country’s Constitution requires a referendum before joining a supranational organisation. However, Armenia should hold one only when the issue “is ripe”. This would mean, in particular, when Armenia applies for EU membership or at least sets out its roadmap. Holding a referendum before that, he argued, would mean asking citizens to go to polling stations before anyone has formulated the question or decided what answers they can choose.

Selling the railway concession is the best solution

Pashinyan said he discussed the future of South Caucasus Railway with Putin. This issue is, incidentally, more important to the Armenian side. For a long time, Armenia’s authorities have been telling their Russian partners that the country is losing its competitive advantage in developing regional railway links because Russia controls the Armenian railway.

Since 2008, the company South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railway under a concession agreement. Russian Railways owns 100% of the company. The agreement grants the concession for 30 years. However, since 2008, freight traffic on Armenia’s railways has halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the investment commitments have remained unfulfilled.

The Armenian prime minister therefore proposed selling the concession to a third country that is friendly to both Armenia and Russia. Russian partners described the proposal as “strange and largely unacceptable”.

However, Pashinyan said the following about the outcome of his meeting with Putin:

“We reached an understanding that the current situation cannot continue for much longer. We need to resolve this issue somehow. Both Armenia and Russia understand that one possible solution would be to sell the concession rights to a third party acceptable to both Armenia and Russia. Frankly, I think this is the best solution. The other options seem unrealistic.”».

Moscow to present proposals for building a new nuclear power plant

According to Pashinyan, Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev will visit Armenia in September.

“He will present Armenia with proposals on what Russia can offer today for the construction of a new nuclear power plant. I have already said that we do not see the nuclear power plant as a geopolitical choice. We need the best value for money. We will go with whoever makes the best offer,” the prime minister said.

He said Armenia would consider all possible options, whether a small modular reactor proposed by Western partners or a conventional Russian nuclear power plant:

“We have never said that the Russian proposal cannot be the best one, including in terms of modular reactors. It is not the case that Russia has no proposal for modular reactors. However, there are a number of important factors: the price, the payback period, the construction time and the financing arrangements.”

Nikol Pashinyan said work on the issue had intensified and that Armenia should make a decision within a year.

He said Armenia initially favoured a small modular reactor, but “desire is one thing and reality is another”.

The problem is that experts are concerned about the lack of experience in building modular nuclear power plants and the potential risks.

According to the prime minister, if there are no operating or licensed modular nuclear power plants anywhere in the world when Armenia makes its decision, this will create “uncertainty” and make the decision very difficult.

At the same time, he said work was continuing to extend the operating life of the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant beyond 2036.

No plans to introduce visas for Russian citizens

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that “if Armenia suddenly introduces visas as well, it will not introduce them against us — it will introduce them against its own citizens”. She also said the move would affect Russian citizens who have relatives in Armenia.

Importantly, no one in Armenia had suggested introducing a visa regime for Russian citizens before her statement.

“We have absolutely no such intention, and never have. It has never even crossed our minds. We are very happy to welcome tourists from Russia. We can see that they have now become very active in promoting Armenia’s tourism attractions. Society also welcomes these people. And they themselves seem to feel quite comfortable in Armenia. We are happy to have them, just as we are happy to welcome tourists from other countries,” the prime minister said.

Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia

World.title: Georgian politicians questioned after ex-prime minister’s claims about Lazare Jorbenadze’s death
World.content:
Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

Georgian politicians have been summoned for questioning over public statements by former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili about the death of Lazare Jorbenadze.

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, investigators have confirmed the suicide theory without ambiguity following investigative work into Jorbenadze’s death on 4 April 2026 and interviews with members of his family.

Nevertheless, because convicted former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili and others have made public statements about the case, investigators will question several political figures further: Irakli Garibashvili himself, Nika Gvaramia, Irma Inashvili, Nanuka Zhorzholiani, Khatia Dekanoidze, Tazo Datunashvili, Gia Khukhashvili, Giorgi Liluashvili, Zaza Davitaia and Ermile Nemsadze.

What happened

On 1 September 2026, former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili published another letter from prison. He called on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Garibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article based on an interview with him.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the suicide theory. In his letter, Garibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the true cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly about the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February with other circumstances.



Lazare Jorbenadze

According to Garibashvili, on 12 February, officials acting on the instructions of Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze gave him an article that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali had published on 2 February 2026.

The article featured a conversation between Dito Chubinidze and Lazare Jorbenadze. Garibashvili says it focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received suggested that he was behind the article. “I received a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article in question,” Garibashvili writes.

Garibashvili says he categorically rejected the accusation and told government representatives that he had never engaged in publishing “commissioned articles”.

What do politicians say?

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, said she would appear in court to testify in the Lazare Jorbenadze case. She said Bidzina Ivanishvili bears responsibility for the system he created, so investigators should question him as well.

“Bidzina Ivanishvili created a system in which people fight for positions and money, testify against each other, fabricate cases and, of course, are deeply involved in corruption. That is why Bidzina Ivanishvili, Kobakhidze, Mdinaradze and everyone who fabricates all sorts of dirt for money should be summoned for questioning. As for the investigation itself, I have made my position clear: I will go to court,” Dekanoidze said.

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili said he did not understand why authorities had summoned him for questioning in the Lazare Jorbenadze death case, as he had made no specific statements about Jorbenadze and only learned of his existence after his death.

“I only learned of Jorbenadze’s existence after his death. I did not comment specifically on the situation involving Jorbenadze. I spoke more broadly about suicide cases that raise questions. Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze should be here instead of me, because Garibashvili named them, but they are not being summoned — I am. And now this has turned into nothing more than a tragicomedy,” Khukhashvili commented.

According to Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, investigators did not ask him about any other subjects during his questioning in the Jorbenadze death case. Gvaramia believes the case may serve two purposes: one could be political propaganda, while the other could involve bringing new charges against the former prime minister.

“The next step, I am sure, will be to bring new charges against Garibashvili, under the article concerning illegal wiretapping. As far as I know, investigators are currently questioning him in prison. Mdinaradze and Kobakhidze should themselves be concerned about such allegations if they are true, although Garibashvili should also provide further explanations,” Gvaramia said after the questioning.

Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

World.title: Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?
World.content:
Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the authorities have raised the income threshold for classifying families as low-income. It would be logical to expect this to increase both the number of people receiving assistance and the amount of support they receive. However, official statistics show the opposite trend: both the number of families receiving targeted state social assistance and the amount paid per person are falling.

According to the State Statistics Committee, as of 1 July, 349,300 people from 78,900 families received targeted social assistance. A year earlier, the system covered 353,300 people from 80,300 families. This means that over the year, the number of families receiving assistance fell by 1,400, while the number of recipients fell by 4,000.

The decline becomes even more striking over the longer term. In mid-2017, 498,400 people received this type of assistance. Over nine years, that figure fell by 149,100, or about 30%. Meanwhile, the country’s population increased during the same period.

These figures raise an important question: have the incomes of low-income families increased enough for them to no longer need social assistance, or has the system stopped reaching some people who still need support?

The income threshold has risen, but social assistance has fallen

Targeted social assistance is not a fixed payment. The authorities calculate it as the difference between the needs-based threshold for all family members and the family’s average monthly income. The calculation takes into account income from the previous 12 months.

In 2025, the needs-based threshold stood at 285 manats (approx. $167.65) per person. In 2026, the authorities raised it to 300 manats (approx. $176.50), an increase of 5.3%. Despite this, the average payment per person fell from 100.37 to 97.94 manats (approx. $59 to $57.70). In nominal terms, the payment fell by 2.43 manats (approx. $1.43), or 2.4%.

Applying the current formula to the average figures suggests that the system calculated recipients’ average monthly income per person at 184.63 manats (approx. $108.60) in 2025 and 202.06 manats (approx. $118.90) in 2026. This represents a nominal increase of 9.4%. Mathematically, the lower payments reflect the fact that, according to the system’s calculations, family incomes grew faster than the needs-based threshold.

However, these figures do not prove that the financial situation of all low-income families has improved. The average for families that remained in the system in mid-2026 is being compared with the average for families that received assistance a year earlier. Families whose payments stopped or whose applications were rejected no longer form part of the new average.

Our calculations, based on official data, show that total monthly payments to recipients fell from about 35.46 million (approx. $20.86 million) to 34.21 million manats (approx. $20.12 million). The government therefore reduced its monthly spending on this group by about 1.25 million manats (approx. $735,300), or 3.5%, in nominal terms.

The assistance has lost even more purchasing power

According to July 2026 data, annual inflation stood at 5.8%, while food inflation reached 7.3%. After taking price rises into account, the purchasing power of the 97.94-manat payment fell by about 7.8% compared with the 100.37-manat payment a year earlier. If we consider only food price increases, the decline approaches 9%.

After receiving assistance, the system brings a family’s calculated income per person up to the needs-based threshold of 300 manats. However, this represents only a 5.3% increase from last year’s level of 285 manats. That increase falls short of overall inflation and especially of food price growth. As a result, even the minimum income of families that remain in the social assistance system has not increased in real terms.

The number of people receiving assistance is not the number of people living in poverty

The State Statistics Committee’s final data for 2025 put the poverty line at 286 manats (approx. $168.20) and the poverty rate at 5.2%. With a population of 10.26 million, this amounts to roughly 534,000 people.

At the end of the same year, 336,000 people received targeted social assistance, or about 3.3% of the population. The authorities use different methodologies and reporting dates to calculate these figures, so we cannot directly compare them. Nevertheless, the gap of about 198,000 people clearly shows that the number of assistance recipients cannot serve as a measure of poverty in the country.

Moreover, earning less than 300 manats does not in itself qualify a person for assistance. Under the rules, a family must show that factors beyond its control have caused its low income. The official criteria allow authorities to reject an application if the family owns or uses a car, has two properties of the same type at different addresses, or has carried out purchase or sale transactions worth more than 12 times the subsistence minimum over the previous 12 months. Authorities can also reject an application if an able-bodied family member has turned down two suitable job offers.

Based on the 2026 subsistence minimum, the threshold for purchase and sale transactions stands at 3,600 manats (approx. $2,118). Authorities can also reject assistance if a family spends 45 manats (approx. $26.50) or more per person each month on utilities and communications. For a family of four, that amounts to 180 manats (approx. $106) in total. The authorities also count money and gifts from relatives, as well as estimated income from a household farm or garden, when calculating family income.

These criteria may help identify hidden income and assets. However, the same rules can exclude a family with a low cash income if it owns an old car, faces high utility bills or mainly survives on financial support from relatives.

The number of pensioners is falling, while more people receive age-related benefits

Another question arises when we examine other social security figures. On 1 July 2025, Azerbaijan had 1,103,300 pensioners. A year later, the figure had fallen to 1.1 million. At the same time, the average pension rose by 10.5% to 594.4 manats (approx. $350). However, the number of pensioners fell by 3,300.

Meanwhile, the number of people who do not qualify for a labour pension but receive a 220-manat age-related benefit (approx. $130) rose from 166,200 to 177,500. We cannot say that the changes in these two groups involve the same people. However, the fall in the number of pensioners as the elderly population grows, alongside the rise in recipients of a lower benefit, requires a separate explanation in terms of access to labour pensions.

What data the government should disclose

To treat a decline in the number of assistance recipients as evidence of falling poverty, we need more than one headline figure. The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population should report how many families entered the system over the past year, how many stopped receiving assistance, how many applicants faced rejection and why authorities rejected their applications.

The government should also report how many families failed to qualify under each criterion, including car ownership, purchase and sale transactions, utility costs, discrepancies in income data and refusal to accept an offered job. It should also disclose how many decisions authorities reviewed following complaints and what share of assistance recipients are children.

Without this data, we cannot conclude that poverty has fallen. So far, the official statistics show only this: the number of people covered by targeted social assistance has fallen, the average payment has declined in nominal terms, and its purchasing power has fallen even further.

Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

World.title: Beslan school siege 22 years on: Where does investigation stand and what did victims achieve?
World.content:
Beslan school siege anniversary

Twenty-two years have passed since the Beslan school siege, one of the most tragic events in the modern history of North Ossetia.

Commemorative events are being held across the republic, but there is still no complete clarity over what exactly happened during the attack.

“Three days in hell”: Timeline of the attack

On 1 September 2004, militants took pupils and teachers at School No 1 in Beslan hostage, including children starting their first year at school, their parents and babies who were with them.

In the first hours of the siege, the militants shot dead the adult male hostages. They held the others in the school’s gymnasium for three days, denying them water and making political demands, including the withdrawal of Russian troops from Chechnya.

The militants also demanded the presence of the then president of North Ossetia, Alexander Dzasokhov, Ingush President Murat Zyazikov, and CIS Executive Secretary and former Russian Security Council Secretary Vladimir Rushailo. None of them complied with the demand.

The North Ossetian authorities attempted to negotiate the release of the hostages, but without success. On 2 September, former Ingush President Ruslan Aushev managed to negotiate with the Ingush members of the militant group. He was allowed into the gymnasium and secured the release of around 20 women with babies.

At noon on the third day, two explosions were heard in the gymnasium.

According to some of the hostages and the official account, one of the explosive devices that the militants had placed along the walls detonated. A fire broke out in the gymnasium and the militants began shooting at the hostages.

An unofficial account, however, maintains that the explosion and subsequent fire were caused by an external strike on the school building using a Shmel rocket launcher.

This account remains disputed, with the North Ossetian and wider Russian authorities rejecting it as unfounded. FSB special forces, who were rehearsing an assault plan in a nearby village when the explosions occurred, were then urgently deployed to Beslan. Fighting with the militants ensued, during which most of the hostages were freed.

However, the death toll was still extremely high. A total of 334 people were killed in the attack, including 314 hostages and 20 members of the FSB special forces, Interior Ministry and Emergencies Ministry. Another 783 hostages were injured.

According to the official account, there were 32 militants. All were killed except Nur-Pashi Kulayev, who was detained and later sentenced to life imprisonment.

However, the criminal investigation launched immediately after the attack has still not been concluded. Relatives of the victims disputed the authorities’ official account and demanded an “objective and fair investigation”. According to some former hostages, there were more than 32 militants and some may have escaped.

There were also claims that the attackers had hidden weapons inside the school in advance and that some of the militants had previously gained access to the building by posing as workers carrying out repairs.

Commemoration ceremony in the gymnasium where the hostages were held

22 года спустя

On 1 September 2026, the Mothers of Beslan public organisation held its annual press conference.

The organisation’s leader, Susanna Dudiyeva, reported some progress in the criminal investigation, which she said had been made possible following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin two years ago, when he visited Beslan ahead of the 20th anniversary of the attack. According to Dudiyeva, Putin subsequently issued instructions to the head of Russia’s Investigative Committee, Alexander Bastrykin.

Dudiyeva told the press conference that investigators had established that there were in fact more than 32 militants and that the criminal case remained open because not all of those killed had been identified. In particular, investigators have been unable to identify one of them, a Saudi national, as the Saudi authorities have not been cooperating with Russian investigators.

The health of former hostages was one of the main issues discussed at the press conference. The Mothers of Beslan committee has successfully campaigned for victims of the attack and their relatives to receive regular social and medical assistance. A comprehensive rehabilitation programme for those affected by the attack has been extended until 2030, while funding for their medical treatment has been increased.

“I would say that rehabilitation at health resorts is going well. There are some problems and some issues, but they can all be resolved. It is particularly encouraging that the children of former hostages who were born after the attack are now also receiving rehabilitation. Almost no other victims of terrorist attacks in Russia have access to this kind of rehabilitation,” Susanna Dudiyeva said.

The question of granting victims an official legal status remains a pressing issue. The adoption of relevant legislation would open up significant new opportunities to provide support to survivors and even their children.

Elvira Tuayeva, a member of the Mothers of Beslan organisation, said the group would continue campaigning for a law establishing the legal status of victims of terrorist attacks, not only those affected by the Beslan siege but by all terrorist attacks that have taken place in Russia.

World.title: Georgian businessman, animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili begins prison hunger strike
World.content:
Activist Elizbarashvili on hunger strike

Georgian businessman, animal rights activist and outspoken critic of the Georgian Dream government Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who was detained earlier, has gone on hunger strike.

Tamaz Elizbarashvili was detained at his home after law enforcement officers searched his car and flat. The Interior Ministry said the search of Elizbarashvili’s car was carried out as part of an investigation into alleged threats and the illegal acquisition and possession of weapons.

According to his lawyer, Elizbarashvili is currently being held in administrative detention.

What is known so far?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Iako Siranashvili, her client was detained by law enforcement officers as he was attempting to jump from a balcony and take his own life.

Siranashvili said Elizbarashvili attempted to take his own life after seeing law enforcement officers use force against his lawyer and witnessing his children in distress.

“Tamaz Elizbarashvili was going to take his own life when he saw me being pushed into the building and beaten. When he saw his children crying and in distress, he tried to jump from the balcony. Tamaz was detained over this and charged with disobeying police orders,” Siranashvili said.

According to the lawyer, law enforcement officers tried to take her phone away when she began filming the search. She alleges that around 20 officers then used physical force against her.

“They tried to take my phone away to stop me filming the search. Anyone is allowed to film, especially a lawyer. They probably wanted to plant a weapon or some other prohibited item, but I prevented them from doing so because I was filming. Around 20 people then attacked me: they grabbed me and snatched the phone from my hands. When I resisted their attempts to take it, they twisted my arms, threw me to the ground and began kicking me,” Siranashvili said.

The lawyer said she had sustained injuries to various parts of her body and was having difficulty walking. Siranashvili said she had left the clinic of her own accord.

“My injuries are such that I can barely walk. I have difficulty moving around. My left arm is in severe pain. My hearing has also deteriorated and I have swelling around my facial bone. I left the clinic of my own accord because I did not think it was necessary to remain there,” she said.

According to Siranashvili, an investigation has been launched under Article 333 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers abuse of official powers. She said, however, that investigators should also examine whether offences had been committed under Articles 364 and 365, which concern obstruction of a lawyer’s professional activities.

“What angers me most is not the fact that I was beaten, but that I was prevented from carrying out my professional duties. That is what makes me most angry, as does the fact that violence was used against a lawyer. Other articles must also be applied; the investigation cannot be limited to Article 333 alone,” the lawyer said.

She said her health had so far prevented her from attending the investigative authorities for a medical examination.

“I feel very unwell and have not yet been physically able to get to the relevant authorities. Investigators have ordered a medical examination, and I hope it will be carried out,” Siranashvili said.

World.title: ADB considers $500,000 grant for Azerbaijan power projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is considering providing $500,000 in grant financing to support the preparation of sustainable power infrastructure projects in Azerbaijan.

The technical assistance is proposed to be financed through the Technical Assistance Special Fund (TASF) and will support the preparation of the first phase of the proposed Azerbaijan Power Distribution Modernization Project, which is included in ADB’s 2026 indicative country pipeline and monitoring report.

The assistance will also finance selected sector studies, capacity-building and gender-related activities aimed at addressing priority needs in the power sector, strengthening project readiness and supporting future ADB operations.

The project is expected to improve the readiness of investments in power distribution grid digitalization and renewable energy integration.

The broader impact of the assistance is expected to be improved electricity supply through the distribution network.

Feasibility study for the power distribution modernization and digitalization project, including assessment of the suitability of digital substation technology has been completed. Moreover, institutional capacity of OJSC Azerishiq for ADB project readiness and gender responsiveness has been strengthened.

According to the latest data from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Azerbaijan secured $2.53 billion in sovereign financing for 10 projects between 2015 and 2024. More than half of that funding (51%) was allocated to regional cooperation and integration projects, representing one of the highest shares among ADB's peer countries. Another 39% supported private sector development, while 18% was dedicated to climate finance and 10% to digital transformation initiatives.

Over the same period, ADB approved nine non-sovereign operations totaling $963.9 million, all of which were directed toward private sector development. Notably, 78% of these commitments were linked to regional cooperation and integration—the highest proportion among comparable upper middle-income economies in ADB's portfolio.

Data from the Central Bank of Azerbaijan show that ADB's foreign direct investment in the country's economy reached $2.075 million in the first quarter of this year, up $455,000, or 28.1%, from the same period a year earlier.

ADB has also expanded its support for Azerbaijan's energy transition. In April 2025, the bank signed a memorandum of understanding with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) and the energy ministries of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan to support the preparation of a feasibility study for the Caspian Green Energy Corridor, a regional initiative aimed at enabling cross-border trade in renewable electricity.

The bank is also providing technical assistance for renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan. Among its recent initiatives is a pilot floating solar power plant on Boyukshor Lake, launched in 2024 to evaluate the commercial viability of floating photovoltaic technology and lay the groundwork for future large-scale deployment.

These efforts are aligned with ADB's 2025–2029 Country Partnership Strategy for Azerbaijan, which identifies green, resilient and diversified economic growth as a central pillar of cooperation, with a strong focus on clean energy, climate resilience and sustainable infrastructure.
