World.title: Uzbekistan’s Fergana, Japan's Mitsui step up investment cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Uzbekistan’s Fergana region and Japanese trading and investment company Mitsui & Co. are exploring new investment projects in energy, water supply, food processing, infrastructure, tourism and education.

This was reflected in the statement by the Fergana regional administration, following a meeting between Governor Khayrullo Bozorov and a delegation led by Tomo Shingo, chief representative of Mitsui & Co.’s office in Uzbekistan, to discuss expanding investment cooperation.

According to the Regional administration, in the course of the meeting, the sides noted the steady development of the strategic partnership between Uzbekistan and Japan and the growing scope of bilateral cooperation.

Moreover, the talks focused on expanding interregional ties, increasing the number of projects involving Japanese investors and supporting new investment initiatives. The parties also emphasized the importance of reciprocal visits by business and government delegations in developing such cooperation.

“Particular attention in the Fergana region is being paid to the introduction of Japan’s advanced experience,” the regional administration said, noting that Japanese teaching methods have already been introduced on an experimental basis in the region’s education system. Higher education institutions are also using modern approaches to train specialists.

During the meeting, the sides put forward proposals for joint projects in the oil industry, water supply, fruit and vegetable processing, infrastructure, tourism and education.

Mitsui & Co. is a major international trading and investment company headquartered in Tokyo and operates in 62 countries. The company opened its representative office in Uzbekistan in 1993 and has investment interests spanning energy, infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and food processing, chemicals, digital technologies and logistics, among other sectors.

The company’s broad sectoral presence could provide opportunities for Fergana to attract Japanese investment and technologies across several priority areas, particularly infrastructure, agricultural processing and water management.

The sides agreed on measures to further expand cooperation, taking into account Mitsui’s areas of expertise and Fergana’s investment priorities.

Meanwhile, Mitsui & Co.’s chief representative in Kazakhstan, Tulkinjon Rakhimov, and Fergana First Deputy Governor Mirzokhid Ubaydullaev also participated in the meeting.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan Industrial Park - synergy of industrial and logistics options
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Diversifying Azerbaijan’s economy is one of the government’s key priorities. One of the important areas of this policy is the establishment of industrial parks and industrial districts in various regions of the country. This policy is already producing results. In the first half of 2026, the volume of production in industrial zones managed by the Economic Zones Development Agency under the Ministry of Economy rose by 8.6% year-on-year to 1.94 billion manat ($1.14 billion). During this period, 554.7 million manat ($326.3 million) worth of manufactured products were exported.

Nakhchivan Industrial Park, expanding geoeconomic opportunities of Azerbaijan

A new stage in the development of industrial zones in Azerbaijan is already beginning. Thus, on August 11 of this year, the foundation of the Nakhchivan Industrial Park was laid. Priority directions for production, processing and recycling, as well as services have been determined here. The industrial park is expected to implement projects in the chemical and food industry, waste processing, ferrous and non-ferrous metal processing, manufacturing of construction materials, machinery and equipment, renewable energy, furniture, textiles, clothing, leather and leather products, packaging, paper and paper products. In addition to production buildings, it's planned to create an administrative building, a social zone including a sports and health center, a repair workshop, a warehouse building, a truck park and a logistics center in the park.

What concessions envisaged in Nakhchivan Industrial Park?

As in other industrial parks, the park will apply a wide range of concessions and support mechanisms to promote the activities of entrepreneurs. Thus, the residents of the park will be provided with ready-made infrastructure created at the expense of state funds. This infrastructure includes gas, electricity, water and sewage systems, internal roads and railways, as well as modern communication lines. In addition, residents of the industrial park are exempt from property, land and profit taxes for a period of 10 years from the date of their registration. Machinery and equipment imported for production purposes are exempt from VAT and customs duties.

What new opportunities does Nakhchivan Industrial Park open up?

Nakhchivan has a strategic position that differs from other regions of Azerbaijan due to its location on the border. This geographical location makes the region an interesting investment destination in terms of access not only to the domestic market of Azerbaijan, but also to foreign markets. The main advantage for the investor here is not only to produce products, but also to organize production in an area close to regional markets. An entrepreneur can consider the possibility of exporting his products to foreign markets by establishing a production line in Nakhchivan without limiting himself to the local market. In this regard, the advantage of Nakhchivan is that it can play the role of a bridge between production and trade. On the one hand, it's possible to use the local raw materials and production potential of the region, and on the other hand, it's possible to benefit from trade relations with neighboring countries.

Nakhchivan Industrial Park located on Zangezur corridor

One of the main factors increasing the strategic importance of the Nakhchivan Industrial Park is its close connection with the future transport and logistics opportunities of the region. In particular, the implementation of the Zangezur corridor can bring new dynamics to the economic and geographical position of Nakhchivan. With the commissioning of the corridor, the role of Nakhchivan in the international transport and logistics routes of the region can also increase significantly.

In this regard, it is not enough to approach the Nakhchivan Industrial Park only as an industrial zone where manufacturing enterprises are concentrated. When assessing the future potential of the park, it is more correct to consider it together with its transport and logistics opportunities. The opening of the Zangezur corridor can strengthen the position of Nakhchivan in terms of freight transportation, warehouse and logistics services, transit, and regional trade.

Another important factor is the future expansion of Nakhchivan's transport and logistics potential. The Zangezur corridor is considered not only as a transport line that strengthens Nakhchivan's connection with other regions of Azerbaijan, but also as a project that can accelerate the region's integration into the wider Eurasian transport network. In this context, Nakhchivan's location on the border is also an important advantage that increases its regional trade and logistics opportunities.

From a broader regional perspective, it's also necessary to consider the potential role of Nakhchivan in the transport links formed along the Middle Corridor. The Middle Corridor is one of the important routes that envisages the transportation of cargo flows from China and Central Asia to Europe via the South Caucasus and the Caspian Sea. The implementation of the Zangezur corridor could create new opportunities for Nakhchivan's integration into this wider transport system.

The synergy created by industry and logistics is particularly noteworthy here. If the industrial park forms a favorable infrastructure and investment environment for production, the expansion of transport and logistics opportunities facilitates the access of that production to markets. In the future, the park can become one of the economic hubs where production, logistics, and trade opportunities of Nakhchivan complement each other. The expansion of access to new markets for the production enterprises established here can also increase the investment attractiveness of the region.

Thus, the main advantage for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park spans beyond the promotion of industrial production. The combination of industrial infrastructure, a strategic geographic location, proximity to foreign markets, future transport links, and the opportunities that the Zangazur Corridor could create may turn Nakhchivan into an economic hub with broader regional prospects for investors.

World.title: Afghan businesses eye textile imports, Islamic banking opportunities in Uzbekistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Afghan business leaders are exploring opportunities to expand trade and financial cooperation with Uzbekistan’s Namangan region, including textile imports and the potential opening of Uzbekistan’s first Islamic bank in the region.

This was reflected in the statement by the Namangan regional administration, following a visit of a delegation led by Muhammad Ibrahim Ghazanfar, chairman of the Balkh Chamber of Commerce and Industry and founder of Ghazanfar Group, and Muhammad Ismail Ghazanfar, chairman of Ghazanfar Bank to Namangan to explore opportunities for cooperation with local businesses.

Namangan Region Governor Shavkatjon Abdurazzoqov received the Afghan business representatives for talks.

The meeting highlighted the strengthening of relations between Uzbekistan and Afghanistan in recent years, particularly growing business-to-business ties, according to the regional administration.

The Afghan businessmen expressed interest in importing textile products from Namangan, including various types of fabrics and textiles, to Afghanistan.

The sides also exchanged views on the possibility of opening Uzbekistan’s first Islamic bank in Namangan.

Such a bank could provide new financing opportunities for businesses and support the development of trade and investment links between companies in Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. It could also create an additional platform for financial cooperation between businesses in the two countries.

The participation of representatives from Ghazanfar Group and Ghazanfar Bank in the talks reflects interest from Afghan businesses in expanding commercial ties with Uzbekistan beyond traditional trade.

The meeting also focused on strengthening direct contacts between entrepreneurs from Namangan and Balkh, with the sides agreeing to further develop business cooperation and pursue mutually beneficial opportunities.

The talks come as Uzbekistan continues to expand economic engagement with neighboring Afghanistan, with trade, logistics and business ties forming an important part of efforts to promote regional economic connectivity.

"At the end of the dialogue, it was agreed to further strengthen cooperation between entrepreneurs from the two regions," the statement said.

World.title: Argentina's Milei vows Falklands oil sanctions in sovereignty push
World.content:
Argentine President Javier Milei says he will sanction oil companies drilling in the Falkland Islands, the British overseas territory claimed by Argentina.

Mr Milei's comments come days after US President Donald Trump said he was reviewing the United States' neutral position on the remote archipelago in the South Atlantic.

It is 44 years since Argentina was defeated by Britain in a war over the islands that killed hundreds, but its sovereignty claim is still enshrined in the constitution and frequently invoked as an expression of national identity.

Now years after a deadly war and unresolved sovereignty claims, tensions are once again escalating.

Javier Milei delivers TV address

Argentina's President Javier Milei delivered a national address on Thursday, local time, and said the "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the archipelago, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

UK urges action over Falklands banner The British government urges FIFA to investigate after Argentine players held up a banner declaring the Falkland Islands were Argentinian.

He then announced sweeping actions aimed at stopping the development of the deep-sea Sea Lion oil project about 220 kilometres north of the islands.

British company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum plan to begin drilling in the coming months and start pumping oil in 2028. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

The companies said in a statement: "The partnership believes that the recent developments are not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development."

The Argentine leader threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in the offshore drilling.

He also announced new funding for a naval base in Argentina's southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego to bolster the country's military presence near the islands.

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Mr Milei said.

" Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security. "

Donald Trump reviewing US position

Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former coloniser, Spain, and that Britain has illegally occupied them since 1833.

Britain rejects that claim, citing the islanders' desire to remain a British overseas territory.

For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing claims while recognising Britain's de facto administration of the islands.

On Monday, Donald Trump stirred concern in Britain when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the decades-old dispute.

"I always review every position," he replied.

"That's just one of many."

Donald Trumps has put UK support in doubt. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Then, in an interview aired Thursday with British broadcaster GB News, Mr Trump dodged directly answering a question about whether the US would "come to the aid" of Britain in another conflict over the Falklands.

Instead, he repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran.

"Your country was not there to help me," Mr Trump said, recalling Britain's former prime minister, Keir Starmer, telling him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign.

"It was pretty sad, the whole thing."

Mr Milei presented Washington's review of its stance as a vindication of his policies and full-throated support for the Trump administration.

"The United States is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner," he said.

Britain, by contrast, is "on a path of decline", he said, alleging it faced "multiple migratory, demographic, and economic crises".

British commitment 'unshakeable'

Britain, which has controlled the islands since 1833, has said that Falkland islanders should determine their own future.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting said on Friday, local time, that the people living there had chosen to be British.

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," Mr Streeting said on X.

"Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable."

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said on X, the UK's position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering.

"The Islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders," he said.

"Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it."

In a 2013 referendum, 99.8 per cent of voters backed remaining under British rule, on a turnout of about 92 per cent. Britain cites the vote as evidence of the islanders' wishes and says it will not discuss sovereignty without their consent.

Argentina rejected the referendum.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Man jailed for recruiting underage girls for sex
World.content:
A North Queensland man motivated by his own "selfish and sinister desires" has been sentenced to 12 years' jail for the rape, sexual assault and recruitment of underage girls for sex.

Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault that some readers may find disturbing.

Charles William Gary Ottaviano previously pleaded guilty to five counts of rape, six counts of indecent treatment of a child under 16 and one count each of repeated sexual conduct with a child and sexual assault over a seven-year period.

During sentencing on Friday afternoon, the Townsville District Court heard that Ottaviano was found to have raped a child and bribed her to recruit other girls for himself and other adult men to abuse.

Four of the five complainants were under the age of 16, with the youngest aged 13 when the offences occurred.

'Your actions are appalling'

In sentencing, Judge Nathan Jarro said Ottaviano's offending was "motivated by your own selfish and sinister desires".

Four of the five complainants were under the age of 16. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

He said the "predatory" behaviour showed "features of manipulation and corruption … money, cigarettes, alcohol, secrecy and recruitment".

The court heard the 39-year-old supplied the girls with cash, alcohol, drugs and cigarettes in exchange for forcing them into sexual acts, committing "routine, repeated sexual conduct".

Judge Jarro said Ottaviano targeted and manipulated "vulnerable" children, exploiting their youth, while ignoring their "obvious pain and distress", and pleas to stop.

The court heard Ottaviano threatened one girl that she would be "bashed" if she told anyone, and laughed at another who struggled to breathe as he abused her.

Judge Jarro told Ottaviano that a complainant who was 13 at the time of offending "never wanted to have sex with you" but she was young and scared.

'History of trauma'

When handing down the sentence, Judge Jarro said he considered Ottaviano's traumatic and "deprived" past, where drugs, sex and violence "sadly became the norm".

Judge Jarro noted Ottaviano had undergone sexual offenders' treatment in late 2024.

Ottaviano has already served two years of his 12-year sentence in pre-sentence custody.

No parole eligibility date has been set.

World.title: Romanian prosecutors indict Tate brothers for trafficking minors, laundering charges
World.content:
Romanian prosecutors has officially indicted manosphere influencer Andrew Tate for trafficking minors, among other charges, alongside his brother Tristan.

On Friday, local time, Andrew Tate was indicted on charges of trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering.

His brother Tristan was indicted for complicity.

The Tate brothers, former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship, were arrested in Miami in late July after Britain requested their extradition.

Mainly based in Romania since 2017, they have been under criminal investigation in the country on charges including human trafficking since December 2022.

They have denied all wrongdoing.

Geek culture' revealed as pipeline to misogyny Researchers say the manosphere has gone mainstream as young men who were suckered into the space reveal how they were recruited into the space.

Romanian prosecutors allege the Tates recruited their victims by seducing them and falsely claiming to want a relationship or marriage, before forcing them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business.

"We will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them."

The Tate brothers remain in jail in the US while a judge decides on the request for their extradition to Britain where they are wanted on rape charges.

Supporters of Andrew and Tristan Tate wait for the latest on their US case. (Reuters: Marco Bello)

The spokesperson for the Romanian anti-organised crime prosecuting unit DIICOT, which is investigating the Tates, said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek their extradition from the United States.

The Tates can be tried in absentia in Romania, but the trial will not start immediately.

Under Romanian law the indictment gets sent to a preliminary court chamber where a judge will inspect the case files to ensure legality.

While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalise the report, indictments routinely take significantly longer.

DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate's victims was 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012, before moving her to the Romanian capital Bucharest and using physical violence and mental intimidation to sexually exploit her by forcing her to produce pornographic content for social media sites.

His brother Tristan was an accessory, the unit said, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.

Prosecutors said the brothers kept $US 1.25 million from the video chat income generated by the victim, roughly 80 per cent of all her gains.

The brothers tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars, they added.

Andrew Tate, a self-described misogynist, previously said he moved to Romania because law enforcement was more lax there.

Both brothers have grown their following of mainly young men by building a lavish, hyper-macho image, and by providing tips on how to coerce women.

Reuters

World.title: Woman charged with murder after body found in creek on NSW north coast

A woman has been charged with murder after the body of a man was found in a creek on a property on the NSW north coast.

Police were called just after midday yesterday to a house on Teven Road, Teven, west of Ballina, after reports of a concern for welfare.

World.title: Ex-MP denies he acted dishonestly in deception case
World.content:
Lawyers for former South Australian MP Fraser Ellis said he admitted he made mistakes but did not "knowingly" act dishonestly, after being convicted of seven counts of deception.

The 34-year-old former member for Narungga on the Yorke Peninsula appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court today ahead of sentencing for the offending, which occurred between November 2018 and May 2020.

The charges relate to the misuse of the Country Members Allowance, a fund used by regional MPs who are required to travel for parliamentary duties.

Ellis was found guilty of four counts of deception in 2024 following a trial but was acquitted of a further 19 counts.

The Director of Public Prosecutions appealed against those acquittals and three were replaced with convictions by the Court of Appeal in July this year.

Scott Henchliffe KC, for Ellis, told the court today the former MP was accused of dishonestly claiming 78 nights costing $18,095, but he was only convicted of 20 nights worth $4,676.

"He accepted that he made mistakes and he was too casual in his approach," Mr Henchliffe said.

"He maintains he did not knowingly act dishonestly."

Fraser Ellis through his lawyers says his reputation has been tarnished. (ABC News)

Mr Henchcliff rejected the idea the fraudulent claims were part of an organised plan orchestrated by Ellis and occurred in a "haphazard nature".

He argued no conviction should be recorded and a good behaviour bond should be considered.

"He feels strongly he has had his reputation tarnished by the outcome, he feels quite depressed about that," he said.

Prosecutors seek deterrence

Prosecutor James Slocombe told the court today the offending was "too serious" to proceed without recording a conviction and a short suspended prison sentence should be imposed.

"The totality of the conduct is simply more than taking from the public purse," Mr Slocombe said.

"Your Honour needs to consider the need for public deterrence in terms of an appropriate sentence."

Mr Slocombe noted Ellis had paid $24,130 as a form of restitution to the House of Assembly before charges were pursued.

Ellis was first elected as the member for Narungga in 2018 at the age of 25 but was unseated at the 2026 state election by One Nation's Chantelle Thomas.

As he left court today, Ellis told reporters he would "wait for the decision and see what happens".

He will return to court for sentencing on September 17.

World.title: Publican jailed for starting hotel fire to pocket insurance
World.content:
A former publican has been sentenced to more than four years behind bars after deliberately burning down a Snowy Monaro pub in order to pocket the insurance payout.

David Culican, 42, was found guilty of intentionally burning down the historical Globe Hotel in Bombala in June 2022.

In Sydney's Downing Centre District Court on Friday, Judge David Scully said Culican destroyed the 1857 building because "the business was in financial stress".

"The offender's motivation was financial gain in potentially very significant amounts," he told the court.

Judge Scully said the pub's insurance policy covered contents up to $480,000 and up to $640,000 in loss of trade, but it was "not clear what the offender would have reaped".

Culican has been sentenced to jail after lighting the fire at the Globe Hotel. (Supplied: Fire and Rescue NSW Station 230)

The court heard that in the day before lighting the fire Culican made plans to rent a truck to transport "items of value" from the pub.

"There was some rudimentary planning … but overall the offending was unsophisticated," Judge Scully said.

The court heard Culican was "clumsy" in his offending which involved him using a blowtorch to light the fire around 4am on June 25, 2022.

CCTV footage from that night which showed Culican exiting the building while carrying a blowtorch and wearing a balaclava was played for the court during the trial.

"The balaclava was a clumsy attempt to hide his appearance," Judge Scully said.

Culican was sentenced to 4 years and 2 months behind bars, with a non-parole period of 2 years and 9 months.

Judge Scully found Culican has showed no remorse. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

'No evidence of remorse'

Culican denied lighting the fire, but a jury found him guilty after a week-long trial and seven-hours of deliberations in the Queanbeyan District Court in May.

Judge Scully said Culican, who watched the sentencing via audio visual link from custody at Junee Correctional Centre, "does not accept responsibility for this offending behaviour" and there was "no evidence of remorse".

The pub was destroyed by the blaze but there was no-one staying there at the time and no-one was injured.

However, Judge Scully noted that both a civilian who was concerned about potential occupants in the building, and the firefighters who responded to the blaze, "put themselves at risk".

A conviction against Culican on a charge of possessing ammunition without authority was also recorded, but no sentence was imposed.

Culican will be eligible for parole in February 2029.

World.title: The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow Adrian Proszenko September 4, 2026 — 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jai Arrow stepped onto South Sydney’s (sometimes) home ground. A packed house, much like the man of the moment, struggled to contain its emotions. They came for what preceded the match as much as for what occurred during it. Loading The clangs of the Legacy Bell, rung by Ron Coote, reverberated around the stadium before the opening notes of Stand By Me rang out over the PA system. And then the moment we had all come for. With both sets of players on the field, it was time for one of the most enduring sporting anthems of them all. You’ll Never Walk Alone.



Those words were also plastered on the banner Arrow walked through after emerging from the tunnel to raucous applause. Arrow, wearing jersey No.23, acknowledged the crowd. Even the Roosters players put their hands together. And thus Arrow brought up an Australian sporting century as unforgettable as any ever struck by Don Bradman. This was Arrow’s 100th and final game in the cardinal and myrtle. It was a moment imagined by Wayne Bennett, who, only a week earlier, had helped the larrikin forward put his socks on for game 99. Tonight, Bennett held the interchange card that allowed Arrow to be replaced by his great mate, Cody Walker. Everyone came together to make the milestone happen. The NRL and the players’ association granted Arrow special dispensation to “play” following his retirement after being diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease.



There was, however, one last obstacle. The Roosters, a feuding foe for well 118 years, needed to agree. Not only did they provide their blessing, their chairman Nick Politis was one of Arrow’s most generous benefactors. “We don’t always see eye-to-eye with the Roosters, but we also know that celebrating Jai tonight will bring us all together,” said Souths chief executive Blake Solly. Jai Arrow’s wife, Berina, and daughter Ayla watch on. Wolter Peeters “On behalf of the Rabbitohs we would like to thank the Roosters for their support of Jai since his diagnosis, and we thank them for supporting this concept of Jai reaching 100 NRL games for our club.” During a half-time interview with Nine’s Danika Mason, Arrow expressed his appreciation for the support he had received.



“It means the world … for me, it’s a great moment,” Arrow said. “I’m so thankful for everyone. I love you all.” Related Article Live

NRL 2026 NRL LIVE updates: Rabbitohs dominating Roosters in Jai Arrow’s 100th game for Souths The guard of honour comprised Rabbitohs old boys, who led fans on a march along Driver Avenue from the Sydney Cricket Ground. Among them was another past player doing it tough, Jason Death. One of the inaugural captains after the Pride of the League was reinstated into the competition, Death has been recovering from a brain bleed suffered after a fall in his Warriewood home. Yet he also wanted to pay homage to the former Maroon. Arrow’s life expectancy is unclear. Yet earlier in the day, he promised to fight on.



“No, no, don’t worry about me,” Arrow told Triple M. “I understand the disease can be very confronting. I give myself every hope to be around for 10 years, at least.” The memories he created tonight will last forever. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead
World.content:
Eating outFood Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead This expansive venue from one of Australia’s best craft brewers is serving classic pub fare with a fun and imaginative twist. Matt Shea September 4, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are Neighbour regulars who will never visit Range Brewing, Matt McIver reckons. “And there are people who love Range for what we do – the beers, the weekly releases – who will never come to Neighbour,” says McIver, who co-owns both venues. Neighbour opened in mid-August at Gasworks Plaza. Markus Ravik If that sounds like a counterintuitive basis on which to open a new bar and eatery, McIver says to think of it as a Venn diagram: some of the punters will overlap, many won’t. Range has become good at this. When McIver and business partner Gerard Martin opened the venue in Newstead in 2018, it quickly developed a reputation for being a craft brewer’s craft brewery. Every week new beers would be released, creating a constantly rotating line-up – one that was actually worth knowing about.



Related Article Fish Lane unveils a glamorous, old-world cocktail boozer Their first expansion was a taproom in Melbourne in 2020 (it subsequently closed in 2024). But ever since, the enterprise has been more well-rounded, with strategically located venues that focus as much on food as they do beer. First there was Patio By Range in Paddington in 2023. That was followed by Rays in Camp Hill the following year. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “Eight years ago, we probably didn’t foresee where this was going … But that modern culture of independent pubs having elevated food menus and nice wine lists and good beer is what we’re trying to create,” McIver says. Neighbour’s fitout feels like a reference to old-school public bars, without being too kitschy. Markus Ravik “We’re not reinventing the wheel, we’re just trying to do the classics well and with love.”



Neighbour opened late August in the Gasworks premises previously occupied by Botany, and it’s the clearest expression yet of that approach. And you can see what McIver means about the Venn diagram: the food menu could be shorthanded as the ultimate pub offering, with a bunch of classics given fun and imaginative twists. There’s a crispy-fried mozzarella in carrozza (think, a fancy cheese toastie) served with a vodka sauce; raw tuna tostadas with salsa macha, cucumber and radish; a parmigiana topped with stracciatella and fresh basil; and an Insta-worthy (and very good) wagyu cheeseburger that’s served on a bed of pepper sauce. The menu pushes pub cuisine in fun and creative directions. Markus Ravik There are also a bunch of smaller snack plates, and a woodfired pizza menu. “It’s meant to be modern Australian pub cuisine,” McIver says. “We’ve taken elements from our other venues that work well and gone from there. It’s food that’s meant to make you go, ‘I can’t stop thinking about that parmy or that steak frites’.”



For drinks, there are six taps pouring Range’s core frothies, backed by a wine list that lines up relatively esoteric Australian producers alongside drops from France and Italy. There’s also a cocktail menu that dishes up classics done “your way” alongside a bunch of approachable signatures. Neighbour’s cheeseburger is up there with the best in town. Markus Ravik All this is served in a fabulously realised fitout by Kate McLean from Soma & Sol that’s slick but welcoming, with glass-brick walls, timber panelling, tile-topped tables and high bars, and burgundy-and-cream houndstooth fabrics. It feels like a reference to old-school public bars without being too kitschy. On a Tuesday night, the place is buzzy and a manager tells me it’s been heaving on the weekends, confirming McIver and Martin’s instinct for what’s been a slightly under-loved space barely a stone’s throw from the original brewery. Neighbour’s bar is serving six tap beers alongside cocktails and small-producer wines. Markus Ravik



But it’s also another expression of a business strategy that’s become sacrosanct in craft beer circles: sell as much product as you can over your own bar. “From the get-go, it was our plan to move as much beer ourselves through our own channels as we could,” McIver says. “We’re still selling 20 kegs of beer through the new venue – that money goes straight into our bank account.” Open Mon-Thu 11am-9pm, Fri-Sat 11am-10pm, Sun 12-9pm 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, (07) 3110 1397 neighbourbyrange.com

For subscribers Matt Shea is Food and Culture Editor at Brisbane Times. He is a former editor and editor-at-large at Broadsheet Brisbane, and has written for Escape, Qantas Magazine, the Guardian, Jetstar Magazine and SilverKris, among many others.

World.title: This 700-page biography, 40 years in the making, is a miracle
World.content:
One day in eighth grade, Nicholas Boggs arrived at his Washington school dressed in a suit. He was giving a presentation on the writer and activist James Baldwin. It might have been around the time Baldwin died. Baldwin was only 63, but he had lived hard: partying, drinking, smoking, lots of sex and endless loving. Loving is the point. Baldwin needed to be in love and spent much of his life doing exactly this, anguishing though it could be – so much so that his biographer, that sweet, earnest boy in the suit, calls his book Baldwin: A Love Story.

Boggs’ biography has taken 30 years to write, 40 to think on. Baldwin (1924–1987) was a massive figure in both literature and civil rights; his insights were electric and well-documented. But reputations are fluid, tastes alter and Baldwin’s elaborate style isn’t easy for later generations. Boggs, in his 708 pages, isn’t much interested in revealing the public man, but in understanding his subject’s intricate dance between creative life and love life.

Writer and civil rights activist James Baldwin (1924-1987). Sophie Bassouls

Baldwin was intersectional before the word was coined. And entirely original. He hated labels and never defined himself as homosexual, although sexually he exclusively liked men. He also had significant deep friendships with women, many of them famous, a few in love with him. Boggs’ original exploration of who Baldwin was, who he became and why, translates him through the four great loves of his life, all men.

The first love, non-sexual, was the artist Beauford Delaney. Baldwin was 16 when he met Delaney, who was in his 30s. Delaney fell in love with the brilliant young man who appeared at his door after a high school classmate suggested Baldwin visit him. Delaney lived in Greenwich Village, the equivalent of Paris’ Left Bank, and was delighted to introduce Baldwin to everyone. Baldwin, the eldest of nine children, his stepfather a street preacher, a man of violence and fury, found in Delaney a spiritual father: Delaney was walking, living proof for him that a black man could be an artist. He never lost touch with Delaney and supported him through difficult later years.

World.title: Greens councillor wins court battle over Gaza newsletter penalty
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Greens councillor wins court battle over Gaza newsletter penalty William Davis September 4, 2026 — 8:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two years after a community newsletter on the history of the Middle East sparked controversy in Brisbane, the Supreme Court has thrown out a costly penalty imposed on the Greens councillor who distributed it. Gabba ward representative Trina Massey mailed a spring pamphlet to residents at the height of the Gaza conflict with a two-page spread titled “Khalil’s Story”. A council ethics committee had ordered Massey to repay $10,000 and issue an apology. But the Supreme Court has now overruled that ruling. Greens councillor Trina Massey published a newsletter in August 2024 with a two-page spread titled “Khalil’s Story”. Monique Westermann “Today’s outcome is a vindication of my decision to challenge the investigation and the findings of the ethics committee,” Massey said in a statement.



“All of this just for speaking openly about the genocide against Palestinians and the human rights of Palestinians living in my ward.” In the August 2024 article – which was written by academic and rapper Dr Jamal Nabulsi – the history of the modern state of Israel was framed as one of violent European colonialism on “stolen Indigenous land”. It attracted backlash from some constituents, who said the language was inflammatory and unfair. They criticised an attached timeline that began with Ottoman rule in the Middle Ages and did not include the Holocaust or October 7 attacks.



In December 2025, Brisbane City Council’s ethics committee – comprising three Labor and three LNP councillors – voted unanimously to endorse the recommendations of a review conducted by FairFact Consulting Services. It found Massey breached several behavioural standards. The report said the article was “essentially propaganda and a ‘call to arms’ for pro-Palestinian support that is not objective to the rest of the community”, and this “could reasonably be expected to make members of the Jewish community feel unsafe, victimised, and targeted”. It rejected other aspects of the complaints, and did not describe the article as antisemitic. Massey was required to issue a public apology in her next ward newsletter and on social media, repay Brisbane City Council half of the $20,000 cost of publication, and undertake training and counselling on the code of conduct.



She took the matter to court, arguing there was a failure of natural justice and her freedom of political communication was being impeded, among other claims. In a judgment handed down by Justice Tom Sullivan in the Queensland Supreme Court in August but finalised on Thursday, previous findings and orders on the matter were quashed, with agreement from council. Brisbane City Council will reinvestigate the newsletter, the lord mayor’s office confirmed. Matt Dennien A judgment listed several reasons why the FairFact report was “invalid and of no effect”, including that it misconstrued section 2.3 of the council code of conduct. Brisbane City Council was ordered to pay Massey’s legal costs.



“Thanks to the LNP’s politically motivated show trial, I was subject to nearly a year of proceedings, along with death threats and attacks on my reputation,” the Gabba councillor said after the decision. Related Article Brisbane development Parents to appeal after new tower approved next to inner-city school “Just three days after the Bondi attack, the LNP lord mayor relied on this ‘invalid’ report to make shameful, defamatory and untrue attacks on me. “The Supreme Court has overturned the report and decisions of the LNP-controlled ethics committee, so I am expecting him to withdraw and apologise for those inflammatory remarks.” The original matter will be reinvestigated by the council ethics committee, the lord mayor’s office confirmed.



Deputy mayor and LNP councillor Fiona Cunningham said in a statement the decision did not change her party’s views on the case. Related Article City council Labor makes case for ‘big workforce’ at Brisbane City Council “The Greens councillor for the Gabba Ward used ratepayer funds to distribute a highly biased, inaccurate and misleading newsletter that local Jewish people called offensive. “This decision doesn’t change the fact that councillor Massey is more interested in Gaza than the Gabba, and still hasn’t apologised for making Jewish people feel unsafe.” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and his council have held the newsletter against Massey for the two years since it was published, discussing it multiple times, including during a council debate just three days before the court decision.



“I am an anti-racist,” Schrinner said on August 25. “I would not like to see any councillor targeting a particular group of people in our community, like your newsletter did, which targeted and made the Jewish community feel completely unsafe.” The remarks provoked strong pushback from Massey and fellow councillor Nicole Johnston. Massey has condemned antisemitism. After the Bondi attack, she posted on social media: “Jewish people have a right to safety. Antisemitism has no place in our community, and this abhorrent attack is an attack on all of us.”

World.title: Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence Jack Gramenz September 4, 2026 — 7:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police should have been patrolling the street where a gunman lay in wait for over an hour before shooting an innocent man dead in the doorway of a western Sydney home, his aunt says. Darlene Norton told Seven News on Friday that police could be doing “so much more” to suppress underworld violence after her nephew Joshua Macdonald was shot at a Merrylands West home on Wednesday afternoon. Loading “The car was sitting there for 90 minutes,” Norton said. “If they already knew that these people next door were being targeted, they had a target on their shoulders, why weren’t they patrolling those streets?”



Police sources with knowledge of the investigation into Macdonald’s murder but not permitted to speak publicly told the Herald on Thursday that the assailants who shot him had been targeting Moshtaba Hafizi, a man police allege has longstanding links to the notorious Alameddine crime family. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on Wednesday. Nine News Police had formally warned Hafizi several times that his life was at risk, including in the days before Wednesday’s shooting, according to several sources. The 30-year-old, who owns the Bruce Street home but does not live there, was aware the property could be targeted. Officers at the scene of the deadly shooting. Wolter Peeters Shortly after 3pm on Wednesday, several shots were fired from the rear of what is believed to be a stolen Audi sedan. It’s believed to be the same vehicle found burned out at Denham Court that night.



Macdonald was not known to police and he has no links to organised crime. Darlene Norton said police should have been patrolling the street where her nephew was gunned down. Seven News He was killed the day after university student Marco Tapia was shot in bed in his Glen Alpine home in another case believed to be mistaken identity. Norton also shared what would tragically be her final message to her nephew, wishing him happy birthday on Sunday. Macdonald replied thanking her and saying he was looking forward to seeing family soon. But three days later, he was dead.



“I thought it was another Joshua [on the news], and then I picked up my phone,” Norton said. The calls she had missed through the night brought the news that her nephew had been shot dead in a broad daylight attack police believe to be yet another case of mistaken identity. Related Article Editorial

Crime Sydney’s newest gangland warriors have no respect for the lives of others The Herald's View Editorial Norton shared a grateful message from Macdonald’s friend, who credited the 40-year-old with saving his children’s lives. “He is my children’s and my own guardian angel,” Norton quoted from the message.



Norton’s husband Trevor criticised Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s refusal to accept that underworld violence on Sydney’s streets was out of control. “What does it take to be out of control?” he said on Seven News. Police Minister Yasmin Catley, centre and Commissioner Mal Lanyon speaking on Thursday after two mistaken identity killings. Oscar Colman Catley on Thursday said she did “not accept that this is out of control”. “Police are working around the clock to address these issues … and they’re not going to stop,” Catley said on Thursday.



Separately, asked if police had lost control of gangland violence in Sydney, Premier Chris Minns said: “For the people who’ve been affected, who’ve been killed, the answer is yes.” Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said he would increase “proactive resources” tasked with combating organised crime and ensure a highly visible police presence to provide reassurance to the public. “Organised crime and the types of crimes we have seen over the last two days will be a priority, and if we need to move further police to address that, we will, because this should not be tolerated,” he said on Thursday. World.title: The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow Adrian Proszenko September 4, 2026 — 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jai Arrow stepped onto South Sydney’s (sometimes) home ground. A packed house, much like the man of the moment, struggled to contain its emotions. They came for what preceded the match as much as for what occurred during it. Loading The clangs of the Legacy Bell, rung by Ron Coote, reverberated around the stadium before the opening notes of Stand By Me rang out over the PA system. And then the moment we had all come for. With both sets of players on the field, it was time for one of the most enduring sporting anthems of them all. You’ll Never Walk Alone.



Those words were also plastered on the banner Arrow walked through after emerging from the tunnel to raucous applause. Arrow, wearing jersey No.23, acknowledged the crowd. Even the Roosters players put their hands together. And thus Arrow brought up an Australian sporting century as unforgettable as any ever struck by Don Bradman. This was Arrow’s 100th and final game in the cardinal and myrtle. It was a moment imagined by Wayne Bennett, who, only a week earlier, had helped the larrikin forward put his socks on for game 99. Tonight, Bennett held the interchange card that allowed Arrow to be replaced by his great mate, Cody Walker. Everyone came together to make the milestone happen. The NRL and the players’ association granted Arrow special dispensation to “play” following his retirement after being diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease.



There was, however, one last obstacle. The Roosters, a feuding foe for well 118 years, needed to agree. Not only did they provide their blessing, their chairman Nick Politis was one of Arrow’s most generous benefactors. “We don’t always see eye-to-eye with the Roosters, but we also know that celebrating Jai tonight will bring us all together,” said Souths chief executive Blake Solly. Jai Arrow’s wife, Berina, and daughter Ayla watch on. Wolter Peeters “On behalf of the Rabbitohs we would like to thank the Roosters for their support of Jai since his diagnosis, and we thank them for supporting this concept of Jai reaching 100 NRL games for our club.” During a half-time interview with Nine’s Danika Mason, Arrow expressed his appreciation for the support he had received.



“It means the world … for me, it’s a great moment,” Arrow said. “I’m so thankful for everyone. I love you all.” Related Article Live

NRL 2026 NRL LIVE updates: Rabbitohs dominating Roosters in Jai Arrow’s 100th game for Souths The guard of honour comprised Rabbitohs old boys, who led fans on a march along Driver Avenue from the Sydney Cricket Ground. Among them was another past player doing it tough, Jason Death. One of the inaugural captains after the Pride of the League was reinstated into the competition, Death has been recovering from a brain bleed suffered after a fall in his Warriewood home. Yet he also wanted to pay homage to the former Maroon. Arrow’s life expectancy is unclear. Yet earlier in the day, he promised to fight on.



“No, no, don’t worry about me,” Arrow told Triple M. “I understand the disease can be very confronting. I give myself every hope to be around for 10 years, at least.” The memories he created tonight will last forever. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead
World.content:
Eating outFood Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead This expansive venue from one of Australia’s best craft brewers is serving classic pub fare with a fun and imaginative twist. Matt Shea September 4, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are Neighbour regulars who will never visit Range Brewing, Matt McIver reckons. “And there are people who love Range for what we do – the beers, the weekly releases – who will never come to Neighbour,” says McIver, who co-owns both venues. Neighbour opened in mid-August at Gasworks Plaza. Markus Ravik If that sounds like a counterintuitive basis on which to open a new bar and eatery, McIver says to think of it as a Venn diagram: some of the punters will overlap, many won’t. Range has become good at this. When McIver and business partner Gerard Martin opened the venue in Newstead in 2018, it quickly developed a reputation for being a craft brewer’s craft brewery. Every week new beers would be released, creating a constantly rotating line-up – one that was actually worth knowing about.



Related Article Fish Lane unveils a glamorous, old-world cocktail boozer Their first expansion was a taproom in Melbourne in 2020 (it subsequently closed in 2024). But ever since, the enterprise has been more well-rounded, with strategically located venues that focus as much on food as they do beer. First there was Patio By Range in Paddington in 2023. That was followed by Rays in Camp Hill the following year. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “Eight years ago, we probably didn’t foresee where this was going … But that modern culture of independent pubs having elevated food menus and nice wine lists and good beer is what we’re trying to create,” McIver says. Neighbour’s fitout feels like a reference to old-school public bars, without being too kitschy. Markus Ravik “We’re not reinventing the wheel, we’re just trying to do the classics well and with love.”



Neighbour opened late August in the Gasworks premises previously occupied by Botany, and it’s the clearest expression yet of that approach. And you can see what McIver means about the Venn diagram: the food menu could be shorthanded as the ultimate pub offering, with a bunch of classics given fun and imaginative twists. There’s a crispy-fried mozzarella in carrozza (think, a fancy cheese toastie) served with a vodka sauce; raw tuna tostadas with salsa macha, cucumber and radish; a parmigiana topped with stracciatella and fresh basil; and an Insta-worthy (and very good) wagyu cheeseburger that’s served on a bed of pepper sauce. The menu pushes pub cuisine in fun and creative directions. Markus Ravik There are also a bunch of smaller snack plates, and a woodfired pizza menu. “It’s meant to be modern Australian pub cuisine,” McIver says. “We’ve taken elements from our other venues that work well and gone from there. It’s food that’s meant to make you go, ‘I can’t stop thinking about that parmy or that steak frites’.”



For drinks, there are six taps pouring Range’s core frothies, backed by a wine list that lines up relatively esoteric Australian producers alongside drops from France and Italy. There’s also a cocktail menu that dishes up classics done “your way” alongside a bunch of approachable signatures. Neighbour’s cheeseburger is up there with the best in town. Markus Ravik All this is served in a fabulously realised fitout by Kate McLean from Soma & Sol that’s slick but welcoming, with glass-brick walls, timber panelling, tile-topped tables and high bars, and burgundy-and-cream houndstooth fabrics. It feels like a reference to old-school public bars without being too kitschy. On a Tuesday night, the place is buzzy and a manager tells me it’s been heaving on the weekends, confirming McIver and Martin’s instinct for what’s been a slightly under-loved space barely a stone’s throw from the original brewery. Neighbour’s bar is serving six tap beers alongside cocktails and small-producer wines. Markus Ravik



But it’s also another expression of a business strategy that’s become sacrosanct in craft beer circles: sell as much product as you can over your own bar. “From the get-go, it was our plan to move as much beer ourselves through our own channels as we could,” McIver says. “We’re still selling 20 kegs of beer through the new venue – that money goes straight into our bank account.” Open Mon-Thu 11am-9pm, Fri-Sat 11am-10pm, Sun 12-9pm 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, (07) 3110 1397 neighbourbyrange.com

For subscribers Matt Shea is Food and Culture Editor at Brisbane Times. He is a former editor and editor-at-large at Broadsheet Brisbane, and has written for Escape, Qantas Magazine, the Guardian, Jetstar Magazine and SilverKris, among many others.

World.title: This 700-page biography, 40 years in the making, is a miracle
World.content:
One day in eighth grade, Nicholas Boggs arrived at his Washington school dressed in a suit. He was giving a presentation on the writer and activist James Baldwin. It might have been around the time Baldwin died. Baldwin was only 63, but he had lived hard: partying, drinking, smoking, lots of sex and endless loving. Loving is the point. Baldwin needed to be in love and spent much of his life doing exactly this, anguishing though it could be – so much so that his biographer, that sweet, earnest boy in the suit, calls his book Baldwin: A Love Story.

Boggs’ biography has taken 30 years to write, 40 to think on. Baldwin (1924–1987) was a massive figure in both literature and civil rights; his insights were electric and well-documented. But reputations are fluid, tastes alter and Baldwin’s elaborate style isn’t easy for later generations. Boggs, in his 708 pages, isn’t much interested in revealing the public man, but in understanding his subject’s intricate dance between creative life and love life.

Writer and civil rights activist James Baldwin (1924-1987). Sophie Bassouls

Baldwin was intersectional before the word was coined. And entirely original. He hated labels and never defined himself as homosexual, although sexually he exclusively liked men. He also had significant deep friendships with women, many of them famous, a few in love with him. Boggs’ original exploration of who Baldwin was, who he became and why, translates him through the four great loves of his life, all men.

The first love, non-sexual, was the artist Beauford Delaney. Baldwin was 16 when he met Delaney, who was in his 30s. Delaney fell in love with the brilliant young man who appeared at his door after a high school classmate suggested Baldwin visit him. Delaney lived in Greenwich Village, the equivalent of Paris’ Left Bank, and was delighted to introduce Baldwin to everyone. Baldwin, the eldest of nine children, his stepfather a street preacher, a man of violence and fury, found in Delaney a spiritual father: Delaney was walking, living proof for him that a black man could be an artist. He never lost touch with Delaney and supported him through difficult later years.

World.title: PM, it’s time for real action on gas, coal and oil
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters PM, it’s time for real action on gas, coal and oil September 4, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The UN Environment Program report concludes that humanity has failed to keep climate change below 1.5degrees (″⁣Pacific anger at Australia after climate target failure″⁣, 3/9). This should be front-page news. Pacific nations, who literally used the slogan ″⁣1.5 to stay alive″⁣, have every right to be angry with the pro-gas Albanese government, whose Resources Minister Madeleine King recently celebrated turning on the tap for fossil gas fracked from the Beetaloo Basin. Climate change, made worse by digging up and burning coal, oil and gas is an existential challenge that affects us all. Like your correspondents (Letters, 3/9), I want to see the Albanese government set out a clear plan to phase out coal, oil and gas and provide permanent protection for Australia’s native forests. That would be real climate action.

Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn I’m doing my bit, but politicians aren’t

I’ve installed solar panels and a battery, switched to efficient electric appliances, drive an EV, moved my savings and super out of fossil fuels, eat mostly local vegetarian food, buy second-hand and minimise waste, and usually take road trips for holidays. I love these healthy changes and feel I’m doing my bit to live a climate-conscious life.

Yet here we are, just 11 years after the historic Paris Agreement, and the UN Environment Program says the world will breach 1.5°C of warming within the next few years. By supporting and enabling the expansion of coal, oil and gas, the industries driving climate change, elected representatives are failing us. As your correspondent argues, it is only the Greens, Community Strong Australia and independent MPs who are prepared to put the public interest ahead of the fossil fuel industry’s interests (″⁣Most politicians should be ashamed″⁣, 3/9). Australians are playing our part; it’s time our politicians played theirs.

Amy Hiller, Kew Policies fuel neighbours’ existence

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called out China for having ″⁣no respect″⁣ for Pacific nations by conducting missile testing in their region (″⁣Albanese blasts China’s missile testing in the Pacific″⁣, 4/9). The acute irony seems to have escaped him. Albanese and his government have shown no respect for Pacific nations by continuing to approve new and expanded coal and gas mines in Australia. The atmospheric pollution they generate by their operations and by the burning of their product worsens the global warming that puts Pacific nations in clear and present danger from rising sea levels. Diplomatic initiatives aimed at warding off Chinese influence in the Pacific are at odds with Australia’s refusal to take responsibility for fuel policies that put our island neighbours’ survival at stake. Perhaps the right word is not irony but hypocrisy.

Tom Knowles, Parkville



THE FORUM All aboard the trams

Finally, the Melbourne tramways general scheme of 1923 gets remembered (″⁣The 100-year-old map that shows what Melbourne commuters are missing out on″⁣, 4/9). The scheme would have doubled the city’s tram network, reaching far into the suburbs.

It’s incredibly pertinent to our times as the city faces an unfolding congestion trap of its own making. In a few short years the city will be experiencing periodic gridlock as our roads and streets fill to capacity. What a shame that the scheme wasn’t implemented but wait, we still have the skills and know how to build it.

Don’t waste our money on the SRL, make trams!

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick Family legacy

How fantastic that reporter Alexander Darling has highlighted the work of our grandfather Tom Strickland who designed one of our famous trams and created their networks. If only modern-day leaders were as committed to public services and access as he was.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Attracting male teachers

Matt Canavan would like to see more male teachers in schools. More men would be interested in teaching if all teachers were much better paid, if classroom supports were improved to reduce the excessive workload, and if politicians stopped sledging teachers.

Eileen Ray, Ascot Vale ... and its obstacles

Nationals leader Matt Canavan attacks what he calls the “feminisation” of curriculum and teaching and asks where all the male teachers are. I can give him three reasons why more men don’t go into teaching. One, the pay is not as enticing as in male-dominated professions; two, society does not respect teachers but instead blames them for all the bad behaviour of children and asks teachers to be a parent/social worker/counsellor and teacher; and three, it’s too much work – it’s not an easy, straightforward, nine-to-five job.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights



Kindness of people

The assistance received when your correspondent had a fall in the street is not at all surprising (Letters, 3/9), because basically people are kind. I think of that as the default position.

However, what is very alarming, is that the default position seems to be progressively swinging the other way.

Barbara Hilling, Watsonia North Smoking factors

Was the price of cigarettes ever a deterrent for smokers in past years? Or was the ending of persuasive advertising a major factor in lessening the injurious habit? Smoking lost its allure for many when the imagery of lighting up a cigarette lost its stylised appeal when the Marlboro man died of cancer and Yul Brynner publicly stated he was dying from lung cancer. Myriad factors over decades have brought down the smoking rates in Australia and it shouldn’t be forgotten the role public education played in doing so.

The effect on health through smoking, particularly lung cancer, became a given fact. Yet now the debate is almost entirely about the price.

There seems to be little acknowledgment of a time when so many factors combined to significantly bring down smoking rates and then raising cigarette prices was seen as the ultimate deterrent. But doesn’t reliance on one policy lever have limitations?

Des Files, Brunswick Scrooge lives

Excuse me but I’m fuming. Scrooge is looming over television sets in aged care homes (“Ask Noel Whittaker”, 2/9). A demand for a daily fee of $5.50 for a resident to watch television in their own room because it’s an “additional service”?

What have we become?

Jane Ross, San Remo Ship as metaphor

Despite the Trump administration’s propaganda spin, the photo of the rusty US super-carrier Abraham Lincoln after “nearly nine months at sea to support US operations against Iran”, is not a good look (“US warship shows strain after long deployment”, 4/9). It’s a visual metaphor for a US president and military, who have bitten off more than they can chew.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills Insanely happy

Here I was feeling unhappy reading all these articles about the devastation that is being and will be caused by AI. I thought something must be wrong for us to so blindly follow the lead of the people from Silicon Valley. Then I realised, AI doesn’t mean Artificial Intelligence, it means Absolute Insanity. I feel happier now.

Stan Thomson, Sandringham



Don’t take it as read

Algorithms ensure people remain in their echo chambers, consuming content that confirms their world view. In the past, we were told: “Don’t believe everything you read.” Nowadays, we need to be told, “Don’t read everything you believe.”

Sarah Russell, Mount Martha Time of dumbing down

I googled for a solution to an electrical problem in my 53-year-old MG Midget and obtained a detailed and very helpful answer that I had no reason to doubt the accuracy of. Looking at videos of people, dogs, dolphins etc, etc that appear uninvited on Facebook I am becoming increasingly unable to tell if they are real or AI fakes. I think I’m reasonably well-educated and able to think for myself, so I’m concerned for all the people who in recent decades have not had the opportunity to develop this for themselves because of the pervasive effect of screens. We are now seeing teachers who have grown up with the insidious dumbing down that occurs due to too much screen time who, probably without realising, now know less than their teachers did. This is how dumbing down occurs from generation to generation, and is the inevitable result of unchecked AI.

Don Jordan, Mount Waverley Don’t follow Queensland

More evidence that the Queensland government is determined to undermine and delay Australia’s transition to a post-carbon economy (“A quarter-million-dollar mistake”, 4/9). Despite the accelerating climate crisis, the greater financial costs, and the greater public health risks, Queensland continues to advance the interests of the fossil fuel industry. The opposition in Victoria has given every indication that it will follow the same path.

There is no doubt that Victorian Labor needs a kick in the pants for the rorts occurring through major infrastructure projects, but its objectives in delivering these projects and pursuing the energy transition remain sound.

Victorians can censure Labor without installing an unstable, economically damaging, and environmentally dangerous Coalition/One Nation alliance by voting for independents and Greens.

Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen Inspiring story

How inspiring to read the story of the Cozzo family (“Cozzo girls ready to baroque Brunswick again”, 4/9). Of course it is a tale of Franco Cozzo’s success as a businessman. It is also a story of a beloved father, whose four daughters are restarting his business in harmony. It is a story of a young man coming here from Italy and working hard to set up a well-loved business. Not mentioned is his wife, who raised 10 children while her husband was busy with his work. Especially inspiring that the community is eagerly anticipating the reopening in two weeks.

We need more families like this.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Nature of things

Mother nature has been sending messages and warnings – together with the scientists – regarding the environment for decades now. All seems to be falling on deaf ears. When nature takes charge of her domain there might not be any survivors.

After all, nature doesn’t need people.

Helena Kilingerova, Vermont



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

If Josh Frydenberg packs his kitbag for another stint in politics, he needs to leave out the lump of coal (″⁣Stars aligning for Frydenberg 2.0″⁣, 4/9).

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton Recycling Tony Abbott, followed potentially by Josh Frydenberg: the Liberals’ aversion to renewables knows no bounds.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton If Josh Frydenberg is the answer to the Liberal Party’s woes, it is in even bigger trouble than we thought.

Annie Wilson, Inverloch



Angus Taylor is promoting price matching between legal and illegal tobacco products. Fantastic. Great move. Well done.

Dawn Richards, Huntingdale The glacier failure in Nepal puts a nail in the coffins of the climate deniers and sceptics frequenting the Coalition and One Nation.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading Warren Pickering, please explain your statement of our ″⁣opportunities to partake in the future of nuclear energy″⁣.

Bill Burns, Bendigo Furthermore

The manosphere and misogynistic attitudes are the urgent problems for teenage boys. They don’t need to have an opinion about abortion.

Kate Ingram, Surrey Hills Having spent a lifetime in sales and sales management I have always believed you’re only as good as your training (″⁣OK, I bottled the interview, but the question was a corker″⁣, 4/9).

Louise Lawson, Point Cook



The NFL has found that about a quarter of deceased former players had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). And they wear helmets (″⁣AFL accused of stalling on head trauma research as chilling NFL findings emerge″⁣, 29/8).

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick Finally

Why not build data centres in the desert? Plenty of space, no neighbours to complain. Plenty of sunshine to make electricity. Plenty of artesian water to cool the computers. What could go wrong?

Doug Springall, Yarragon

World.title: Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Shot man’s family say police need to do more to control gang violence Jack Gramenz September 4, 2026 — 7:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police should have been patrolling the street where a gunman lay in wait for over an hour before shooting an innocent man dead in the doorway of a western Sydney home, his aunt says. Darlene Norton told Seven News on Friday that police could be doing “so much more” to suppress underworld violence after her nephew Joshua Macdonald was shot at a Merrylands West home on Wednesday afternoon. Loading “The car was sitting there for 90 minutes,” Norton said. “If they already knew that these people next door were being targeted, they had a target on their shoulders, why weren’t they patrolling those streets?”



Police sources with knowledge of the investigation into Macdonald’s murder but not permitted to speak publicly told the Herald on Thursday that the assailants who shot him had been targeting Moshtaba Hafizi, a man police allege has longstanding links to the notorious Alameddine crime family. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on Wednesday. Nine News Police had formally warned Hafizi several times that his life was at risk, including in the days before Wednesday’s shooting, according to several sources. The 30-year-old, who owns the Bruce Street home but does not live there, was aware the property could be targeted. Officers at the scene of the deadly shooting. Wolter Peeters Shortly after 3pm on Wednesday, several shots were fired from the rear of what is believed to be a stolen Audi sedan. It’s believed to be the same vehicle found burned out at Denham Court that night.



Macdonald was not known to police and he has no links to organised crime. Darlene Norton said police should have been patrolling the street where her nephew was gunned down. Seven News He was killed the day after university student Marco Tapia was shot in bed in his Glen Alpine home in another case believed to be mistaken identity. Norton also shared what would tragically be her final message to her nephew, wishing him happy birthday on Sunday. Macdonald replied thanking her and saying he was looking forward to seeing family soon. But three days later, he was dead.



“I thought it was another Joshua [on the news], and then I picked up my phone,” Norton said. The calls she had missed through the night brought the news that her nephew had been shot dead in a broad daylight attack police believe to be yet another case of mistaken identity. Related Article Editorial

Crime Sydney’s newest gangland warriors have no respect for the lives of others The Herald's View Editorial Norton shared a grateful message from Macdonald’s friend, who credited the 40-year-old with saving his children’s lives. “He is my children’s and my own guardian angel,” Norton quoted from the message.



Norton’s husband Trevor criticised Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s refusal to accept that underworld violence on Sydney’s streets was out of control. “What does it take to be out of control?” he said on Seven News. Police Minister Yasmin Catley, centre and Commissioner Mal Lanyon speaking on Thursday after two mistaken identity killings. Oscar Colman Catley on Thursday said she did “not accept that this is out of control”. “Police are working around the clock to address these issues … and they’re not going to stop,” Catley said on Thursday.



Separately, asked if police had lost control of gangland violence in Sydney, Premier Chris Minns said: “For the people who’ve been affected, who’ve been killed, the answer is yes.” Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said he would increase “proactive resources” tasked with combating organised crime and ensure a highly visible police presence to provide reassurance to the public. “Organised crime and the types of crimes we have seen over the last two days will be a priority, and if we need to move further police to address that, we will, because this should not be tolerated,” he said on Thursday. World.title: Four injured after car crashes into Dunsandel pub in Canterbury
World.content:
Four people have been injured after a car crashed into a pub in Dunsandel in Canterbury this evening.

RNZ understands the pub in question is the Dunsandel Bar and Cafe.

Police said they were called about 6.15pm after a car collided with a building on Main South Road near Boundary Creek Road.

Two people suffered serious injuries, one moderate injuries and one minor injuries.

Police said it appeared the injured people were inside the pub, although a person in the car may also be among those hurt.

World.title: UN human rights commissioner visit to West Papua on track, says Indonesia
World.content:
Indonesia's government has indicated that a visit by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua is on track.

This comes as Melanesian Sperarhead Group (MSG) countries agreed to push Jakarta to facilitate the visit, after years of apparent inaction.

A request for the visit was made by Pacific Islands Forum countries back in 2019, but it has still not gone ahead, despite ongoing human rights violations in Papua.

A statement issued by MSG states from this week's Pacific Forum leaders meeting in Palau appeared to reflect frustrations that the visit has still not been facilitated.

The statement said that if a visit by the UN Commissioner's office was not facilitated by Indonesia in order for a report on human rights issues in West Papua to be produced by their next summit in 2027, then Indonesia's associate member status in the MSG will be reviewed.

The full members of the MSG are: Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia's FLNKS Kanak Movement. The United Liberation Movement for West Papua has observer status at the MSG, and Indonesia has associate member status.

In a response to RNZ Pacific following the statement, a spokesperson from Indonesia's embassy in New Zealand said there was "no discussion to review our membership within the MSG".

"We are always in constructive discussion on the issues deemed important by other members of the MSG, and we can also confirm that the said proposed visit is on the right path.

Ongoing conflict in Papua

The long-running conflict between the West Papua Liberation Army and Indonesian military forces in Papua has escalated in recent months, causing mass displacement of some Papua village communities in the region around Highland Papua province.

In the latest reported violence, human rights workers told RNZ Pacific that four members of the Liberation Army had been arrested and killed by Indonesian forces in Yahukimo Regency in recent days, and another member seriously injured, while six civilians were also arrested during the incident.

The spokesperson for the embassy said that during the 62nd Session of the Human Rights Council, the High Commissioner assessed "that force must not be used to pursue territorial claims or political demands".

"The sovereign equality of States, territorial integrity, and non-interference remain the foundation of the international order; respect for international law and the principles of UN Charter is non-negotiable."

World.title: New Zealand Transport Agency cuts road funding for some councils
World.content:
The NZ Transport Agency is cutting the amount of funding it gives some councils to help with essential infrastructure, prompting calls for a review of how the calculations were done.

Among them is Tararua District Council, which said the agency's decision to cut it's contribution to the roading network will cost the district more than $1.2 million over three years.

Tararua District Council is one of more than a dozen councils that have seen their Financial Assistance Rate, or FAR, from NZTA reduced over the next three years.

The move has left councils struggling see how they can fund road maintenance, public transport and other costs at a time they're also being forced to keep rates down.

NZTA currently contributes 73 cents towards every eligible dollar spent on Tararua roads. Next year that will reduce to 72 cents, before dropping again to 71 cents for the following two years.

Tararua District Mayor Scot Gilmore told Checkpoint while a couple of cents doesn't sound like a lot, it will all add up.
