Tech.title: How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
Tech.content:
“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.

Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.

It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.

Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.

“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.

The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.

“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.

Tech.title: The 6 Best Monitors That Actually Work Well With Macs
Tech.content:
Just about any monitor can work with a Mac. It doesn’t need to be made by Apple or have any official certification. There’s a case to be made for using a cheap 1080p monitor, but most Mac users will want something a bit more premium. As you can see from options like the Dell 27 Plus 4K, that doesn’t have to mean overly expensive. Either way, here are the four elements to consider when shopping for a good monitor to go with your Mac.

Size and resolution: 27- and 32-inch monitors are the most common sizes these days, but there are larger options. I would also consider a 34-inch ultrawide monitor if you like the wider 21:9 aspect ratio with the curved shape. With Apple, resolution is king. There's a reason it invests so much in high pixel density for every screen it sells, even in midrange options like the MacBook Air. Pixel density is what gives a screen its sharpness, and you need a lot more pixels when they're stretched across a large external monitor. If you want to keep fidelity up, I wouldn’t buy anything less than 4K, and bumping up to 5K or 6K on a 32-inch monitor can be helpful. Read more to learn the details on the funky way macOS handles resolutions and scaling. You should also consider the refresh rate: a 120-Hz refresh rate is what the MacBook Pro supports, offering smoother animation, especially in games.

Adjustability: Apple monitors and iMacs aren’t exactly known for adjustability. They often have none at all, and cost more when they do. That isn’t the best for your posture and ergonomics. Famously, the discontinued Pro Display XDR charged an extra $1,000 for a Pro Stand with proper adjustability (now a $400 add-on for the newer Studio Display XDR). For ergonomics, the top of the screen you're working on should be as close to eye level as possible, and that ranges depending on someone’s height. If a monitor doesn’t have height adjustability, you’ll need a separate monitor stand or arm. Beyond height adjustment, many monitors also have stands that can swivel, tilt, and rotate, all of which matter when using multiple monitors. This is also needed if you want to use a second monitor vertically, which has become increasingly popular.

Ports: Even the cheapest monitors will always have HDMI, which is all you need to connect directly to a Mac Mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, or MacBook Pro. Some monitors have USB-C that supports video, which will let you connect to one of a Mac’s Thunderbolt ports. The Mac Mini comes with three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an Ethernet jack. The Mac Mini Pro model has the same ports, except three of them support faster Thunderbolt 5 instead of 4. You’ll need to use at least one of these Thunderbolt ports to connect more than one external monitor. These monitors also tend to have other ports, such as USB-A. These can be useful, as the Mac Mini doesn't have any on its own.

Image quality: Apple prides itself on the image quality of its Macs, so in the case of the Mac Mini, you’ll likely want to get something worthy of your Mac. This is especially important for content creators, photographers, and designers. So, consider a monitor’s brightness, color accuracy, color coverage, and contrast. While some IPS displays offer decent color and contrast, mini-LED or OLED displays will guarantee better image quality. These also have significantly higher peak brightness in HDR content, which really brings games and movies to life.

Tech.title: Measles Outbreaks Are Forcing Immunocompromised Kids to Make Impossible Choices
Tech.content:
As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.

Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.

Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”

While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.

Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.

Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.

“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.

The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.

Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.

“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.

Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.

Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.

“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.

Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.

Tech.title: ICE Wants to Know Who Bought a Certain Green Beanie From REI in the Last 2 Years
Tech.content:
Did you buy a beanie from REI recently? The Department of Homeland Security might be looking for you.

New court filings allege that Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed the outdoor retailer in March, requesting the transaction information for “all persons” in the greater Minneapolis-St. Paul area who had purchased a specific type of dark green beanie from the company since 2024. REI did not respond to questions about whether it had complied with the request and, if so, how many people are affected.

The filings are part of a broader lawsuit by the federal government against 39 people who attended an ICE protest at a church whose pastor also worked as an acting ICE field office director. Both protesters and journalists who were attempting to cover the event, including former CNN host Don Lemon, are now defendants.

The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent as part of HSI’s investigation into the defendants, according to the court filings. Other recipients included social media companies, airlines, telecom providers, a car rental company, and a state employment agency. At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline, the filings allege, asked not only for information about a defendant’s past flights, but also requested that the airline give HSI a “lookout notification” about the defendant’s travel in the future. DHS declined to comment. The US Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, which is litigating the case on behalf of the government, did not respond questions about why it was necessary to identify everyone in Minnesota who purchased the beanie from REI, or why it specifically targeted REI customers, since the beanie is sold on other platforms as well.

The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are also known as 1509 customs summons, and are meant to be used to request information related to imports and exports. However, since the start of the Trump administration, WIRED and other news outlets have reported on DHS’s attempts to unmask online critics using the legal tool, which can be sent without the oversight of a judge or a jury.

Tech.title: AI Use in the Job Market Is Creating an Infinite Doom Loop
Tech.content:
Being in a low-fire, low-hire economy only makes matters worse. Job postings are scarce. Scams and ghost jobs are enough of a problem that some states are looking to write new laws to combat them.

Both job seekers and employers say they're experiencing a breakdown of trust. Candidates sink so much time into their search and hear nothing. Applying to jobs is a black box.

Some employers, meanwhile, say they receive hundreds of applications that look nearly identical. So they feed them into the AI rating system of their ATS to try and get some quick differentiation.

Chait says we're in an AI doom loop. “We've got this tragic situation where each side has a problem. They're using AI to solve their own problem, but in ways that make the problem worse. And so more AI use begets more AI use, to no one's benefit. The more it's happening, the worse it gets.”

Comparing Human Vetting to AI

I spoke with dozens of recruiters and HR managers, as well as small business owners who do their own hiring. Some admitted they use automated candidate ranking, and some were adamant that they do not. The division has nothing to do with the size of the organization or even the number of applicants received. It seems driven by philosophy and culture.

Kim Jones is vice president of human resources at Toshiba. “We have humans review every application,” she says. She doesn't mind applicants using AI to polish up their materials, but “it's not really going to help with getting through the ATS.” Culling applicants comes down to job requirements, salary expectations, and a few other factors, like whether the person would be a rehire.

Where she has seen unwanted AI usage is in the interviewing stage. “You hear the pause, maybe hear the typing, then they come up with a verbose answer,” Jones says.

Another company that relies more on humans than technology for hiring is Doist. It's a small, fully remote company that hires internationally, which means when they have an opening, they're flush with applications.

Nadia Vatalidis, head of people at the company, says her team experimented to see if ATS rankings could help. They took roles that had already been filled and fed in the job descriptions as well as all the applicant materials that they had saved from the hiring process. They wanted to know “what would happen if AI had to short-list the same batch of candidates and whether the folks we interviewed would show up in those same categories,” Vatalidis says. “In two instances that we tested, the person we hired wasn't in the short list.” She says there was overlap in who got an interview, but their new hires—people who were working out great after about six months—didn't make the cut.

Using AI Differently

When James Jacobsen started his job search five months ago, the amount of time he sank into searching and applying to jobs was equivalent to a full-time role. As a design professional, he knows AI can't match him when it comes to creativity, but he experiments with it heavily and knows it's a powerful tool for certain tasks. He used Claude and ChatGPT to polish up his application materials and make sure they were in line with the job description, but it wasn't moving the needle.

Instead of focusing only on his application materials, he started using Claude to streamline and track his job search from top to bottom. He instructed it to comb job listings, analyze descriptions, and log them. He devised an elaborate scoring system based on the type of work, seniority, and his salary requirements, which varied for in-person, hybrid, and remote roles. His AI assistant highlighted the top jobs he should apply to. When he rejected one, he added a note, so if the same position got reposted weeks later, his AI could immediately remind him why he wasn't interested. He spent less time searching to find more high-quality positions. He got a few bites but no offers.

Tech.title: What the Heck? Another Perfect Geometric Shape Has Been Detected on Saturn
Tech.content:
A team of astronomers discovered a strange polygonal atmospheric structure on Saturn near the planet’s south pole. This 10-sided shape, known as a decagon, joins one of the gas giant’s most famous features: a hexagon near the north pole that was first observed 44 years ago. Images of the new decagon were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, and the discovery was recently published in the journal Science Advances.

The formations at both the north and south poles aren’t solid structures, like a wall or a rock formation. Saturn doesn’t even have a defined solid surface like Earth’s crust. If you were to descend through the atmosphere of the ringed planet, the pressure and density would progressively increase, but you would never reach a “ground” on which to land. Instead, what astronomers have witnessed are patterns formed by clouds, albeit very unusual ones.

Each side of the decagon measures approximately 16,800 kilometers, which is a few thousand miles longer than the diameter of Earth. Near the feature is a jet stream reaching speeds of 116 meters per second, or nearly 260 miles per hour. By way of comparison, a Category 5 hurricane—the most intense storm level possible on Earth—is defined by winds above 157 miles per hour. Interestingly, although the jet stream circulates at tremendous speed, the decagon pattern shifts at a mere 2.5 meters per second—less than 6 miles per hour.

Photograph of the new decagon at Saturn’s south pole Photograph: Courtesy of Space Telescope Science Institute Office of Public Outreach

The south pole feature appears to have formed recently. For decades, scientists have been searching for a counterpart to the famous northern hexagon. However, major missions that observed the planet have previously not been able to find an equivalent, long-lasting structure in the south. The search was further complicated because, due to Saturn’s tilt, its southern hemisphere was not clearly visible from Earth for many years.

The first clues of the decagon came from ground-based observations, some by amateur astronomers. As the images accumulated, it became evident that something strange was happening in Saturn’s southern cloud bands. Data from the Hubble Space Telescope made it possible to trace the pattern back to images taken in 2023. Monitoring continued, and by 2025 its 10 vertices had become much more clearly defined, confirming the presence of a new polygonal feature in the ringed planet’s atmosphere. Science, however, hasn’t settled on an explanation for how these structures came to be.

Various hypotheses have been proposed since the discovery of the north polar hexagon. One is that the polygons are the visible manifestations of enormous atmospheric waves confined by powerful jet streams. You can think of these as similar to ocean waves, which are not simply objects traveling across the ocean but rather disturbances propagating through the water.

A wave’s behavior changes depending on the space in which it moves and the boundaries it encounters. On Saturn, waves of atmospheric gases may be encountering jet streams that confine them, in a sense, like the edge of a beach. Except in this case, the “beach” wraps all the way around the planet.

Tech.title: Silicon Valley Is Having a ‘Hot Girl Renaissance’
Tech.content:
Since the dawn of Silicon Valley, there’s been a widespread perception that San Francisco is, put gently, not exactly a dating mecca.

The city famously has a skewed male-to-female ratio (per census data, there are about 105 men for every 100 women), and there’s a perception among many women that men who work in tech tend to have poor social and emotional skills and a lack of style—opting for Patagonia vests and Meta glasses rather than putting substantive effort into their appearance.

On August 31, however, Celeste Amadon, the founder of the AI-powered dating app Known, valiantly attempted to reverse that stereotype. In an X thread accompanied by a moody, upward-angled selfie, she announced that she and her team were compiling a list of “SF’s most dateable people,” titled “San Francisco’s Hot List.” She attached a link for people to nominate their single friends according to criteria like “ambition,” “accomplishment,” “reputation,” and “aura.”

The post was skewered online by many in and outside of the tech scene, with some referring to it as “cringe” or mocking the lack of eligible singles in San Francisco: “The solution to dating in SF is to leave SF,” posted one female founder. But it was an extremely effective bit of marketing for Known, garnering more than 15,000 submissions 24 hours after the tweet was posted, according to Amadon. It was also an effective piece of counter-propaganda to the stereotype of San Franciscans, officially heralding that San Francisco Is Hot.

“Not to be cheesy, but I think the SF dating scene deserves some defending,” Amadon tells WIRED. “It gets so much flak for being a place where it’s hard to meet people, but there are many people who are super eligible in not just their physical attractiveness but in their holistic dateability.”

Known’s Hot List is part of a broader conversation focused on the general attractiveness of the San Francisco populace—and why some locals seem to be placing more importance on being perceived as hot.

Last summer, two women who work in tech—Madison Kanna (who is on the Hot List) and Cat Orman—threw an “enforced ratio” party at a Tesla showroom in the city, ensuring that there were as many women as men. The invite stipulated that the vibe would be “unapologetically feminine and fun” and that “​Patagonia vests will be turned away at the door.” On August 28, Mantis Biotech startup founder Georgia Witchel posted an X thread titled “Tech Is Having a Hot Girl Renaissance.” In the thread, Witchel describes how social media has been deluged with “young, attractive women taking tastefully slutty duck-faced mirror selfies” to promote their startups, citing Known and the insurance company Corgi as examples.

Witchel says her argument is not so much that she objects to young women using their attractiveness as a marketing strategy—it's more to explain how and why it has emerged as a marketing strategy to begin with, telling WIRED the trend is a result of “a renaissance of sales culture in SF.”

Throughout much of Silicon Valley, software marketing was “nerds selling to other nerds,” she says—but with the emergence of vibe coding, the barrier to entry for the industry has gotten lower, and the standards for marketing a product higher. “The fact that you are able to build a complicated product is not enough to give you the leeway of not being charismatic,” says Witchel. “People are recognizing that.”

When reached for comment, Brooke LeBlanc, head of community at Corgi, who Witchel cites in her thread, referred WIRED to an X post. “My mom just heard about the hot girl in tech renaissance and she’s absolutely thrilled by the news,” she wrote. “No one in my family from Georgia can believe that it’s breaking news for a woman to care about how she looks.”

Amadon says the Hot List has “minimal” connection to Witchel’s thread, but she understands why Known’s marketing “draws interest” (though she notes that X specifically is “not a primary marketing channel” for the app). She concedes that the list was intended to capitalize on the discussion and create “positive discourse” around dating in San Francisco.

And it’s working: On September 1, Known posted the first round of Hot Listers, including LeBlanc and startup founders like Jasper Carmichael-Jack, the CEO of the AI-driven company Artisan. There was nary a Patagonia vest in the bunch.

Tech.title: Xbox Game Pass Subscribers Are Losing a Big Perk This November
Tech.content:
Unlimited Xbox Cloud Gaming is going away. Starting in November, the service will have monthly limits based on the Xbox Game Pass subscription tier, according to a Microsoft post on Thursday. Cloud gaming hours will be capped at:

15 hours for Game Pass Ultimate

10 hours for Premium

5 hours for Essential

Microsoft said it’s making these changes due to the increased cost of cloud gaming. “Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance,” the company said in the post. “We understand that for some players the practical result is a higher cost.”

The limited hours will impact 4% of Xbox Game Pass subscribers, Microsoft said. If you fall into that group, you’ll have the option to purchase more cloud gaming time, and it will also be available to gamers without an Xbox Game Pass subscription.

Also see: Gaming Has Never Been Better. So Why Does It Feel Like the Worst Time to Be a Gamer?

Details about how much additional playtime will cost will be revealed in November, but Microsoft did say cloud gaming features will vary by market. However, it’s unclear whether that means it will be priced differently in certain cities or whether there will be throttling to reduce stream quality.

Microsoft also noted that the service change gives Xbox One owners an opportunity to play Xbox Series X and S games without buying a new console, which has gone up in price due to the sharp rise in hardware costs driven by ongoing component shortages. The Xbox division has been hit with setback after setback, starting in May 2025 with the first price hike for the Xbox Series X and S consoles.

A second jump in price for the console came last October, along with a 50% price increase for Xbox Game Pass the following month. Microsoft did reduce the cost of Game Pass subscriptions this past April, but this move to cut cloud gaming hours shows how it’s trying to continue to reduce costs, even after laying off 1,600 employees in the Xbox division and closing four game studios the company owned in July.

Xbox Cloud Gaming was a central part of Microsoft’s This is an Xbox campaign in late 2024 that pushed the idea of gamers using their phones, tablets, laptops and smart TVs as their Xbox through the Xbox app and cloud gaming. The marketing move was to drive more people to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass while also masking disappointing hardware sales for the Xbox Series consoles.

A lack of a proper universal ecosystem across the board due to the absence of an official Xbox app on some platforms, no universal controller options to play the games and an uneven playing experience contributed to the campaign’s failure. It was cited as offending some Xbox employees after Phil Spencer stepped down as the boss of the Xbox division in February.

Tech.title: A Smart Innovation at IFA Wants to Light Your Home With All-New Sensor Combos
Tech.content:
I’ve found past Aqara products, like the multipurpose security sensor, particularly useful, but at IFA 2026, the security company is swerving in an entirely new direction: smart lighting.

Entering the lighting world is a bold move for Aqara, but I’m not totally surprised. Showing off a suite of products that looks to confront lighting maestro Govee, Aqara wants to differentiate itself with several tricks connecting the lighting products back to its previous security specialties. Here’s what I noticed.



New lamps, LED strips and outdoor lighting

Aqara’s colorful floor lamp looks directly inspired by Govee products. Aqara

Aqara isn’t just dipping its toes into smart lighting at IFA — it’s unveiling a packed product line with entries for basically every part of the home. It takes most brands years to expand into so many areas, so a large launch like this is particularly unusual.

Indoors, Aqara is showing off both a standing lamp and table lamp, with a focus on multicolor options (through app control, of course). The standing lamp, for example, has 18 different zones to control separately or cycle colors through. The line will also include a smart downlight for low ceilings, plus a smart LED strip with 108 LEDS per meter — which sounds like a whole lot to me based on my past tests of LED strips.

Then Aqara moves outdoors, with a new outdoor string light product that has a broad color temperature range to mimic different kinds of natural light. The company is also planning to release permanent, weatherproof outdoor lights designed to stay under eaves and provide lighting year-round.

Hmm, where have I seen colorful, permanent outdoor eave lights just like this? Oh yes, Govee again. Aqara

I don’t have info on release dates or pricing for all these lighting products yet, but it’s immediately clear how similar they are to Govee lights, including the floor lamp and the permanent outdoor lights. It looks like Aqara is taking the smart lighting king head-on with this release, giving consumers an alternative that hasn’t been easy to find in past years.

Of course, seeing the products, even in person at IFA, can only say so much about their design quality and ease of use. I’ll want to test these new lines ASAP to get a better feel for how they, well, feel and to see how durable they are and if newcomers can easily adopt them.

Aqara sensor and switch support

Aqara’s products are designed to work easily with its security sensors, too. Aqara

Here, Aqara is taking a road less traveled by using artificial intelligence, diverging from Govee into what Aqara calls “AI-driven spatial intelligence.” That’s not as bland as it may sound: Aqara plans to connect its lighting to past sensors that I already like, giving them ways to work easily together. The approach also means you could use a previous security sensor for broader, more convenient purposes or connect more to an existing Aqara switch.

To this end, every lighting product Aqara announced will be compatible with Zigbee, Thread and Matter, which means it can also work with Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and so forth. In my experience with Aqara products, you typically get the most choices with Aqara’s own Aqara Home app, but there’s certainly flexibility here.

When connected to a large smart device ecosystem, like Aqara presence sensor or movement sensor, users can set rules based on what they are already using. A door sensor that gives you an alert when a door is opened can now quickly change an Aqara light to a different color or turn on an entry light to welcome someone home. Overhead lights can brighten when people enter the room, detected by Aqara’s presence sensor. And Aqara switches can control indoor or outdoor lights with custom routines at a touch.

You could connect other smart lights to Aqara sensors with Matter support before, but now that Aqara has its own lights, the process should be more seamless and open up new routine options.

A little bit of generative AI in the mix

Aqara is also adding AI and crowdsourcing assistants to the mix. Aqara

One of Govee’s points of pride — and I’ve seen it in other smart lighting like Lepro’s, too — is its many scenes and the ability to create new lighting scenes on the fly by using its generative AI lighting assistant with voice or text prompts, as well as downloaded images.

Aqara is again taking a page out of this book, debuting what it calls “Gen-Scene,” an AI ability to generate lighting scenarios. Aqara’s tool seems more focused on building entire scenes across home zones than simply creating color schemes. I’m interested in trying it out as part of Aqara’s whole kit.

The company is also introducing something more unique for planning, and I like the sound of it. Aqara showcased a platform called Aqara Builder, a gathering place for users to post their projects, inspirations and literal automation walkthroughs. I like the idea of crowdsourcing ideas like this, and we’ve already seen how so many people collaborate over platforms like Home Assistant to share solutions. If Aqara can create a similar community for its products, that would be a smart home win.

Tech.title: This New Robot Vacuum Wants to Remove Dust Mites and End Your Allergies
Tech.content:
Ecovacs makes some of the best robot vacuums we’ve tested here at CNET, and for a long time, their unique combo T90 Pro Omni was our top choice for its incredible versatility. The new Ecovacs Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is a bit more iterative than its predecessor, the X12, but it makes key improvements to tackle dust mites and allergies.

“A dust mite allergy isn’t something you just get over. You clean around it,” said Michelle Jones, associate brand marketing director at Ecovacs Americas. “Most robots skim the top of a carpet. We built the X12S to get down to where the dust actually sits.”

The X12S was tested by the SGS Testing & Control Services Singapore and, in testing, removed an average of 97.44% of dust mite allergens and 95.45% of dust mites from carpet. Ecovacs points out that dust mites live in soft material, especially carpet. Since carpet is underfoot, it traps dust mites and allergens deeper in the pile that a conventional robot vacuum can’t reach.



This might sound niche, but as someone who has three asthmatic cats and occasionally seasonal allergies, I’m interested to see if it lives up to the testing claims. The feature sounds similar to Anker’s new Omni E35, which also claims the ability to remove 99% of dust mites and has Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America certification.

The X12S also has 53 air watts of effective suction, 60% more than the previous-generation X12; Ecovacs claims this gives it handheld-vacuum-level cleaning power, which I’ll be interested to see if that is true in CNET’s lab testing.

The OZMO Roller 3.0 is self-washing, as is increasingly common among robot vacuums from different manufacturers, so the roller keeps refreshing itself with clean water. Reprising its role from the previous generation is the FocusJet stain spray, which shoots water to loosen and break up older and dried-on stains — this is another feature we’ve seen other manufacturers adopt after Ecovacs showed it off on the X12 earlier this year.

The rest of the cleaning system carries over from the X12, including the 15-millimeter auto-mop lifting and the Mop Roller Smart Cover, which keeps the mop clear of the carpet. It has AIVI 3D 4.0 dual obstacle avoidance, which pairs camera vision with 3D laser sensing to navigate cluttered rooms. There’s also a 3D edge sensor to clean close to walls and baseboards without leaving gaps.

Interestingly, the X12S has a physical privacy shutter, not just software privacy. It covers the AIVI camera so you can be sure that when it’s closed, the lens is blocked.

“A cover you can see is easier to trust, because you can look at it,” Jones said. “As these robots take in more of the home, people will want to ensure they have their privacy.”



This is a first for robot vacuums, at least with the ones I’ve seen, and it’ll be interesting to see if other companies choose to adopt it. Lastly, it also comes with the fast-charging system we liked on the X12 that can top the robot vacuum up more quickly between mop washing dock cycles.

Price and availability

The Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is available in the United States at an MSRP of $1,300. Buyers can order it on Amazon or at ecovacs.com. From Sept. 4 through Sept. 11, an Amazon launch deal brings the price to $1,000.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: The Best of IFA 2026: AI Dishwashers and Earbuds and Toothbrushes, Oh My!
Tech.content:
CNET staffers have touched down in Berlin and are on the floor at IFA 2026, one of the world’s largest tech events where the future is on full display. From a camera-equipped dishwasher and Dyson’s largest air purifier yet to a repairable laptop and a speaker designed to soothe you to sleep, we’ve laid eyes on devices that could change how we live, breathe, clean, work and play.

If you, too, would like to peer into the future and see what’s ahead, this is the best tech we’ve spotted at IFA 2026.

An all-seeing dishwasher

Miele’s Diamond G8 isn’t your average dishwasher. David Watsky/CNET

Miele’s new Diamond G8 dishwasher has an AI-powered internal camera that scans your dishes and decides how to wash them so it doesn’t miss a single spot. Though Home and Kitchen Managing Editor David Watsky, who saw the dishwasher in person, was skeptical about this feature, he was left impressed.

But the Diamond G8’s scrubbing smarts don’t stop there. If you want the Diamond G8 to run only when electricity is most affordable, it can do that too, waiting for the hours when power costs less.

Note-taking earbuds

Plaud One: your AI note-taking assistant earbuds. Plaud/CNET

Going beyond its AI note-taking wearable pin and credit card-like device that you can attach to your phone, Plaud launched the Plaud One earbuds to capture and transcribe your conversations and calls. You can even talk to Plaud’s AI by saying, “Hey Plaud,” and then ask it your questions or give it directives.

“We’d always recommend informing people that you’re using a recording device, and it’s important to note that recording phone calls without permission from all participants can be illegal in some states,” principal writer Katie Collins wrote when covering the Plaud One announcement.

A robot vacuum that seals itself to carpet

The Roomba Max 875 Combo is all about clean carpet. iRobot

While robot vacuums are great for taking the effort out of keeping your floors clean, CNET’s testing has found that they don’t offer the same suction power as traditional vacuums. iRobot aims to improve on that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which uses SealForce technology to seal itself to carpet and better suction up spots that need extra cleaning.

In a video call with Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar prior to IFA 2026, Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said SealForce is like pressing harder with a traditional vacuum to thoroughly clean a specific patch of carpet, but in a robot vacuum format.

A smart ring puts contactless payments at your fingertips

Imagine how cool it will feel to use your ring for contactless payments. Circular

In addition to having the health-tracking capabilities we expect of smart rings, Circular has added contactless payments, a feature typically found on smartwatches and smartphones, to its new subscription-free Ring 3 Pro and Ring 3 Slim. When covering the launch, principal writer Vanessa Hand Orellana wrote that the company also gave both rings haptic vibration alerts, a feature previously available on its first Circular Ring, along with advanced sleep metrics, glucose trend estimates and access to its AI health coach.

A laptop built to be repaired

The Vero 16 comes with its own repair guide. Acer/CNET

With its new fourth-generation Vero 16, Acer brings the “right to repair” conversation into focus, as CNET writer Tyler Graham explained that the modular laptop is designed to let users easily upgrade its components themselves. There’s even a repair guide engraved on it to help with these swaps.

The Vero 16 didn’t come alone, as it was announced alongside Acer’s compact 14-inch Swift Blade 14 and sleek 16-inch Swift Air 16.

A speaker that lulls you to sleep

Sleep has never sounded so sweet. Katie Collins/CNET

Alongside its Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro with a touchscreen case, Anker introduced the SleepLab Pro speaker, which uses radar to track your sleep, breathing and heart rate, then customizes its audio to help you drift off to dreamland and stay there. “It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table,” Collins wrote when describing the device. It also triples as a sunrise alarm clock and a nightlight that glows in a range of shades.

A non-Pro SleepLab has the same features, minus radar sleep tracking.

Dyson’s largest air purifier

Air purifier or Dune sandworm? You decide. Dyson

The new Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde (try to say that five times fast) was designed to purify multiple rooms using the company’s most powerful processor. As Kumar put it, it looks like a Dune sandworm with its nozzle head that can be rotated and tilted. While operating quietly, the purifier can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns for a breath of fresh air.

Lenovo’s first rollable work laptop

Lenovo is on a roll. Josh Goldman/CNET

Lenovo’s Project Swan concept is a laptop that expands horizontally at the touch of a button, transforming its display from 14 to 17 inches. But unlike the Legion Pro Rollable Graham spotted at CES 2026, this isn’t a gaming laptop – it’s for work. Perfect for work trips when you want a more compact 14-inch display for travel, but a 17-inch for getting the job done (or watching movies during your downtime).

Dyson’s first toothbrush

Plaque begone! Tara Brown/CNET

Dubbed the CameraJet, Dyson’s first toothbrush has a built-in, AI-powered camera that detects gaps between your teeth within 100 milliseconds so that it can floss while you brush. To do so, the brush has an anti-gravity tank that its charging dock fills with mouthrinse, which its jet uses to floss.

You can even use the CameraJet’s camera as an endoscope to see your teeth in the app, where brushing and flossing insights, coverage maps and guided cleaning are also available. However, this high-tech toothbrush comes at a cost: $500.

As IFA runs from Sept. 4 to Sept. 8, this is just the beginning. We’ll continue updating this list as we see the best that the tech event has to offer.

Tech.title: GPT-6 Stole the Show, but Anthropic, Meta and Google Also Had New AI Models This Week
Tech.content:
While OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra is making a big splash in the AI world with its debut, it was far from the only one to be announced this week. When there’s a new, updated model seemingly every other day, it’s hard to stay up to date, let alone be excited, but the onslaught of new offerings is something to note.

It wasn’t just OpenAI: Fellow AI heavy hitters Anthropic, Meta, and Google also announced updates to AI models. While each new model has its own strengths, a focus we’re seeing more and more often is advancements in agentic AI workflows, and each new announcement spotlight on those capabilities.

Below, we’ll break down all of the latest models from this week and give you the details.

GPT-6 Astra

Of all models released this week, OpenAI’s is the only one that’s not a “.x” update. GPT-6 Astra is said to excel in cybersecurity and software engineering, and OpenAI calls it its most intelligent model yet. The performance benchmarks for Astra have it ahead of its competitors in a lot of ways, making it one of the most advanced models we’ve seen to date.

OpenAI is also touting Astra’s strength in multi-step agentic workflows, scientific discovery and financial modeling. The model is also said to be much better at computer use, which was a focus of its predecessor, ChatGPT 5.6, when it was released in July.

ChatGPT-6 Astra is rolling out to people with Daybreak access, its program for “vetted enterprise customers and cybersecurity practitioners.” OpenAI says that the new model will roll out to Plus, Pro and Business users over the coming days.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1

Anthropic announced updates for its Fable and Mythos models — both of which are some of the best available today. Anthropic says that both Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but each has a different set of safeguards. Fable is the model that the average person can use, and Mythos is typically reserved for researchers and cybersecurity experts.

Anthropic says its latest models have significantly better performance over their predecessors, and the release “sets a new standard” for coding, knowledge work and long-running problem-solving tasks. It also says that Fable 5.1, when set to low or medium effort, has performance similar to Fable 5 but at a much lower cost.

Fable 5.1 is available to the general public, whereas Mythos is limited to Anthropic’s trusted access programs.

Muse Spark 1.3

Meta released a model this week that should bring it back up into the conversation about the most capable models around. Muse Spark 1.3 brings more advanced reasoning and better performance in agentic and coding tasks.

Meta said this model is trained to collaborate with the person using it, and will ask clarifying questions when a prompt is vague and check to confirm the actions it will perform in agentic workflows.

Must Spark 1.3 is available in Muse Code and Meta’s Model API.

Gemini 3.8 and 3.8 Flash Cyber

Google released two new models in the form of Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber. This was hot on the heels of the release of Gemini 3.7 Flash on Aug. 13. The latest additions to the family are said to offer “next-generation intelligence” for agentic workflows and cybersecurity.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is available to enterprise, consumer and developers across Google products, where 3.8 Flash Cyber is currently available in limited access to participants of the Fairwind Program, which was also announced the same day as the new models.

Tech.title: The New iPhones Could Cost 10-20% More, an Analyst Predicts. Thanks a Lot, RAMageddon
Tech.content:
Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event is days away, and there are plenty of rumors swirling about new devices we can expect, like a new Apple Watch and the first foldable iPhone, which could be called the iPhone Ultra.

When we asked CNET readers one thing they’d change about the iPhone in our Big Guessing Game, 16% said they want it to cost less. But that’s not happening. In fact, you should expect new models to cost significantly more.

TrendForce, a global market research firm, released a report on Thursday suggesting you can expect higher prices instead of steep discounts. The firm expects the iPhone 18 series to cost 10 to 20% more due to the ongoing RAM shortage and higher hardware costs.

“For the 256GB Pro model, memory costs in [the third quarter of 2026] are expected to be nearly 400% higher than a year earlier,” TrendForce said. “Despite Apple’s efforts to negotiate lower prices for other components, these savings are unlikely to offset the resulting pressure on overall [materials] costs.”

Apple raised prices on select products in June due to the RAM shortage, but excluded iPhones from the price hikes. Now there’s a chance that Apple could release some iPhone 18 models with higher prices at the September event. TrendForce said it expects Apple to absorb some of the costs to keep prices for the new models as part of a “relatively moderate” pricing strategy.

So exactly how much more are we talking about? Some analysts believe the foldable iPhone Ultra could cost between $2,000 and $2,500. TrendForce predicts the starting price will be slightly higher — between $2,099 and $2,299. The phone could go up to $3,000. TrendForce didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment.

But higher costs aren’t equivalent to big improvements.

TrendForce says we shouldn’t expect major performance upgrades from Apple’s upcoming iPhone lineup. Instead, we should expect a more powerful processor for AI features and power efficiency, better chip cooling technology and power-efficient displays. And the iPhone 18 Pro models’ main camera could have a “mechanical variable aperture” to improve depth-of-field control and dynamic range for different lighting settings.

The really big upgrade is the potential release of the folding iPhone Ultra and bigger batteries for premium iPhone 18 models, TrendForce predicts. The iPhone 18 Pro Max could see the biggest upgrade due to a larger chassis. CNET’s Patrick Holland tested smartphone batteries last year and found that the iPhone 17 Pro Max was the best for battery life, so iPhone 18’s premium models could be an even bigger upgrade from the current model.

Tech.title: Ultrahuman Eyes Gesture Control for Future Rings With Qualcomm Boost
Tech.content:
Smart ring company Ultrahuman is up there with Samsung as the biggest rivals to Oura, but it has some lofty ambitions for its next steps, which it hinted at on Thursday at IFA here in Berlin. The company announced it had raised $70 million from Qualcomm Ventures, Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume and others to develop next-generation AI wearables.

The smart ring market is currently dominated by Oura, but Ultrahuman is finding ways to set itself apart. It has already evolved rapidly over the past few years into a health company offering a range of complementary products and services, including blood testing and an ambient sleep monitor that sits by your bed. Earlier this year, it launched the Ring Pro, which has better battery life than its predecessors and also doesn’t require a subscription, unlike some of its rivals.

The new funding is set to further boost this growth, putting the Ultrahuman Ring at the center of an ecosystem where data about your body is used for more insightful and actionable purposes. Ultrahuman plans to invest the money in sensing, materials, electrical engineering, algorithms, physiology and clinical science to build future rings and ultimately make the human body more understandable with AI.

The partnership with Qualcomm draws Ultrahuman into a much wider ecosystem of AI products, many of which are also wearable, with which the Ultrahuman Ring could become interoperable. One example is the Meta Glasses, which the Ultrahuman Ring could be linked to for purposes of gesture control, said Bhuvan Srinivasan, the company’s chief business officer, in an interview.

“What we’re really thinking is you could have a ring that helps you control what’s happening in the glasses, but then at the same time at night it measures all your sleep and all your health,” he said. “So it’s valuable to you both in the day and the night.”

This won’t be possible with the Ring Pro, he added. “There’ll be another Ring level that we are working on with them.”

The partnership with diagnostic and drugs company Labcorp is also important to bringing Ultrahuman’s vision to life, due to the support it can provide to Ultrahuman’s Blood Vision preventative blood-testing service that it’s been building out for the past two years, Srinivasan said.

“The idea behind Blood Vision is really to bring together all the things you cannot measure on a wearable, but you can measure in your blood, which is also very valuable,” he said. “And now we really want to roll that out and make preventive health blood testing much more mainstream. And that’s really why we tied up with them over time.”

The funding could help Ultrahuman position itself as a bridge between people’s health, AI agents and other AI-equipped devices. “Ultrahuman is pioneering a new generation of personal AI devices that make personalized insights effortless,” said Quinn Li, senior vice president of Qualcomm Technologies and global head of Qualcomm Ventures. “We look forward to supporting their journey as they expand the possibilities of personal AI devices.”

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: The Weirdest and Wackiest Tech We Found at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
IFA is in full swing, and the Berlin expo has gathered advanced tech from across the globe to show off, from all-new vacuum features to ultra-advanced AI ecosystems ready to help manage your home. Then there are the products that made us go, “…Huh.”

When tech companies are throwing everything they’ve got at IFA, things can get a little weird. Here’s the wackiest tech we spotted, what it’s supposed to do, and how useful we think it could be out in the real world.

Govee’s mood-reading skylight

Govee’s giant mood light was on display at IFA. David Watsky/CNET

Govee has long been at the forefront of strange home lighting creations, from literal curtains of light to spread across your garage to table lamps that look more like alien artifacts. Now Govee is showing off one of its oddest products yet: a dome-like ceiling light designed to mimic the sky and be “mood-responsive.”

In this case, mood-responsive means you can use Govee’s AI to talk about your mood or how you’re feeling, and the Govee app will suggest ceiling light color schemes to match. But the light can also create a specific blue wavelength designed to evoke blue skies and natural daylight.

Govee’s mood-interpreting light may not be as far-fetched as you think. Govee

Too weird to work? Not as weird as you may think. I’ve tested Govee’s AI before, and you really can generate lighting patterns based on your mood or random musings. But Govee already has so many lighting scenes in its app that I didn’t find it very practical — although definitely fun. I wonder how well it will work with a full ceiling light.

A gigantic tofu maker

The Nuvell plant protein maker is about the size of an espresso machine. David Watsky/CNET

If your two problems are not eating enough plant protein and having too much counter space, the Nuvell is here. This massive bean cooker and compressor is the size of an espresso machine and churns out blocks of tofu in as little as 30 minutes. It can make other vegan proteins depending on the legume you stick inside.

Plant protein made in the comfort of your kitchen. David Watsky/CNET

I asked the rep on duty whether the Nuvell could make cheese if you poured cow’s milk in. She claimed it could, but didn’t seem too confident.

Too weird to work? While it wasn’t operational at IFA, we assume the Nuvell does what it’s supposed to, since turning soybeans into tofu isn’t rocket science. The real question is whether or not it’s worth the space on your counter for this one-trick pony kitchen appliance.

A tiny robot vacuum… for your bed

Yep — a whole robot vacuum, just for the bed. Creatulize

Creatulize came to IFA to show off the smallest robot vacuum in all of Berlin. The X1 Pro is the brand’s second-gen bed robot vacuum, designed to clean your bedding and mattress.

Using precision mode, the vac moves slowly and steadily across a mattress, sucking up dust, mites, hair and whatever else lurks. It can clean a king-size in about 20 minutes and has an easy-to-empty debris canister. Special sensors keep it from tumbling off the bed. When it hits an edge, it stops, turns and keeps on keepin’ on.

That’s one itty-bitty robot vac. David Watsky/CNET

Too weird to work? Mattress vacuums are becoming a thing, based on the idea that dirty mattresses exacerbate allergies. Nobody wants a dusty mattress, but whether or not you need a dedicated vacuum for it is up for debate. We’ll be testing the X1 Pro to find out.

Midea’s AC unit that follows you around (sort of)

Midea’s new voice-controlled air conditioner follows you around the room with a stream of cool. David Watsky/CNET

One of the highlights we saw – and felt – was an air conditioner unit that sends custom cool air to you wherever you are. Midea’s new system uses spatial imaging and sensors to track your position in the room and deliver a stream of cool air your way. That means a cooler you and less energy wasted.

Midea’s smart AC works with the brand’s other air-quality appliances, including the humidifier. The two work in harmony through Midea’s smart sync to keep your home’s air at your desired temperature and humidity, no matter what Mother Nature has planned.

It’s also voice-activated, so you can turn it on or off, or activate the “mmWave sensor system” without getting up or even opening your phone.

Too weird to work? While the AC wasn’t officially up and running at IFA, Dyson launched a similar freestanding fan and air purifier that tracks humans in the room and spits fresh, cool air their way. We’re still testing that one in our lab, but would be surprised if the technology doesn’t live up to at least some of its promise.

SwitchBot’s AI shirt pin, the MindClip

SwitchBot’s AI clip sort of… spies on everyone around you. SwitchBot

If you thought AI was already in everything, just wait: SwitchBot is announcing the launch of its AI shirt device, the MindClip, at IFA. It’s made to clip onto your shirt pocket, collar, nearby strap or even belt. Once in place, it, well, essentially listens to everything that happens within a 3-meter radius for up to 20 hours and saves it for you.

The MindClip can recognize people by their voices and summarize conversations or events, ostensibly to help you with planning after a busy day. As far as AI goes, it’s no spying Meta glasses, but it is fairly invasive, especially for strangers you may be chatting with.

Too weird to work? This isn’t the first time we’ve seen an AI pin, although it is the smallest and least distracting version I’ve spotted. The problem is that none of them really took off, and some companies even pivoted to an entirely different product. So yes, it’s too weird to work for now, but maybe the rumored AI capabilities in Apple’s AirPods will be an exception.

The AI-powered companion doll from Lovense

Lovense’s updated AI companion doll also made an appearance at IFA. Lovense

Singaporean intimacy and sex toy company Lovense has brought the latest version of its AI “companion doll” to IFA, aiming to make it more lifelike than ever before. In addition to talking, remembering past facts and adjusting its personality, the silicone doll can blink, smile and look when called by its custom name. Users can also chat with the doll at a distance via a phone app and set up roleplay scenarios, if they prefer.

Too weird to work? Yes, the age of AI sex dolls is here. But it’s such an eclectic — and expensive (between $4,000 and $8,000) — proposition, this one is only for those with very specific tastes and a, ahh, particular relationship with AI. For others, Lovense also debuted several more conventional, AI-free toys.

A Eufy sensor that asks if you fell down

Eufy’s new sensor has a very, very specific purpose in the home. Eufy

When today’s home sensors can do nearly anything from recognizing when dogs bark to knowing when someone is tampering with a mailbox, it may sound strange to make a sensor specifically to say, “Oops, it looks like you fell down!” But that’s just what Anker’s Eufy brand has done.

There’s method behind this madness. The wall sensor uses a combo of algorithms and presence sensing with mmWave technology, no cameras necessary. It’s made to help those aging in place or living in rest homes without creating privacy concerns. The sensor even supports two-way audio, so family members or nurses can check in if they get an alert about a potential fall.

Quick note: As Anker consolidates its brand names, Eufy products are staying with us, but the Eufy name may not be around forever, so keep that in mind when shopping.

Too weird to work? In this case, not at all. I’ve already seen mmWave technology tap into Wi-Fi signals to help those aging in place, although Eufy’s sensor is the first I’ve seen that focuses on falls and enables two-way audio for a quick checkup. It’s a strong use of the technology.

A smartphone for your pet

The Petphone certainly makes a lot of claims about AI pet powers. Petpogo

Ucloudlink has brought the newest version of its award-winning PetPhone to IFA this year, showing a world where cats and dogs have their own smartphone, too. Sort of.

The Petpogo PetPhone is technically a smart pet collar, and we’ve reviewed many of those. But this version comes with two-way audio to talk to your pet with an app and AI features that interpret behavior and motion so pets can theoretically initiate a call themselves, as well as emotion analysis of barks, meows and other actions. It also supports more traditional capabilities like tracking and geofencing, and it alerts pet parents to out-of-routine behaviors.

Too weird to work? No AI features can accurately interpret specific barks or meows into moods and feelings. That’s (currently) nonsense. And trying to get your pet to “call” you with specific behaviors sounds dubious at best. So most of the innovations here are too weird, but the underlying collar functionality looks usable.

These headphones that turn into a Bluetooth speaker

TDM’s Bluetooth speaker headphone hybrid is confusing. TDM

TDM is showing off its unique Neo headphones, with a literal twist. In normal mode, they look like a typical pair of wireless headphones. But twist and collapse the earcups, and they form into a small Bluetooth speaker with up to 8 hours of music playback. The dual-device comes with an aux port, a USB-C charging port and a carrying case.

Too weird to work? When was the last time you saw someone with headphones and thought, “What a pleasant, private music experience that person is having, I wish there was a way for them to share it with all the people nearby?” Nope. No one likes it when you play music out loud in public spaces, especially when the same device could let you listen privately. I’m calling these headphones too weird to work.

A soundwave-creating smart bed

Amada’s acoustic mattress claims many different applications. Amada

Amada brought a fascinating mattress to IFA called the Soundwave Smart Mattress. Yes, it connects to a phone app. And yes, it really does produce sound waves or at least a “vibroacoustic experience” with vibration modes for presleep relaxation, meditation, focus and recharging. I’m not sure how vibration is supposed to help with those things, but CNET health expert Anna Gragert told me vibration therapy does have applications for recovery and disease treatment. The bed is made of polyurethane foam and polyester fabric, with a four-pin power connector.

Too weird to work? Well, Magic Fingers did have their day in hotel rooms across the US, but that day ended pretty fast. I don’t know if a bed with good vibrations is what the average home is looking for, but if you’ve tried it and it works for you, this could be a shakingly good upgrade.
